हाल इस क़दर हमने अब तक सँवारे नहीं हैं,
हम उन्हीं के हैं अब तक... जो हमारे नहीं हैं।
​बस गया है इस क़दर वो इन आँखों में,
आँसू भी अब इनके... खारे नहीं हैं।
​जीता क्या इक दफ़ा उसने दिल ये हमारा...
वो दिल हम किसी पर... अब तक हारे नहीं हैं।
​यूँ तरस ना खाओ तुम देख कर हालत हमारी,
इश्क़ के मारे हैं... बेचारे नहीं हैं।
​वो कहते हैं हम भुला देंगे उनको पुरानी आशिक़ी की तरह,
लगता है किसी शायर से वो... दिल हारे नहीं हैं।

Childhood


A longing memory of solitude
Lingers in the heart.
How beautiful were those days...
A joint family, filled with emotions
In every relation...
Carefree, unbound dreams filled with 
Joy and playfulness...
When the pain itself didn’t feel painful
In the laps of elders...
It didn’t realise
How hardships this life will carry,
When this shed of love will be gone...
How many endless, innocent memories
Of festivities are still embedded in the
Corner of heart....
How much we enjoyed together
The celebration of colours
And relished our favourite dishes
Prepared lovingly by ma...
How a huge big home with open aangan
Embraced everyone in its arms....
How our mango orchard 
Used to bear the fragrance of ripening mangoes...
How the summer afternoon
Used to be playing lots of games together
Among the siblings and cousins...
How the grandparents used to take us
To visit small carnivals...
How wandering everywhere in the small town
During learning the bicycle
Had made us remember every street...
How we, a bunch of kids used to play
On the huge rooftop in sultry  evenings
Till the sunset...
How enthusiasm never used to lessen...
How life was itself a story in the
Colourful pages of story books...
How i wish, we could have shared
And spent our childhood together...
When time didn’t run on the watch,
It used to flow gradually in accordance 
With life....
Beautiful and soulful memories appears
Like a flow of wind...
And make me feel like a swing,
Will you accompany me with
Your childhood here...

When the sun hides him behind the clouds,  
When a breezy wind begins to blow,  
Oh, Almighty of the world,  
Why does this surrounding fill with divine glow?

When woodsmoke mingles with the village breeze,  
It feels like You're hiding behind the haze.  
I can't tell if Your presence is imaginary or real,  
But whatever it may be, I always see You and start praise.

The butterflies and the dragonflies make the surroundings so enchanted,  
As if they too rejoice to welcome Your presence,  
The flowers dance and spread their fragrance in the air,  
Seems like the sweet scent of incense.

Oh, Divine of divinity,  
When are You coming to lift my spectacles?  
My eyes have been yearning for years,  
Only to see Your divine miracles.

Taking two steps, I may stumble, I may fall,
Yet I will rise again, I will move forward...
On my tiny feet, I may wobble, I may feel afraid,
Yet I will walk, I will move forward...
A hundred times I will fall, a hundred times I will rise,
Until I master the way to walk,
I will keep falling and rising again;
Tripping over stones, writhing in pain,
Yet I will rise again, I will move forward...
Some paths will be difficult, while some will be easy,
Somewhere I will meet noble humans, somewhere monsters,
I will embrace all these troubles with a smile,
Even amidst the pain, I will stay smiling,
Yet I will rise again, I will move forward...

— Sarfaraj Ahmad

title.stringValue: Beyond Survival: The Barefoot Roots of a Developed India

content.stringValue:
Beyond Survival: Why India’s Dream of 2047 Begins in Its Barefoot Classrooms


Dreams do not discriminate. Wealth or poverty should not determine who is allowed to imagine a better future. Yet we live in a society where one child dreams of building the next great technology while another dreams simply of having a proper meal.
On a quiet morning in a small town, I met a boy of about six. His eyes were welling with tears. He wore a faded, worn school shirt, while his bare feet told a story his words could not. When I asked why he was standing outside during school hours, he looked away in quiet shame. After I gently asked again, he told me that he had no proper shoes to wear and that his family could not afford them. His mother had left three years earlier, and his father struggled with alcohol dependence.
In that brief encounter lay a jarring contrast: a child dressed for the future, yet held back by the present.
As India sets its sights on becoming a developed nation by 2047, a century after independence, we must confront a sobering reality: a nation's future cannot walk forward when its children lack the ground on which to stand.

Where Tomorrow Stands Barefoot

We often speak of India's demographic dividend, imagining a future driven by scientists, innovators, entrepreneurs and global leaders. But the foundations on which these minds are shaped—our schools—must be strong enough to nurture them.
For millions of children, learning can become a struggle against their surroundings rather than an exciting journey of discovery. During the monsoon, rain can find its way through damaged roofs; inadequate furniture and basic facilities can turn a classroom into a place of endurance rather than inspiration.
India's latest UDISE+ 2024–25 data covers 1,471,473 schools nationwide. While the country has made substantial progress in school infrastructure, gaps remain. The data shows that 1,377,945 schools have electricity and 1,352,061 have functional electricity, while 1,221,231 have playgrounds. These figures represent progress, but they also remind us that essential facilities are not yet universal.
And infrastructure is only one side of the problem. Being enrolled in school is not the same as truly learning.
ASER 2024 highlights the continuing challenge of foundational learning in rural India. Among children in government schools, only 23.4% of Class III students could read a Class II-level text, although this marked an improvement over 2022.
The numbers are not merely statistics. Behind every percentage is a child whose opportunity to learn can shape the rest of their life.
For some disadvantaged children, school may also be one of the few places where they can access nutritious food, books, teachers, sports and opportunities beyond their immediate surroundings. The school meal matters. But education must offer something greater than survival: it must offer the possibility of a different future.
A child deserves a classroom that sparks curiosity, a playground that allows them to discover their abilities, books that expand their imagination, teachers who encourage questions, and an environment that makes them proud to say, “This is my school.”
A child's background should never determine the height of their dreams.

When Survival Becomes the Size of a Dream

When a child grows up surrounded by hardship, success can naturally come to mean earning enough to eat, securing a roof over their head and finding a stable job. There is nothing wrong with wanting these things; they are basic human needs. But a developed nation needs more than a generation that merely survives.
It needs a generation that questions, imagines, innovates and creates.
Critical thinking and creativity need space to grow. When a child is constantly preoccupied with basic needs, discomfort or insecurity, that space becomes harder to find.
This is why primary schools should be regarded not simply as administrative institutions, but as the nurseries of India's human potential. The children sitting in today's classrooms will become tomorrow's scientists, engineers, teachers, entrepreneurs, artists, administrators and leaders.
They are not merely preparing for India's future.
They are India's future.
When families cannot provide every resource or opportunity a child needs, society and the state have a responsibility to help level the field. A child's birthplace, income or family circumstances should not become a ceiling on their imagination.

Lessons from Nations That Chose to Nurture Their Young

India does not need to copy another country's education system. But it can learn from nations that have treated education as a long-term investment in human potential.
Singapore offers one striking example. In PISA 2022, Singapore ranked highest among participating countries and economies in mathematics, reading and science. Estonia also performed above the OECD average in all three core subjects.
The lesson is not that India should become Singapore or Estonia. The lesson is that strong education systems are built deliberately, consistently and over time.
India has already begun several efforts in this direction. The PM SHRI scheme, for instance, aims to strengthen more than 14,500 existing government schools as exemplar schools that provide high-quality, equitable and inclusive learning environments.
But schemes alone cannot transform education. Their success depends on implementation at the last mile—where the policy finally reaches the child.
Every rupee allocated for a child's classroom, learning material, nutrition or infrastructure must reach its intended purpose. Transparency, monitoring and accountability are essential. Public resources meant for children must never be lost to leakage, corruption or administrative failure.
Because when a resource meant for a child does not reach that child, it is not merely a financial loss. It is a lost opportunity to shape a life.

To Reach 2047, We Must First Reach the Child

If we want the next generation to carry the weight of a developed India, we must first give them firm roots.
A child deserves a school where rain stays outside the classroom, where a proper seat is not a luxury, where books invite curiosity, where a playground encourages teamwork, and where learning is something to look forward to rather than endure.
Our greatest national investment cannot be measured only in highways, factories, laboratories or technology parks. It must also be measured in the confidence of a child who believes that they can build something the world has never seen.
India's first great innovation should begin not only in our laboratories, but in the minds of our youngest learners.
Only when we free children from the struggle for basic dignity can we expect them to dream beyond survival.
Because the India we hope to see in 2047 is not waiting somewhere in the future.
It is already sitting in our classrooms today.

Without folded hands and prayers unsaid
Life was simple and content to look
God was there in every step I made
And in every breath I took

Without much stroke and style
Life was a colourful sketch unquote 
God was there in every rack and file
And in every detail I noted 

Without the angels choir singing
Life was a melody echoing in my ears
God was there in every agony clinging 
And in every bunch of cheers

Without the medals and glorious feat
Life was ignited with many a compliment 
God was there in every fall and defeat
And in every occasion of achievement 

Without folded hands and prayers unsaid
Life was simply a beauty to look
God was there in every flower I laid
And in every thorn I took

The Bulb Above The Desk

What have we done with our children?
Alas! What have we done?

We put clocks beside their hearts and call the ticking discipline.
We make them sit still while childhood runs barefoot through the corridors within.
And when it catches its breath,
“Why are you tired? Why are you behind? Behind whom?”
Who began this race? Who drew the finish line across a life, then called the running grace?

A child raises a hand, and we teach him to fear being wrong.
Where mistakes are embarrassing, we teach - life is for the strong!

Who decided a number could become a verdict?
Ninety-nine. Ninety-eight. Ninety-seven - as though a mind were a staircase, and someone must always stand below.
We teach them to climb, but never ask where they are meant to go.

We teach friends to count each other in percentages, row by row.
We teach parents to swallow pride in decimals and praise.
Another child's victory becomes another child's loss,
and still we ask them to smile - Congratulations! Well done!

Tell me, when did education become a polite word for comparison?
When did learning become a race where someone must always lose?
If one child rises, why must another fall?
Who decided there was only room for one, not all?

Where did the questions go?
The strange ones - the silly ones - the beautiful ones we used to know?
Who explains why the bus follows the moon, why a mother's croon tastes like honey, why a bright day ends too soon?

We sharpen pencils, answers, ranks - until curiosity bleeds into desks and blanks.
And still we say, study harder, as if exhaustion were virtue and sleep were crime.
What exactly are we educating out of them, one lesson, one silence, one perfect answer at a time?

Enough!

Not mathematics. Not ambition. Not wanting to become more.
Just stop counting the score!

Let them fail - let failure remain an attempt, not a prophecy.
Let them ask questions with no answer sheet waiting beneath them.
Let them become strange. Let them become different. Let them become themselves.

We were meant to teach them how to think - not how to win, not how to outrun one another.
Give me the child back.
Let the future keep the marks.

ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ,

ಅದೂಂದು ಒಂದು ದೊಡ್ಡ ವಠಾರ ಅದರಲ್ಲಿ ದೊಡ್ಡ ಮನೆ ಮತ್ತು ಸಣ್ಣ ಮನೆ ಸುಮಾರು ನಲವತ್ತು ಮನೆಗಳು ಇರುವ ಬಡಾವಣೆ ಅಂತಾನೇ ಹೇಳಬಹುದು.
ಈ ವಠಾರದಲ್ಲಿ ವಾಸಿಸುವ ಜನರುಗಳಿಗೆ ಯಾವುದೇ ಜಾತಿ ತಾರತಮ್ಯ ಇರಲಿಲ್ಲ ನೋಡ್ರಿ.
ಅಲ್ಲಿ ಎಲ್ಲ ರೀತಿಯ ಜನ ಅಂದ್ರೆ ಹಿಂದು.ಮುಸ್ಲಿಂ. ಕೇರಳ. ತಮಿಳು. ತೆಲುಗು. ಮರಾಠ.ಗುಜರಾತಿ.ರಾಜಸ್ತಾನಿ‌ಹೀಗೆ ನಾನಾ ಸಮುದಾಯದ ಜನರು ಅಲ್ಲಿ ವಾಸಿಸುತ್ತಿದ್ದರು.
ಆ ವಠಾರದಲ್ಲಿ ಹಬ್ಬ ಹರಿದಿನಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಒಬ್ಬರಿಗೊಬ್ಬರು ಪರಸ್ಪರ ಹೊಂದಾಣಿಕೆ ಮಾಡಿಕೊಂಡು ಹಿಂದುಗಳ ಮನೆಗೆ ಮುಸ್ಲಿಂರು ಬಂದರೆ ಅವರ ಮನೆಗಳಿಗೆ ಹಿಂದುಗಳು ಹೋಗಿ ಖುಷಿ ಪಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದರು.ಇದರಂತೆ ಬೇರೆ ಬೇರೆ ರಾಜ್ಯದಿಂದ ವಲಸೆ ಬಂದಂತಹ ಜನರು ಪರಸ್ಪರ ಪ್ರೀತಿ ವಿಶ್ವಾಸದಿಂದ ಇರುತ್ತಿದ್ದರು.

ಕೆಲವೂಮ್ಮೆ ಸಣ್ಣ ಪುಟ್ಟ ಜಗಳ ಗಳು  ನಡೆಯುವುದುಂಟು ಅದರಲ್ಲಿ ಮುಖ್ಯವಾಗಿ ನೀರಿನ ಸಲುವಾಗಿ ಜಗಳಗಳು ನಡೆಯುತ್ತಿದ್ದ ಕಾರಣ ಏನೆಂದರೆ ನಲವತ್ತು ಮನೆಗಳು ಇರುವ ವಠಾರದಲ್ಲಿ ಕೇವಲ ಎರಡೇ ನೀರಿನ ನಲ್ಲಿಗಳು ಇದ್ದವು.ಅದರಲ್ಲಿ ನೀರು ಈಗಿನಂತೆ ಇಪ್ಪತ್ನಾಲ್ಕು ಗಂಟೆ ನೀರು ಬರುವಂತಹ ನಲ್ಲಿ ನೀರು ಅಲ್ಲಾ.ಆ ಎರಡು ನಲ್ಲಿಯಲ್ಲಿ ಬೆಳಿಗ್ಗೆ ಏಳು ಗಂಟೆಯಿಂದ ಹತ್ತು ಗಂಟೆಯ ಮಟ ಬಂದರೆ ಅದೇ ಪುಣ್ಯ.
ಇನ್ನು ಬೇರೆಯ ಸಮಯದಲ್ಲಿ ವಠಾರದ ಜನಕ್ಕೆ ಕೈ ಪಂಪ್ ನಿಂದ ಹೊಡೆಯುವ ಬೊರ್ ವೆಲ್ ನೀರೇ ಗತಿ.
ಅದರಲ್ಲೂ ವಠಾರದ ಜನರ ಜೊತೆ ಸರತಿ ಸಾಲಿನಲ್ಲಿ ನಿಂತು ಆ ವಠಾರ ಓನರ್ ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬ್ ಮತ್ತು ಮಕ್ಕಳು ನೀರನ್ನು ಹಿಡಿಯುತ್ತಿದ್ದದು ನಿಜ.ಹೀಗೆ ನೀರಿನ ಸಲುವಾಗಿ ಗುದ್ದಾಟ ಹೊಡೆದಾಟ ಮಾಮೂಲಿ.ಇನ್ನು ಕೆಲವೂಂದು ವಿಚಾರಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಎಂದರೆ ಈ ಆಗೆಲ್ಲಾ ಈಗಿನ ಹಾಗೆ ಟಿವಿ ಇರಲಿಲ್ಲ ಅದು ಓನರ್ ಬಿಟ್ಟರೆ ಒಬ್ಬ ಬಾಡಿಗೆದಾರರ ಮನೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಒಂದು ಟಿವಿ ಇತ್ತು.
ಹಾಗಾಗಿ ಇನ್ನು ಕೆಲವರು ಈ ರೇಡಿಯೋ. ಟೆಪ್ರಿಕಾರ್ಡ್ನಲ್ಲಿ ಹಾಡನ್ನು ಕೇಳುವ ಸಲುವಾಗಿ ಜೋರಾದ ಧ್ವನಿಯಲ್ಲಿ ವ್ಯಾಲೂಮ್ ಆನ್ ಮಾಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದರು.
ಆಗ ಸಣ್ಣಪುಟ್ಟ ಜಗಳಗಳು ಖಾಯಂ.ಮತ್ತೆ ಈ ಹುಡುಗ ಹುಡುಗಿ ಅನ್ಯ ಜಾತೀಯರು ಓಡಿಹೋಗಿ ಮದ್ವೆ ಆದ್ರೆ ಆವಾಗ ಒಂದು ವಾರ ಎರಡು ಕುಟುಂಬಗಳ ನಡುವೆ ಗಲಾಟೆ ಜೋರಾಗುತ್ತಿದ್ದು ‌.ಇನ್ನು ಉಳಿದವರಿಗೆ ಮಜಾ ಬರುತ್ತಿತ್ತು ಆ ಜಗಳ ನೋಡಲು.
ಕೆಲವೊಂದು ಸಲ ಹಿಂದು ಧರ್ಮದವರು ಮನೆಗಳನ್ನು ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ ನೋಡಿಕೊಳ್ಳುವರು ಎನ್ನುವ ದೃಷ್ಟಿಯಿಂದ ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬ್ ರು ಜಾಸ್ತಿ ಬಾಡಿಗೆ ಹಿಂದು ಮಂದಿಗೆ ಬಾಡಿಗೆ ಕೊಟ್ಟಿದ್ದರು.ಈ ವಿಚಾರ ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬ್ ಅವರು ಹೆಂಡತಿ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನುಗೆ ತುಂಬಾ ಇರಿಸುಮುರಿಸು ಆಗುತ್ತಿತ್ತು.ಆದರೆ ಏನು ಹೇಳುವ ಪರಿಸ್ಥಿತಿ ಇರಲಿಲ್ಲ.ಹಬ್ಬ ಹರಿದಿನಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಹಿಂದು ಮಂದಿ ತಮ್ಮ ತಮ್ಮ ಮನೆಯ ಅಂಗಳದಲ್ಲಿ ಸೆಗಣಿ ಸಾರಿಸಿ ದೊಡ್ಡ ದೊಡ್ಡದಾದ ಚೆಂದದ ಬಣ್ಣ ತುಂಬಿದ ರಂಗೋಲಿ ಹಾಕಿತ್ತಿದ್ದರು.ಆಗ ಇಡೀ ಸುಂದರವಾಗಿ ಕಾಣುತ್ತಿತ್ತು.ಇದನ್ನು ಸಹಿಸದೆ ನಮ್ಮ ಧರ್ಮಕ್ಕೆ ಸಗಣಿ ಸಾರಿಸಿದರೆ ನಮಗೆ ನಮಾಜ್ ಮಾಡಲು ತೊಂದರೆ ಆಗುತ್ತದೆ ಅಂತ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಬಕೆಟ್ ತುಂಬಾ ನೀರನ್ನು ಇಡೀ ವಠಾರ ಅಂಗಳದಲ್ಲಿ ಹಾಕಿ ಬಿಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು.
ಆಗ ಹಿಂದು ಮಂದಿ ಸುಮ್ಮನೆ ಇರುತ್ತಿದ್ದರೇ ನೀವು ನಮ್ಮಂತಹವರಿಗೆ ಏಕೆ ಬಾಡಿಗೆ ಕೊಟ್ಟಿರಿ ನಮ್ಮ ಅಡ್ವಾನ್ಸ್ ಹಣ ವಾಪಸ್ ಕೊಡಿ ಇವತ್ತೇ ಮನೆ ಖಾಲಿ ಮಾಡುತ್ತೇವೆ ಎನ್ನಲು ಆಗ ಓನರ್ ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬ್ ಹೊರಗೆ ಓಡಿ ಬಂದು ಹೆಂಡತಿಯನ್ನು ಬೈದು ಒಳಗೆ ಕರೆದುಕೊಂಡು ಹೋಗುತ್ತಿದ್ದರು.
ಆದರೆ ಅದು ಆಗಿನ ಸಂದರ್ಭಕ್ಕೆ ತಕ್ಕಂತೆ ಅಷ್ಟೇ ಸೀಮಿತವಾಗಿತ್ತು.

ಆಮೇಲೆ ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬರ ಹೆಂಡತಿ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಮತ್ತೆ ಸಂಜೆ ಹೊತ್ತು ಎಲ್ಲರ ಜೊತೆ ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ ಮಾತನಾಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು.
ಆಮೇಲೆ ನನ್ನ ಗಂಡಂಗೆ ನಿಮ್ಮದು ಹಬ್ಬದ ಸಾರು ಇಷ್ಟ ಕೊಡಿ ಅಂತ ಕೇಳಿತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು.
ಆಮೇಲೆ ರಂಜಾನ್ ಹಬ್ಬದಲ್ಲಿ ಎಲ್ಲರಿಗು ತುಂಬನೇ ಗೂಡಂಬಿ.ದ್ರಾಕ್ಷಿ.ಬಾದಮಿ ತುಪ್ಪ ಬರೇ ಹಾಲಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಮಾಡಿದ ಹಾಕಿ ಕೀರನ್ನು ಹಂಚುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು.
ಅವಳ ವರ್ತನೆ ಸ್ಪಲ್ಪ ವರಟು ಆದರೂ ಸ್ವಭಾವ ಗುಣ ತುಂಬಾ ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿತ್ತು.
ವಠಾರದ ಒನರ್ ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬ್ ಸುಮಾರು ಎಂಬತ್ತು ವರ್ಷ ತುಂಬಿತ್ತು ಅವರ ಹೆಂಡತಿ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಅವರಿಗೆ ಅರವತ್ತು ವರ್ಷ ಆಗಿತ್ತು ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬ್ ಮತ್ತು ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನುಗು ಇಪ್ಪತ್ತು ವರ್ಷಗಳ ಅಂತರವಿತ್ತು.
ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಹದಿನಾರು ವಯಸ್ಸು ಇರಬಹುದು ಆವಾಗ ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬ್ ಅವರ ತಂದೆಗೆ ಒಬ್ಬನೇ ಮಗನಾಗಿದ್ದು ಲಾಯರ್ ಆಗಿದ್ದ ಮತ್ತೆ ಹಣ ಆಸ್ತಿ ತುಂಬಾನೇ ಇತ್ತು ಎನ್ನುವ ಕಾರಣಕ್ಕೆ ವಯಸ್ಸಿನ ಇತಿಮಿತಿ ನೋಡಿದೆ ಇವರಿಬ್ಬರ ಮದುವೆ ಮಾಡಿಸಿದ್ದರು.
ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬ್ ಮತ್ತು ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಮದುವೆಯಾಗಿ ನಲವತ್ತು ವರ್ಷಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಹತ್ತು ಮಕ್ಕಳು ಅದರಲ್ಲಿ ಐದು ಗಂಡು ಐದು ಹೆಣ್ಣು ಮಕ್ಕಳನ್ನು ಮಾಡಿಕೊಂಡು ಹೇಗೂ ಜೀವನ ನಡೆಯುತ್ತಿತ್ತು.
ಆದರೆ ಸರ್ಕಾರಿ ಲಾಯರ್ ಇದ್ದ ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬ್ ರನ್ನು ಬಹಳ ಮುದ್ದಿನಿಂದ ಬೆಳೆಸಿದ ಅವರ ತಂದೆ ತಾಯಿ ನಮ್ಮದೇ ತುಂಬಾ ಆಸ್ತಿ ಇದೆ ಕೆಲಸ ಮಾಡುವುದು ಬೇಡ ಅಂತ ಲಾಯರ್ ಕೆಲ್ಸಕ್ಕೆ ರಾಜಿನಾಮೆ ಕೊಡಿಸಿದರು.
ಆಗ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಕೆಲಸ ಬಿಡುವುದು ಬೇಡಾ ಅಂತ ತುಂಬಾ ಹೇಳಿದರು ಕೇಳಲಿಲ್ಲ.
ಒಂದಿಷ್ಟು ವರುಷಗಳ ನಂತರ ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬ್ ತಂದೆ ತಾಯಿ ತೀರಿಕೊಂಡರು.
ಕೂತು ಉಂಡೆರೆ ಕೊಪ್ಪರಿಗೆ ಹೊನ್ನು ಸಾಲದು ಎಂಬಂತೆ.
ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬ್ರು ಸಂಸಾರ ಜೋತೆ ಹತ್ತು ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಜೀವನದ ನಿರ್ವಹಣೆಯ ಸಲುವಾಗಿ ಒಂದೊಂದಾಗಿ ಆಸ್ತಿಯನ್ನು ಮಾರಿದರು.
ಇನ್ನು ಹೀಗೆ ಮುಂದುವರೆದರೆ ಎಲ್ಲ ಆಸ್ತಿಯನ್ನು ಮಾರುವರು ನಮಗೇನು ಉಳಿಸುವುದಿಲ್ಲ ಅಂತ ಜಗಳ ಮಾಡಿ ಈಗಿರುವ ಈ ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬರ ವಠಾರವನ್ನು ಉಳಿಸಿಕೊಂಡು ಎಲ್ಲ ಜವಾಬ್ದಾರಿಯನ್ನು ತಾನೇ ನಿಭಾಯಿಸಲು ಸಿದ್ಧಳಾದಳು.
ಎಲ್ಲ ಮನೆಗಳ ಬಾಡಿಗೆ ರೇಟು ಜಾಸ್ತಿ ಮಾಡಿ ಹೇಗೂ ತಕ್ಕಮಟ್ಟಿಗೆ ಜೀವನ ಸಾಗಿಸುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು.

ಆದರೆ ಇತ್ತಿಚೆಗೆ ಗಂಡನನ್ನು ನೋಡಿದರೆ ಸಾಕು ಉರಿದು ಬಿಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು.
ವಠಾರದ ಹೆಣ್ಣು ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಜೊತೆ ಹರಟೆ ಹೊಡೆಯುತ್ತಾ ಗಂಡನಿಗೆ " ಓ ಬುಡ್ಡಾ ಹೈ ನಾ ಮೇರಾ ಮರದ್ ಉಸಕಾ ಗಾಲಾ ತಬಕೇ ಛಾತಿಕೂ ಚೀರಕರ್  ಔರ್ ಉಸಕೇ ಫರ್ ಬೈಠಕೇ ಉಸಕಾ ಕುನ್ ಪೀ ಜಾವುಂಗಿ "( ಆ ಮುದುಕ ಐತಲ್ಲಾ ನನ್ನ ಗಂಡ ಅವ್ನ ಕತ್ತು ಹಿಸುಕಿ ಅವನ ಎದೆಯನ್ನು ಸೀಳಿ ಅದರ ಮೇಲೆ ಕೂತ್ಕೊಂಡು ಅವನ ರಕ್ತ ಕುಡಿಯುವೆ) ಅಂತ ಏನೇನೋ ಹೇಳ್ತದ್ದನ್ನು ಕೇಳಿ ಎಲ್ಲರು ನಗುತ್ತಿದ್ದರು.
ಹೇಗೂ ತಕ್ಕಮಟ್ಟಿಗೆ ಜೀವನ ಸಾಗಿಸುತ್ತಿದ್ದ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ತಾನು ಯಾವುದರಲ್ಲೂ ಕಡಿಮೆಯಿಲ್ಲ ಎಂಬಂತೆ ನಾಲ್ಕು ಗಂಡು ಮಕ್ಕಳು ನಾಲ್ಕು ಗಂಡು ಮಕ್ಕಳದು ಮದುವೆ ಮಾಡಿದಳು.
ಹೆಣ್ಣು ಮಕ್ಕಳು ಗಂಡನ ಮನೆಗೆ ಹೋದರೆ ನಾಲ್ಕು ಗಂಡು ಮಕ್ಕಳು ತಮ್ಮ ತಮ್ಮ ಹೆಂಡತಿಯರನ್ನು ಕರೆದುಕೊಂಡು ದುಬಾಯ್.
ಬೆಂಗಳೂರು. ಮಂಗಳೂರು ಬಾಂಬೆ ಅಂತ ಕೆಲಸದ ನೆಪ ಹೇಳಿ ಹೋದರು.
ಇನ್ನು ಉಳಿದಿದ್ದು ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬ್ರು ಅವರು ಹೆಂಡತಿ ಇಬ್ಬರು ಮಕ್ಕಳಾದ ಹೀನಾ ಮತ್ತು ಸಲೀಂ ಉಳಿದರು.
ಎಂಟು ಮಕ್ಕಳ ಮದುವೆ ಮಾಡಿದ ಕಾರಣ ತುಂಬಾ ಸಾಲ ಆಗಿತ್ತು.
ಮಕ್ಕಳು ಹಣ ಕಳುಹಿಸುತ್ತಿದ್ದರು.
ಆದರೆ ಅದು ಸಾಲುತ್ತಿರಲಿಲ್ಲ.
ಇನ್ನು ವಠಾರದ ಮನೆಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ಕೆಲವೂಂದು ಮನೆಗಳನ್ನು ಭೋಗ್ಯಕ್ಕೆ ಕೊಟ್ಟ ಕಾರಣ ಬಾಡಿಗೆಯು ಕಡಿಮೆಯಾಗಿತ್ತು.
ಇನ್ನು ಸಲೀಂ ಮತ್ತು ಹೀನಾಳ ಓದು ಮುಗಿದಿರಲಿಲ್ಲ.
ತುಂಬಾ ಕಷ್ಟಕರವಾದ ಜೀವನ ಸಾಗಿಸುತ್ತಿದ್ದರು.

ಹೀಗೆರುವಾಗ ಸಲೀಂ ಓದು ಬಿಟ್ಟು ಕೆಲಸಕ್ಕೆ ಹೋಗಲು ಶುರು ಮಾಡಿದ ಆದರೆ ಹೀನಾಳಿಗೆ ಓದಬೇಕು ಎನ್ನುವ ಆಸೆ ತುಂಬಾ ಇತ್ತು.
ಅವಳು ಮೊದಲ ಪಿಯುಸಿ ಓದುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು.
ಪರೀಕ್ಷೆ ಹತ್ತಿರ ಬಂದಿದ್ದ ಕಾರಣ ಅಮ್ಮನಿಗೆ ಹಣವನ್ನು ಕೇಳಿದಳು ಅದಕ್ಕೆ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು "ಮೇರೆಕನೇ ಪೈಸೆ ನಹಿ ಓ ಅಂಟಿ ಹೈ ಉಸ್ ಪಾಸ್ ಜಾಕೇ ಮಗಂಲೇ"(ನನ್ನ ಹತ್ತಿರ ಹಣ ಇಲ್ಲ ಆ ಅಂಟಿಗೆ ಹೋಗಿ ಕೇಳು ತಗೂ) ಅಂತ ಹೇಳಿದಳು.
ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಹೀಗೆ ಹೇಳಲು ಒಂದು ಕಾರಣವಿದೆ ಏನೆಂದರೆ ಹೀನಾ ಯಾರು ಜೋತೆನೂ ಬೇರತು ಮಾತನಾಡಿದ ಹುಡುಗಿ ಆದರೆ ಆ ವಠರಾದ ಮನೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಬಾಡಿಗೆಗೆ ಇದ್ದ ಸವಿತಾಳನ್ನು ತುಂಬಾ ಹಚ್ಚಿಕೊಂಡಿದ್ದಳು ಅವರ ಜೋತೆ ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ ಮಾತನಾಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು.
ತನಗೆ ಯಾವಾಗಲಾದರೂ ಏನಾದರೂ ತೊಂದರೆ ಬಂದರೆ ಅಥವಾ ಹಣದ ಅವಶ್ಯಕತೆ ಬಂದರೆ ಸಾಕು ಸವಿತಾಳ ಮನೆಗೆ ಹೋಗಿ ತೆಗೆದುಕೊಂಡು ಬರುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು.
ಆಮೇಲೆ ಹೀನಾ ಹಾಗೆ ಹಣವನ್ನು ಸುಮ್ಮನೆ ತೆಗೆದುಕೊಂಡು ಬರುತ್ತಿರಲಿಲ್ಲ ಒಂದು ವಾರ ಇಲ್ಲ ಎರಡು ವಾರಗಳ ನಂತರ ಅವರ ಅಣ್ಣಂದಿರ ಹತ್ತರ ಹಣವನ್ನು ಇಸ್ಕೊಂಡು ವಾಪಸ್ ಸವಿತಾಗೆ ತಂದುಕೊಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು .
ಇವರ ಈ ವ್ಯವಹಾರದಲ್ಲಿ ಸವಿತಳ ಗಂಡ ಆಗಲಿ ಮಕ್ಕಳಾಗಲಿ ತೆರೆ ಕೆಡಿಸಿಕೊಳ್ಳದೆ ಹೋಗ್ಲಿ ಬಿಡು ಹೀನಾ ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ ಓದಲಿ ಅಂತ ಹೇಳಿತ್ತದ್ದರು.
ಸವಿತಾಳಿಗೆ ಹೀನಾಳ ಶಾಂತ ಸ್ವಭಾವ. ಗುಣ ಓದುವ ಹವ್ಯಾಸ ಮಾತನಾಡುವ ರೀತಿ ಎಲ್ಲ ಇಷ್ಟವಾಗುತ್ತಿತ್ತು.
ಹೀಗಾಗಿ ಕೌಸರ್ ಸವಿತ ಅಂಟಿಗೆ ಹೋಗಿ ಕೇಳು ಅಂತ ಹೇಳಿದರಲ್ಲಿ ಏನು ತಪ್ಪು ಇರ್ಲಿಲ್ಲ.ಈ ವಿಷಯ ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬ್ರುಗು ಗೋತ್ತತ್ತು.
ಹೀನಾ ಅದೇ ಖುಷಿಯಲ್ಲಿ ಸವಿತಾಳ ಮನೆಗೆ ಹೋಗಿ "ಆಂಟಿ ನಂಗೆ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ಕೂಡಿ ಕಾಲೇಜು ಫೀಜ್ ಕಟ್ಟಬೇಕಿತ್ತು"
ಅಂತ ಕೇಳಿದಳು ಅದಕ್ಕೆ ಸವಿತ ಕೂಡ ಹಿಂದೆ ಮುಂದೆ ಏನು ವಿಚಾರ ಮಾಡಿದೆ ಒಂದು ಸಾವಿರ ರೂಪಾಯಿ ಕೂಟ್ಟಳು.
ಆಗ ಹೀನಾ "ಅಯ್ಯೋ ಅಂಟಿ ಇಷ್ಟೂಂದು ಬೇಡ ನಂಗೆ ಬರೀ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ಕೂಡಿ ಹಾಕು"ಎನ್ನಲು 
ಸವಿತ "ತಗೂ ಪುಟ್ಟ ನೀನು ತುಂಬಾ ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ ಓದುತ್ತಿ ಅಂತ ನಂಗೆ ಪರ್ವಾಗಿಲ್ಲ ನೀನು ಕಾಲೇಜ್ ಫೀಜ್ ಕಟ್ಟಿ ಉಳಿದಿದ್ದು ನೋಟ್ಸ್ ತಗೋ ಬರೆಯಲು"ಎಂದಾಗ 
ಹೀನಾ "ಬೇಡ ಅಂಟಿ ನನ್ನ ಹತ್ತಿರ ಎಲ್ಲ ನೋಟ್ಸ್ ಇದೆ ಸುಮ್ಮನೆ ಹೆಚ್ಚಿಗೆ ಹಣ ಬೇಡ ನಾನು ಬೇಕಾದರೆ ಮತ್ತೆ ಕೇಳಿ ಇಸ್ಕೊಂತಿನಿ ಈಗ ನಂಗೆ ಬರೀ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ಕೂಡಿ ಅಷ್ಟೇ"ಅಂತ ಹೇಳಿ ಒಂದು ಸಾವಿರ ರೂಪಾಯಿಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ತನಗೆ ಬೇಕಾದ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ತಗೊಂಡು ಉಳಿದ ಹಣವನ್ನು ವಾಪಸ್ ಸವಿತ ಅಂಟಿಗೆ ಕೊಟ್ಟಳು 
ಸವಿತ ಅಂಟಿ "ಸರಿ ಬಿಡಮ್ಮ ನಿನ್ನಷ್ಟ" ಅಂತ ಹೇಳಿ ಉಳಿದ ಹಣವನ್ನು ಇಸ್ಕೊಂಡಳು.
ಆಗ ಹೀನಾ" ಅಂಟಿ  ಇವತ್ತು ಸೋಮವಾರ ನಾನು ಈ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿಯನ್ನು ಮುಂದಿನ ಸೋಮವಾರ ಕೊಡುವೆ"ಎಂದಾಗ 
ಸವಿತ "ಯಾವಾಗಲಾದರೂ ಕೊಡಮ್ಮ  ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ ಓದು ಪಸ್ಟ್ ನಾನು ನಿಂಗೆ ಹಣ ಕೇಳಲ್ಲ "
ಹೀನಾ "ಇಲ್ಲ ಅಂಟಿ ಮುಂದಿನ ಸೋಮವಾರ ನಮ್ಮ ದೊಡ್ಡಣ್ಣ ದುಬಾಯ್ ನಿಂದ ಮನಿ ಆರ್ಡರ್ ಮಾಡುತಾನೆ ನಾನು ಆವತ್ತೆ ಈ ದುಡ್ಡುನ್ನು ತಂದುಕೊಡತಿನಿ ಸರಿ ಅಂಟಿ ನಾನು ಬರುವೆ "ಅಂತ ಹೇಳಿ ಹೀನಾ ಹೋದಳು

ಇದರ ಮಧ್ಯೆ ಹತ್ತಿರವೇ ಇದ್ದ ಅವರ ಸಂಬಂಧದ ಡಾಕ್ಟರ್ ಒಬ್ಬರನ್ನು ಕರೆಯಿಸಿ ಹೀನಾಳ ಹೆಣವನ್ನು ಕೆಳಗೆ ಇಳಿಸಿ ಎಲ್ಲರನ್ನು ಹೊರಗೆ ಕಳುಹಿಸಿ ಕೈ ಕಾಲು ಎಲ್ಲ ನೆಟ್ಟಿಗೆ ಮಾಡಿ ಬಿಗಿಯಾಗಿ ದಾರ ಕಟ್ಟಿ ಮತ್ತೆ ಚಾಚಿದ ನಾಲಿಗೆಯನ್ನು ಕತ್ತರಿಸಿ ತೆಗೆದು ಹಾಕಿ ಕೆಳಕ್ಕೆ ಹೆಣವನ್ನು ತಂದು ಹಾಲ್ ನಲ್ಲಿ ಮಂಚದ ಮೇಲೆ ಹಾಕಿ ಅದಕ್ಕೆ ಏನು ಸ್ಪಲ್ಪ ಸೆಂಟು ಹಾಕಿ ಊದುಬತ್ತಿ ಹಚ್ಚಿ ನೋಡುವವರಿಗೆ ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ ಕಾಣುವಂತೆ ಮಾಡಿದರು.ಆಮೇಲೆ
ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ವಠರಾದ ಮಂದಿಯನ್ನು ಕರೆದು  "ನೋಡು ಯಾರಾದ್ರೂ ಕೇಳಿದರೆ ಹೀನಾ ಮೆದುಳಿನ ಜ್ವರದಿಂದ ಬಳಲಿ ಸತ್ತಿದ್ದಾಳೆ ಅಂತ ಹೇಳಬೇಕು ಇದು ನಮ್ಮ ಮರ್ಯಾದೆ ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆ ನಿಮ್ಮ ಮಕ್ಕಳು ಹೀಗೆ ಆಗಿದ್ದರೆ ನೀವು ಏನು ಮಾಡುತ್ತೀರಿ ನೋಡಿ"ಎಂದು ಅಳುತ್ತಾ ಹೇಳಿ ಒಳಗೆ ಹೋದಳು.

ಎಲ್ಲ ವಠಾರದ ಮಂದಿಗೆ ಹೀನಾ ತುಂಬಾ ಒಳ್ಳೆಯ ಹೀಗೆ ಹೇಗೆ ಮಾಡಿಕೊಳ್ಳಲು ಸಾಧ್ಯ ಎಂಬ ಅನುಮಾನವಂತೂ ಬಂದಿದ್ದು ನಿಜ ಆದರೆ ಹೋಗ್ಲಿ ಬಿಡಿ ಇದು ಅವರವರ ವೈಯಕ್ತಿಕ ವಿಚಾರ ಮತ್ತು ಮರ್ಯಾದೆ ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆ ಎಂದು ನಿಟ್ಟುಸಿರು ಬಿಟ್ಟರು.
ಯಾರಾದ್ರೂ ಬಂದು ಹೀನಾಳ ಸಾವಿನ ಬಗ್ಗೆ ಕೇಳಿದೊಡನೆ ಜ್ವರದಿಂದ ಬಳಲಿ ಸತ್ತಿದ್ದಾಳೆ ಅಂತಾನೇ ಹೇಳಿದ್ರು.
ಇತ್ತ ಹೀನಾಳ ಶವದ ಮುಂದೆ ಅವತ್ತು ಐದು ಆರು ಮಹಿಳೆಯರಿಂದ ಕುರಾನ್ ಓದಲು ಶುರು ಮಾಡಿದ್ರು.ಹೀಗೆ ರಾತ್ರಿ ಕಳೆದು ಹಗಲು ಆಯಿತು ಬೆಳಗ್ಗೆ ಬೇಗನೆ ಶವ ಸಂಸ್ಕಾರ ಮಾಡಲು ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಸಂಬಂಧಿಕರಿಗೆ ಹೇಳಿದಳು.
ಹೀನಾ ಶವವನ್ನು ಒಂದಿಷ್ಟು ವಯಸ್ಸಾದ ಮಹಿಳೆಯರು ಬಿಸಿ ನೀರಿನಿಂದ ಲಕ್ಸ್ ಸೋಪು ಶಾಂಪೂ ಎಲ್ಲ ಹಾಕಿ ಸ್ನಾನ ಮಾಡಿಸಿ ಅವರ ವಿಧಿ ವಿಧಾನಗಳಂತೆ ಕುರಾನ್ ಮಂತ್ರಗಳನ್ನು ಹೇಳುತ್ತಾ ಹೀನಾಳನ್ನು ಅತಿ ಸುಂದರವಾಗಿ ಅಲಂಕಾರ ಮಾಡಿ ಶವದ ಪೆಟ್ಟಿಗೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಮಲಗಿಸಿದರು.
ಎಲ್ಲರು ನೋಡಿ ಎಷ್ಟು ಸುಂದರವಾಗಿದಾಳೆ ಒಳ್ಳೆ ಮದುಮಗಳಂತೆ ಕಾಣುತ್ತಿದ್ದಾಳೆ ಎನ್ನತ ಕಣ್ಣೀರ ಧಾರೆ ಆರಿಸಿದರು.
ಅದುವರೆಗೂ ಸವಿತ ಮಗಳು ರಾಣಿ ಅವಳ ಶವವನ್ನು ನೋಡಲೇ ಇರ್ಲಿಲ್ಲ.ಈಗ ಅಲಂಕಾರ ಮಾಡಿದ ಹೀನಾಳ ಹೆಣವನ್ನು ನೋಡಿ ಸವಿತ ನಿನ್ನೆ ನನ್ನ ಎಷ್ಟು ಚೆಂದ ಮಾತನಾಡಿದಿ ಹೀನಾ ಈಗ ನಿನ್ನನು ಈ ಸ್ಥಿತಿಯಲ್ಲಿ ನೋಡಲು ನನಗೆ ಸಾಧ್ಯವಾಗುತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ ಹೀನಾ ಬಾನು ಅಕ್ಕ ನೋಡಿ ಹೀನಾ ಹೆಂಗೆ ಸುಮ್ಮನೆ ಮಲಗಿದ್ದಾಳೆ ನನ್ನನು ಅಂಟಿ ಅಂಟಿ ಅಂತ ಯಾವಾಗಲೂ ಕರೆಯುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು ಎಂದು ಹೀನಾ ಏನಾಯ್ತು ಪುಟ್ಟ ನಿಂಗೆ ಈ ಮಾಡಿದ್ದು ಸರಿಯೇ ಪುಟ್ಟಿ ಎಂದು ಬಿಕ್ಕಿ ಬಿಕ್ಕಿ ಅಳುತ್ತಿದ್ದರು.
ಸುಮಾರು ಬೆಳಿಗ್ಗೆ ಹನ್ನೊಂದು ಗಂಟೆಗೆ ಹೀನಾಳ ಶವದ ಕೊನೆಯ ಮೆರವಣಿಗೆ ಮನೆಯಿಂದ ಹೊರಟಿತ್ತು.
ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬ್ರಿಗೆ ದಿಕ್ಕೆ ತೋಚದೆ ಕಂಗಾಲಾಗಿದ್ದರು ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಎದೆ ಹೊಡೆದುಕೊಂಡು ಅಳುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು ಎಲ್ಲ ಅಕ್ಕಂದಿರು ಅಣ್ಣಂದಿರು ಬಂದಿದ್ದರು.ಇಡೀ ಕುಟುಂಬದವರ ಆಕ್ರಂದನ ಮುಗಿಲು ಮುಟ್ಟಿತ್ತು.
ವಠಾರದ ಎಲ್ಲರು ಕಣ್ಣೀರು ಹಾಕಿದರು. ಹೀನಾಳ ಶವವನ್ನು ಸ್ಮಶಾನಕ್ಕೆ ಹೋಗಿ ದಫನ್ ಮಾಡಿ ಬಂದ ಮೇಲೆ ಇಡೀ ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬರ ವಠಾರವೇ ಸ್ತಬ್ಧವಾಯಿತು.
ಹೀನಾಳ ನಲವತ್ತು ದಿನದ ಎಲ್ಲ ಕ್ರೀಯಾ ಕ್ರಮಗಳು ಮುಗಿದವು.
ಎಲ್ಲ ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬರ ಮಕ್ಕಳು ಎಲ್ಲ ಕೆಲಸ ನಿಮಿತ್ತ ತಮ್ಮ ತಮ್ಮ ಊರುಗಳಿಗೆ ತೆರಳಿದರು.
ಈಗ ಮನೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬರ ಹೆಂಡತಿ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಹಾಗೂ ಸಲೀಂ ಮೂವರೇ ಉಳಿದಿದ್ದು ಮುಂಚನ ಹಾಗೆ ವಟವಟ ಅನ್ನುತ್ತಿದ್ದ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಸುಮ್ಮನೆ ಇದ್ದರು ಯಾರು ಜೋತೆನೂ ಬೇರತು ಮಾತನಾಡಿ ದಿನಗಳೇ ಕಳೆದಿದ್ದವು.

ಹೀಗೆ ಇರುವಾಗ ಒಂದಿಷ್ಟು ದಿನಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ವಠರಾದ ಮಂದಿಗೆ ಹೀನಾ ಓಡಾಡಿದಂತೆ ಮಾತನಾಡಿದಂತೆ ನಿಂತಂತೆ ಭಾಸವಾಗುತ್ತಿತ್ತು.ಬೇಗನೆ ಕೆಲಸದಿಂದ ಮನೆಯೊಳಗೆ ಹೋಗುವರು ಆದರೆ ಸಂಜೆಯಾದರೆ ಸಾಕು ಮನೆಯಿಂದ ಹೊರಗೆ ಬರಲು ಭಯಪಡುವಂತಹ ಸ್ಥಿತಿ ತಲುಪಿದ್ದರು.
ಮತ್ತೆ ಕೆಲವರು ಹೀನಾಳನ್ನು ಅವರ ತಾಯಿ ತಮ್ಮ ಸೇರಿ ಕೊಂದಿದ್ದಾರೆ ಅವಳ ಮೈಮೇಲೆ ಗಾಯದ ಕಲೆ ಇದ್ದವು ಏನೇನೋ ಸುದ್ದಿಯನ್ನು ಹರಡಿದರು.

ಇಷ್ಟೆಲ್ಲಾ ಆದರೂ ಸವಿತ ಮಗಳು ರಾಣಿಯ ಕಣ್ಣಿಗೆ ಒಂದು ದಿನ ಕೂಡ ಕನಸಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಆಗಲಿ ಅಥವಾ ಭೂತದ ರೂಪದಲ್ಲಿ ಆಗಲಿ ಕಾಣಿಸಲಿಲ್ಲ.ಸವಿತ ರಾಣಿ ಬೆಳಿಗ್ಗೆ ಮುಂಜಾನೆ ನಾಲ್ಕುಕ್ಕೆ ಎದ್ದು ಅಕ್ಕ ಪಕ್ಕದ ಓಣಿಯಿಂದ ಕತ್ತಲೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ನೀರನ್ನು ತರುತ್ತಿದ್ದರು.
ಮತ್ತೆ ಅವರಿಗೆ ಯಾವುದೇ ಭಯ ಏನು ಆಗುತ್ತಿರಲಿಲ್ಲ.
ಸವಿತ ತನ್ನ ಪಾಡಿಗೆ ತಾನು ಸುಮ್ಮನೆ ಇರುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು.ಹೀನಾಳ ನೆನಪು ಮರುಕಳಿಸಿದಾಗ ಮೌನವಾಗಿ ಕುಳಿತು ಬಿಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು.
ಇದುವರೆಗೆ ಒಂದು ದಿನವೂ ಕನಸಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಬರದ ಹೀನಾ ಈಗ ಸತ್ತು ಎರಡು ತಿಂಗಳ ಕಾಲ ಕಳೆದಿತ್ತು ಆಗ ಇದ್ದಕ್ಕಿದ್ದಂತೆ ಒಂದು ರಾತ್ರಿ ಸುಮಾರು ಎರಡು ಗಂಟೆಯಾಗಿತ್ತು.
ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಕನಸಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಹೀನಾ ಬಂದು "ಅಮ್ಮಿ ಓ ಅಂಟಿ ಕೂ ಮೈ ಸಾಥಸೂಪಚಸ್ ರೂಪಾಯ್ ದೇನಾ" ( ಅಮ್ಮ ಆ ಅಂಟಿಗೆ ನಾನು ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ಕೂಡಬೇಕು) ಎನ್ನುವ ಧ್ವನಿಗೆ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಹೆದರಿ ಬಿಟ್ಟಳು.
ಯಾರಿಗೆ ಕೊಡಬೇಕು ಅಂತ ತಿಳಿಯದೇ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಸುಮ್ಮನೆ ಆದಳು.
ಆದರೆ ಹೀಗೆ ಸುಮ್ಮನೆ ಇರದೆ ಹೀನಾ ಸರಿಸುಮಾರು ಒಂದು ತಿಂಗಳುಗಳ ಕಾಲ ಕನಸ್ಸಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಬರತೊಡಗಿದಳು.
ಹೀನಾ ಏನು ಕೇಳುತ್ತಿರಲಿಲ್ಲ.
ಬರೇ "ಓ ಅಂಟಿ ಕೂ ಮೈ ಸಾಥಸೂಪಚಸ್ ರೂಪಾಯ್ ದೇನಾ"
ಕಣ್ಣಾಮುಚ್ಚಾದರೆ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನುಗೆ ಬರೀ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ಕೂಡಬೇಕು ನಾನು ಎನ್ನುವ ಕನಸು ಮತ್ತೆ ಮತ್ತೆ ಬೀಳ ತೊಡಗಿತು.
ಏನು ಮಾಡಬೇಕು ಯಾರಿಗೆ ಹೇಳಬೇಕು ಅಂತ ತಿಳಿಯದೇ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಎಲ್ಲ ವಠಾರದ ಮಂದಿಗೆ ಕೇಳಿದಳು ಎಲ್ಲರು ನಮ್ಮ ಜೋತೆಗೆ ಮಾತನಾಡುವುದೇ ಕಷ್ಟ ಇನ್ನು ಹಣ ಎಲ್ಲಿಂದ ಕೇಳುವಳು ಎಂಬ ಉತ್ತರ ಹೇಳುತ್ತಿದ್ದರು.
ಹೀಗೆ ಒಂದು ವಾರ ಕಳೆಯಿತು.
ಹೀನಾ ಈಗಂತೂ ನೇರವಾಗಿ ಬಂದಂತೆ ಕಾಣಿಸಿ ಆ ಅಂಟಿಗೆ "ಅಮ್ಮಿ ಓ ಅಂಟಿ ಕೂ ಮೈ ಸಾಥಸೂಪಚಸ್ ರೂಪಾಯ್ ದೇನಾ ಅಬ್ ತು ದೇ " (ಅಮ್ಮ ನಾನು ಆ ಅಂಟಿಗೆ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ಕೂಡಬೇಕು ಈಗ ನೀನು ಕೊಡು) ಎನ್ನುವಂತೆ ಅಪ್ಪಣೆ ಮಾಡಿ  "ತು ನಹೀ ದಿಯೇ ತೂ ಮೈ ತುಜಿ ಚೂಡುಂಗಿ ನಹೀ "
(ಕೊಡಲಿಲ್ಲ ಅಂದ್ರೆ ನಾನು ನಿನ್ನನು ಸುಮ್ಮನೆ ಬಿಡಲ್ಲ) ಎಂದು ಪೀಡಿಸುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು.

ಕಡೆಗೆ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಮತ್ತೂಮ್ಮೆ ವಠರಾದ ಜನರಿಗೆ ದಯಾ ಮಾಡಿ ಹೇಳಿ ಯಾರು ನನ್ನ ಮಗಳು ಹೀನಾಗೆ ದುಡ್ಡು ಕೊಟ್ಟಿದ್ದೀರಿ ತಿಳಿಸಿ ಇಲ್ಲಾಂದ್ರೆ ಅವಳು ನನ್ನನ್ನು ಸುಮ್ಮನೆ ಬಿಡಲ್ಲ ಎಂದು ಬೇಡಿಕೊಂಡಳು.
ಆಗ ಅದರಲ್ಲಿ ಒಬ್ಬರು "ಬಾನು ಅಕ್ಕ ಹೀನಾ ನಮ್ಮ ಜೋತೆನೇ ಮಾತನಾಡುತ್ತಿರಲಿಲ್ಲ.
ಇನ್ನು ಹಣ ಎಲ್ಲಿಂದ ಕೇಳುವಳು ಹೇಳಿ ಅವಳು ಯಾವಾಗಲೂ ಆ ಸವಿತ ಅವರ ಮನೆಗೆ ಹೋಗುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು ತಾನೇ ಬಹುಶಃ ಅವರೇ ಕೊಟ್ಟಿರಬೇಕು ನೋಡಿ" ಎಂದಾಗ 
ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನುಗೆ" ಯಾ ಅಲ್ಲ ನಾನೇ ಮರೆತು ಬಿಟ್ಟೆ ಸವಿತ ಅವರನ್ನು ಹೀನಾ ಸಾಯುವ ಒಂದು ಆರು ದಿನಗಳ ಹಿಂದೆ ಹೀನಾ ಹಣ ಕೇಳಿದ್ದಳು ನಾನೇ ಆ ಸವಿತ ಹತ್ತರ ಇಸ್ಕೂ ಅಂತ ಈಗ ನೆನಪು ಆಯಿತು"ಎನ್ನುತ್ತಾ ತಡಮಾಡದೆ ಸವಿತಳ ಮನೆಗೆ ಹೋಗಿ"ರೀ ಸವಿತ ಹೀನಾ ನಿಮ್ಮ ಹತ್ತರ ಹಣವನ್ನು ಇಸ್ಕೊಂಡಳು ಅದನ್ನು ಯಾಕೆ ಹೇಳಲಿಲ್ಲ ನೀವು"ಎನ್ನಲು 

ಸವಿತ "ಇಲ್ಲ ನನ್ನ ಹತ್ತಿರ ಹಣ ತೆಗೆದುಕೊಂಡಿಲ್ಲ "ಅಂದಳು.

ಆಗ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು "ಇಲ್ಲ ನಿಮಗೆ ಗೋತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ ನನಗೆ ಈ ನಿಮ್ಮ ಹಣ ಕೊಡುವವರೆಗೂ ನಂಗೆ ಸಮಾಧಾನವಿಲ್ಲ ನನ್ನನ್ನು ನೆಮ್ಮದಿಯಿಂದ ಬದುಕಲು ಬಿಡುವುದಿಲ್ಲ ಹೀನಾ ನಿಮ್ಮ ಕಾಲಿಗೆ ಬಿದ್ದು ಬಿಡುವೆ ಈ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ನೀವು ತೆಗೆದುಕೊಳ್ಳಿ"ಎಂದು ಆ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ಹಣವನ್ನು ಸವಿತಗೆ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಕೊಟ್ಟು"ನಂಗೆ ಈಗ ನೆಮ್ಮದಿಯಾಯ್ತು ನೋಡಿ"ಎನ್ನುತ್ತಾ ನಾನು ಬರುವೆ ಎಂದು ಹೊರಟು ಹೋದರು.

ನೋಡಲು ಹೋಗಿ ಜ್ವರ ಬಂದು ಮಲಗಿದರು. ಇದರ ಮಧ್ಯೆ ಹತ್ತಿರವೇ ಇದ್ದ ಅವರ ಸಂಬಂಧದ ಡಾಕ್ಟರ್ ಒಬ್ಬರನ್ನು ಕರೆಯಿಸಿ ಹೀನಾಳ ಹೆಣವನ್ನು ಕೆಳಗೆ ಇಳಿಸಿ ಎಲ್ಲರನ್ನು ಹೊರಗೆ ಕಳುಹಿಸಿ ಕೈ ಕಾಲು ಎಲ್ಲ ನೆಟ್ಟಿಗೆ ಮಾಡಿ ಬಿಗಿಯಾಗಿ ದಾರ ಕಟ್ಟಿ ಮತ್ತೆ ಚಾಚಿದ ನಾಲಿಗೆಯನ್ನು ಕತ್ತರಿಸಿ ತೆಗೆದು ಹಾಕಿ ಕೆಳಕ್ಕೆ ಹೆಣವನ್ನು ತಂದು ಹಾಲ್ ನಲ್ಲಿ ಮಂಚದ ಮೇಲೆ ಹಾಕಿ ಅದಕ್ಕೆ ಏನು ಸ್ಪಲ್ಪ ಸೆಂಟು ಹಾಕಿ ಊದುಬತ್ತಿ ಹಚ್ಚಿ ನೋಡುವವರಿಗೆ ಚೆನ್ನಾಗಿ ಕಾಣುವಂತೆ ಮಾಡಿದರು.ಆಮೇಲೆ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ವಠರಾದ ಮಂದಿಯನ್ನು ಕರೆದು  "ನೋಡು ಯಾರಾದ್ರೂ ಕೇಳಿದರೆ ಹೀನಾ ಮೆದುಳಿನ ಜ್ವರದಿಂದ ಬಳಲಿ ಸತ್ತಿದ್ದಾಳೆ ಅಂತ ಹೇಳಬೇಕು ಇದು ನಮ್ಮ ಮರ್ಯಾದೆ ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆ ನಿಮ್ಮ ಮಕ್ಕಳು ಹೀಗೆ ಆಗಿದ್ದರೆ ನೀವು ಏನು ಮಾಡುತ್ತೀರಿ ನೋಡಿ"ಎಂದು ಅಳುತ್ತಾ ಹೇಳಿ ಒಳಗೆ ಹೋದಳು.  ಎಲ್ಲ ವಠಾರದ ಮಂದಿಗೆ ಹೀನಾ ತುಂಬಾ ಒಳ್ಳೆಯ ಹೀಗೆ ಹೇಗೆ ಮಾಡಿಕೊಳ್ಳಲು ಸಾಧ್ಯ ಎಂಬ ಅನುಮಾನವಂತೂ ಬಂದಿದ್ದು ನಿಜ ಆದರೆ ಹೋಗ್ಲಿ ಬಿಡಿ ಇದು ಅವರವರ ವೈಯಕ್ತಿಕ ವಿಚಾರ ಮತ್ತು ಮರ್ಯಾದೆ ಪ್ರಶ್ನೆ ಎಂದು ನಿಟ್ಟುಸಿರು ಬಿಟ್ಟರು. ಯಾರಾದ್ರೂ ಬಂದು ಹೀನಾಳ ಸಾವಿನ ಬಗ್ಗೆ ಕೇಳಿದೊಡನೆ ಜ್ವರದಿಂದ ಬಳಲಿ ಸತ್ತಿದ್ದಾಳೆ ಅಂತಾನೇ ಹೇಳಿದ್ರು. ಇತ್ತ ಹೀನಾಳ ಶವದ ಮುಂದೆ ಅವತ್ತು ಐದು ಆರು ಮಹಿಳೆಯರಿಂದ ಕುರಾನ್ ಓದಲು ಶುರು ಮಾಡಿದ್ರು.ಹೀಗೆ ರಾತ್ರಿ ಕಳೆದು ಹಗಲು ಆಯಿತು ಬೆಳಗ್ಗೆ ಬೇಗನೆ ಶವ ಸಂಸ್ಕಾರ ಮಾಡಲು ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಸಂಬಂಧಿಕರಿಗೆ ಹೇಳಿದಳು. ಹೀನಾ ಶವವನ್ನು ಒಂದಿಷ್ಟು ವಯಸ್ಸಾದ ಮಹಿಳೆಯರು ಬಿಸಿ ನೀರಿನಿಂದ ಲಕ್ಸ್ ಸೋಪು ಶಾಂಪೂ ಎಲ್ಲ ಹಾಕಿ ಸ್ನಾನ ಮಾಡಿಸಿ ಅವರ ವಿಧಿ ವಿಧಾನಗಳಂತೆ ಕುರಾನ್ ಮಂತ್ರಗಳನ್ನು ಹೇಳುತ್ತಾ ಹೀನಾಳನ್ನು ಅತಿ ಸುಂದರವಾಗಿ ಅಲಂಕಾರ ಮಾಡಿ ಶವದ ಪೆಟ್ಟಿಗೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಮಲಗಿಸಿದರು. ಎಲ್ಲರು ನೋಡಿ ಎಷ್ಟು ಸುಂದರವಾಗಿದಾಳೆ ಒಳ್ಳೆ ಮದುಮಗಳಂತೆ ಕಾಣುತ್ತಿದ್ದಾಳೆ ಎನ್ನತ ಕಣ್ಣೀರ ಧಾರೆ ಆರಿಸಿದರು. ಅದುವರೆಗೂ ಸವಿತ ಮಗಳು ರಾಣಿ ಅವಳ ಶವವನ್ನು ನೋಡಲೇ ಇರ್ಲಿಲ್ಲ.ಈಗ ಅಲಂಕಾರ ಮಾಡಿದ ಹೀನಾಳ ಹೆಣವನ್ನು ನೋಡಿ ಸವಿತ ನಿನ್ನೆ ನನ್ನ ಎಷ್ಟು ಚೆಂದ ಮಾತನಾಡಿದಿ ಹೀನಾ ಈಗ ನಿನ್ನನು ಈ ಸ್ಥಿತಿಯಲ್ಲಿ ನೋಡಲು ನನಗೆ ಸಾಧ್ಯವಾಗುತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ ಹೀನಾ ಬಾನು ಅಕ್ಕ ನೋಡಿ ಹೀನಾ ಹೆಂಗೆ ಸುಮ್ಮನೆ ಮಲಗಿದ್ದಾಳೆ ನನ್ನನು ಅಂಟಿ ಅಂಟಿ ಅಂತ ಯಾವಾಗಲೂ ಕರೆಯುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು ಎಂದು ಹೀನಾ ಏನಾಯ್ತು ಪುಟ್ಟ ನಿಂಗೆ ಈ ಮಾಡಿದ್ದು ಸರಿಯೇ ಪುಟ್ಟಿ ಎಂದು ಬಿಕ್ಕಿ ಬಿಕ್ಕಿ ಅಳುತ್ತಿದ್ದರು. ಸುಮಾರು ಬೆಳಿಗ್ಗೆ ಹನ್ನೊಂದು ಗಂಟೆಗೆ ಹೀನಾಳ ಶವದ ಕೊನೆಯ ಮೆರವಣಿಗೆ ಮನೆಯಿಂದ ಹೊರಟಿತ್ತು. ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬ್ರಿಗೆ ದಿಕ್ಕೆ ತೋಚದೆ ಕಂಗಾಲಾಗಿದ್ದರು ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಎದೆ ಹೊಡೆದುಕೊಂಡು ಅಳುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು ಎಲ್ಲ ಅಕ್ಕಂದಿರು ಅಣ್ಣಂದಿರು ಬಂದಿದ್ದರು.ಇಡೀ ಕುಟುಂಬದವರ ಆಕ್ರಂದನ ಮುಗಿಲು ಮುಟ್ಟಿತ್ತು. ವಠಾರದ ಎಲ್ಲರು ಕಣ್ಣೀರು ಹಾಕಿದರು. ಹೀನಾಳ ಶವವನ್ನು ಸ್ಮಶಾನಕ್ಕೆ ಹೋಗಿ ದಫನ್ ಮಾಡಿ ಬಂದ ಮೇಲೆ ಇಡೀ ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬರ ವಠಾರವೇ ಸ್ತಬ್ಧವಾಯಿತು. ಹೀನಾಳ ನಲವತ್ತು ದಿನದ ಎಲ್ಲ ಕ್ರೀಯಾ ಕ್ರಮಗಳು ಮುಗಿದವು. ಎಲ್ಲ ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬರ ಮಕ್ಕಳು ಎಲ್ಲ ಕೆಲಸ ನಿಮಿತ್ತ ತಮ್ಮ ತಮ್ಮ ಊರುಗಳಿಗೆ ತೆರಳಿದರು. ಈಗ ಮನೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬರ ಹೆಂಡತಿ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಹಾಗೂ ಸಲೀಂ ಮೂವರೇ ಉಳಿದಿದ್ದು ಮುಂಚನ ಹಾಗೆ ವಟವಟ ಅನ್ನುತ್ತಿದ್ದ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಸುಮ್ಮನೆ ಇದ್ದರು ಯಾರು ಜೋತೆನೂ ಬೇರತು ಮಾತನಾಡಿ ದಿನಗಳೇ ಕಳೆದಿದ್ದವು.  ಹೀಗೆ ಇರುವಾಗ ಒಂದಿಷ್ಟು ದಿನಗಳಲ್ಲಿ ವಠರಾದ ಮಂದಿಗೆ ಹೀನಾ ಓಡಾಡಿದಂತೆ ಮಾತನಾಡಿದಂತೆ ನಿಂತಂತೆ ಭಾಸವಾಗುತ್ತಿತ್ತು.ಬೇಗನೆ ಕೆಲಸದಿಂದ ಮನೆಯೊಳಗೆ ಹೋಗುವರು ಆದರೆ ಸಂಜೆಯಾದರೆ ಸಾಕು ಮನೆಯಿಂದ ಹೊರಗೆ ಬರಲು ಭಯಪಡುವಂತಹ ಸ್ಥಿತಿ ತಲುಪಿದ್ದರು. ಮತ್ತೆ ಕೆಲವರು ಹೀನಾಳನ್ನು ಅವರ ತಾಯಿ ತಮ್ಮ ಸೇರಿ ಕೊಂದಿದ್ದಾರೆ ಅವಳ ಮೈಮೇಲೆ ಗಾಯದ ಕಲೆ ಇದ್ದವು ಏನೇನೋ ಸುದ್ದಿಯನ್ನು ಹರಡಿದರು.  ಇಷ್ಟೆಲ್ಲಾ ಆದರೂ ಸವಿತ ಮಗಳು ರಾಣಿಯ ಕಣ್ಣಿಗೆ ಒಂದು ದಿನ ಕೂಡ ಕನಸಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಆಗಲಿ ಅಥವಾ ಭೂತದ ರೂಪದಲ್ಲಿ ಆಗಲಿ ಕಾಣಿಸಲಿಲ್ಲ.ಸವಿತ ರಾಣಿ ಬೆಳಿಗ್ಗೆ ಮುಂಜಾನೆ ನಾಲ್ಕುಕ್ಕೆ ಎದ್ದು ಅಕ್ಕ ಪಕ್ಕದ ಓಣಿಯಿಂದ ಕತ್ತಲೆಯಲ್ಲಿ ನೀರನ್ನು ತರುತ್ತಿದ್ದರು. ಮತ್ತೆ ಅವರಿಗೆ ಯಾವುದೇ ಭಯ ಏನು ಆಗುತ್ತಿರಲಿಲ್ಲ. ಸವಿತ ತನ್ನ ಪಾಡಿಗೆ ತಾನು ಸುಮ್ಮನೆ ಇರುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು.ಹೀನಾಳ ನೆನಪು ಮರುಕಳಿಸಿದಾಗ ಮೌನವಾಗಿ ಕುಳಿತು ಬಿಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು. ಇದುವರೆಗೆ ಒಂದು ದಿನವೂ ಕನಸಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಬರದ ಹೀನಾ ಈಗ ಸತ್ತು ಎರಡು ತಿಂಗಳ ಕಾಲ ಕಳೆದಿತ್ತು ಆಗ ಇದ್ದಕ್ಕಿದ್ದಂತೆ ಒಂದು ರಾತ್ರಿ ಸುಮಾರು ಎರಡು ಗಂಟೆಯಾಗಿತ್ತು. ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಕನಸಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಹೀನಾ ಬಂದು "ಅಮ್ಮಿ ಓ ಅಂಟಿ ಕೂ ಮೈ ಸಾಥಸೂಪಚಸ್ ರೂಪಾಯ್ ದೇನಾ" ( ಅಮ್ಮ ಆ ಅಂಟಿಗೆ ನಾನು ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ಕೂಡಬೇಕು) ಎನ್ನುವ ಧ್ವನಿಗೆ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಹೆದರಿ ಬಿಟ್ಟಳು. ಯಾರಿಗೆ ಕೊಡಬೇಕು ಅಂತ ತಿಳಿಯದೇ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಸುಮ್ಮನೆ ಆದಳು. ಆದರೆ ಹೀಗೆ ಸುಮ್ಮನೆ ಇರದೆ ಹೀನಾ ಸರಿಸುಮಾರು ಒಂದು ತಿಂಗಳುಗಳ ಕಾಲ ಕನಸ್ಸಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಬರತೊಡಗಿದಳು. ಹೀನಾ ಏನು ಕೇಳುತ್ತಿರಲಿಲ್ಲ. ಬರೇ "ಓ ಅಂಟಿ ಕೂ ಮೈ ಸಾಥಸೂಪಚಸ್ ರೂಪಾಯ್ ದೇನಾ" ಕಣ್ಣಾಮುಚ್ಚಾದರೆ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನುಗೆ ಬರೀ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ಕೂಡಬೇಕು ನಾನು ಎನ್ನುವ ಕನಸು ಮತ್ತೆ ಮತ್ತೆ ಬೀಳ ತೊಡಗಿತು. ಏನು ಮಾಡಬೇಕು ಯಾರಿಗೆ ಹೇಳಬೇಕು ಅಂತ ತಿಳಿಯದೇ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಎಲ್ಲ ವಠಾರದ ಮಂದಿಗೆ ಕೇಳಿದಳು ಎಲ್ಲರು ನಮ್ಮ ಜೋತೆಗೆ ಮಾತನಾಡುವುದೇ ಕಷ್ಟ ಇನ್ನು ಹಣ ಎಲ್ಲಿಂದ ಕೇಳುವಳು ಎಂಬ ಉತ್ತರ ಹೇಳುತ್ತಿದ್ದರು. ಹೀಗೆ ಒಂದು ವಾರ ಕಳೆಯಿತು. ಹೀನಾ ಈಗಂತೂ ನೇರವಾಗಿ ಬಂದಂತೆ ಕಾಣಿಸಿ ಆ ಅಂಟಿಗೆ "ಅಮ್ಮಿ ಓ ಅಂಟಿ ಕೂ ಮೈ ಸಾಥಸೂಪಚಸ್ ರೂಪಾಯ್ ದೇನಾ ಅಬ್ ತು ದೇ " (ಅಮ್ಮ ನಾನು ಆ ಅಂಟಿಗೆ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ಕೂಡಬೇಕು ಈಗ ನೀನು ಕೊಡು) ಎನ್ನುವಂತೆ ಅಪ್ಪಣೆ ಮಾಡಿ  "ತು ನಹೀ ದಿಯೇ ತೂ ಮೈ ತುಜಿ ಚೂಡುಂಗಿ ನಹೀ " (ಕೊಡಲಿಲ್ಲ ಅಂದ್ರೆ ನಾನು ನಿನ್ನನು ಸುಮ್ಮನೆ ಬಿಡಲ್ಲ) ಎಂದು ಪೀಡಿಸುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು.  ಕಡೆಗೆ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಮತ್ತೂಮ್ಮೆ ವಠರಾದ ಜನರಿಗೆ ದಯಾ ಮಾಡಿ ಹೇಳಿ ಯಾರು ನನ್ನ ಮಗಳು ಹೀನಾಗೆ ದುಡ್ಡು ಕೊಟ್ಟಿದ್ದೀರಿ ತಿಳಿಸಿ ಇಲ್ಲಾಂದ್ರೆ ಅವಳು ನನ್ನನ್ನು ಸುಮ್ಮನೆ ಬಿಡಲ್ಲ ಎಂದು ಬೇಡಿಕೊಂಡಳು. ಆಗ ಅದರಲ್ಲಿ ಒಬ್ಬರು "ಬಾನು ಅಕ್ಕ ಹೀನಾ ನಮ್ಮ ಜೋತೆನೇ ಮಾತನಾಡುತ್ತಿರಲಿಲ್ಲ. ಇನ್ನು ಹಣ ಎಲ್ಲಿಂದ ಕೇಳುವಳು ಹೇಳಿ ಅವಳು ಯಾವಾಗಲೂ ಆ ಸವಿತ ಅವರ ಮನೆಗೆ ಹೋಗುತ್ತಿದ್ದಳು ತಾನೇ ಬಹುಶಃ ಅವರೇ ಕೊಟ್ಟಿರಬೇಕು ನೋಡಿ" ಎಂದಾಗ  ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನುಗೆ" ಯಾ ಅಲ್ಲ ನಾನೇ ಮರೆತು ಬಿಟ್ಟೆ ಸವಿತ ಅವರನ್ನು ಹೀನಾ ಸಾಯುವ ಒಂದು ಆರು ದಿನಗಳ ಹಿಂದೆ ಹೀನಾ ಹಣ ಕೇಳಿದ್ದಳು ನಾನೇ ಆ ಸವಿತ ಹತ್ತರ ಇಸ್ಕೂ ಅಂತ ಈಗ ನೆನಪು ಆಯಿತು"ಎನ್ನುತ್ತಾ ತಡಮಾಡದೆ ಸವಿತಳ ಮನೆಗೆ ಹೋಗಿ"ರೀ ಸವಿತ ಹೀನಾ ನಿಮ್ಮ ಹತ್ತರ ಹಣವನ್ನು ಇಸ್ಕೊಂಡಳು ಅದನ್ನು ಯಾಕೆ ಹೇಳಲಿಲ್ಲ ನೀವು"ಎನ್ನಲು   ಸವಿತ "ಇಲ್ಲ ನನ್ನ ಹತ್ತಿರ ಹಣ ತೆಗೆದುಕೊಂಡಿಲ್ಲ "ಅಂದಳು. ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು "ನೋಡಿ ಸವಿತಮ್ಮ ನೀವು ಸುಳ್ಳು ಹೇಳಬೇಡಿ ನಮ್ಮ ಹೀನಾ ನಿಮ್ಮ ಹತ್ತರ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ಇಸ್ಕೂಂಡಿದ್ದಾಳೆ ತಾನೇ ನೀವು ಸುಳ್ಳು ಹೇಳಿದರೆ ನನ್ನ ಮೇಲೆ ಅಣೆ ನೋಡಿ "ಎಂದಾಗ  ಸವಿತ"ನಿಮಗ್ಯಾರು ಹೇಳಿದ್ದು ಅಂದ್ರೆ ಅಷ್ಟೂಂದು ಇಲ್ಲ ಬಿಡಿ ಏನು ಒಂದು ಇನ್ನೂರು ಇರಬಹುದು ಅಷ್ಟೇ " ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು"ಇಲ್ಲ ಇಲ್ಲ ನಿಮಗೆ ಗೋತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ ನೋಡಿ ನಂಗೆ ಒಂದು ತಿಂಗಳಿಂದ ನನ್ನ ಕನಸಿನಲ್ಲಿ ಹೀನಾ ಬಂದು ಕಾಡುತ್ತಿದ್ದಾಳೆ ಓ ಅಂಟಿ ಕೂ ಮೈ ಸಾಥಸೂಪಚಸ್ ರೂಪಾಯ್ ದೇನಾ ಅಂತ  ನಾನು ಈಗ ನಿಮಗೆ ಹಣ ಕೊಡಲಿಲ್ಲ ಅಂದ್ರೆ ಅವಳು ನನ್ನನ್ನು ಸಾಯಿಸಿ ಬಿಡುತ್ತಾಳೆ ಸವಿತ ಈಗ ಹೇಳಿ ನಿಜ ನನ್ನ ಆಣೆ"ಎಂದಳು  ಆಗ ಸವಿತ ನಿಟ್ಟುಸಿರು ಬಿಟ್ಟು "ನಿಜ ಬಾನು ಅಕ್ಕ ಅವತ್ತು ಹೀನಾ ಬಂದು ನನ್ನ ಹತ್ತಿರ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ಹಣ ಕೂಡಿ ಅಂತ ಕೇಳಿದಳು ನಾನು ಅವಳಿಗೆ ಒಂದು ಸಾವಿರ ರೂಪಾಯಿ ಕೊಡಲು ಹೋದೆ ಅವಳು ತೆಗೆದುಕೊಳ್ಳುಲಿಲ್ಲ ಅವಳು ತನಗೆ ಬೇಕಾದ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ಮಾತ್ರ ತೆಗೆದುಕೊಂಡು ಹೋದಳು. ಆಮೇಲೆ ಅವಳೇ ಈ ಲೋಕ ಬಿಟ್ಟು ಹೋದ ಮೇಲೆ ನನಗೆ ಹಣ ಏಕೆ ಬೇಕು ಹೇಳಿ ಅಕ್ಕ ಅದಕ್ಕೆ ನಾನು ಸುಮ್ಮನೆ ಆದೆ ನನಗೆ ಹಣ ಬೇಡ ಅಕ್ಕ ಎನ್ನುತ್ತಾ ಸವಿತ ಕಣ್ಣಿರು ಹಾಕಿದರು.  ಆಗ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು "ಇಲ್ಲ ನಿಮಗೆ ಗೋತ್ತಿಲ್ಲ ನನಗೆ ಈ ನಿಮ್ಮ ಹಣ ಕೊಡುವವರೆಗೂ ನಂಗೆ ಸಮಾಧಾನವಿಲ್ಲ ನನ್ನನ್ನು ನೆಮ್ಮದಿಯಿಂದ ಬದುಕಲು ಬಿಡುವುದಿಲ್ಲ ಹೀನಾ ನಿಮ್ಮ ಕಾಲಿಗೆ ಬಿದ್ದು ಬಿಡುವೆ ಈ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ನೀವು ತೆಗೆದುಕೊಳ್ಳಿ"ಎಂದು ಆ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ಹಣವನ್ನು ಸವಿತಗೆ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ಕೊಟ್ಟು"ನಂಗೆ ಈಗ ನೆಮ್ಮದಿಯಾಯ್ತು ನೋಡಿ"ಎನ್ನುತ್ತಾ ನಾನು ಬರುವೆ ಎಂದು ಹೊರಟು ಹೋದರು. ಇತ್ತ ಅವರು ಕೊಟ್ಟ ಆ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿಯನ್ನು ನೋಡುತ್ತಾ ಹೀನಾಳ ಮಾತು ನೆನಪಾಗಿ "ಅಂಟಿ ನಾನು ಈ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ಕೊಟ್ಟೆ ಕೊಡುವೆನು" ಎನ್ನುವ ಧ್ವನಿಯು ಮರುಕಳಿಸಿ ಸವಿತಳ ಕಣ್ಣಿರು ಹಾಗೆ ಧಾರೆಯಾಗಿ ಹರಿಯುತ್ತಿತ್ತು. ಅಂದು ರಾತ್ರಿ ಕೌಸರ್ ಬಾನು ನೆಮ್ಮದಿಯಾಗಿ ನಿದ್ದೆ ಮಾಡಿದ್ದಳು. ತುಂಬಾ ಸ್ವಾಭಿಮಾನಿಯಾಗಿದ್ದ ಹೀನಾ ಸತ್ತ ಮೇಲೆ ಅವಳು ಆತ್ಮವಾಗಿ ತನ್ನ ಏಳುನೂರು ಐವತ್ತು ರೂಪಾಯಿ ಸಾಲವನ್ನು ಕೊನೆಗೂ ತೀರಿಸಿಕೊಂಡಿದ್ದು ಆ ಇಬ್ರಾಹಿಂ ಸಾಹೇಬರ ವಠರಾದ ಮಂದಿಗೆಲ್ಲ ಒಂದು ಆಶ್ಚರ್ಯ ಎಂಬಂತೆ ಮೂಡಿತ್ತು.  *ಧನ್ಯವಾದಗಳು* I wonder what the pages I left hanging feel—
all the things I promised I would write on them,
gone, poof. 


Do they still have faith in me?
Will they ever be able to trust a human's touch? 
if someone else finds the body! 

I feel sorry for those pages.
But I do have a reason.
I may not be the best person that there is, 
but I do wish for every page to be finished—
pages full of words, proud and complete.

But if I were to deliberately finish one
just for the sake of finishing for forsaking it—  
wouldn’t that be unfair to the page?

Therefore, I made a painful decision:
to leave it unfinished.
Unfinished it may be, so,
but at least it will still carry 
the essence of something meaningfully tragic. 

I know the page can't forgive me 
for what I took away from it.
But I hope I would've done better.  

-Asher Graves

The morning sun over the Deomali hills is not like the sun anywhere else in the world; it does not simply rise, it spills over the rim of the jagged peaks like molten honey, turning the mist in the valleys into a vast, moving sea of silver. I was fifteen that year, a boy with dusty sandals and a heart that was always a little too restless for the confines of a classroom or the neat, organized rows of my father’s garden. My father, a quiet man who worked for the forest department, had been posted to a remote station near the base of these hills in southern Odisha. It was a land of red earth, shifting shadows, and the kind of silence that makes you hear your own thoughts with startling clarity. While my father spent his days counting saplings, marking timber, and arguing with local contractors, I spent mine wandering the narrow goat tracks, deserted landscapes and paths that wound upward toward the highest point in the state. I didn't have many friends my own age in the village, but I didn't mind the solitude; the hills were companions enough, with their ever-changing moods and the secret languages of the wind whistling through the crags. One afternoon, when the air was heavy with the scent of wild sage and the distant, rhythmic thud of a woodcutter’s axe echoed across the gorge, I found myself higher than I had ever climbed before. The wind up there had a sharp, cold edge to it, smelling of impending rain and the ancient scent of distant pines. I sat down on a flat granite boulder to catch my breath, watching a hawk circle lazily in the blue void below me. It was then that I noticed a small, narrow path hidden behind a screen of tall, swaying elephant grass. Being a boy driven by that peculiar mountain curiosity, I followed it. The path led to a small, hidden dip in the hillside, sheltered from the biting wind, where a tiny patch of yellow mustard flowers grew in stubborn defiance of the rocky, unforgiving soil. Standing in the middle of this patch was a girl. She was wearing a traditional hand-loomed sari of a dull, earthy red, and her dark hair was tied back with a simple piece of dried vine. She wasn't doing much of anything—just standing there with her hands at her sides, looking out at the range of hills that stretched away toward the horizon like the humps of a great, sleeping dragon. I must have made some noise, for she turned her head and looked at me. Her eyes were large and dark, reflecting the vastness of the landscape, and she didn't look frightened or surprised to see a stranger in her secret garden. She looked as though she had been expecting me, or perhaps as though she expected no one and was therefore prepared for anyone the mountain might bring. I asked her if she lived nearby, and she pointed a slim, sun-darkened finger toward a cluster of low stone huts, nestled where the spring emerged from the rock. Her name was Bini, and she told me she came to this spot every day to watch the clouds and see which birds were migrating toward the plains. As we sat together on the grass, she began to talk about the hills in a way I had never heard before. She showed me how the grass leaned in a certain direction hours before a storm broke, and how the rocks changed their color from gray to a deep charcoal just before the sun dipped behind the western ridge. She told me that the mountains were old, far older than the stories the village elders told around their fires, and that if you sat very still and held your breath, you could hear the earth shifting beneath you. We became friends in that quiet, effortless way that children do in the mountains, where words are often less important than the shared observation of the world. I would bring her little things from the town at the base of the hill—a shiny glass marble that caught the light, a packet of sweet lemon drops that made her squint, or a comic book with bright, garish pictures that she would study with intense, silent gravity even though she couldn't read the text. In return, she taught me the names of the birds that nested in the high crags and showed me where the wild strawberries grew, tiny and tart and bursting with the concentrated flavor of the mountain soil. One evening, as the sky turned a deep, bruised purple and the first stars began to pierce through the twilight, Bini told me that her family would soon be moving down to the plains. Her father had found work in a brick kiln near the coast, and they had to leave before the heavy winter mists settled in and made the high paths impassable. There was a profound, quiet sadness in her voice, not because she was afraid of the new place, but because she couldn't imagine a life where she couldn't see the peaks of Deomali every morning when she woke up. On our last day together, the hills were draped in a soft, thick veil of white fog. We couldn't see the valley at all; it was as if the rest of the world had vanished, leaving us floating on a tiny island in the sky. Bini reached into the folds of her red sari and handed me a small, smooth stone. It was a piece of white quartz, worn perfectly round by the action of some ancient, long-vanished stream, and it felt strangely warm in my palm. She told me that as long as I held the stone, I would always have a piece of the mountain with me, and so would she, wherever she went. I watched her walk away down the narrow path until the mist swallowed her red sari, and the only sound left was the mournful sighing of the wind through the elephant grass. A week later, my father was transferred again, this time to a bustling town in the north, and the Deomali hills became a memory tucked away in the back of my mind. The years skipped by like stones thrown across a pond. I grew up, moved to the capital, and studied with a fierce intensity that left little room for mountain dreams. I eventually found myself in the polished, high-ceilinged corridors of power in Bhubaneswar. In the wake of the 2024 elections, I was appointed as a political advisor to the new government. I became a man of schedules and strategies. Yet, on the corner of my mahogany desk, tucked amidst the weight of legislative papers, sat that same small, smooth piece of white quartz. It looked entirely out of place in the sterile city office, but it was the only thing that kept me grounded when the politics grew too loud. Just recently, due to a sudden reshuffling of the cabinet, I was transferred to a field office back in the southern districts to oversee tribal welfare. The transition was abrupt, leaving me with a suitcase full of reports and a strange sense of returning to a previous life. Driving back toward the Koraput heights in a government jeep, the air began to change, gaining the crisp, sharp bite of the highlands. The mustard flowers were long gone, replaced by wild ferns, and the stone huts on the slope were ruins. I sat on the same granite boulder and took the white quartz stone out of my pocket. The silence was just as I remembered it—deep, ancient, and full of the mountain's breath. I realized then that my work in the city was small compared to the enduring spirit of this place. Bini was right; the mountains don't forget. I didn't find her, but as I looked out at the golden light spilling over the ridges, I felt a sudden sense of peace. I left the stone there, on the flat rock, returning it to the earth. I drove away as the stars began to blink, knowing that the hills of Deomali would always keep our secrets, wrapped in the clouds and the quiet music of the wind. I was no longer just an advisor; I was a son of the hills coming home. I knew then that to serve these people, I first had to remember the girl from the clouds and the simple truth she taught me: that we do not own the land, we only belong to it for a little while. This realization gave my work a new purpose. As the jeep descended, I looked back at the darkening silhouette of Deomali and felt exactly where I was meant to be. The ghosts of the past were not there to haunt me, but to guide me through the mists.

One day, my son,
troubled by a small disappointment
that had grown large in his heart,
looked at me and said,
“Life is unfair.”
I did not tell him
that his hurt was trivial—
for no pain is small
to the heart that bears it.
I only held his sorrow gently
and said,
“My child,
life may not always be fair.
But it can still be faced
with courage, grace,
and an unbroken heart.

Think life is unfair?
Remember Rama—
Born to inherit a throne,
yet exiled to the wilderness
on the eve of his coronation.
He left behind Ayodhya’s splendour,
the love of his people,
and the crown that was already his—
not in defeat,
but in obedience to a promise
made before his time.
Through forests and hardship,
he walked as a prince without a kingdom,
with Sita beside him
and Lakshmana guarding his path.
Then fate struck deeper:
Sita was stolen away,
and Rama searched through grief,
across mountains, forests, and seas,
while his heart carried
the ache of separation.
He fought a war
not for conquest,
but to restore honour,
love, and righteousness.
He returned victorious,
yet even victory
did not spare him sorrow.
For a king belongs not only
to his own heart,
but to the burdens
of an entire kingdom.
For the sake of a kingdom’s faith,
he let Sita go—
while she carried within her
the future of his lineage.
In the quiet sanctuary of the forest,
she gave birth to Lava and Kusha;
and Rama, though king of Ayodhya,
did not witness their first steps,
their childhood laughter,
or the unfolding of their years.
He ruled an empire
while a father’s emptiness
ruled within him.
When his sons finally stood before him,
they came not as children
who knew their father’s embrace,
but as young voices
singing the story
of the man they did not know.
So when life takes away
what you believed was yours—
a home, a dream, a loved one,
or a long-awaited reward—
remember Rama.
Dharma is not always easy.
Sometimes it asks us
to walk barefoot through loss
and still keep our integrity
unbroken.
Think life has been merciless?
Meet Krishna—
the sovereign of serenity,
whose smile concealed
a lifetime of separation.
Born to Devaki and Vasudeva
within the iron womb of a prison,
he was torn from his parents
before he could know
the warmth of their embrace.
He was carried through a storm-swept night
into the tender refuge
of Yashoda’s lap
and Nanda’s loving home.
Yet even Gokul was not forever.
Fate called him away
from the flute-filled lanes of Vrindavan—
from the Gopikas whose devotion
made love a form of prayer,
from the laughter of cowherd companions,
and from Yashoda,
whose eyes forever searched
for the child she had raised as her own.
He was derided by Shishupala,
hounded by the implacable Jarasandha,
and forced to abandon Mathura
to preserve its people.
Still, from exile and threat
he raised Dwarka—
a resplendent citadel by the sea,
a city of jeweled palaces,
wide avenues, lofty gateways,
and golden spires
mirrored in the sapphire waters.
Dwarka was not merely a kingdom;
it was a vision made stone—
prosperous, radiant, unconquered,
where wealth flourished
beneath the shelter of wisdom
and justice wore a crown.
Yet the architect of that splendour
became, at Kurukshetra,
a charioteer.
The Lord who could command creation
held the reins of Arjuna’s horses,
guided the chariot through dust and blood,
tended to the weary steeds,
and accepted the humble duties of service
without surrendering his majesty.
He spoke the Gita—
an ocean of eternal wisdom—
while standing amid the thunder
of conches, weapons, and grief.
And still, he could not prevent
the ruin of all he loved.
He witnessed the Yadavas,
his own radiant clan,
fall to fratricidal madness;
he watched magnificent Dwarka—
its towers, courts, gardens,
and gilded splendour—
yield at last
to the engulfing sea.
Then, in the hush of a forest,
the guide of kings,
the beloved of Vrindavan,
the sovereign of Dwarka,
was struck by an arrow
loosed by a hunter.
Even the gods were not spared
when they chose
to walk among us.
Through their avatars,
they did not promise
a life untouched by pain.
They taught us instead
to endure without bitterness,
to rise without arrogance,
to surrender without defeat,
and to accept
without becoming numb.
So, my child,
when life does not give you
what you hoped was yours,
do not let disappointment
teach your heart to harden.
For perhaps grace is not
the absence of suffering,
but the strength to remain gentle,unshaken 
, unperturbed even when life turns 
tumultuous

The Boy Who Stayed

Prologue — The Result

The day Saanvi Sharma's NEET result came out, it rained.

She would remember the rain more clearly than the marks.

She had not qualified for the medical college she had dreamed of. She hadn't failed completely either. She had simply been close—close enough for everyone to tell her she could try again.

Her mother said, "We can try again."

Her father said, "You should have worked harder."

Saanvi nodded, but something inside her quietly broke.

She didn't want another year of coaching, mock tests and expectations. She didn't want to spend another year watching her friends begin college while she remained behind.

Three months later, she left home for college.

She packed clothes, books and everything else a person carries when they aren't ready to admit that their old life is over: photographs of her school friends, friendship bracelets, poems, her annual-function badge—and her old school uniform.

It belonged to the girl who had once believed she knew exactly who she would become.

Part One — The Girl Who Was Supposed to Be a Doctor

College began on a Monday.

By Friday, Saanvi had already decided she hated it.

Her roommate, Meera, found her complaints entertaining. Saanvi missed home, but more than home, she missed school. She missed her three best friends—Rhea, Sana and Nandini—and the familiarity of knowing exactly where she belonged.

Every night she called her mother.

Every week her father called and asked about grades, attendance and NEET.

"Don't waste your potential," he always said.

Saanvi hated that word.

Potential meant she was never quite enough as she was.

Her relationship with her father had always been complicated. He wasn't cruel. He simply never knew how to be present. He missed school functions, forgot important days and responded to disappointment with instructions rather than comfort.

So Saanvi had grown up searching for reassurance elsewhere.

Unfortunately, she had developed a terrible taste in boys.

She liked emotionally unavailable people. Boys who disappeared and returned. Boys who made her jealous. Boys who gave affection in small, unpredictable doses.

Her best friend Rhea once told her, "You don't want love. You want proof."

Saanvi had been offended.

Years later, she understood.

She wanted someone to choose her because, somewhere inside, she was afraid she wasn't worth choosing.

So, on her first night in college, she wrote in her notes app:

NO MORE LOVE.

She had no idea how quickly that promise would become complicated.

Part Two — The Boy Who Didn't Look Like Trouble

Saanvi first noticed Aarav Malhotra in the library.

She had taken a seat he usually used.

"You're sitting in my seat," he said.

"There isn't a reserved sign."

"I know."

"Then?"

He smiled awkwardly. "I just thought I'd ask."

She stared at him.

"You're strange."

"Probably."

He picked up his books and left.

What irritated her most was that he didn't look back.

The next day she deliberately sat somewhere else.

Aarav arrived, saw her and smiled.

"Happy?" she asked.

"A little."

She laughed.

That was how it began.

Aarav was nineteen, academically brilliant but unpretentious. He liked books, old songs, coffee and quiet places. He had never had a girlfriend because he didn't understand casual relationships.

If he ever loved someone, he wanted it to mean something.

Saanvi, meanwhile, was impossible to understand.

She was loud with people she trusted and quiet with everyone else. She complained about college constantly, talked about school like it was a country she'd been exiled from, danced whenever music played and wrote little thoughts in the margins of her notebooks.

Aarav noticed everything.

He simply didn't tell her.

Part Three — The Girl Who Danced

The college fest arrived in November.

Saanvi joined the dance team despite not having danced properly since school.

During rehearsal, Aarav saw her.

She was different when she danced.

The sadness disappeared. The insecurity disappeared. For those few minutes, she wasn't a NEET dropper or a disappointing daughter.

She was simply Saanvi.

That was when Aarav began falling for her.

During the performance, their eyes met from opposite sides of the stage.

He smiled.

She smiled back.

Later, he found her backstage.

"You were amazing."

"Really?"

"Really."

"Why?"

"I don't give compliments I don't mean."

She looked at him for a moment.

That answer stayed with her.

A few days later came the ramp walk.

Saanvi hadn't wanted to participate, but her friends forced her.

When she walked onto the stage in a deep blue outfit, Aarav looked up.

For three seconds, neither moved.

There was no dramatic confession.

Just recognition.

He wasn't looking at her marks or her failures.

He was simply looking at her.

Afterward, she found a bottle of water backstage with her name on it.

"You brought this?"

"You're always thirsty after events."

"You remembered?"

"You mentioned it."

Aarav shrugged.

"I pay attention."

Saanvi didn't know what to do with someone who noticed things without being asked.

Part Four — The Slowest Fall

Saanvi didn't fall in love with Aarav suddenly.

It happened in pieces.

The library became their place.

She would arrive late, and he would silently move his bag from the chair beside him.

She constantly lost pens.

One morning, when hers stopped working, a blue pen appeared beside her notebook.

"I have another," Aarav said.

She didn't know he had bought extra blue pens because he had noticed she preferred them.

He never made a performance out of caring.

He simply cared.

One afternoon, Saanvi walked into the cafeteria and immediately looked around.

"Where's Aarav?"

Meera smiled.

"Why are you looking for him?"

"I'm not."

"You literally just asked where he is."

Saanvi spotted him near the vending machine.

Something inside her relaxed.

She hated that feeling.

Aarav was becoming important.

And important people could leave.

That frightened her.

She had spent years confusing unhealthy love with passion. Aarav was different.

If he was busy, he said so.

If he couldn't talk, he explained.

If she was upset, he listened.

If he made a mistake, he apologized.

There was nothing to decode.

For the first time, affection didn't feel like a test she had to pass.

Part Five — Two in the Morning

One night, Saanvi couldn't sleep.

She was looking through old photographs when she stopped at her Class XII farewell picture.

Her three best friends stood beside her.

Her father wasn't there.

He hadn't come.

Her phone buzzed.

Aarav: Awake?

She replied yes.

Can't sleep?

No.

Want to talk?

She hesitated.

Then answered:

Okay.

They talked until nearly three.

Saanvi told him everything.

Her school.

Her friends.

Her dreams.

Her disappointment.

Her father's absence.

The feeling that everyone had moved forward while she had been left behind.

Aarav didn't interrupt.

When she finally fell silent, he said,

"You don't have to become the person everyone expected."

Saanvi swallowed.

"What if I don't know who I am?"

"Then you can figure it out."

"And if I fail again?"

"Then you fail."

She laughed weakly.

"That's your advice?"

"No."

He paused.

"My advice is that failing at something doesn't make you a failure."

Saanvi closed her eyes.

Nobody had ever said it like that.

Part Six — The First Fight

Their friendship became something neither named.

They ate together.

Studied together.

Walked across campus together.

Sometimes they said nothing for an entire hour and still felt comfortable.

Then Saanvi's past caught up with her.

An old boy from school messaged her.

He apologized.

He said he missed her.

Saanvi knew better.

But part of her still wanted the validation.

Aarav noticed she was distracted.

"You okay?"

"Yes."

"You're lying."

She became defensive.

"You don't get to question everything I do."

"I didn't mean—"

"You don't have to act like you know me."

He went quiet.

For the first time, they walked away from each other without saying goodbye.

That night, Saanvi realized something painful.

She had been waiting for Aarav to become difficult.

She had been waiting for the hidden red flag.

She had been preparing herself to leave before he could.

Because people had always left her eventually.

The next morning, she found him outside the library.

"I'm sorry," she said.

Aarav nodded.

"I'm sorry too."

"Why?"

"I should have trusted you to tell me what you needed."

She looked at him.

"You don't have to apologize for caring."

He smiled.

"Neither do you."

And somehow, the fight made them closer.

Part Seven — When Friendship Wasn't Enough

By the end of the semester, Saanvi knew.

She knew when Aarav was tired by the way he rubbed his eyes.

She knew he drank coffee when stressed.

She knew he called his mother every Sunday.

She knew he hated crowded places but always accompanied her to events.

She knew he preferred silence to unnecessary conversation.

Most importantly, she knew she felt safest around him.

One evening, they sat on the steps outside the academic block.

"Do you ever think about the future?" Saanvi asked.

"Sometimes."

"What do you want?"

He looked at her.

"Something peaceful."

She smiled.

"That's boring."

"Maybe."

"What about love?"

He was silent for a moment.

"I think love should feel like home."

Her smile disappeared.

Because that was exactly what she had been missing.

Not excitement.

Not jealousy.

Not someone who made her chase.

Home.

She looked away.

"I think I like you."

Aarav blinked.

"You think?"

She laughed nervously.

"Fine. I like you."

"I like you too."

"Since when?"

He smiled.

"The dance."

Her cheeks turned pink.

"That's so unfair."

"Why?"

"Because I was busy dancing."

"I know."

Part Eight — The Boy Who Stayed

They didn't become a dramatic college couple.

There were no grand gestures.

Their relationship began quietly.

A hand held while walking.

Shared headphones.

Notes left inside books.

Coffee after difficult exams.

Arguments that ended in conversations instead of silence.

Aarav never tried to rescue Saanvi from her insecurities.

He simply stayed beside her while she learned to face them herself.

Saanvi slowly understood that love wasn't supposed to make her anxious.

She didn't need to earn affection.

She didn't need to decode messages.

She didn't need to compete with other girls.

She didn't need to become someone else to be chosen.

One evening, she called her mother.

"I'm not preparing for NEET."

There was a pause.

"I know."

"I think I'm going to be okay."

Her mother's voice softened.

"I know."

For the first time, Saanvi believed it.

Later that night, she found the old school uniform at the bottom of her suitcase.

She unfolded it.

Once, it had represented the girl who thought her future had to follow one perfect path.

Now she understood something.

Sometimes life doesn't destroy your plans.

Sometimes it simply gives you a different life.

Epilogue

Years later, Saanvi would remember the rain from the day her NEET result came out.

But she would remember other things too.

The library chair.

The blue pen.

The bottle of water.

The dance.

The three seconds on the ramp.

The conversation at two in the morning.

And Aarav.

The boy who had never arrived like a storm.

He hadn't swept her away.

He hadn't promised to fix her.

He hadn't made her chase him.

He had simply been there.

Quietly.

Patiently.

Consistently.

He had stayed.

And perhaps that was the greatest love story of all—not about the person who made her heart race, but the person who finally taught her that love could make her heart feel safe.

Some people arrive like storms.

Some arrive quietly, carrying books.

And sometimes, the quiet ones are the ones who stay.

Warmth

The Warmth

I built my house with only one door. Not because I didn't want windows, or walls, or a roof that held the rain, but because a door was the only thing I could control. A door opens because I decide it opens. A door stays shut because I decide to keep it shut. Everything else in my life had been decided for me, by a mother who left before she ever really arrived, by people who said they loved me and then said other things about me when I wasn't in the room, by a world that laughed at a little girl standing alone and mistook her silence for something to mock instead of something to ask about.

There was a boy once, before any of this, who I loved the uncomplicated way you love someone at that age, completely, and without any evidence that it was a bad idea. And when it ended, the way those things end, he didn't just walk away. He told people I had betrayed him, a lie so much simpler to believe than the truth, whatever the truth even was, and the story spread through a school the way stories do at that age, gaining teeth as it went, until I was the girl who couldn't be trusted, before I even understood what trust was supposed to feel like from the other side. No one asked me what happened. They just laughed, in the hallway, in the way only children can laugh, cruel without knowing the weight of it.

So I built the wall. And I put one door in it. And I promised myself: I decide.

Before I understood anything else about love, I understood my parents' marriage, which is to say, I understood two people who shared a house and stopped, somewhere along the way, sharing anything else. My father stayed, technically. He came home every night, sat at the same table, slept in the same bed. But staying and loving are not the same verb, and I learned that difference before I learned to read. I watched my mother look at him like he was furniture. I watched him look at her like she was a door he'd already stopped knocking on. No one raised their voice. No one ever left. That was the cruelest part, I couldn't even blame a slammed door, because nothing ever slammed. It just quietly rotted, for years, in front of a child who was taking notes without knowing it.

So by the time she died, I didn't just lose a mother. I lost the only proof I might have had that love, when it's real, doesn't have to look like two people slowly going numb in the same room.

I still remember the exact shade of the classroom wall the day I found out, a chalky, institutional blue, the kind that never quite looks clean. I remember I was halfway through copying a spelling word when the door opened and it was my father, not a teacher, not the front office, my father, still in his work clothes, too early in the day to make any sense. I remember thinking, before I let myself think anything else, that fathers do not come to schools in the middle of a Tuesday unless something has already ended.

He didn't say the words in the hallway. He didn't say them in the car. He said them in the driveway, engine still running, both of us still buckled in, like some part of him thought if we didn't get out of the car yet, the day hadn't fully started. Your mother's gone. There's no more of her to go back to. I don't remember crying. I remember, very specifically, deciding, the way children decide things without knowing they've decided them, that I would never again let information that big reach me without warning.

That was the first brick. I didn't build the rest of the wall consciously. But that was the day the ground for it got laid, in a driveway, with the engine still running, my father's hands still on the wheel because he didn't know what else to do with them either.

I decided, somewhere very young and very wordlessly, that love was either a performance people kept up out of duty, or a door someone eventually stopped walking through. Either way, it wasn't safe. Either way, it ended the same, with someone still in the house, but gone.

For years, that was enough. I would close the door when I was fine, and I was fine most of the time, because being fine was easier than finding out, again, that no one was there. And on the nights I wasn't fine, the nights the walls felt more like a coffin than a house, I would let myself hope, just once, just a crack, and I would open the door. And there was never anyone standing there.

So I stopped hoping. I told myself the door was decoration. A door doesn't have to be opened to be a door. It can just be a shape in a wall that says once, there could have been a way in.

Then he came.

I found out later, much later, in pieces, the way you find out anything about a person who'd rather show you than tell you, that he had known me before the door. Not well. Not the way people mean when they say they know someone. He'd only ever seen me from a distance: in a hallway, at a table, in the kind of rooms where I made myself small on purpose. He told me once, through the wood, in a voice that didn't know I was listening as closely as I was, that he used to watch for the rare, involuntary moments I forgot to guard my own face, and that when I smiled, actually smiled, it did something to the room that no one else in it seemed to notice but him. He said my sadness had never once looked like weakness to him. He said it looked like depth, like a well he wanted to know the bottom of, not because he wanted to fix it, but because he thought it was the truest part of me. He said he saw something in my eyes, even in the worst of my silences, that looked like love with nowhere left to go. And that was the night, he told me, he decided the nowhere might as well be him.

His own reasons for staying didn't come from a broken heart, not the way mine had. No one had ever betrayed him, no one had lied to him or turned a room against him or blamed him for things he didn't do. It was smaller than that, and somehow heavier: people simply left. Easily. Without cruelty, without a single dramatic exit, friends who drifted, a father who moved on to a second family like changing a coat, people who said let's stay close and then didn't, not out of malice, just out of the ordinary carelessness of people who've never had to learn how to stay. Nothing in him ever broke. It just dimmed, year by year, the way a light left on too long loses its shine without ever going out. He didn't know how to make people stay. He only knew, with total certainty, what it looked like when they left, and he'd promised himself that if he ever found someone worth it, he would be the one who simply didn't.

So when he found me, and found a door instead of a person, he didn't see a wall to be afraid of. He saw, maybe for the first time, somewhere he could finally practice the one thing no one had ever done for him.

He made a rule for himself early on, one he never told me about until it no longer mattered: he would not leave. Not for an hour, not for dry clothes, not even on the nights the rain came down hard enough that leaving would have been the reasonable thing to do. He told me later it started almost like an experiment, he wanted to know, factually, physically, how long a person could stay if they simply decided not to be the kind who left. He'd watched everyone in his life treat staying as conditional, contingent on comfort, on convenience, on whether the weather or the mood made it easy enough. He wanted, just once, to find out what staying looked like with every one of those conditions stripped away, to see if it was even possible to do for someone what no one had ever done for him. So he didn't go home to dry off. He didn't leave to eat properly, or sleep somewhere his body could actually rest. Each refusal was its own quiet proof, to himself more than to me, that he was not going to be one more person who left easily. He was so intent on proving he could stay forever that he never noticed he was spending himself to do it, that the very thing meant to prove his love was also, slowly, the thing that would keep him from being alive long enough to receive it.

I don't know when he first sat down outside it. I only know that one evening, mid-storm, mid-nothing, I heard a voice through the wood, low, unhurried, like he had nowhere else in the world to be:

"I will not knock. I will only wait,

the way the shore waits for a tide

that has every right never to come back."

I froze. I didn't answer. I didn't have to, I could hear, even through a door, that he wasn't asking me to.

He came back the next night. And the next. Always at the door, always in whatever weather the sky decided to throw at him, never asking to come in, never asking anything at all. Just, reciting. Fragments. Half-poems, sometimes finished, sometimes trailing into the sound of rain like even he didn't need the ending.

I told myself it didn't touch me. I told myself a voice through a door is just a voice, and a poem is just words, and none of it could reach the parts of me I'd sealed off years ago. But my heart didn't get that memo. Every night his voice came through the wood, something in my chest would ache in a place I thought had gone numb for good. I never told him. I never opened the door. I would just sit on the other side of it, back against the wood, and let the ache happen in silence, because silence was the only language I still trusted.

Once, just once, that early on, I opened the door for him. Not out of courage. Out of a leak in a roof three streets over that had turned into a joke he wouldn't let go of, some absurd story about a neighbor's cat and a fully collapsed ceiling, told with the kind of comic timing that made it impossible to keep listening from behind wood without wanting to see his face while he told it. So I opened the door, just a crack, just enough to prove to myself I still could.

He didn't lunge for the opening, didn't say anything dramatic about the moment. He just grinned, soaked, ridiculous, hair plastered to his forehead, and said, "Took you long enough. I was starting to think I'd have to write a poem about a cat that never gets to the point either."

I laughed. An actual laugh, the kind that surprises the person doing it. "Your poems get to the point eventually?"

"Rarely. But it's a nice walk there."

"I opened a door for you and this is the material you brought?"

"I've been workshopping it for weeks. I had higher hopes too."

I closed the door on him, still laughing, and I remember standing with my back against it afterward, hand over my mouth like I'd been caught doing something I wasn't supposed to enjoy. It terrified me more than any storm ever had, not the joke, not him, but how easy it had been, for four whole minutes, to just be a person talking to another person instead of a wall being tested. But I think, in those minutes, he understood something about me that no one had bothered to before: that the wall wasn't cruelty. It was scar tissue. And scar tissue, given the right joke at the right moment, can still laugh.

He never tried to break down the door after that. He just kept sitting. Kept speaking. Like he'd decided that understanding didn't need a key, it just needed time.

As the weeks went on, his poems changed. In the beginning they'd been careful, almost distant, a stranger testing whether a locked door could hear at all. But somewhere in the second month, they turned warmer, bolder, like he'd stopped speaking to a wall and started speaking to a woman he was falling for on the other side of it:

"I have seen you smile exactly four times.

I did not mean to count. I could not help it,

the room forgets itself when you forget to guard your mouth,

and so, apparently, do I."

And then, one night, warmer still, a poem that didn't sound like distance at all anymore, but like a confession he'd been holding back out of respect for the wood between us:

"People tell me eyes are windows.

Yours are something older than that,

a well I have been staring into for months,

not to see myself reflected,

but because even at the bottom of your sadness

there is a light I have never seen anywhere else.

I do not love you despite what your eyes carry.

I love you because they carry it so honestly.

If I ever get to see them without a door between us,

I already know: that is the exact place

I will choose to stay."

I sat on my side of the wood that night with my hand pressed flat against it, as close to touching him as I had let myself get in years, and I did not open the door. But something in me had already started to.

He had a habit, I noticed, of resting his palm flat against the door while he spoke, I could hear it, the faint drag of skin on wood whenever he shifted, and sometimes, if I put my own hand where I guessed his was, I swore I could feel the shape of it through the grain, like the door was thin enough to carry warmth but not thin enough to carry him. It didn't make sense, logically, wood doesn't transfer heat like that, not through inches of oak, not from a man who spent half his nights soaked and shivering in weather that should have made him cold to the touch. But some nights, when my palm found the exact place his had been, I would feel something unmistakably warm bloom under my skin, and I never once let myself examine why. I only knew that his hands must have been getting used to being cold everywhere except in the one place they were trying to reach me.

There was one night I didn't hear him at all.

No poem. No rustle of wet cloth against the step. No breathing I'd learned to recognize even through solid wood. Panic did something to me that even my own grief never had, it made me move. I crossed to the door on shaking legs and pressed my eye to the keyhole, half-certain of what I'd see: nothing. Empty step. The oldest wound reopening. Instead I saw him. Curled on the ground, soaked through, exhausted past the point of holding himself upright, asleep in the rain outside a door that had never once let him in.

Something broke in me that had nothing to do with the wall.

I didn't open the door. I couldn't, even for him, even then, my hand wouldn't move on the latch. But I did something I had not done in all the nights he'd spoken to me. I spoke back. Quietly, brokenly, my voice raw from disuse:

"Don't sleep out there. Don't leave me

the way silence always does,

stay awake, if nothing else,

so I know the waiting is a person

and not a ghost I've made up

to survive the nights alone."

He stirred. He didn't understand, maybe, that I'd finally spoken, only that a voice had reached him, warm even through wood, and pulled him back from wherever exhaustion had taken him. He sat back up against the door. And after a moment, in a voice rough with sleep and cold, he answered with a poem of his own, quieter than before, like he was saving something of himself for later.

I never told him I'd been the one to speak. I don't think I needed to. I think some part of him already knew the wall had a heartbeat behind it.

There was an old gap in the wood, low near the hinge, small enough that I'd never thought of it as anything, a flaw in the carpentry, nothing more. But one evening, laughing at something he'd said, something small and unguarded, I forgot myself enough that my face did the thing it used to do before I taught it not to. I didn't know he could see through that gap until he went quiet mid-poem, quiet in a way that wasn't exhaustion. Later, much later, he told me that was the fifth time. He said he'd been counting since the hallway, years before the door, and he'd started to believe he might never see a sixth. He said that on the nights afterward, when his body wanted to stop, when the cold had gotten far enough into him that stopping would have been easier than staying, he thought of that gap in the wood and made himself last one more hour, and then one more, on the chance there might be a sixth. I don't know if there ever was. I only know that a five-second accident of my own face may have bought him more nights outside my door than any poem he ever gave me.

The storm came back the night everything ended. Worse than any before it. I lay on my side of the door and waited for his voice the way I used to wait, as a child, for a knock that never came. And it came, thinner now, and slower, like each word cost him something he didn't have much more of.

Then it stopped.

I don't know how long the stopping lasted before I understood it wasn't a pause. I only know that I was on my feet before I decided to be, that my hand was on the latch before I gave it permission, that for the first time since I built this house, the door was not a decision I made slowly. It was the only thing left.

It opened.

Rain. Cold. And him, still there, still sitting, soaked through to something past shivering, looking up at the open door like it was the one thing he'd been waiting his whole life to see and the one thing he no longer had the strength to walk through.

"Your wall is gone," he said. His voice was barely a voice at all. "I don't have anything left to give you. All my love, I already gave it to the door."

I knelt down. I took his hands, finally, without a door between them and mine, and they were nothing like the warmth I had felt through the wood all those nights, they were cold, actually cold, shaking with a chill that had clearly been sitting in his bones for hours, maybe days, and I understood, too late, that whatever warmth I'd felt through the grain had never been the wood carrying his heat to me. It had been the only heat he had left, and he had been giving all of it to a door, on purpose, night after night, so that some part of him could reach me even when the rest of him couldn't come in.

I said his name. I said stay. I said all the words I had swallowed for years, all at once, too late, spilling out of a mouth that had finally learned how to open at the exact moment his eyes were learning how to close.

The door stood open behind me. Open, at last, exactly like I had always feared it, open onto no one.

Not because he had left.

Because he had stayed until there was nothing left of him to walk through it with.

I did not keep the door open. I could not tell you, even now, why I closed it again, except that an open door with no one behind it was somehow crueler than a shut one had ever been. Some nights I still put my palm flat against the wood, in the exact place his hand used to rest, waiting to feel that warmth again. It never comes. Wood, it turns out, was never what was warm. I just didn't understand that until there was nothing left on the other side of it to keep me warm at all.
