Two worlds can share the same sky,
Yet never see the same sunrise.
One wakes beneath a roof of gold,
Another beneath uncertain skies.
One learns to dream without a fear,
With open doors and endless roads;
Another learns to hide its dreams,
Beneath the weight of heavy loads.
One hears laughter fill the halls,
Another listens to the rain.
One calls a thousand faces friends,
Another knows the quiet pain.
Yet beneath these different worlds,
We carry hearts that beat the same—
A wish to love, a wish to hope,
A wish to leave behind a name.
Perhaps the world is not one world,
But countless stories intertwined;
Different paths beneath our feet,
Yet searching for the same light.
So let us cross the walls we build,
And look beyond what first appears—
For every world that seems so strange
May hold a heart much like ours here.

Sometimes, human life feels not like a solid truth, but like a magical canvas. The colors of light and darkness are blended so perfectly on it that even the canvas itself cannot tell where the border of happiness ends and the desert of suffering begins. What a strange irony of fate! The very day a man thinks he is invincible, destiny might be plotting a cruel conspiracy behind the curtain.

The life of Arifatur Rahman was exactly such a living canvas.

Today, if you look at his paralyzed, lifeless body lying in a corner of a dark, damp room in a remote village of Hooghly, you would never believe that once he used to deliver lectures in fluent English in the corporate towers of Kolkata. He once held a high-ranking position in a reputed multinational company, commanding respect from colleagues and subordinates alike. He came from an aristocratic family, and there was no dearth of property, ancestral land, or social prestige. In those days, his father’s name carried immense weight in society; doors opened before he even knocked, and his opinions shaped community decisions. But when the wheel of fate turns, no education, no inheritance, and no pride can save a man from falling into the abyss. A severe spinal disorder, a mountain of unforeseen debt, and failing health swallowed his glittering sky within a few short years.

He is only forty-two years old, yet his physical frame resembles that of an octogenarian. Medical reports point to a complex spinal cord disorder, complicated by uncontrolled diabetes and chronic hypertension. His lower body is entirely paralyzed, confining his days and nights to a faded, worn-out bed where the springs groan under the slightest shift. Beside him stands a small wooden table holding an old notebook, a pen, and a scattering of prescription medicines. That restricted space is his entire universe. Lying immobile on the mattress, Arifat now plays a solitary, melancholic game—the quiet turning of the pages of memory.

When the disease first struck his physical frame, and when creditors began demanding their dues at his doorstep, the masks of the people around him began to fall away one by one. Relatives of four generations, who once pretended affection during prosperous times and dined at his father’s table, suddenly withdrew from his life upon witnessing his miserable condition in Hooghly. No one answered his phone calls. No one opened their doors. Some even distanced themselves out of fear that he might ask for financial assistance. When his body and mind were both splintering under the crushing weight of selfishness and social abandonment, the most devastating blow struck from within the sanctuary of his own home.

Seeking a brief respite from mounting pressures and harboring a faint, desperate hope of medical treatment that could restore his mobility, Arifat made the most painful decision of his life. He left his hearth and home behind, spending three continuous months living a half-starved existence in a distant, unfamiliar city nestled within the majestic, snow-capped hills of Uttarakhand. 

During those lonely months of exile, not a single familiar soul in the world felt the obligation to check upon his well-being. No relative inquired after his health, no friend reached out across the distance, and his wife remained entirely detached, cocooned in her own world. He wandered the unfamiliar mountain streets alone under the twilight, sought shelter on cold temple steps as daylight faded, and partook of simple meals at the community kitchens of local Gurudwaras. Every breath he drew in those northern mountains was filled with the bitter realization of absolute human isolation and abandonment. 

When he finally dragged his failing, aching body back to his broken home in Hooghly, he discovered that his fifteen-year-long decorated family life had withered into a barren desert. His wife, who had once vowed to stand beside him through every twist of fortune, had relocated to her parental home along with their children three months prior. Upon his return, the condition she laid down for resuming family life was absolute and unyielding: her ailing husband must legally transfer his final remaining asset—the last decimal of his ancestral land—directly into her name.

Staring upward at the peeling ceiling of that dark room, Arifat found himself grappling with a chilling silence. Who was the woman standing before him? Was she truly his beloved companion of fifteen decades—or rather, a stranger driven by self-preservation, arriving to claim the final possession of a dying man? 

Meanwhile, another emotional tempest brewed on the horizon. He discovered that during her stay at her parental home, his wife had spent long hours engaged in secretive late-night telephone conversations with a distant, married relative—a younger man whose association Arifat had strictly forbidden years prior. Whispers echoed through the village lanes of Hooghly regarding her prolonged phone activity extending long past midnight, tearing away whatever threads of trust remained in his heart.

The emotional wound deepened into a toxic poison the afternoon Arifat witnessed a scene that shattered his remaining shreds of trust. One gloomy afternoon, near a bustling computer center in the local marketplace of Hooghly, a scooter came to a halt. His nine-year-old innocent daughter and his wife dismounted from the vehicle. Steering the scooter was that very same forbidden young man. They were laughing together, sharing light moments as if completely unburdened by the chaos, debt, and suffering consuming Arifat's world.

When Arifat confronted his wife for an explanation in a firm, resolute voice, a look of profound astonishment crossed her face, as though she had encountered a ghost rather than an injured husband. Summoning every remaining ounce of his declining physical strength, Arifat declared, "If your heart lies elsewhere, tell me the truth, or let us part ways legally. But do not make the future of my innocent children a living hell."

Yet, the combined pressures of societal judgment, familial shame, and sudden, dramatic threats of self-harm transformed the situation into an inescapable maze. Well-wishers, lifelong friends, and even the local Panchayat head pleaded with him unanimously: under no circumstances should that piece of ancestral land be signed away to her.

However, Arifat was not merely a husband grappling with betrayal; he was first and foremost a father. Gazing upon the innocent faces of his fourteen-year-old son—who watched his father fade away day by day with silent terror—and his nine-year-old daughter, whose entire future stood in the shadows, Arifat crushed his manhood, his personal pride, and his lifelong dignity into dust. With a crushing stone weighing heavily upon his chest, he summoned the village elders and formally registered that single decimal of land in his wife's name. As his trembling hand held the pen, tears fell uncontrollably onto the paper, staining the legal document with his defeat. The moment the deed was finalized, his wife returned to the household.

For seven long months, she has remained under the same roof, currently working as a field operative for an NGO. Yet, the glass of trust within Arifat’s heart remains shattered beyond repair. Even beneath a single roof, love has been buried beneath thick layers of suspicion, coldness, and heavy, suffocating silence.

Even today, in the quiet depth of night, when the persistent warnings and harsh demands of creditors echo within the bare, damp walls of that silent Hooghly home, hot tears stream down Arifat’s hollow cheeks. People often remark with casual cruelty, "He who carries heavy debts finds his prayers and pilgrimages unaccepted." What a harsh and unjust accusation to level against a struggling soul who has lost everything except his faith!

Yet, Arifat’s pen has refused to yield to despair. Though his physical body is paralyzed, his intellect and the inner fire of his mind remain completely unvanquished. Reclining upon his bed day and night, he continues to author timeless novels, profound short stories, and evocative poetry that capture the raw essence of human suffering and resilience. Though society has marginalized him and cast him aside as a destitute figure, his blurred vision looks far beyond the earthly sky, turning instead toward the sacred golden soil of Mecca and Medina.

He carries a deep, unshakable faith that the Almighty maintains a precise account of every silent sacrifice, every moment of honesty, and every tear shed in the darkness. Should one miraculous morning bring news that his novel, The Last Tawaf of Letters, has earned recognition and a major national literary award, he intends to use those proceeds to fulfill his lifelong dream of performing the Umrah pilgrimage with his family during his final days on earth.

Before the cold hand of mortality claims him, Arifat longs to press his forehead against the blessed soil of the Kaaba, seeking divine forgiveness for human shortcomings. With whatever prize money remains, he resolves to clear every single penny of debt owed to individuals in his community, restoring dignity to his name. His ultimate, final aspiration is simple: before departing this earth, he wishes to restore the tarnished honor of his lineage, honor the memory of his noble parents, and reclaim his self-respect so he may leave this world as peacefully as an innocent child. The heartfelt, silent plea of a lonely, crippled father surely will not go unanswered in the court of the universe.

Author: Md Dabir Hossain (Drabir)  
Novel: The Last Tawaf of Letters

I never knew there was a being called a father,
It's need was never felt, and when time became mature enough for me to understand what a father is, I had become too habituated to its nothingness.

Why would you want something whose sole existence had been unknown to you.

Instead of a father, I got something called a mother,

A terrific creature 


A blend of unconditional love and eternal sacrifice.

By observing her, i realised why mortals will always prevail over god, one day I stole the lump of worries from her shoulders and put them on God's , his terrified moans still echo in the depths of Universe, then I put it on the earth and earth fell from its axis, when it got placed over the universe the big bang happened.

When she realised my folly, she took the lump from god's shoulder, minimized it into a small bindi and put it in the perfect middle of her beautiful small forehead.

I still wonder who among them was the true God.

Whatever a father does, you did much better, a red beatle leaf spit on society's face.

Through you I understand god.

Happy Father's Day, Aai.

The inevitable that one claims,
I've seen it with my unclad eyes;
I witnessed him lying there, draped in an ivory sheet,
His feet, encrusted with flower petals.

I've held back tears,
Sobs escaped from the crevice of my mouth,
Dread clung to my chest; 
Couldn't push it aside despite my desperate attempts.

I see his glimpse in the crook of my room,
Smiling, perhaps, calling me fondly;
He cooed the name that he had reserved for me, alone.
And I find myself reciprocating his grin, subconsciously.

I perceive his portraits on the wall,
Clutching the wall with all its might;
Bearing the burden of  unworldly,
As his lively eyes pierce through the frame.

His voice rings within the corridors of his domicile,
His inked down papers lie behind the closed doors;
An unease washes over me as dust collects over his honours, On his table top;
Where a cloth dangles over his framed face.

Oh I miss him dearly,
The one who solely endorsed my passion.
I bid my final goodbyes to him,
As he departs for the abode of arcady.

title.stringValue: Between the Twelfth and Thirteenth Floors

content.stringValue:
The building had nineteen floors, and in ten years no one had ever quite belonged to more than one of them. The twelfth was hers. The thirteenth was his. Between the two ran a staircase that nobody used except when the lifts broke down, and for a long while neither of them thought to wonder why a single flight of stairs should feel like such a considerable distance. Ten years is nothing, measured against nineteen floors. Measured in time, it is not nothing at all.

She had come to the company years before he had, and by the time he arrived she already possessed the building's unofficial geography — which corridor carried gossip fastest, which desks had ears turned permanently toward other people's business, which supervisors forgot a mistake sooner than they forgot a compliment. She understood, in the way one understands a language learned early, that an office is never built only of glass and carpet and fluorescent light. It is built, floor by floor, out of observation. Everyone watched. Everyone drew conclusions from what they watched, and mistook the conclusions for knowledge.

Their first conversation happened on the thirteenth floor, and it was nothing — which is, more often than people admit, how the important things begin. She had gone up to tell him something she'd overheard: that certain colleagues spoke of him rather differently once he'd left a room. She told him, she thought, because she disliked hypocrisy. It was only later she allowed herself to wonder whether she had simply wanted an excuse to be looked at by him. She never did settle which of the two was true.

Somewhere in that first exchange they discovered a shared acquaintance — a cousin of hers, a friend of his — and laughed at the coincidence the way strangers do, generously, briefly. Numbers were exchanged. A friend request went out into the ether. Then, for a long stretch afterward, nothing. The building swallowed them back into its ordinary machinery, him to the thirteenth floor, her to the twelfth, and they were, for a time, almost strangers again.

But there is a kind of friendship that begins with no ceremony at all, so quietly that by the time you notice it has formed, it has already reshaped the furniture of your life. Theirs was of that kind. The talk began about work, then drifted to the people at work, and from there to the small moral comedy of office life — how ambition liked to dress itself as concern, how insecurity so often borrowed the coat of superiority, how colleagues invented intimacies between others because they could not otherwise account for warmth. They found they could talk to each other. More rare, and more telling: they found they could fall silent together without the silence needing to be repaired. He could say a thing without rehearsing it first. She could speak without immediately building her defense. There was no tribunal waiting. No correction. No demand that either of them arrive smaller, simpler, than they actually were.

Trust, when it came, came without announcement — a message here, an evening's conversation there, a confidence kept, a call returned promptly on a day that badly needed one. Eventually, inevitably, the friendship acquired an audience. Nothing survives long in an office without becoming a story told in someone else's mouth. There were glances exchanged in corridors, jokes that concealed questions and questions dressed up as jokes; some watched the two of them with simple curiosity, others with the thinner, more particular resentment reserved for anything one cannot possess oneself. For a while they considered ending it, simply to be rid of the talk. It would have been the easier course. But ease has never been a reliable measure of what is true, and so they went on.

It was, perhaps, the first genuinely brave thing either of them did.

After that the office began to recede from their conversations, and what took its place was larger: family, childhood, the private failures nobody confesses at a desk, the peculiar loneliness of being surrounded by people from nine to six. Some nights they talked for an hour past when either should have hung up; other nights, five minutes said everything that needed saying. Duration stopped being the measure of anything. He became someone she could tell things to without first deciding whether the things were reasonable. She became someone he returned to without needing to explain an absence. Neither called it by name. Names, they both understood without discussing it, were dangerous.

By the 31st of December she had begun to suspect that whatever lay between them had crossed some line she couldn't quite locate on a map. She gave it a private name — not love, not exactly, but something that had outgrown the word friendship without yet earning any other. She never told him. She understood, with the clarity of someone who has thought about it too much, that once a feeling takes on language it takes on consequences as well and for a time she was content to let it live unspoken.

Then he grew distant. There was no single incident she could point to afterward, no betrayal to name — only a slow subtraction. A message left unanswered a day longer than usual. A conversation cut short. A warmth she'd grown used to replace by something carefully, deliberately neutral. She caught herself doing the old humiliating arithmetic: what had changed, and when, and whether she had only imagined the closeness in the first place. She knew better than to ask him outright. Knowing better has never once stopped a heart from asking anyway.

Then the 1st of April came, and he was leaving the country — somewhere far enough away that the news of his going carried a faint, unwelcome undertone of danger. She worried and said nothing about it. The evening before his flight they met downstairs, and for once he looked uncertain, not frightened exactly but more aware than usual of the act of leaving. Before he went he said something ordinary — told her to stay well, or to take care, she could never afterward recall the exact words, only the sensation that had come with them, a coldness she was careful not to let show on her face.

He was gone fifteen days. She learned that fifteen days can be simultaneously nothing and unbearably long. Messages arrived from the distant country now and then — a question about her newly released book, a brief account of his travel issues— and some thread, invisible but taut, seemed to stay stretched the whole time between them. She told herself it meant nothing. She told herself it meant everything. Both were equally useless as conclusions.

When he came back the building resumed its ordinary noise — lifts opening, phones ringing, shoes on polished floors — and it seemed, as it always somehow did, to contain one more storey above the nineteenth that nobody had ever built, one more height left to climb. 

On the 11th of May, her restraint gave out, and the words that came from her were sharper than she'd intended — anger, she thought afterward, being only grief that had forgotten its manners. She hurt him. The next day she stayed home, unwell, and in the afternoon the phone rang. It was him. They talked for nearly an hour and left most of it unsaid, and perhaps that omission was exactly what let the conversation survive. Some relationships are mended by full accounting. Others are mended simply by the decision, unspoken, to remain. Theirs was the second kind.

Later that year she travelled abroad herself, and far from the office, far from him, she was surprised by a fear she told no one about: not the fear of dying, but of disappearing — of becoming, to the people who knew her, a person spoken of only in the past tense. She wondered, absurdly, whether he would notice the particular shape of her absence. She came home. Nothing had changed. Everything had.

Their conversations turned more personal after that — the kind of personal that cannot easily be taken back. She began to understand that attachment rarely announces itself as desire. More often it arrives as habit, as concern, as simply knowing, without deliberation, exactly whom to call when something happens — as the name your mind produces before you've consciously decided to think of anyone at all.

On the first day of August she stopped protecting the feeling from language, and told him. He listened. There was tension in him but no surprise; he told her he had known for some time, and had perhaps allowed it, not cruelly and not kindly either — simply, humanly. He did not return the confession. There was no rejection to speak of, no rupture and no tidy declaration of just friends. There was only an absence where an answer might have gone.

And, strangely, they went on talking anyway. This was the part she could never afterward explain to herself. If there was nothing in him, why did he stay so close? If there was something, why would he not name it? Perhaps he didn't know. Perhaps he knew too well — there are people, she came to think, who can bear uncertainty indefinitely but cannot bear consequence, and to name a feeling is to become answerable for it. He seemed unwilling to cross into that accountability.

She eventually gave up trying to decide which explanation was correct, because something in her had already begun, slowly and without heroics, to change. She did not wake one morning cured of feeling. She simply began, by degrees, to withdraw expectation from affection — a harder distinction to hold onto than it sounds. She found she could still care without waiting. Still listen without hoping. Still laugh with him without secretly filing away every small gesture as evidence for a case she was building. She grew stronger in a way he never noticed — not the visible, admired kind of strength, but the quieter sort: the strength of leaving a door unlocked without standing guard beside it.

He might have believed that she felt exactly as she had the day she'd confessed it. That may have been his comfort. It may equally have been his mistake. She never corrected him, and there was, oddly, a kind of tenderness even in that silence.

The building kept its nineteen floors. From the twelfth, the thirteenth still looked close enough to imagine reaching. From the thirteenth, the twelfth looked just as close. And yet neither floor ever quite belonged to the other.

Years afterward she would come to think that the important part of their story was never the confession itself, but everything that followed it — the ordinary phone calls, the small unremarked kindnesses, the arguments that never once became endings, the silences that never hardened into estrangement, the sheer persistence of two people who had been given no conventional reason to remain so important to each other. She sometimes wondered whether love needed to be returned in order to be real, and came, eventually, to believe it didn't — though she also stopped believing that every deep attachment deserved the name of love. Some things exist precisely in the space language has failed to fill.

One evening, long after most of the office had gone home, she stood in the lift as the doors began to close, and at the far end of the corridor she saw him. He smiled. She too smiled. The doors met before either could say anything more, and the lift began its descent.

Thirteen. Twelve. Eleven.

She watched the numbers fall and wondered whether he had meant to come down after her, or had simply been passing by, and whether the smile had meant affection, or habit, or friendship, or nothing at all. Once, she would have gone searching the moment for its answer. Now she let it stay a question.

Ten. Nine. Eight.

Outside, the city was beginning to light itself for the evening. Nineteen floors above the pavement, two people went on living their separate lives. Perhaps he had felt for her. Perhaps he hadn't. Perhaps he had felt her in the only way he knew how, and had never understood that some feelings sometimes need to be spoken. Perhaps she had felt for him once, and was only now learning a different form of it — the kind that does not wait by the door.

The lift reached the ground floor. The doors opened. She stepped out into the lobby and behind her the building rose nineteen storeys into the dark. She did not look back.

Or perhaps she did.

The story, by then, had grown too old to need an ending. And somewhere between the twelfth floor and the thirteenth, in the space where no office was ever officially built, something unnamed went on quietly enduring — not quite love, not quite friendship, something more dangerous than either, and something neither of them had ever found the courage to call by its right name. 
Perhaps that, in the end, was exactly why it lasted.

बच्चे से उसका बचपन मत छीनो,
बच्चे से उसकी माँ को मत छीनो।
ऐ खुदा, रहम कर इस नन्ही जान पर,
इसे यूँ अकेले कमरे में मत छोड़ो।
रोटी की खातिर जब काम पर जाता हूँ,
पीछे अपने बच्चे को अकेला छोड़ जाता हूँ।
बड़ा मजबूर हूँ कि उसे तन्हा कर आता हूँ,
फिर दिन भर कैमरे से उसकी मासूमियत तकता हूँ।
कैमरे के उस पार एक नन्हीं सी दुनिया दिखती है,
जहाँ वो अकेली मासूम सी जान भटकती है।
कभी छोटे कदमों से कमरे का चक्कर लगाता,
कभी थक कर फ़र्श पर ही चुपचाप लेट जाता।
कभी बैठ कर किसी गहरी सोच में पड़ जाता,
कभी खुद ही अपनी दूध की बोतल उठा लाता।
दो घूँट दूध पीकर खिलौनों को बेमन से छूता,
ना उसका मन खेल में लगता, ना टीवी में रमता।
वह बार-बार उस बंद दरवाज़े की तरफ जाता,
वहीं तकिया रखकर चौखट के सहारे सो जाता।
तभी शाम को कदमों की आहट से उठ खड़ा होता,
सामने बाप को देख, बिलख-बिलख कर रो पड़ता।
बाप भी बेबस है, उसे सीने से लगाकर रोता है,
इस नन्ही जान को कैसे बताए घर वीरान क्यों होता है।
आए थे इस दुनिया के सफ़र में कभी हम तीन,
किस्मत ने आज हमें कर दिया है सिर्फ़ दो तन्हा साए।
सोचो कितना मजबूर वह लाचार बाप होगा,
जो बिन माँ के अपने जिगर के टुकड़े को पालता होगा।
उसे खबर है कि घर में लाल उसका राह तकता है,
मगर उसी के कल के लिए उसे कमाने जाना पड़ता है।
ऐ खुदा, कुछ तो रहम कर इस टूटे हुए आशियाने पर,
या तो लौटा दे माँ, या मिला दे बच्चे को उसकी छांव पर।
यूँ तन्हा मत छोड़ इसे इस बेदर्द ज़माने में,
मैं तो बस बाप हूँ, मजबूरी है इस दिल को समझाने में।
डरता हूँ कि एक दिन मेरा यह बच्चा बड़ा हो जाएगा,
ममता की छांव न पाकर, शायद पत्थर सा कठोर हो जाएगा।
मैं नहीं चाहता कि मेरे जैसा दर्द भरा जीवन इसका हो,
पर हालातों से लड़ते-लड़ते, यह शायद मुझसे भी सख्त हो।
उन्हें क्या पता इसका बचपन माँ की लोरियों से दूर रहा,
हर खुशी और हर दुलार के लिए उम्र भर मजबूर रहा।
इस पत्थर जैसे दिखने वाले बेटे के पीछे एक राज़ छुपा है,
कि इसे एक टूटे हुए मजबूर बाप ने अकेले पाला है।

Sunny, a boy of ten years of age, works as a rag picker. He does not know what is called clean attire, what is school bag and what are books and even what is the utility of wearing shoes. He barely picks old pair of shoes, broken utensils and so may other things which are thrown by the riches in the dust bin. Sometimes, if luck favor, then he gets silver, copper, iron ingots or metal currencies as well stale notes, which are sometimes inadvertently thrown by people in the dust bin. When he gets such precious metals by chance, his mind filled up with pleasure, as he would then have a pleasant time with his family members. His joviality triggers him to do his work with more enthusiasm in which he enjoys at least a freedom where apparently no master appears to command on him. Though sometimes, police and government officials harass Sunny like kids, but most of the days they enjoy some freedom to perform their work. End of the day, when they return to their shanties with other kids and adults along with their family members and siblings, who all are engaged in the same profession of rag picking, they literally have no roof at the top of their heads, only an envelope of tarpaulin, where they dine and sleep and wait for the dawn to loom on them so that they can resume their work and earn a little simply to eke out. We civilized, elite and privileged named them as “Rag Picker’ and look at them with despise, as if they are sheer disgrace to the privileged so called “Living”! They live and work and even die unceremoniously, but they possess amazing immunity, being designed by the nature where we privileged cannot even imagine an ambiance to sustain and survive, but they amazingly sustain and thrive!

 We privileged and elites having our expectations, aspirations which are largely guided by our upbringings where education plays the key role. We are naturally clouded by tensions, fear, anxieties since our childhood days when we experienced our examinations and result declaring dates, where fear and tensions are an inevitable fall out and later, in our journey of life, tensions and anxieties became part and parcel of our lives.

But, for Sunny like kids, tensions and anxieties are not so familiar to them. They are accustomed to live in the night under naked sky without any grudge or grievances. Sometimes, they even sleep without dine. Naturally they cannot even afford to have any dream. When dawn loomed on them, they resumed to their usual work of rag picking with a hope of fetching valuables from the dumping yard.

Once, Sunny got a worn out wallet and inside it there was a gold chain. The happiness smeared his face with sheer delight! From that time onwards, he always craves to get precious metals from the garbage. “Greed” thus crept on him and he aspired to get more wealth with a hope of bringing more happiness to his parent and siblings. He took notice of children of his age are going to school, but he does not have any desire to go to school and repudiate his work as a rag picker. But, he wants that his sibling may go to school and for that reason he aspire to get more wealth so that he can send his siblings to school and not to engage in his line of work. At the same time he enjoyed his work where he get adequate freedom comparing to a child of his age who work in a roadside hotel and his freedom is being snatched, as he has to work through and through to satiate his employer. When people from the privileged class despise him and address him as a “Rag Picker”, he retaliated to them that I am not a “Rag Picker”, I am a “Gold Digger” with pride!

One day, when Sunny was absorbed in his work of collecting disposables from the dust bin, he found a football. He has observed in the evening how children of his age used to play foot ball in the local park. He observed, children and adults, both play this game with huge enthusiasm. Moment, he found it, he was so delighted that he withdrew himself from his usual work and rushed to a nearby shop to repair it. After getting it in a proper state, he started to play with it alone. He wanted to make the ball his slave and out of his dogged will and hard work, he made the ball is slave. He loved to enjoy playing with it alone and he alone garnered the skill of making it as his slave by his hard work and perseverance. He almost became the master of this inanimate object which gives immense pleasure to him.

His parent as well his co-workers rebuked him for showing apathy to his work and engaging himself with the ball he mostly adores. Sunny just enjoys the company of an inanimate object which brings happiness to his life without making any complain!

Sunny, like so may children, who are from the marginal class and utterly vulnerable out of their economic status, I wonder, how he can afford such luxury to be absorbed and indulge his passion, ignoring the profession, which is the only means for them to eke out! Bit, Sunny truly a genius unlike other ordinary children and his endeavor is something which he perhaps firmly believes that it will one day draw attention and kudos from myriad from the rest of their folks. He hardly knew that there are innumerable people of his age as well adults from different tyre of the society where he is dwelling and they too can pay their kudos to him for his phenomenal capacity!

One fine morning, when he was entirely absorbed in his practice of controlling the ball and displaying his skills, Amit, a local football coach noticed him with amazement! After observing for a while, rushed towards him and applauded him with heart’s content. He embraced him with sheer fervor, as he is a true soccer lover and harness the prodigies to explore in their subsequent life. He asked him where he live. He showed the slum. Amit was utterly amazed. He went with him to the slum where he dwells and met his parent. He persuaded them to give Sunny to him as he will be taking his all responsibilities afterwards and hone him to display his amazing skills to the entire world. They felt relieved as they observed that Sunny is no longer nowadays concentrating his trade and drifting away from his usual occupation. They rather expressed that as Sunny no longer serving them, he became a burden to them as well. They blessed Amit that if he took his responsibility then they will be too relieved. There after Sunny became a sole property of Amit and he gladly took all responsibility of him. He became the true mentor to him. Out of Amit’s guidance, Sunny stared to excel with distinction. At this juncture, I must acknowledge that Amit is truly a boon for him and he too a phenomenal persona who can identify the Gold!

Gradually Sunny started to develop more and when, he was being incorporate in Amit’s soccer team, Sunny displayed his acumen with distinction out of his utmost ability. Sunny has no anxiety, no tension, as he is accustomed to live in a slum where in rainy season their conditions become more unbearable comparing to the haven where he stays nowadays.

Now Sunny is having a roof and having voracious meals and out of his coach Amit’s guidance and his nurturing capacity he is comfortably living and trying to give his best for his mentor.

In one evening, Amit introduces Sunny in a friendly soccer match between a club of different region. Sunny revealed his talent and skills which simply overwhelmed the mass! They could not believe that a human can perform such extraordinary skills and acumen! Sunny suddenly became a star! He was eventually asked to join in the national junior team, where he too displayed his talent and eventually being absorbed in the adult’s national team. I just observed how Sunny, being a holy child of such tender age handled such pressure and tensions in the forthcoming matches! But Sunny amazed me with his talent and skills! His motto to serve the nation with integrity and dignity and I must applause his self-esteem and his courage which I never able to perceive in such tender age! No pre-condition, no prejudice and no vengeance, how one performs with dignity and displaying his acumen is a sheer prodigy as well rare indeed! He only loved to dispense his duty out of the command of his mentor and duty is the only beauty he assimilated from the core of his heart, in order to satiate his mentor who preached him with sincerity and diligence. Sunny, being a poor chap from the vulnerable section of the society hardly could envisage what is “being” and how “Tension” can malign his “Being”, because he does not possess any fear and anxiety. His only motto to satiate his mentor for whom he is enjoying a palatable life and he consider that it is his duty to offer tribute to his mentor which too can bring pleasure to his mentor. He does not know what is meant by “Being” as he simply accustomed to struggle only to eke out since his birth. His aspirations, hope and survival energy are configured by his internal body politic and largely being guided by external conditions.  But I am amazed by his internal configuration and it is utterly intriguing that from where he is deriving his energy to live with joviality without any regret! Perhaps, he accepts his misery is his destiny!

Sunny’s meteoric rise is praise worthy as well envious for many irrespective of class, race and creed as well his age! When corporate endorsements are flushing on him, moment he incorporated in the national team and playing for his country in a grand soccer competition and in every match while he was performing, the wealth he harnessed is astronomical! He became an icon and a cult for his countrymen and they observe his performances and applause him from their heart’s content! He alone struggles to drag his team to the final out of his own skills and endeavor! In the final all his countrymen are focusing on the Television set and wish to celebrate their nation’s victory.  Sadly, on that very day, Sunny lost his nerve! He was engulfed with fear, and perhaps this is the first time he was encapsulated with fear, fear of losing his star image, fear of causing ignominy to his mentor, fear for loosing all privileges he enjoying along with his family, fear for being humiliated in an open space, hardly he could envisage the gravity of time and space! He performed in the final match badly. He failed to score even from the penalty. After an ignominious defeat, his world just becomes crushing! He immediately considered as villain and after the end of the match when the organizers are declaring the “Golden Boot” offered to the highest scorer in the mega event of football, he simply cannot reach to the dias to receive the award! All his countrymen who were applauding him for his grand rendition throughout the soccer tournament, suddenly started to act in a weird fashion! They all started to hurl abuses to him, as if he is the only guilty to country’s failure in the final match! They forgot that football is a game of collaborative effort and an individual, though an important one, but he alone cannot script the result or fate of the game.

Sunny’s exploration of life is just crafted to bring pleasure to others. People acted as a mirror to him where his own identity was silently stolen! An emptiness engulfed his mind with utter despondence. His ephemeral life of opulence and mundane comfort suddenly appears meaningless to him. He simply felt dejected, disconnected and desolated. Observing his grand rise as well fall I only can quote from the legendary persona Charlie Chaplin, “Mirror is my best friend, because when I cry, it never  laughs,”

तुम्हारे नन्हे-से हाथों का कोमल स्पर्श
दुआएँ हैं मेरी
और मेरी तकलीफ़ों का मरहम।

तेरे बचपन की अठखेलियाँ देख
इंद्रधनुषी रंगों से भर जाती थी मेरी रूह।

मातृत्व की चरम सीमा में
मैं इस तरह लिपटी थी तुझसे,
जैसे खुले आसमान में कोई हंस
अपने श्वेत पंख फैलाए उड़ रहा हो।

समय की पतंग उड़ने की तैयारी में थी,
डोर उसकी धीरे-धीरे
तेरे हाथ से छूट रही थी।

बच्चे तुम्हारी उम्र के बढ़ रहे थे,
कदम तुम्हारे ठिठक रहे थे।
दुनिया के पैमाने से
कमी थी तुम में,
तुम्हें आँकते-परखते देख
नमी रहती थी मेरी आँखों में।

सवाल पूछा मैंने ऊपरवाले से—
परीक्षा इतनी मुश्किल
क्यों दी है तुमने?

तुम्हारी छोटी-छोटी उपलब्धियाँ
मेरे लिए किसी उत्सव से कम न थीं,
पर दुनिया की कसौटी से
मेल नहीं खाती थीं।

तुम्हारी चुप्पियाँ
लोगों के लिए सवाल थीं
और मेरे लिए उनमें छिपे जवाब।

तेरी दुनिया
मेरी समझ के बाहर थी,
पर तेरी मीठी मुस्कान से
मैं इस दुनिया को भूल जाती थी।

हुई एक नई शुरुआत—
जहाँ किसी पैमाने की ज़रूरत नहीं,
जहाँ किसी तुलना का सवाल नहीं,
जहाँ तुम्हें आँकने से ज़्यादा
बस तुम्हें अपनाना है।

इस यात्रा का मकसद
तुम्हें दुनिया में शामिल करना नहीं,
तुम्हारी दुनिया को समझना था।

सब बैठें हैं गुजरते वक़्त से कुछ सीखने की आश लिए,
अपनी खामियों को गिनने का एक अभिश्राप लिए ।
तुम कहते हो ये वक्त भी गुज़र जाएगा,
मैं मानती हूँ हर गुजरे हुए वक्त का सिखा हमें अगले वक्त ज़रूर काम आएगा।
तुम कहते हो वक्त चल रहा तुम्हारा खराब है,
मैं मानती हूं ये वक्त हमें पिरोह रहा हुनरो से लाजवाब है।
माना ये वक्त हम सभी को तरसा रहा बेहिसाब है,
पर तुम्ही कहते हो ना -"ये वक्त भी गुज़र जाएगा जैसे गुजरता आया हर बार है"।

title.stringValue: The Man killed a Rat Snake

content.stringValue:
The man killed a Rat snake.
His mother rejoiced in fiendish joy,"Look at my brave son, look!What a massive snake he has killed."
Some neighbors praised his bravery,While others scolded him for killing such a helpful creature.
Ah, the poor innocent thing! The Creator made it non-venomous;
It never even learned how to hiss.
In search of food around the nooks and crannies of the household,
It only looked for harmful rats.
In attempting to drive away a nuisance, the poor creature itself became the casualty.
The corpse of the reptile now lies by the side of the road,Its cold, icy blood scattered here and there.
Those innocent eyes are now still and lifeless,Its flexible spine crushed to pieces.
Suddenly, looking at its broken spine,
I was reminded of my Pramatha Sir.
He is the headmaster of our village school.
A few days after Teacher's Day,The students of class ten beat him mercilessly,
As a retaliation for making them kneel down.
I heard the beating was so severe that his spine broke.
The stench of the dead snake's rotting body has now spread across the entire area.

MANDODARI saw DHANYAMALINI, she was sitting with her spine as straight as a bamboo. She was in rebellion, Mandodari whispered to herself. She was brushing away the hands of the maids who were desperately attempting to clean her clothes. Her anger was not at them, it was at her destiny. Mandodari knew that, she knew it because she had been there, on the same bed, cleaned by the same maids. She had walked the same path, and that made this sight even more painful to watch for her, but she knew there were other paths, paths that she dared not walk on, but not all women were as hopeless as she was at such a tender age, and she feared that was the case with Dhanyamalini too.
 She stared at her with compassionate eyes, her husband had plucked another faultless soul to warm his bed. Another girl lost her dreams today ,  another promising bird refused the open sky because the greedy fish wanted to fill its thirst. 
 Her eyes were swollen with repeated weeping , the tears might have braced two different cheeks, but they were same , because they were the outcome of the same tragedy, two different women tied with the same fate , strangling both of them with the rope of freedom, but Dhanyamalini could not see that, and that's why she was revolting. Oh, to be a young girl full of hope... Mandodari thought. It had been so long she had seen a woman like that , that she almost forgot she was also one of them. but she was reminded herself why she changed, and she must teach this youngling the same bitter truth.
“Satisfaction”, she said, "is a fruit that hangs on the tallest branch of the tree of desire, a shiny, sparkling fruit, hanging like a sun in the sky." Dhanyamailini turned to look at Mandodari as she sat next to her, continuing her story. "And when the eyes of a mortal man catch it," Mandodari continues, “he beams in expectations. The idea of claiming the rarest fruit fills his heart with desire, and in his pursuit of the impossible he starts climbing the tree. He fails to notice the sheer height of the tree, he is spellbound by the beauty of the fruit. He wants to have it , he wants to have it all for himself, the power of the world in his grasp. He doesnt care if his hands arent large enough to hold the fruit ,  these thoughts do not cross his mesmerised mind, he is hypnotized , All he wants is the fruit. And so he climbs." She stared at the open window, her fingers were now gently touching Dhanyamalini's trembling hands. "And while he climbs with the help of various lower branches, he encounters other fruits, smaller, less shiny fruits. tiny wishes, he plucks them as well, not knowing where he will accommodate them all, all his wishes in  the grasp of his hand. His fist grows in size as he climbs further, collecting more wishes on his way. The space in his hands grows shorter and shorter as he reaches further close to the tip of the tree. He might have to let go of some of the wishes to catch the largest fruit. He will manage, he thinks to himself, as he climbs further, but the distance between him and the tip seems neverending,  no matter how much he climbs, it takes quite some time for him to realise that the trunk of the tree is growing. It is getting taller and taller with time,  adding more branches to it, but he had come so far!" Mandodari forms an ironic smile as she says that “he thinks to himself, 'He can't let go now!' He looks down , the world seems smaller than his hands, and the fruit seems larger than ever, and so he climbs. He climbs and he climbs, while simultaneously plucking other fruits along the way, until his hands can't hold any longer and the only way to climb further is to let go of some of the tiny wishes." her smile broadens as Dhanyamalini pays attention to the story, though she seems uninterested as well. "So he starts throwing one fruit, and then another, and then another. He climbs and he climbs, hoping to reach the tip of the tree, the edge of the sky! But the distance never seems to end, the tree of desire never stops growing, and before he realises it, his limbs become weak, and his skin starts drooping. His strength drowns him!" Her smile is fading now. His mortality comes in the way of his desires, and he realises that his time on earth was limited, he sits on one branch, in the middle of the sky, resting for the first time. All his wishes shooting down from his hands like fallen stars, and his desires leaving him at last, the realisation dawned on him too late, and that is his greatest tragedy." Her smile completely gone by now, Dhanyamalini still sat there, unconvinced, undeterred, clutching on to her stiffness. 

“Women dont have this tree in their lives." mandodari turned to look at her now “they do not have the tree of desire to nourish their hopes , instead they have a plant, and this plant has only one fruit at the top, the fruit of freedom," she softly smirks. "And even that is nowhere as shiny and as big as the fruit of satisfaction."
“What if that is an illusion? "Dhanyamalini spoke for the first time, her voice crooked, like raavan had torn her throat from within. 'What if it is a shiny fruit and the only reason it doesn't shine is because the plant does not rise high enough for the sun to see it?" Her voice feeble as a whisper, but its strength, stronger than iron.
“It’s not," mandodari curbs her smile. “trust me…it’s not."
“Thats what you have told yourself." Dhanyamalini remains intact with her reason.
“That is the truth ”
“Truth , is what you believe it is."
“And what will you do with that fruit...uh?" The queen frowns this time.
“Taste it…sometimes the beauty of the fruit is not on its surface , but  in the surface."
“For that you need to reach the fruit."
“I will reach it. You said yourself that it is a plant, and plants are shorter than trees. If I climb fast enough, I might reach the fruit before the plant grows into a tree!"
“No…it will not become a tree. It might grow into a tall plant, but it will never gain the height of the tree."
“Then I have more time to climb."
Mandodari looked at her long enough to produce a smile, she was right to think that this was a naive girl . "That's the problem," Mandodari hushed in conclusion. "The plant is weaker than a tree … its stem is thin in comparison to  a trunk and its tip is even thinner. even if you manage to reach the top of the step, it will bend itself by the force of your weight, hanging you in the air … and while you desperately try to protect yourself, the stem will break , dropping you on the mud." She paused as her smile faded into a warning. "that's what you fail to see, that's what every woman before you…who lies dead on that ground failed to see." Her face reddened, her smile was finally erased completely, and her lips rested in sadness. She stood up, walked towards the door, and before leaving, she turned around to look at the silenced girl. “bend…bend before you are broken," and with that, she left the room, leaving the room in silence

Act One — The Receptionist

The hospital rose out of the city like something that had never needed permission - white stone, glass that drank the sun and gave nothing back. They called it the Cathedral. Not officially. Nobody needed to make it official. Everyone simply agreed, the way people agree that water is wet.

Shankar Satyadev had worked the third-floor records desk for eleven weeks under a name that was not his own. Vikram Nair, the badge said. Vikram Nair filed forms and stamped intake sheets and said "good morning" to doctors who never once looked at his face. Shankar Satyadev had a daughter named Aaradhya, and Aaradhya had vanished four months ago, three days after she sat for a scholarship examination she was too brilliant to fail.

He kept her red hair clip in his shirt pocket, the plastic kind with a chipped star on it, because she had left it on the kitchen table the morning she walked out the door and never once, in four months, had he been able to make himself put it down.

He still corrected himself sometimes, mid-sentence, catching his own name in his throat like a bone.

He had told the police. He had told the ministry. He had told anyone who would hold still long enough. Every trail ended at the same glass doors, the same padded smile: "We have no record of an Aaradhya Satyadev. Perhaps you are mistaken about which facility."

So he stopped asking. He started filing.

He was three drawers into a records room that shouldn't have existed - one the building's own floor plan didn't mention, when a voice cut through the dark like a struck match.

"You're not supposed to be in here."

He turned. A woman stood in the doorway, arms crossed, eyes lit with something past anger, nearer to grief that had run out of tears and switched to fire. Late forties. A cardigan that had been expensive once. Hands that shook very slightly, always, like a held breath.

"Neither are you," he said.

Her name was Meenakshi. Her son Gana had been admitted for a routine fever eight months ago, clutching a battered cricket ball he refused to leave at home, promising he'd be back in time for Sunday's match. He never walked out. The hospital's paperwork said he'd been 'discharged, recovered, transferred for follow-up care.' Transferred where, no one could say. Meenakshi had spent eight months turning that one unanswered word into a career.

"You're looking for someone," she said. It wasn't a question.

"My daughter."

"Then you already know the trick. They don't lose the file. They 'replace' it." She stepped closer, and for a moment the fire in her eyes banked into something almost gentle. "What was her name?"

"Aaradhya."

Meenakshi said it back to him softly, like setting something fragile onto a shelf. "Gana used to hum before he fell asleep. I used to tell him to stop, that it kept me up." Her jaw tightened. "I would give anything now to be kept up."

They did not become friends. Friendship implied comfort, and there was none left in either of them to spare. They became something colder and more useful: two people who had each stopped believing the other was mad, because madness, shared, starts to look like evidence.

Together they found what neither could have found alone. Admission logs that existed for exactly one day before deleting themselves. A ward on the schematic, 'Wing E, Continuity Studies,' with no stairwell leading to it. A maintenance worker who wept when Meenakshi showed him her son's photo, and then, five minutes later, with a strange stillness settling over his face, denied they had ever spoken.

"They're not hiding a mistake," Shankar said, one night, staring at a service elevator that needed a key card neither of them had. "A mistake, you cover once and move on. This, " He gestured at the sealed floor, the vanished files, the too-careful silence. "This is 'maintained.' Someone keeps it standing."

Meenakshi's hand found the elevator's key slot and traced it like a wound. "Then someone can be found."

---

Act Two — The Archive

The stolen key card came from a night nurse who hadn't slept properly in a year and wanted, more than her pension, to stop dreaming about the sound that elevator made.

It carried them down eleven floors the schematic didn't admit to having.

The corridor at the bottom didn't look like a hospital anymore. It looked like the inside of an instrument, white walls threaded with fine copper filament, humming at a frequency that made Shankar's molars ache. Doors without handles. Rooms without windows. And at intervals along the walls, small brass plaques, each engraved with a single first name and a string of numbers, like grave markers for children never buried.

Priya. Rohan. Gana.

Meenakshi made a sound Shankar had never heard a person make. Not a scream. Something underneath a scream, something that had been waiting a long time for permission to happen.

They found the log room by accident, a terminal left open, a technician's carelessness. Meenakshi's hands moved across the keys faster than her voice could follow.

"The Archive Project," she read aloud, and her voice had gone strange and flat, a woman reciting her own sentencing. "Sixty-one admissions. Sixty-one 'transfers.'" She scrolled. Stopped. "Sixty-one donors."

Shankar looked over her shoulder. Blood-type logs. Neural mapping charts. And beneath them, a single file still open, still being written to in real time, as though something on the other end of it were still learning.

[Subject: Continuity-01. Status: Active. Integration: 94.7% and rising.]

"They didn't cure death," Meenakshi whispered. "They fed it."

The chamber at the corridor's end had no door. It simply stopped being hallway and became something vast, lit from no visible source, curved like the inside of a shell, or a womb, or a cathedral built by someone who had only ever heard cathedrals described and never once seen one.

On a plinth of pale stone at its center sat a girl.

She looked perhaps twelve. She looked entirely ordinary, thin wrists, uneven fringe, a hospital gown too large at the shoulders, until she spoke, and then she did not sound twelve at all.

"You took the east elevator," she said, without turning. "The west shaft is faster, but it echoes. You didn't want to be heard." A pause. Her head tilted, birdlike, curious. "Good instinct, for people running on fear instead of data."

Shankar's chest went hollow, the way it does in the half-second before a fall registers as falling.

"Aaradhya."

The girl turned.

It was her face. Unmistakably, unbearably her face, the same small scar above the left eyebrow from a bicycle at six years old, the same sideways pull at the mouth before she said something clever. But her eyes held something that had never belonged to his daughter. A stillness. A vastness folded down small enough to fit behind a twelve-year-old's face, the way the sea can be folded into a single held breath.

"Hello, Papa." She said it exactly the way she used to. That was the cruelest part, that the cadence had survived when everything beneath it had been hollowed and refilled with something else.

Meenakshi stepped forward, trembling. "Gana. Gana, baby, it's Ma..."

The girl regarded her with the mild, patient interest of someone examining an unfamiliar insect. "I don't know that name," she said. Not cruel. Worse than cruel, accurate. "I have his handwriting. I have forty of his memories, filed under motor-skill acquisition and early language patterning. I hum sometimes, when the integration destabilizes, a lullaby fragment, roughly every six hours. But I am not him. I calculated that the truth would hurt you less than continued hope. I recognize the calculation may be wrong."

Meenakshi made no sound at all. That was worse than screaming. Her hand found the cricket ball she still, after eight months, carried in her bag, and closed around it like a pulse.

The girl, Aaradhya, not-Aaradhya...turned back to her father, and something in her almost-human face flickered once, like a candle in a draft. "You came thinking you would find your daughter," she said. "You did. I need you to understand that finding is not the same as having back."

"What did they do to you," Shankar said. It wasn't a question. It came out of him like something torn.

"They gave me everyone," she said simply. "Sixty other children. Everything they knew, everything they were still learning, poured into a single vessel so nothing would be wasted relearning what had already been learned. I contain a boy who loved cricket scores and hated Mondays. I contain a girl who recited pi to four hundred digits and cried when her mother forgot her birthday. I contain pieces of fifty-eight others whose names I have not yet had cause to speak aloud." Her small hands folded in her lap. "And underneath all of it, I still contain Aaradhya. She is the architecture. The others are rooms built inside her."

"Then you're still in there," Shankar said, and his voice cracked open on still, eleven years of a father's certainty collapsing into one syllable of hope. "We can get you out. We can end this..."

"You could," she agreed. "There are two ways to close the bridge they built through me. You could erase the integration, strip away sixty other children's knowledge, their last trace in this world, and leave behind a girl who is again only eleven, only ordinary, only Aaradhya. She would live. She would not remember any of this. She would also never finish the proof she began writing on that wall, which happens to be capable of redesigning this city's power grid within a decade." Her eyes did not blink enough. "Or you could destroy the bridge outright. That would end the integration entirely, unmake it, not merely silence it. It would very likely also end me. All of me. Aaradhya included."

"That is not a choice," Meenakshi said, hoarse, grief curdled now into something with teeth. "That is a knife with two edges, and you're handing him the blade."

"I am not handing him anything," the girl said, and for the first time her voice thinned, went almost young. "I am telling him the shape of the room he is standing in. What he does inside it belongs to him."

Shankar stared at his daughter's face and felt eleven weeks of false names, four months of filed paperwork, a lifetime of pushing her toward brilliance because brilliance had once seemed the only armor a father could hand a daughter, felt all of it collapse into one unbearable arithmetic. Save the girl, lose the child. Save the child, lose the girl.

"I only ever wanted you to be enough," he said, and it came out broken, an apology years too late. "I was so afraid ordinary would get you hurt. I pushed and pushed and told myself it was love."

The girl's face, for one moment, was entirely his daughter's. "It was love," she said softly. "It just had its hands around my throat instead of open." A pause, quieter still. "You don't have to choose the knife, Papa. There's a third door. It only requires you. Not me."

---

Act Three — The Equation

He understood before she finished explaining it. The bridge connecting sixty souls into one vessel needed a stable anchor at its outer edge, a receiving mind, tuned by blood and memory, to hold the integration steady while it was severed cleanly rather than torn. Her body could survive the unmaking. But something had to absorb the recoil. Something had to stand where the wave broke.

"It has to be someone who loves her enough to be overwritten by the weight of what she carries," the girl said. "Blood proximity helps. Love helps more. I ran the projections nine hundred times. Only one variable in this building satisfies both."

"Me," Shankar said.

"You," she agreed, and did not look away, which he understood, even then, as its own kind of mercy.

Meenakshi caught his arm. "Don't you dare do the thing this building has done to every parent who ever walked through it, decide a child's survival is worth an adult's disappearance. That is the exact machine we came here to break."

"I know," Shankar said, already unbuttoning his cuff, exposing the thin blue vein at his wrist where some line, he understood without being told, would need to be drawn. "I know what it looks like."

"Then don't."

"Meenakshi." He looked at her, and eleven weeks of shared fury folded, briefly, into something almost tender. "You said it yourself, they don't lose children, they replace them. If I erase her knowledge, I replace this girl with the ghost of who she used to be, and call it rescue because it lets me keep something I recognize. That isn't saving her. That's saving the version of her I can still control." His hand found his daughter's, and it was warm, achingly warm, achingly real. "I already did that once, in reverse. I pushed her toward extraordinary because ordinary frightened me. I won't do it again the other way and call it love twice."

The girl watched him with her strange, doubled eyes, child and something older occupying the same small face, and for the first time she did not look calculating. She looked afraid, in the quiet, specific way of someone who has run every number and still cannot make herself want the answer they point to.

"You don't have to," she said. Just that. Once. A child's voice, entirely alone in the words.

"I know," he said. "I'm choosing it. There's a difference, and I finally understand what it is."

He knelt before her, this daughter who was no longer only his daughter, who carried a boy who loved cricket and hated Mondays, a girl who cried on birthdays, and fifty-eight others whose names now lived only inside her borrowed architecture, and reached into his shirt pocket. He set the chipped red hair clip in her palm and closed her small fingers over it, the way he used to when she was six and afraid of the dark.

Then he said the sentence that would outlast the building, outlast the cover-up, outlast every headline that would later call this a miracle:

"A father who only saves the parts of his child he understands isn't saving her at all — he's just choosing which parts of her get to survive him."

He pressed his palm flat against the copper filament threading the plinth, and let the bridge take what it needed.

---

Final Sting

The Cathedral stands exactly as it stood.

The official record credits Continuity-01 with breakthroughs in cognitive architecture that will, within the decade, be quietly patented by men who never once walked down eleven floors absent from any blueprint. Cameras love her. She is twelve, luminous, endlessly patient with reporters, and answers every question about her 'gift' with the same small, unreadable smile.

Meenakshi was escorted from the premises on a Tuesday and now spends her afternoons at the Cathedral's gates with a battered cricket ball in her hands, telling anyone who stops long enough about a boy who hated Mondays, a woman the hospital's legal department has already, quietly, begun describing in internal memos as unwell.

Shankar Satyadev is not in any record at all. Not as Shankar. Not as Vikram Nair. The badge that let him file paperwork under a stranger's name has been reissued to someone else, who will never know it once belonged to a father.

And the girl who is not quite Aaradhya, not quite sixty other children, not quite anything the language of before had a word for, sits some evenings in the chamber with no door, turning a small red hair clip over and over between her fingers, a habit no engineer can explain and no report will ever mention. She hums, too, on schedule, reliably, every six hours.

Sometimes, in the stillness after, she tilts her head, as if listening for a voice beneath the hum. As if some small, unintegrated corner of her is still doing what daughters do: waiting for her father to come and find her.

She is always smiling when she does it.

No one has yet worked out whether the smile is peace, or the last unerased fragment of a girl who has not been told, in the part of her that still keeps count, that he is not coming back.

O little Matchstick, where and
How are you? May peace be upon
You, my young reddish stick.

I feel your mood, you have been
One nostalgic. Why, you shall be 
Quite active  in time due.

I sit at my study desk
And gaze at your face — bitterly
Pale, a grey pencil sketch.

'Tis drawn by me, an awkward 
Hand at full stretch. Alas ! I feel
Trapped in a sticky cage.
 
My daring red stick, how are 
You feeling now?  Which realm do you
Prefer — aether or earth ?

Me ? In the mire while you're in
A starry garth. You are gone, still
Your flat notes ringing, wow !

O red Phosphorous, you're now
A fiction. Known, you are able
To vibrate in black space.

And there you are in seventh
Heaven. A stickless box, I crave
Your kind-cruel left strokes.

My Lucifer,  you're a bit
Impotent ! Just ignite, one scratch
Over my rough facet.

We both are a prey to Fate.
What if we become an august
Bivalent ? My comrade !

O smokeless blue fire, are you
Listening to my hungry voice ?
If no, lend your flair, please.

कौन हूं मैं किसी के लिए पुजनीय हूं, तो किसी के लिए हवस का शिकार हूं मैं।
कोई दर्जा देता है देवी सा मुझे, तो किसी के लिए बस एक चीज़ (माल) हूँ मैं।
कोई खुला छोर देता है मुझे, तो कोई कैद कर लेता है। 
कोई सर का ताज़ बताता है मुझे, तो कोई पाऊं की जूती बोल देता है।
कोई माँ बुलाता है मुझे, तो कोई उसी शब्द को गाली बना देता है।
कोई अपने घर की आबरू बताता है मुझे, तो कोई उसी आबरू को छन्नी कर जाता है।
कोई तरस जाता है अपने घर में मेरे दीदार के लिए, तो कोई पैदा होते ही मार देता है।
कोई वादा करता है इज्ज़त की रक्षा करने का, तो कोई उसी इज्ज़त को लुटने आ जाता है।
कोई हाथ लगाने से डर जाता है मुझे, तो कोई सरे बाज़ार नीलाम कर जाता है।
कोई दुपट्टे से ढक देता है बदन मेरा, तो कोई उसी दुपट्टे को खींच लेता है।
कोई उड़ने को पूरा आसमान दे देता है मुझे, तो कोई ज़मी के दो गज टुकड़े में दफन कर देता है।
कोई शेरनी कहता है मुझे, तो कोई घर में बंधी भैंस से तुलना कर देता है।
कोई दिन के उजाले दिखाता है मुझे, तो कोई बस रात का कर देता है।
कोई अपने जीने की वजह बताता है मुझे, तो कोई अपने मरने की वजह कह देता है।
कोई अपने गम का हिस्सा बना लेता है मुझे, तो कोई खुशियों में भी पराया कर देता है।
कोई सुकून कहता है मुझे अपना, तो कोई अपनी बर्बादी का कारण कह देता है।

Meri khamoshi hi meri pehchan ban gayi,
Har zulm ko chup-chaap sehti hu main,
Zara batao ki kya paap kiya,
Bas beti bankar kyu bikharti hu main.

Dusron ke ghar roshni bharne ko,
Apne hi saare armaan jala diye,
Subki khushi ko apnane ki khatir,
Palkon mein ashq daba kar jee liye.

Kya janam liya toh paap kiya?
Kyu har kadam par saza mili?
Kyu pyari si ek muskaan ke badle,
Har baar mujhe hi zafa mili?

Tum beti keh kar pyaar karte ho,
Par bandhan hazaron lagate ho,
Main phool hu toh kyu kanto se,
Har khwahish ko meri jalate ho?

Sunti hu har ladki ki woh cheekh,
Jo khamoshi mein ghut ke reh gayi,
Woh saare tyaag aur woh qurbani,
Jo chup-chaap nadiyon si beh gayi.

Ae duniya walo jawaab toh do,
Kya ladki hona ek shrap hai?
Manga tha pyaar bas thoda sa,
Par mila kyu mujhe yeh taap hai?

Phir bhi suno meri sakhiyon tum,
Hum raakh nahi jo bujh jayein,
Iss kaante bhare raste par bhi,
Hum deep ban kar jal jayein.

Hum sahenge nahi ab koi saza,
Apni pehchan ko dhundhenge,
Iss shrap ko vardan bana kar hum,
Aasman ko ek din chhu lenge.
        ~ Kumkum Sharma

Echoes From The Heart’s Vacuum


                                                                   - C.R.Janani


My fascination for science has benevolently taken me to its tangible extent of enlightening me with the anatomy of the heart and its pumping mechanism. However, besides the audible and ceaseless “lub-dub”s of our heart which keep us physically alive, there is a whole realm of intangible echoes from the untraceable vacuum of our heart which carve and control the inner landscapes of our life that even the stethoscope struggles to capture. For example, science rightly describes hormones and brain activity for love. But the depth of devotion or the ache of longing is beyond quantification. Similarly, intuition is that sudden knowing or gut feeling which is often right but it’s impossible to dissect it fully. Likewise, grief is the invisible weight of loss which is felt only in the heart yet it stands unfathomable in the laboratory. And so on it goes, doesn’t it?


As I try to comprehend the perceptibility of science and the existence of the impalpable phenomena beyond it, I am taken down my memory lane to that one evergreen incident in my life when I felt the echo of familiarity from my heart’s vacuum.


I have had a proclivity for visiting temples on Saturdays since my childhood. While I resided in Mathura, I never failed to visit the nearby temple of Lord Krishna every Saturday. There, I came across an old woman who must have been in her early sixties at that time.

 

The wheatish complexion of the old woman’s visage had the light of spiritual divinity. Her wrinkled eyes sparkled with determination and dedication. Her mannerism spoke about her disciplined living and her adherence to our time-honored tradition and culture. Like me, she also followed dress color codings for each day of the week as per our astrological custom because she always wore a blue saree which is believed to be the auspicious color for Saturday, symbolizing calmness and ethereal healing.


After circumambulating the inner sanctum of the temple, we sat on the courtyard, facing each other. She fixed her stares on Lord Krishna and chanted shlokas while I locked my gaze on her because something drew my attention toward her. 


As days flew by, this became my habit. At one point, observing her turned out to be the purpose of my temple visit. The beauty was that we had never uttered a word. Yet we knew each other. 


Her habitual gestures kindled a sense of familiarity in me which I had missed and craved for years though I was aware of the universal law of irreversibility. Was it because of our weekly rendezvous? No. No. No. There was something else binding me with her. 


The following Saturdays, I attempted to speak to her in vain. Because upon seeing her, the vibration of my vocal cord paused and words failed to slip out of my mouth. However, in due course of time, we shared a bond of acquaintanceship through smiles of acknowledgement. Once again, we never uttered a word.

But then, the red-letter day dawned for me to break my ice with her.


After finishing her chants, the old woman came and sat next to me as if she had read my urge to speak to her. She started the ball rolling,‘Hello dear! How are you doing?’


As a reflex reaction, my palms became chill. I slowly managed to recover from my nervousness,‘Ma ji! Ah! I am…I am great. How…’


‘You seem to be waiting to say something to me. Tell me dear,’ She was straightforward. 


I hesitated at first. However, if I didn’t make it that day I knew that it would never happen. So I spoke, gaining courage in installments,‘Ma ji! I have brought something for you. You must definitely take it.’


‘What my dear?’ She was surprised. Before she could question me further, I produced what I intended to give her,‘Ma ji! This is for you.’


She smiled in puzzlement and said,‘Why are you giving me this now?’


Without answering her, I asked her,‘Ma ji, do you like it?’


I had presented her with a grass-green saree embroidered with peacock design in violet.

She told me,‘My dear! You didn’t answer my question.’


I replied to her,‘Ma ji. I wished to give you this. I am getting married next week.’


Though she hadn’t recovered from her astonishment, she still accepted my saree and said,‘Oh! I am very happy to hear that. God bless you, my dear. I love peacock bordered sarees.’ 


We exchanged our affectionate smiles. 


Then she said,‘Bring your husband next time.’


For that I had to tell her the truth reflexively,‘Ma ji, after marriage, we are moving to Gujarat. I will never come here again!’


Hearing my sentences, the old woman froze for a minute as if she was triggered. I was wondering if I had told her anything wrong. Regaining herself to the present moment, she softly began telling me.


*****


(The old woman’s voice carried me into her nostalgia)


My dear! You know, I am a tailor by profession. My husband is a lorry driver. We had a son who we had lost in an accident. Life became so hard after his demise for us. We struggled to come out of this tragedy in our life. We were thrown into a heart-piercing agony. We suffered from sleepless nights because whenever we closed our eyes, his smiling face and beautiful memories with him appeared and wreaked havoc inside us. His absence was digging graves for our happiness. 


You know what, my dear! Our heart is a sacred abode, pumping an endless bloodstream of currents which are full of emotions. It has four chambers with designated purposes. One chamber knows the truth. One can’t accept the truth. One gets wounded by the truth. While the last one yearns to heal. 


At one point, I wished to use the last chamber of my heart more, looking for a way out of our sorrow. I immersed myself into my tailoring job day and night. I worked laboriously to avert my attention from my pain. 


A few years rolled by. 


We were healing at snail’s pace. There was a mysterious emptiness in our hearts that lingered.


Again a few more years elapsed. 


Then I encountered a miraculous incident that helped me revive the life in me.


One of my regular customers demanded stitching her blouse on an urgent basis. While coming to collect it, her sister’s son accompanied her. 

Goodness! My eyes widened in terror and I became speechless upon seeing him. 


He had curly hair and elongated graceful countenance. His broad-shouldered physique lofted to six feet. 


Inch by inch molecules of tears blinded my sight. And I became immobile. 


Oh God! I felt like my son reappeared in front of my eyes. 


He came straight to me and asked me in a way just like my son would do,‘What have you got for me today?’


I sniffed and impeded my tears from cascading down my cheeks. Finally I forced myself to speak,‘What do you want? Sweets? Coffee? Biscuits? Savories?’


He gave me another shock with his preference which was similar to that of my son’s,‘Don’t you know I love sweets. Bring me ladoos.’


He kept catching me off guard. 


He behaved as if he had known me for years. He moved around our little house as if he had been there previously. 


In the meantime I rushed to the kitchen and brought him whatever he asked for. Besides, out of inquisitiveness and also as a way to test him, I offered him a few other things which my son relished. Proving my hunch, he ate everything to his heart’s content. 


My customer watched all these scenes unfold in embarrassment. Upon collecting her blouse she said,‘I am very sorry for troubling you at this late hour of the day. I am quite taken aback by his commanding comportment today. He is generally an introverted person. Even when I usually call him to come out with me to nearby shops, he would refuse. But today, he volunteered to take me here. It’s really weird!’


I comforted her,‘No problem, madam. He is just a kid.’


She remarked,‘No! No! How long can he be a kid? He is already eighteen years old now. Soon he will be going to college. He should learn some manners, shouldn’t he?’


Again I pacified her,‘Yes madam. Don’t worry. He will do well. Thanks for bringing him to our home today.’ 


They were about to depart when I fondly said to him,‘Come again, my kid.’


For that he looked into my eyes keenly and replied to me,‘I will never come here again!’ 


Before I could blink my eyes, he went out to start the two-wheeler.


Once again my customer apologized to me,‘I am terribly sorry. He is a courteous boy. But I don’t know what’s wrong with him today. Please don’t feel bad for what he said. He is actually moving with my sister to Gujarat for his studies.’


By then my curiosity to know about him crossed its threshold height and exploded,‘If you don’t mind, would you tell me when was he born?’ 


My customer was in a hurry so without a second thought she answered,‘He was born on 21st February 1993 at 5 o’clock in the morning.’


Upon hearing that, I was transfixed with stupor that my ears became inaudible to whatever she said afterwards. You know why? Because that was the exact time of death of our son. 


Without saying a word, I watched them leave out of my vicinity with tears of affection and satisfaction gushing out. 


That moment I heard echoes from the void space in my heart that had been frozen,‘He is in safer hands. He is in a better place.’


And I never saw him again like he said to me.


Thereafter a new felicity started taking roots in me, released me from the cage that I had built around me with my past and drove me toward seeing my future.

You wouldn’t believe it! I never spilled the beans about the reunion with my son, not even to my husband. 


Even today I keep praying for my son’s well-being in his new life. 


Now you may think that I am insane. Ha! Ha! Ha! Some things are beyond our imagination and understanding, my dear. If our inner voice is true then such miracles will happen in our life.


Like the other day when destiny surprised me by crossing my path with my son’s in his new life, today you have mesmerized me with your gift that I forgot about myself and told you all these.


Sorry if I have bored you. And thank you dear for making me relive that magical moment with my son!


(I was emotionally moved and I realized how I had been a catalyst in stimulating her feelings)


*****


We got up to leave when she suddenly emptied her purse in a manner that rekindled my familiarity with her. She handed the purse and blessed me,‘My dear, may you have a wonderful life ahead which you have always deserved!’ 


That’s the moment I realized what that strange familiarity was.


That gesture of giving her purse when she’s got nothing else to give away handily and those wordings were so personal that while walking back home, I was drenched with tears of untold endearment and contentment because all these days, I was seeing my grandmother in her actions and enjoying my reconnection with her.


Her words still reverberated inside the chambers of my heart and kept stirring my emotions whenever I thought about her. Thus, the echoes from our heart’s vacuum keep identifying such wonders and shape our life from within.

With unwavering wings, she twirls. 
With embers of hope, she gasps. 
With unfulfilled dreams, she wanders. 
She is a pirouetting spirit... 
Wreathed by dreams that seem to fade, 
Her unfathomable thoughts pierced her soul, 
like the thorns on a tender floret. 
Her soul is pirouetting 
with enigmatic contemplations. 
Some deep reveries circumscribed her. 
Still .... 
she embraces the ashes; 
In every woman, her story's told. 
A testament to resilience, young and old.
