The biggest hearts bleed the most. 
She tries and tries to pump her life blood throughout the world, 
but try as she might the blood only pools and weighs her down, 
until she can no longer walk and run and play. 
She will eventually succumb to her very gift, 
having given too much and lost too much, 
she will drown in it.
She will try to swim to the surface but she is chained to the sea bed,
she will try to scream and beg but her lungs are empty.
People may try to save her, to help her, but the moment she thinks she's escaped, she will return to those familiar waters.
This cycle will continue until the day she's accepted her fate interwoven with countless lives,
even then she will never be able to fly weightlessly,
she will forever remain a broken shell of what she was.

They called it as a story with a quote that goes – “Lots Of Eyes On One Glass Piece.” 
It was a cold night. I had been waiting for a long time. Finally, the rose glowed. Then I closed my eyes. Cleared my mind. Got my senses under control. Sitting on a tree branch. My vitals. My Bluereds. Those blue-roses are somehow connected to my soul. When they glow, it’s time for me to do the work. They crawled with their glowing petals. Straight into her room through the window. 
I can feel what happens around them. I can see wherever they go. I can hear whatever they want me to. 
It was almost ten p.m. The roses crawled a little closer and higher. That was when, I first saw her. In a building full of busy people. Working to their limits for the sake of survival. She lived on the second floor. She was sitting on a couch with a laptop on a table. I could see her tense face in the mirror in front. 
Her hair was loose. Her lips were wet. Her dress was stunning. 
Every part of her made me realise how good my petals’ choice was. Then, her phone gave a soft buzz. She got a message. And in a split second, her ex-pression changed to something amazing. Smiled with excitement. The message was from her fiancé. But she seemed a little young to get married. 
She was so pretty with that smile. 
She noticed the branch of my blue-roses peeping in. She came closer. And she threw them away and closed her window. The lights went off. But I couldn’t stop myself from pushing my vitals closer to her. The smallest of the roses made its way–through the vent, into her bedroom, on the second floor. By the they reached, she was sitting on the bed. With a locket in her hand. The locket had a photo.
 I just needed to get a little closer to see what was in it. But she didn’t give me a chance. She sighed and put the locket inside a drawer just beside her bed. The lamp was off. Her bedroom was kind of cozy but a little small. It barely had any room for two people to share. No wonder why she had a narrow bed. Leaving my Bluereds there, I took a deep breath. And regained consciousness.  
As a matter of fact, their garden had these tall trees and cozy bushes, making it so comfortable for someone like me to stalk someone like her. But at night, anyone can only stare until the lights went off. And thanks to Mother Nature, I have better eyes. I can see better in the dark. Even from far away. 
It was so satisfying to watch her sleep. I stayed there for a long time. Couldn’t help myself. 
At exactly 11:55 p.m., I got the letter I had been waiting for, from the passenger pigeon. It was from my darling, Jean. 
The letter was made from bamboo pulp from the envelope to the paper. The tradition came from humans. It had a seal made from natural gums. Pressed with a coconut shell. 
The night was dark and silent. Gave me a peaceful environment to read my letter. I slid down the tree. I walked across the buildings with my hoodie on. And my letter in my hand. I finally got out of the city. Then, I sped away in the air at the speed of sound. I finally reached my favourite spot. The bridge over the Morvan River. It was old and there wouldn’t be any vehicles passing over it. 
Rested my legs against the railing. In the midnight moonlight, my hand glowed. My blue power emerged from my hand. Just like the fire from dead leaves, like the lightning from clouds—so natural. 
My tattoos revealed themselves. At my neck, on my hands, across my chest, and along my back. Then I opened her letter. Written in beautiful handwriting. And with intense emotion. I spent an hour reading what my darling had written. 
We don’t need sleep. It’s been a long time since I’ve been to our place. I might not even be able to get there anymore. Not for a long time. 
After reading the letter, I jumped straight into the water. The Morvan was one of the purest waters nearby. And I spent the whole night underwater. It was so relaxing being with the fish and playing with the clams hiding shyly. 
The beauty underwater is something more than just pretty. 
The tides drifting on surface.
The fish mating underneath.
 The plants waving on ocean floor. 
The sharks biting the flesh.
 It’s inexplainable. 

Mother Nature gave us a better life. Breathing underwater, speed same as that of sound, vision sharper than an eagle’s, a sense of smell stronger than a hound’s, jaws fiercer than a crocodile’s, and power that humans can call SUPERNATURAL. 

By the time I came out of the river, it was already seven in the morning. I went back to my place, far away from the city. It was an old building, nothing special, but it was enough for one person to stay in for a while. As usual, I paid the rent to the old man who had been waiting for me for the past three days. And now it was time for me to leave for a better place. I knew what was best for my Jean.
I made the palace myself.
It was huge & surrounded by long, high walls. I built most of it with dark volcanic stone, with marble staying around the entrances, pillars, and parts of the floors. The windows were tall and covered with smoked glass, so dark that you could barely see what was behind them from the outside. Wood was worked into the walls and ceilings, and I used it together with the stone and the black marble because I wanted the place to feel warm without making it look bright.
Most of the palace was dark. Not completely black, but dark enough that even during the day it never felt like the sunlight could reach every corner. From the outside, it looked more like a massive shadow than a home. Sometimes, even I had to stop and look at it for a moment. To admire what I have done. I had built every part of it myself, yet there were times when it didn’t feel like I had. I didn’t believe it at first. Now I confidently say that it was built by me. It might be the best artwork I ever made. 
I sealed the entire place with my power from the moment I finished building it. No one outside could see it, touch it, or even get close to it. I made sure of that.
Anyone who tried to come near would start feeling some-thing wrong. The closer they got, the worse it became. A strange pressure. An uncomfortable vibration they couldn’t explain. They would usually stop, turn around, and leave without knowing why. If they tried to keep going, the force would push-’em back.
It became our palace of nights whenever we met.
I covered the entire floor with mosses and flowers grew around the walls. Their smell stayed in the air even when there was no wind. Somehow, all of it worked together—the dark stone, the marble, the old wood, the moss, and the flowers. I love the way I used the volcanic stones in every part of the floor and thick walls. They stayed stronger than I expected. 
It was beautiful.
But there was always something about the place that made it feel like we weren’t the only ones there. However, it was suitable to spend intimate nights–just like we did. As if you don’t wanna stop, the night goes on and on till the sunlight enters through the window. 
The huge palace did take a lot of time to clean. And it was almost sunset when I suddenly remembered about my next victim. 
The next second I flew into the sky searching for my rose that only glows when viewed with my eyes and only when they were near the chosen victim.
 I saw her. 
She wasn’t at her building this time. It was her work place. The Ace restaurant. I sped away like a shooting star in the sunsetting sky, leaving trail of a disturbed air.  I did land on a tree. I never miss my target. My power shut off its glow allowing the darkness to spread all around. I waited there for a while. She finally came out. 
Smiling. 
And laughing. 
With some other who also worked there. May be they are still working at Ace. Or maybe there are not. 
Zara, was her name that I heard in the conversation among them. She had blonde hair, seductive eyes, modern dress, high heels and an engagement ring. 
I went closer. 
Unnoticeable in the bushes on road side. I needed to crouch because of my height making it easier for someone to notice me if I stood. Then, I used my power, glowing only to my eyes, and mere dark dust to any other who sees it. No one could see me. 
I kept taking deep breathes. 
With my eyes closed, my mind cleared, my senses transferring themselves magically into the BLUE-ROSES that chooses my victims. That’s why I call them as my Vitals. Then, I lost my consciousness. It was like a quick glimpse. Like a neuron transmitting a signal. Like a lightning from cloud reaching the earth. Then I could see her. 
Her beautiful face with that extremely attractive smile. It made me wanna hear her moan. 
May be with pain. 
May be with love. 
I could hear her laughter. I saw her waving goodbyes to some of her co-workers. And then, I saw her boss. He had quite an intention on Zar. I could see it in his eyes. I had better ones than his intentions. The way he tries to get close and touch her for every small reason possible. It’s obvious. 
But Zar is a smart-chick. She cut the conversation and gave some hugs to the leaving workers but some stayed with her. And she gave one to the boss too. That freaky old man should have been in his limits.  Zara moved on along the pathway on road side. Her co-workers accompanied her. It was five of them in the closest circle. I could see their names on their batches - Edward, Barbra, Melanie and Rosalin. And by their looks, it was quite a friend group with issues. Only one man for four ladies. That’s interesting. 
And it was hard for me to leave that bastard boss unharmed who misbehaved with my victim. 
He got what he deserved for the harassment. It might be known tomorrow. In news. Then everyone knows my style. Or maybe I should give them some clues that it was his body. I didn’t care then. 
Soon, one by one started to take off the path. Leaving the others, going to their home. First, it was Rosalin, she seemed like a chilled beer in a cold night. Her words, they can change anyone in sad mood. I knew her. She was the younger sister of my last victim. But the sisters hadn’t talked in like a year. She gave a hug and smiled at her before going into the house she had problems with. 
Melanie stopped before going inside and asked Zar to wait. She came out after a while with a bottle of cheap wine. She couldn’t afford much but her love was infinite. She was the shortest in the group. 
So cute and little. I wish she was my victim. But no worries, I had Zar, much sexier than the shorty. 
Soon, Barb and Rosalin started to leave the path. 
Barb said “I couldn’t afford a gift now… but I’m saving money to get it to your wedding” 
Zar replied “You don’t need to. You’re both my favourite. I just want you to be there.”
She gave them a hug and the last two continued their way home. 
It was finally Ed’s turn to leave Zar alone. That’s when I got the chance I’ve been waiting for. 
Ed stopped and said “Zar… just don’t forget that we all love you.” 
He kissed her on the FOREHEAD and said “And this is from me..” If it wouldn’t have been the forehead or if it would have been her cheeks, I swear I wouldn’t have left him alive. My victim is mine. Only mine to enjoy. Mine to do whatever I want to. Kiss. Kill. Or any thing.
His gift probably was the only one that lasts longer. It was a ring. May be not made of real gold but shiny enough for her to use. 
I could see it in his eyes. The way he concerned about her. The way he kissed her forehead and hugged her in a tight, warm, cozy hug. Wiping off the tear before she could notice. It was all emotional. But he kept watching until she left the lane. And now it’s my turn to emerge. 
The connection wasn’t lost but I came to my senses. Following the crawling branch that gives me the invisible signals, I finally got close. To her.
But what fun would there be if I just came face to face and take her away!
Let’s do it my way.
The night breeze trembled her legs. Making her trip on my branches. She got an ankle sprain. It was her left ankle. I could see the pain in her face from far. She dragged herself to the nearest tree. Thinking she was safe, though she wasn’t, she checked on her left ankle. It did bulge. I mean, like a swelling. To be honest, I learnt English from my first victim. It’s kinda hard to maintain all that freakish grammar. 
Anyways. That cute pinkish thing. Who doesn’t want to be that thing on her leg. It made her moan a bit at least. 
It was time to execute my plan. 
Cutting through the dark night streets with the yellow lights, the cab came. It was me in the driver seat. I stopped right beside her. Having no choice she accepted to enter my cab. We talked about the fare. I mean… not that it matters cause I am not going to take her money anyway. 
I could see her tired face from the mirror. She sat in the back seat. In fact, I didn’t even know the exact route she asked. 
The moonlight makes my skin more sensitive to reveal my power. Just as I said, it glows in BLUE colour only to my eyes and appears dark dust to any other. Like an Unholy ghost!
I managed to hide that from her sight. 
She looked at her phone. The battery died. My Bluereds took control over the situation. 
The cab became extremely cold. I could see the discomfort in her face. She was trembling and shivering. I gave her a coat I was saving for every of my victim. It was made with fur of a hound. That gave her the warm she needed. 
The car windows went utterly black. Nothing except the front view was visible. As if we were trapped in another black dimension from three sides. Before she could even notice, the power blocked the sound from reaching her ears. She bend her head and tried to close her eyes once. The black windows got cracks and got smashed with an invisible force. They blasted outward. But she could hear nothing but silence. 
The deadly silence was so addictive. 
What I was pondering is that she had a lot of eyes on her. I mean from work, from neighbourhood, almost everywhere, she had someone that would flirt with her. She was like a delicate glass piece in the hands of that person, she was gonna marry. 
My branches slowly surrounded the cab. They slowly crawled in just like a snake. The glowing petals revealed themselves to her. Making her eyes realise the truth of blue power. She opened her eyes disturbed by brightness. She saw them glowing. She noticed the darkness. 
Before she could make a sound, my BLUEREDS crawled on her body and entwined around her neck making her voice difficult to come out. I could see her struggle as she was getting choked with some flexible-strong branches. Just a plant but not as safe as a Holy Basil. I wanna choke her too.

She could barely see anything in that pain. 
Then she saw me. With the blue power, glowing around my skin, smearing all around like smoke. The power can only be seen when the death comes closer to my victims. 
Until then it was just dark dust to them. I could see her eyes almost getting popped out. I could see her struggle to gasp for little air. I could hear her mumbling voice too low to hear. My BLUEREDS hold her neck so tight that she couldn’t even breathe properly.
Then, I looked at her from the mirror and talked to her. 
It was all fleshy bones and two eye balls hanging at the bushes right beside the ACE. The night screamed tremendously.
All I said to her in the night was “Hello, Zar.”
In the next morning, the Ace was in terror. Blood dripping off the tips of leaves. Dangling strings of tendons and flesh hanging from high branches made me crave more but this wasn’t the right time. I should wait. 
But I should also remember what my Jean. 
“May be my breathe forgets you.
Or may be even my soul. 
But never my physical body for what you did. 
For the tainted pleasure you gave.”

The air is thick with the metallic ting of concrete which follows an explosion. The boy with a rhythmic pace walks with the weight on his back familiar, yet terrifying. His little brother’s head rests on the back of his shoulder and the little puffs of his breath against his neck are long gone. They are now replaced with a heavy silence that screams louder than the explosion itself. He isn’t walking towards a destination, he is just walking. His feet are tired but he doesn’t stop because that would mean he has acknowledged that the world has ended around him. With every step he feels the weight of failure to protect his little brother. He is consumed by guilt, feeling less and less as a person and more like a hollow vessel, carrying the ghost of “what could have been”. To him the surroundings present a picture of absurdity and indifference. The shattered buildings, the sirens, the dust- all seem cruel. He wanders aimlessly as if the universe has already done its worst and nothing can surprise him any longer. He speaks to the silence trying to bridge the gap between ‘before’ and ‘now’. “Hold on tight, Sam. Okay? We are almost there.” referring to the shambles which once housed their entire lives. “Keep your eyes closed. I’ll wake you up when everything is over.” The realization that the world has stopped for his brother while he must keep going feels like an unimaginable task, turning his grief into a physical burden. He decides to bury him right next to their home because it contained all the love they ever knew. Struggling, he tries to clear off the debris to make place for his brother’s innocent lifeless body; marking the end of a childhood ruined too soon and a maturity that came far too early for him to bear.

Brahmarakshasa

Brahmarakshasa is not a subject normally discussed at any home but paranormals are topics of high interest to the world of social media. But I was forced to think about this recently.  The day after Diwali, I and my family were sitting around the dining table. My father was sharing his memories about his childhood. He spoke extensively about the deaths of his siblings in childhood. My father is the second child. Three of his siblings died during their early childhood due to illness. My father said that in those days, such negative incidents sparked what would be loosely translated as "divine fact-finding missions" or "prashnam veykal" in Malayalam. The family believed that there must be some reason or dosham which has triggered the loss of these children.
My father often speaks about his "Veliachan" (Maternal Grandfather) very highly. Veliachan has made a strong impression in my father’s mind and heart. Though Veliachan had no such blind beliefs, he gave in to pressure from his compatriots, and agreed to have a consultation with an astrologer. The arrangements were made and an astrologer was brought. As the family lore goes, the astrologer started the process in the evening. The astrologer asked for a lamp to be lit, threw some kavadi (shells), chants Sanskrit slokas and then finally came up with some prophecies.
While the lamp was lit, there sounded 3 loud blasts resembling firecrackers(vedi) and he immediately prophesied that there should have been 3 deaths in the family. Naturally, Veliachan disagreed immediately as he suspected that the person who brought him there could have provided the background information. Also, this astrologer's knowledge of Sanskrit was quite weak as he was making mistakes in his interpretations. He finally inferred that there was an impact of some Brahmarakshasa due to which these children lost their lives at an early age and advised the family to conduct a special pooja and do an offering of paal payasam (sweet-porridge made of milk, rice and sugar) in any Shri Krishna temple. 
Listening to this story, I fully agreed with Veliachan that this was a hoax but my reasons differed with his. In the beginning, I was under the belief that if such a ritual should have been conducted, then it should have been done in a temple aligned to Mother Goddess or Lord Shiva as both the Divine Beings have direct control over such paranormal entities. But later I was inclined to correct myself as this is a Brahmarakshasa. The astrologer's inference of 3 deaths based on the 3 firecrackers felt questionable to me as temples in Kerala have strict adherence to time and discipline. This person should have come at a time when there was some ongoing special pooja in the temple and naturally firecrackers would be burst. Even though I found it hard to believe, I still could let go of this argument but how did he come to the conclusion of a Brahmarakshasa? There must be some evidence based on the being's behaviour to come to that conclusion.
So, who is a Brahmarakshasa? We usually do not hear the words, "Brahma" and "Rakshasa" in the same word in today's world. As per my research there are many theories about the origin of a Brahmarakshasa. One such theory is that a Brahmin who is learned and strictly follows austerities; yet has committed sins in his life will fall into a "pret" (ghost) yoni due to his severe sins. But a Brahmarakshasa cannot be categorized as just an ordinary "pret atma". He gets the rank of a Rakshas because, this is a Brahmin who has done his studies in Vedas, is very learned and therefore a very strong being at a soul level. Unlike ordinary “pret atma”, a Brahmarakshasa is believed to be very powerful and holds strong abilities. Anyone born as a Brahmin but who does not follow or live as a Brahmin (like no janau ritual and does not follow the traditions of Brahmins) is considered to be just an ordinary person. Even if he has sinned, he cannot become a Brahmarakshasa on his death. 
Another belief is that any Brahmin who had an untimely death also could become a Brahmarakshasa. In this belief, an unmarried Brahmin who follows his austerities but has an untimely death is believed to become a very powerful Brahmarakshasa. This is because he has lot of goals and desires which are unfulfilled due to untimely death. Another theory is that a Brahmin is expected to impart knowledge through a shishya. Failing to do so will turn him into a Brahmarakshasa on his death. Such a mention is there in the legend of Chakravarthy Vikramaditya whose father Vidyasagar gained lot of knowledge from a Brahmarakshasa. This particular being was him cursed as he did not impart his knowledge to anyone during his lifetime and that his salvation would be if he found a deserving pupil and imparted his entire knowledge to him. These are common beliefs in this Yuga. 
There is yet another literature on these beings. The literature on Brahmarakshas and the wisdom of Brahmarakshasa is infused into the Kaulantak Peeth tradition whose Mahaguru is Shukracharya himself. According to the Siddha Dharma, the Brahmarakshas is the first rakshasa created by Lord Brahma with pure tamas characteristics. The rakshasa learnt a lot of tamasic vidyas from Lord Shiva himself through "Guru/Shishya" sampradaay. Shukracharya learn't this from Lord Shiva and imbibed it to Kali Rakshasa. In this Siddha Dharma, the Brahmarakshas sadhana is done to attain sookshtar body. The iconography of the Brahmarakshasa mentioned as per Siddha Dharma is completely different from the popular believes in the examples mentioned above. A lot of literature on Brahmaraksha is available in "Brahma Raksha Kalpa" authored by the first Brahmarakshasa (literature credits to kaulantak peeth)
Brahmarakshasa - Abode and traits: Popular belief says that Brahmarakshasa identifies a Peepul tree and chooses to live there until such time they get liberated from such an existence. In Hinduism, the Peepul tree is believed to be the abode of Lord Brahma. So how does one identify if a Peepul tree is occupied by a Brahmarakshasa or by Lord Brahma?  When a Peepul tree rots from the bottom but is fresh on the top such a tree is supposed to be the abode of Brahmarakshasa. The moment the Brahmarakshasa leaves the tree, the Peepul tree is believed to immediately catch fire or die. This reference is seen in the life history of Sant Tulsidas who inadvertently gives moksha to a Brahmarakshasa. In return, the being tells Tulsidas that only Lord Hanuman can lead him to Lord Ram. The Brahmarakshasa also informs Tulsidas that Lord Hanuman attends his Ram Katha sessions every day. The being goes so far as to help Tulsidas to identify Lord Hanuman from his audience.  
The Brahmarakshasa are reputed to be more than 7 to 8 feet tall, powerful beings with canine teeth and in some references sport the Brahmin's choti (traditional tuft of hair at the back of the head as per the Brahmin tradition). It is said that these beings are very learned and can recite Sanskrit slokas and mantras in much more purity than living human beings. They will even accompany you in your chants of the mantras, if done in their presence. They retain their original knowledge and acquire more knowledge with immense powers and special abilities. These powerful beings prefer to reside silently on Peepul trees and are never ever visible to anyone. When humans disturb their abode or malign their surroundings, they get irritated and start to trouble the humans. They are hugely powerful beings with various abilities and they can either destroy the peace or lives of humans, sometimes even consuming them or they can even grant lots of success and wealth if they are pleased. It is reputed that if you get on the wrong side of a Brahmarakshasa, then no human has sufficient powers to save you. Only the Gods can protect you from their attack. It is said a Brahmarakshasa cannot be easily killed, it can be liberated only by an equally powerful and learned Brahmana (case in point, Sant Tulsidas). There have been references to true incidents related to the presence of Brahmarakshasa at least in 2 incidents that I have heard (one from Madhya Pradesh and another from Bihar) where these beings have been disturbed and have therefore troubled the surrounding humans. There is still a lot of information that is yet to be known about these dangerous beings. All my knowledge come from people who research on this topic or the tantra saadhaks.
So why this lengthy write-up about the Brahmarakshasa? Let me come back to my father's tale in the morning. Did those children really lose their lives due to the attack of a Brahmarakshasa? No, I do not personally believe so. None of my father’s explanations point towards any evidence of the presence of a Brahmarakshasa around the area. The children of India in those times were prone to lot of diseases thereby, many of them died an early death due to lack of knowledge and/or poor medical facilities. While I personally believe this to be the case in these children, Father also mentioned other interesting facts. Though Veliachan did not believe in this, the family did complete the pooja and the offering in a far-away Shri Krishna temple. Father also mentioned that in those days, there was a custom of installing "parakuttichaathan" in any new place that the people buy. Though no one in their right mind will willingly invoke and install a Brahmarakshasa around their living abodes, a parakuttichaathan is a different case. But that is a story for another day.

- Pramila Sankarankutty

​Chapter 1: The Illusion of Perfection
​The rain over Mumbai fell not in drops, but in heavy, rhythmic sheets that washed over the paved driveway of the Roy mansion. Outside the iron gates, bright flashes from media cameras illuminated the deluge every few seconds.
​Reporters shoved microphones toward Mr. Indrajit Roy, a high-profile politician whose face was a carefully crafted mask of sorrow, and his wife, Sunita, a former leading actress weeping dramatically into a silk handkerchief.
​"Please, give our family privacy during this tragic hour," Indrajit pleaded into the sea of microphones, his voice cracking with rehearsed emotion. "Our daughter Tia has been our rock through all of this. She is a blessing."
​Standing quietly under the shaded archway of the grand entrance, eighteen-year-old Tia watched her parents' performance. Her face was completely still, her eyes reflecting the cold grey of the storm. As another camera flash caught her profile, her lips subtly parted.
​Away from the reporters, away from her parents' sight, a cold, chilling smile spread across Tia’s face. She knew the truth. Her parents didn't care about their children; they only cared about the headlines. But what nobody in that media circus realized was that the girl standing in the shadows wasn't who they thought she was.
​Chapter 2: Shadows in the Corridor
​The next morning, the sky cleared over the bustling grounds of St. Xavier’s College. In the BBA department corridor, the air was thick with the usual noise of students, but near the end lockers, a quiet cruelty was unfolding.
​Tisha, a shy second-year student, stood pinned against the locker doors. Three senior bullies surrounded her, mocking her clothes and knocking her notebooks onto the floor. Dozens of students walked past, casting brief glances before looking away, unwilling to get involved.
​"What's the matter, Tisha? Forgot your voice today?" the lead bully sneered, shoving her shoulder.
​Before he could strike again, a heavy hand grabbed the bully’s collar and violently shoved him back.
​"Touch her again, and you’ll answer to me," Riyansh growled, stepping in front of Tisha like an impenetrable shield. Riyansh was well-known on campus—protective, headstrong, and fearless.
​Behind him stood Tia, watching silently as Riyansh scattered the bullies with a single glare. Tia stepped forward, her voice soft and comforting as she helped Tisha gather her scattered books. "Are you okay, Tisha? Don't let them scare you."
​Lequally, down the long, sunlit corridor, another figure stood in the shadows near the stairs.
​It was Megha. Dressed in standard college attire, her face was a exact mirror image of Tia’s. She watched Riyansh shield Tisha, and as she looked at his hands, her eyes narrowed. Slowly, terrifyingly, her calm expression morphed into a look of raw, unhinged venom.
​Megha marched down the hall, her footsteps echoing loudly. She grabbed Tia’s wrist with a grip so tight it left white marks.
​"Is Riyansh falling for you... or for that pathetic girl he just saved?" Megha whispered, her breath hot against Tia's ear. Her eyes darted wildly. "He belongs to me, Tia. You know what happens when someone takes what's mine."
​Tia kept her face completely blank, her voice remaining unnervingly calm. "You're overthinking, Megha. He was just helping her."
​Chapter 3: Sins of the Past
​The roots of this obsession were planted ten years ago inside the cold, marble walls of the Roy estate.
​When Tia and Megha were eleven, their home was not a sanctuary, but a gilded cage. Indrajit Roy was climbing the political ladder, while Sunita was consumed by her acting career. The twins were left entirely to paid caretakers. To their parents, the identical girls were indistinguishable—just two identical props for family photo shoots.
​Starved of affection, Megha’s mind twisted. She realized early on that good behavior got no attention, but destruction did. She began small—sabotaging the kitchen appliances, pushing an elderly servant down the back stairs, and burning Tia's school projects. But instead of love, she received screams and harsh punishments, which only fed her internal darkness.
​The breaking point came when they turned thirteen. Tia won first place in a prestigious state mathematics Olympiad. Spotting an opportunity for political PR, Indrajit hosted a lavish victory gala at their mansion.
​Under the blinding party lights, Sunita showered Tia with kisses for the news cameras, while Indrajit paraded her in front of high-society guests. In the dark corner of the second-floor terrace, thirteen-year-old Megha watched the parents she craved love from treat Tia like a queen.
​"It should have been me," Megha spat, stepping out onto the stormy terrace where Tia stood taking a breath of fresh air.
​"Megha, please, calm down—" Tia started, but she never finished her sentence.
​With a scream of pure rage, Megha lunged forward and shoved Tia over the stone balustrade.
​Tia’s body hit the courtyard below with a sickening thud.
​Chapter 4: The Great Theft
​The night of the fall was total chaos. Rain poured over the ambulance as paramedics rushed Tia's broken body to the ICU. Outside the emergency room, reporters swarmed Indrajit Roy.
​Panicked, flustered, and having never taken the time to actually learn the subtle differences between his twin daughters, Indrajit spoke blindly into the microphones: "Our heart breaks tonight. Our daughter... Megha... has fallen from the terrace and is in a coma."
​Inside the waiting room, thirteen-year-old Megha overheard her father’s mistake. Her heart hammered against her ribs. In that split second, a horrific idea took root.
​If the world believed Megha was the one lying half-dead in the hospital, then the girl standing in the hallway was Tia. The golden child. The loved one.
​From that night on, Megha stepped into Tia’s life. She moved into Tia’s room, wore her clothes, and sat at the dining table receiving the praise she had craved her entire life. To keep up the lie, Megha spent her nights staying up until dawn with private tutors, desperately studying advanced mathematics and copying Tia's graceful handwriting until her fingers bled.
​Meanwhile, miles away in a state hospital, the real Tia lay in a deep, lifeless coma. Deemed the "troublesome, broken child" by her parents, she was placed in a private room with paid nurses and completely forgotten.
​Four years passed. One rainy afternoon, the real Tia opened her eyes.
​When she finally recovered and returned home, she discovered her entire existence had been stolen. But Tia did not scream, nor did she go to the police. She looked at her sister—who was now drowning in anxiety, terrified of being caught—and played the ultimate long game.
​Tia forced Megha into a silent compromise: Megha would take a separate entrance exam and enter St. Xavier’s as a BCom first-year student, while Tia reclaimed her rightful place in the BBA second-year program under Megha's former identity.
​Chapter 5: Room Number 7
​Back in the present day, Megha’s mind had fractured completely. Being separated from Riyansh by different academic blocks drove her into a state of acute paranoia.
​It was 6:00 PM on a Friday. The campus was nearly empty.
​In the abandoned basement of the arts block—Room Number 7—the air smelled of damp concrete and rust. Tied to wooden chairs were three female students, including Tisha. Their mouths were taped, their eyes wide with sheer terror.
​Standing before them was Megha. On a dusty desk nearby, a laptop was live-streaming a camera feed directly to a monitor in an adjacent room where Riyansh had been lured and locked inside.
​"He looked at you," Megha whispered, her voice dangerously soft as she caressed a heavy iron rod. "He smiled at you in the corridor. Nobody looks at what belongs to me."
​Suddenly, a loud bang echoed through the building. The flickering overhead bulbs buzzed violently before dying completely. The entire college was plunged into pitch-black darkness as the main power grid failed.
​From the dark corner of Room 7, a figure stepped out of the shadows.
​It was Tia.
​Before Megha could react, Tia swung a heavy wooden plank, striking Megha across the shoulder and knocking her to the ground. Tia quickly ripped the tape off Tisha's mouth. "Run! Get to the main gate and find the security guards!" Tia ordered.
​Tisha and the girls scrambled out into the dark hallway, their frantic footsteps fading into the distance.
​Chapter 6: The Final Smile
​Tia turned and ran toward the upper floors to free Riyansh, but the shadows in the hallway seemed to move.
​Emerging from the darkness behind her was Megha. Her hair was completely wild, her uniform torn at the shoulder, and a terrifying, demonic laugh echoed off the concrete walls. She sprinted with supernatural, frantic speed, her fingernails scraping against the locker doors.
​"You took my life once, Tia!" Megha shrieked, lunging at her sister as they burst through the double doors onto the stormy first-floor balcony. "This time, I’m not sending you to a coma! I’m finishing you!"
​Rain lashed against their faces as the twins grappled on the slick stone floor. They fought with a viciousness born of ten years of hidden hatred.
​Riyansh, having kicked open the basement door, raced up the stairwell and burst onto the balcony. The sight stopped him dead in his tracks.
​In the dim emergency lights and blinding rain, two identical faces were locked in a deadly struggle. Their clothes were soaked, their hair matted over their faces.
​"Riyansh! Help me! She's crazy!" one screamed.
​"Don't listen to her! She tried to kill those girls!" the other shrieked.
​Riyansh took a step back, his dimaag completely sunn. He couldn't tell who was Tia and who was Megha.
​Before he could make a move, police sirens blared from the courtyard below. Red and blue lights flashed against the pouring rain. Tisha had brought the authorities.
​In that second of distraction, the sister on top delivered a brutal strike to the other's temple, dazing her. She stood up smoothly, grabbed the dazed girl by her collar, and with a single, ruthless movement, heaved her over the stone balcony railing.
​A sickening crash echoed from the courtyard below as the body struck the pavement near the police cruisers.
​Riyansh screamed in horror, running past the surviving sister and sprinting down the stairs to help the officers surrounding the motionless body in the rain.
​Up on the dark, empty balcony, the storm raged on.
​The surviving twin stood alone at the ledge, watching the flashing red and blue lights below. Down in the courtyard, her parents were already arriving, stepping out of their luxury car and bursting into fake, hysterical tears for the news cameras that had followed the police.
​Slowly, the girl on the balcony wiped the rainwater from her face. Her shivering stopped. Her chest settled into a calm, steady rhythm.
​She turned her face toward the dark sky. The terrified, tear-streaked expression melted away entirely.
​In its place, a cold, calculated, and deeply evil smile spread across her lips—a smile full of dark victory, identical to the one born in the shadows ten years ago.
​She looked down at her hands, adjusted her posture, and smoothed down her clothes. The game was over, and the golden child had taken back her throne.
​[THE END]

दूसरा प्रेम तब हुआ जब जीवन की समझ कम थी मगर दिल में बेचैनी और ख़ुशी के सारे ऐहसासात थे वो लड़की भी बहुत प्यारी थी हम साथ में ट्यूशन पढ़ते थे, एक किस्सा है वो ट्यूशन सुबह जल्दी आ गई थी, अकेले बैठना उसको मंजूर नहीं था तो उसने आके मेरा दरवाजा खटखटाया और कहा साथ चलो, मैं उसके साथ बिना सवाल किये चला गया, उन दिनों मौसम सर्द था तो मैंने कुछ कागज लिए और उन्हें जलाया फिर अपने हाथ गर्म करने लगा, हुआ यूँ उसने भी अपने हाथ मेरे हाथों पर रख दिये, वो पहला स्पर्श इतना प्यारा, सारे दिलों को उसने हाथों की तरह नर्म होना चाहिये, खैर मैं कभी इज़हार तो नहीं कर पाया शायद वो समझती थी, ये प्रेम गीता-क़ुरान की तरह पाक था, मगर इसको पाना ना मुमकिन था, और इस जगमगाते प्रेम का गला एक गलतफहमी ने घोंट दिया……..

Was never bestowed upon me

Was most alluring to me
And maybe I felt like I had something to prove
A deep pressure, an internal struggle roaring within me
Backed by the years of taunts of the demons whose origins I did not know
Were they born in my own mind
Or did they arise from subtle remarks gradually accrued from the world
Telling me that my life is meaningless unless I pushed myself
To be unique, to defy the norm
And head towards the path travelled by few
The trail, though having soft impressionable soil, was devoid of footsteps I could walk in
A rose-coloured mist suffused throughout the road, enticing me, yet obstructing my view
For hidden amongst the soft blades of grass
Were thorns I could not navigate and thickets I could not clear
Interlaced with a dense fog, suffocating me with every step
Brambles scratching mercilessly at my thighs
The effects of which still relentlessly persist in the form of jagged, immortal scars

And here I find myself on yet another journey
Standing before a fork in the road once more
And this time, I gingerly take the first step onto the path familiar to me
A road where every pebble knows my name
Where the trees bow to the sound of my footsteps

I'll step onto the trodden road this time

The sky was painted with the colour of devotion,
The universe was awaiting a divine creation.

She ran towards Him with Her anklets jingling in ecstasy.
The dried leaves that touched Her feet on the way
Were blessed with life; nothing could make Her path delay.

Her long hair decorated with jasmine and marigolds,
With every step, pure dignity she holds.
Her mind lost in His flute’s euphony,
Her heart built of sanctity, reflecting pure transparency.

The blue butterflies sat on Her forehead,
To be witness to love that’s painted in red.
Her face reflected the euphoria she could experience,
Who else could explain that the art of waiting is also a deep science?

She passed through the breeze, and pebbles did hurt Her heel,
But the jubilation she had, no other could feel.
Her eyes waited only to dive into His,
Her lips chanting His name and feeling the bliss.

The old memories flashed back in Her mind,
Her love helped Her see the absolute truth and not be blind.
The colours of Holi that filled the air of Vrindavan,
And with Him she gazed at the rising moon and the setting sun.

The pots He used to break and the Maakhan He used to eat,
Their strong bond, no enmity could defeat.

Radha and Krishna are eternal, not like a couple dating.

They were two bodies with one soul,

Krishna left Vrindavan for the duties He had to fulfill,
Radha waited behind, to meet Her love who was in Her heart, still.

They came to teach that true love never makes you hold,
But gives you the courage to stand strong and bold.
Radha taught the world the art of waiting in love and devotion,
Krishna’s duty was to teach how to deal with life’s most threatening situation.

THE COUNTRY I LEFT TWICE : 

A Medical Student’s Story of War, Escape, and Finding Home Again

Before the War -

When I first chose Ukraine, I did not know that one day I would measure my life by the moments before and after a war.

I had finished school and was looking for a place where I could study medicine. There were several options in front of me. Italy. Poland. Ukraine.

In the end, Ukraine felt familiar.

I had studied about the country in history. I knew its name before I knew its streets. I knew that Kharkiv had once been the capital of Soviet Ukraine and that the city carried a strong Russian influence. I knew almost nothing about what it would feel like to live there.

I arrived in Kharkiv with my father and my maternal uncle.

For the first few days, I did not even stay in my hostel room.

A room had been allotted to me, but everything felt unfamiliar—the country, the language, the city, the idea of living so far from home. So I stayed at the Iris Art Hotel while my father and uncle were still with me.

Those first days remain among the warmest memories I have of Ukraine.

We ate at the hotel. We walked around the city. We went to Eco Park and Gorky Park. We saw V. N. Karazin University and Kharkiv National Medical University. I was beginning to understand the place that would become my home for the next few years.

Then, after about five days, my father and uncle had to leave.

I cried.

I had not expected their departure to affect me so much. They had brought me there, helped me settle in, and suddenly I was standing in a foreign country without them.

Before leaving, they had bought food for me.

Some of it remained uneaten.

I kept it.

At the time, I could not explain why. Perhaps I simply wanted something that belonged to the life I had known before Ukraine.

I did not know then that I would eventually become the person who would leave Ukraine carrying memories instead of luggage.

⸻

The Country I Came to 'Love' -

Life slowly became ordinary.

And ordinary life, I later learned, is one of the things war takes away first.

Ukraine was beautiful.

The air often felt fresh. The country seemed spacious and full of nature. There were parks, trees, long streets, old buildings, lively places, quiet corners and the particular feeling of a city in which you were gradually becoming comfortable.

I was a medical student. My days were filled with lectures, classes, practicals, books, exams and the usual worries of medical school.

I learned Ukrainian.

I learned Russian.

In Kharkiv, both languages were part of everyday life.

Eventually, I was no longer living in the hostel. I had an apartment with Dr. Shrivastava, and life had settled into a routine.

The future still seemed predictable.

I would finish medical school.

I would become a doctor.

I would go home.

War belonged to history books.

At least, that was what I believed.

⸻

The Morning Everything Changed - 

For months, there had been rumours.

Tensions were rising. People talked about Russia. News reports appeared. Conversations changed.

But rumours are strange things.

They can become part of everyday life without ever becoming real.

At our university, students had been reassured repeatedly. We had heard variations of the same message for months.

Nothing had happened.

Why would something happen now?

The question sounded reasonable.

Until one morning, something did.

It was early—around six in the morning.

I saw flashes outside.

For a moment, they looked almost like fireworks.

Then my phone rang.

It was Dr. Swain.

Shelling.

Not fireworks.

Shelling.

I was confused. Frightened. Still half inside sleep.

Dr. Shrivastava was already awake. She told me that the shelling had been going on for two or three hours.

I had slept through calls.

I had slept through the beginning of the war.

That realization was terrifying.

Outside, Kharkiv was changing.

The city I knew was still physically there, but something invisible had broken.

The word war was no longer something I read in a newspaper.

It was outside my window.

⸻

Five Days - 

The first instinct was survival.

Food.

Water.

Money.

Information.

People rushed to shops.

The shelves emptied.

Prices rose.

Things that had seemed completely ordinary became valuable.

Chips, for example, could suddenly cost two or three times what they normally did.

I bought what I could.

Ten packets of noodles.

Four large cans of water.

Chocolates.

We already had flour, rice, lentils and vegetables in the apartment, but suddenly even the food already sitting in our kitchen looked different.

It was no longer simply food.

It was time.

Every packet meant another meal.

Every bottle of water meant another day.

At one point, I found an ATM that still had cash. Other ATMs were empty.

The electricity remained.

The water remained.

The gas remained.

That almost made the situation stranger.

How could everything still be functioning when the world outside was falling apart?

We began using blackout curtains.

We used phone torches when necessary.

We tried to cook.

I made one thin roti for myself.

I also made half a packet of noodles for Dr. Shrivastava and kept the other half for myself.

It sounds insignificant now.

But during those days, every small action carried weight.

There were shelters.

There was the metro.

Kharkiv’s metro stations became places of refuge.

I remember their beauty even in those circumstances.

Marble.

Lights.

Large underground spaces.

At times, the stations looked almost like wedding halls.

But people were not there to celebrate.

They were there because the ground above them was dangerous.

And something else happened underground that I will never forget.

People shared.

Ukrainians offered food.

They understood that many Indian students had dietary restrictions, particularly around beef and vegetarian food. In shelters, metro stations, shops and during evacuation, Indians were often given consideration.

In the middle of a war, strangers tried to make sure strangers could eat.

That is one of the memories I carry with me.

War can reveal cruelty.

But it can also reveal kindness.

Sometimes the kindness comes from people who have no reason to offer it.

⸻

Mr. and Mrs. Livon - 

Our apartment owner was Mr. Livon.

He was an older man and a former police officer.

His wife was kind.

They were not simply names connected to an apartment anymore. They had become part of the strange community of people surrounding us during those years.

There were birthdays when they brought chocolates and flowers.

There were ordinary conversations.

There were moments that now feel impossibly distant from the war.

I remember Mr. Livon singing the Raj Kapoor song, “Mera joota hai japani…”

A song from India, sung by a Ukrainian man.

Those moments became precious because they belonged to the world before everything became about survival.

I still hope that one day, after completing my licensing exams and beginning to earn as a doctor, I can return and visit Mr. and Mrs. Livon.

Some people become part of your life without ever knowing how deeply you remember them.

⸻

The Decision to Leave - 

For five days, we stayed.

Five days of uncertainty.

Five days of trying to understand whether things would improve.

Five days of hearing explosions and wondering what would happen next.

By the sixth day, we decided to leave.

It was not one simple decision.

Leaving meant abandoning our apartments.

Our belongings.

Our books.

Our clothes.

The small things we had collected while building a life there.

We packed documents.

We packed only what we could carry.

The rest remained in the wardrobe.

I remember believing that perhaps we would return.

That thought made leaving possible.

We would go temporarily.

The situation would settle.

We would come back.

That was what I told myself.

We planned to leave with Dr. Shrivastava, her friends and my friends.

Taxi applications were not working properly.

Eventually, sometime around 3:30 or 4:00 in the morning, we began walking toward the railway station—Vokzal.

It was roughly a kilometre away.

The streets were dark.

We carried what we could.

The city that had once felt alive was almost unrecognizable.

I kept thinking about the things I had left behind.

Clothes.

Books.

Memories.

An entire version of myself.

We reached the station.

And eventually, we boarded the train.

⸻

The Train - 

The train moved slowly.

Very slowly.

The lights were kept off because of the danger from fighter jets.

Inside the darkness, people were trying to remain quiet.

Trying to understand where they were going.

Trying not to think too far ahead.

The train eventually reached the Poland–Ukraine border.

There was another reality there.

Women and children were being prioritized.

Men remained behind.

People were separated by circumstances none of them had chosen.

I watched.

I listened.

I tried to understand what was happening.

Only days earlier, I had been a medical student going to classes.

Now I was a person crossing a border because the country where I lived was at war.

⸻

Leaving Without Leaving - 

I eventually reached Poland and then India.

But reaching safety did not mean the story ended.

That is something people who have never experienced displacement may find difficult to understand.

You can leave a dangerous place physically while remaining there emotionally.

Part of me was still in Kharkiv.

In the apartment.

In the metro.

On those streets.

With the things I had left in the wardrobe.

With the people I had met.

With the ordinary life that had disappeared almost overnight.

For a while, I thought leaving Ukraine meant I had lost the country that had become my second home.

But life is rarely that simple.

I returned to Ukraine.

Not to Kharkiv.

This time, I was in Ternopil.

Perhaps returning was my way of proving to myself that Ukraine was not only the place where a war had happened.

It was also the place where I had once been happy.

Where I had studied.

Where I had grown.

Where I had imagined my future.

But the war had changed the meaning of return.

Missiles and uncertainty were still part of reality.

Eventually, I left Ukraine again.

The country I had once entered with luggage and excitement was now a country I was leaving with memories.

Twice.

⸻

The War Inside - 

People often imagine war as explosions.

They imagine buildings collapsing.

Sirens.

Smoke.

Soldiers.

Trains full of refugees.

Those things are real.

But there is another war that is harder to explain.

The war that continues inside you.

It changes the way you hear sounds.

The way you react to silence.

The way you think about safety.

Before the invasion, I could hear a sudden loud noise and simply hear a loud noise.

Afterward, a sound could make the body react before the mind understood why.

War changes your relationship with ordinary things.

A packet of noodles can remind you of scarcity.

A train can remind you of escape.

A metro station can remind you of shelter.

A song can take you back to a room thousands of kilometres away.

A piece of uneaten food can remind you of your father.

And an empty wardrobe can remind you that sometimes you leave a place without knowing whether you will ever return.

⸻

What I Learned - 

I went to Ukraine to become a doctor.

I learned medicine there.

But I also learned things no textbook could have taught me.

I learned that plans can disappear overnight.

I learned that certainty is fragile.

I learned that people can be afraid and still move forward.

I learned that strangers can become helpers.

I learned that a country can become part of you even if you were not born there.

Most importantly, I learned that home is not always a single place.

Sometimes home is a city.

Sometimes it is a person.

Sometimes it is a language.

Sometimes it is a memory.

And sometimes home is simply the version of yourself that existed somewhere and somewhen.

⸻

The Country I Left Twice - 

I often think about the girl who first arrived in Kharkiv.

She was nervous.

She was carrying the expectations of a family that had sent her abroad to become a doctor.

She did not know the streets.

She did not know the language.

She did not know that the country she had chosen would eventually teach her more about fear and courage than any classroom could.

She did not know that she would one day run toward a railway station before dawn.

She did not know that she would leave her belongings behind.

She did not know that she would return.

And she certainly did not know that she would have to leave again.

If I could speak to that girl now, I would tell her something simple:

You will be afraid.

You will not understand everything.

There will be days when you will want to go home.

There will be days when you will miss the life you had before.

But one day, you will understand that surviving something does not mean forgetting it.

It means carrying it differently.

Ukraine was not only the country where I experienced war.

It was also the country where I became an adult.

It gave me memories before it gave me fear.

It gave me friendships, education, independence, beauty and countless ordinary days.

And perhaps that is why leaving was so difficult.

I was not simply leaving a country.

I was leaving a part of my life.

The first time I left Ukraine, I believed I would return.

The second time, I understood that some returns are not meant to be physical.

Sometimes you return through memory.

Through photographs.

Through stories.

Through the people you remember.

Through the places that remain alive inside you long after you have gone.

I still remember Kharkiv.

The parks.

The university.

The apartment.

The metro.

The food.

The streets.

The people.

The darkness of that early morning.

The slow train.

The border.

And the feeling of looking back at a country that had become home without ever asking permission.

I left Ukraine twice.

But Ukraine never completely left me.

⸻

Epilogue - 

Years later, when I think about those days, I no longer see only the war.

I see the life that existed before it.

That matters.

Because a country should not be remembered only by its destruction.

Ukraine was more than the explosions.

It was the fresh air.

The parks.

The old streets.

The languages.

The university corridors.

The people who shared food.

The couple who brought chocolates and flowers.

The song Mr. Livon sang.

The thin roti I made when I was frightened.

The noodles divided into two portions.

The belongings left in a wardrobe.

The train that carried us away.

And the young medical student who believed she would return.

Maybe that is what memory does.

It takes a place that history reduces to a headline and gives it back its ordinary life.

I cannot change what happened.

I cannot bring back the days before the war.

I cannot erase the fear.

But I can remember.

And I can write.

Because sometimes writing is another way of returning home.

And this is my return.

To the country I left twice.

To the country that taught me that survival is not merely escaping danger.

Sometimes survival is finding the courage to remember what you loved before the world changed.

And continuing to live after it does.

If I could choose!
How I live,
Even for just a day.

I would start as a blind,
Keeping my eyes wide open
Just to admire darkness!

And continue as a deaf,
Keeping my ears tuned in
Just to vibe to silence!

Why not a mute,
Having my thoughts engulfing me
Just to scream hush!

Let Alzheimer’s take over me,
Making enchanting memories
Just to remember void!

Where will they live? 

If a bird and a fish fall in love, where will they stay?
One was made for the sky, the other couldn't live that way.
She dreamed of flying beside him through the blue,
He dreamed of finding a world where she could too.

She'd wait by the water when the evening grew cold,
He'd swim to the surface just to watch her unfold.
They knew they were different, but love felt so right,
So they kept choosing each other, night after night.

She tried to stay closer, he tried to come near,
They both knew the distance, but ignored every fear.
She wished for the ocean, he wished for the air,
Both slowly forgetting that neither belonged there.

Then one day she whispered, “Maybe we should let go,”
He smiled like he knew, though it hurt him to know.
She flew toward the sunset, he sank with the tide,
And neither looked back at the other that night.

The next morning, the shore looked just the same,
The waves kept moving, the sky stayed the same.
No one knew why neither had come back that day,
Or why their little meeting place felt so far away.

She went looking for him where her wings couldn't fly,
And he followed her there, forgetting he couldn't survive the sky.

Chapter 1 — The Past We Carried

Maya had always believed that the sea remembered people.

Every morning in Blackwood Cove, the tide arrived carrying the same salt air, the same gull cries, and the same distant rhythm of boats returning to the harbor.

Yet the town never felt exactly the same.

People changed.

Children grew older.

Friendships became complicated.

Promises were made and sometimes broken.

She first met Nikki in Class 6.

They were classmates, and the friendship began easily.

Nikki was confident and outspoken, the sort of girl who could turn a quiet classroom into a conversation.

Maya was quieter, thoughtful, and careful about what she shared.

They studied together, traded jokes during lunch, and walked home along the same road after school.

One afternoon, Nikki invited Maya to her house to study.

Books covered the table, but neither girl was paying much attention to them.

They talked about school, teachers, and the future.

Then Nikki crossed a boundary Maya did not want crossed.

Maya immediately stepped back.

“Nikki, what are you doing?

I don’t like this.

I’m straight, and I want us to just be friends.”

Nikki went quiet.

The room suddenly felt much smaller.

Before either girl could say more, Nikki’s mother entered and understood that something was wrong.

She spoke firmly to Nikki and reassured Maya that she had done nothing wrong.

Maya left that afternoon with the uncomfortable feeling that childhood had changed in a single moment.

She did not hate Nikki.

In fact, she continued to care about her as a friend.

But Maya learned to keep a clear boundary.

Years later, she would remember that lesson whenever she felt uncertain about where friendship ended and something deeper began.

As Maya grew older, her life appeared simple from the outside.

She fell in love with a boy she had known since school.

He was kind, familiar, and part of the future she imagined.

When they began a relationship, Maya believed she finally understood herself.

Marriage, a home, a career, perhaps children—her future seemed like a road already marked on a map.

Chapter 2 — New Beginnings

What had begun as friendship slowly became the most anticipated part of Maya’s day.

She and Elena studied together, shared meals, and walked along the coast after classes.

Sometimes they talked for hours.

Other times they sat without speaking, watching fishing boats move across the horizon.

Maya was surprised by how comfortable silence felt with Elena.

With her boyfriend, she often felt she needed to explain herself.

With Elena, she could simply exist.

Then Elena told Maya that she had to leave the country with her parents for a family visit.

The trip was supposed to be temporary, but no one could say exactly how long it would last.

“I don’t know how long I’ll be gone,” Elena said at the harbor.

“Take care of yourself,” Maya replied.

“You too.”

Neither moved for a moment.

Maya wanted to hug her but hesitated.

Elena seemed to notice the hesitation, yet she did not make Maya uncomfortable.

She only smiled and stepped closer.

“I’ll message you,” Elena said.

Maya watched her leave.

“Maya?” She turned.

Chapter 3 — Something Unspoken

When Elena returned from abroad, Maya discovered that distance had not weakened her feelings.

If anything, the time apart had made them impossible to ignore.

The moment Elena appeared on campus, Maya felt the old rush of happiness.

Elena smiled as though no time had passed.

“You missed me?” Elena asked.

“Maybe a little,” Maya said, looking away.

“Only a little?”

Maya laughed.

“Don’t get used to compliments.”

Their friendship became closer.

They shared lunches, studied late, and explored parts of Blackwood Cove Maya had never noticed before.

Elena introduced her to a small viewpoint above the harbor where the ocean seemed endless.

Meanwhile Nikki prepared to leave again for a job abroad.

Before leaving, she met Maya for coffee.

Maya smiled.

Chapter 4 — Closer Than Before

Maya and Elena became inseparable.

Their days developed small rituals: coffee in the morning, messages during lectures, walks after class, and long conversations near the harbor.

Maya still had a boyfriend, and that fact increasingly troubled her.

She knew she was keeping part of her life hidden.

The guilt did not disappear simply because her feelings were genuine.

One evening, Elena found Maya sitting alone near the beach.

“Are you happy?” Elena asked.

Maya hesitated.

“I don’t know anymore.”

Elena sat beside her but kept a respectful distance.

“You don’t owe me an answer,” she said.

Maya looked at her.

“That’s the problem.

I think I owe myself one.”

The words frightened her.

Saying them aloud made the uncertainty real.

Elena slowly reached for Maya’s hand.

Maya looked down.

She knew she could pull away.

She didn’t.

Chapter 5 — The Confession

For several days Maya rehearsed words she could never say.

She wrote messages and deleted them.

She imagined conversations and ended each one before it began.

Eventually she understood that silence was becoming another form of dishonesty.

She met Elena near the sea at sunset.

The sky was pale gold, and the first evening lights were appearing along the harbor.

“I need to tell you something,” Maya said.

Elena waited.

“I don’t understand what is happening to me.”

Maya took a breath.

“But I think I’ve fallen for you.”

Elena’s expression softened.

“I’ve been waiting for you to say that.”

Maya looked down.

“What does this make me?”

“It makes you Maya,” Elena said.

“Someone who discovered a feeling she didn’t expect.”

Maya laughed through her tears.

“You make everything sound simple.”

“It isn’t simple.

Chapter 6 — The Distance Between Us

Maya’s past returned sooner than she expected.

Her childhood boyfriend came home from abroad after completing his higher education.

Seeing him at the harbor brought back memories of school corridors, shared plans, and years of believing they would always be together.

He quickly learned about Elena.

The truth was painful because Maya had not ended the old relationship before beginning the new one.

Whatever her feelings had become, she had cheated on him.

“You could have told me,” he said.

Maya lowered her eyes.

“I was afraid.”

“Afraid of hurting me?”

“Yes.

And afraid of what the truth meant about me.”

He was silent for a long time.

“The truth still hurts,” he said.

Maya nodded.

It was measured in broken trust.

Chapter 7 — A Night by the Ocean

After the difficult weeks that followed, Maya and Elena needed one evening without explanations.

They walked to a quiet beach after sunset.

The moon painted a silver path across the water.

“I don’t want to lose you,” Maya said.

Elena reached for her hand.

“You don’t have to lose me tonight.”

They walked barefoot beside the waves.

Maya told Elena stories from childhood.

Elena told Maya about learning to sail and about the first time she realized The Blue Horizon was more than a family business—it was a part of her identity.

They laughed over small memories.

Then they sat together on the sand.

“Sometimes,” Elena said.

Maya closed her eyes.

Chapter 8 — Falling a Little Deeper

Love did not arrive for Maya as one dramatic transformation.

It arrived through ordinary moments.

Morning coffee.

A message during a busy afternoon.

Elena remembering exactly how Maya liked her tea.

Maya leaving a note in Elena’s bag before an early sailing trip.

Their relationship became a collection of small acts that slowly made a life.

Maya began accepting that her feelings were real.

She no longer woke each morning asking whether she was allowed to feel them.

One morning, Elena was laughing at a mistake she had made while preparing supplies for The Blue Horizon.

Maya watched her and laughed too.

“What?” Elena asked.

“Nothing.

I just like seeing you happy.”

Elena smiled.

“No.

Chapter 9 — Under the Same Sky

Maya and Elena began imagining a future together.

They talked about traveling along the coast, building their careers, and perhaps one day living near the ocean.

Their dreams were not extravagant.

They were personal and ordinary, which made them feel real.

One night they lay beneath a clear sky outside the harbor.

“Do you think we’ll still be together years from now?” Maya asked.

Elena turned toward her.

“I hope so.”

“That’s not a very confident answer.”

Elena smiled.

“The future isn’t something we can promise.

But I can promise what I feel tonight.”

Maya moved closer.

“What do you feel?”

“That I love you.”

Maya smiled.

Elena looked toward the horizon.

Chapter 10 — The Kiss We Couldn’t Forget

They returned to the place where they had first admitted their feelings.

The evening was warm, and the fading sunlight turned the sea gold.

Maya looked at Elena.

“I remember being afraid of these feelings.”

“And now?”

“Now I’m afraid of losing them.”

Elena stepped closer and embraced her.

They shared a long, emotional kiss.

It was not simply romantic; it carried everything they had survived—the confusion, the guilt, the courage, and the decision to remain honest.

When they separated, Elena looked toward the horizon.

Chapter 11 — Love Before the Storm

The next few days carried an uneasy quiet.

Elena continued working with The Blue Horizon, but Maya noticed that she checked her phone more often.

She received messages she would not explain and sometimes stood alone near the harbor, staring toward the water.

Maya wanted to ask questions, but she also respected Elena’s need for privacy.

One evening they shared dinner and talked about the future.

“Promise me something,” Elena said.

Maya smiled.

“What?”

“Keep moving forward, no matter what happens.”

Maya frowned.

“Why are you saying that?”

“Because life changes quickly.”

Maya took Elena’s hand.

“Then we’ll change with it.

Together.”

Elena smiled, but sadness remained in her eyes.

They spent the rest of the evening talking about ordinary things.

Maya never imagined it would become one of their last ordinary nights.

The next morning, Maya received a call.

Elena had been killed.

For several seconds Maya could not understand the words.

Chapter 12 — The Climax

Grief made the first days after Elena’s death almost impossible.

Maya barely slept.

Yet every time she closed her eyes, she remembered Elena’s final warnings.

She began reviewing the events of the previous week.

A message Elena had received.

A meeting she had never explained.

A person Maya had noticed near the harbor more than once.

Small details began connecting.

Maya returned to The Blue Horizon and spoke with people who had been around Elena.

One detail contradicted another.

A timeline did not make sense.

A message had been deleted, but Maya remembered seeing its notification.

The more she investigated, the more certain she became that Elena’s death had not been a simple accident.

Someone had been watching Elena.

Maya discovered evidence pointing toward a person connected to a dispute surrounding the boat charter.

The confrontation that followed was frightening, but Maya refused to back down.

Maya finally understood why Elena had seemed frightened in her final days.

When the truth finally came out, Maya felt no satisfaction.

Chapter 13 — After the Storm

Weeks passed before Maya learned how to live with the silence.

At first, every familiar place hurt.

The coffee shop reminded her of Elena.

The harbor reminded her of Elena.

Even the ocean, once a place of comfort, became a collection of memories she could not escape.

Then one morning Maya returned to the beach where they had spent their happiest nights.

She sat alone and listened to the waves.

For a long time she said nothing.

Then she smiled through her tears.

“You were right,” she whispered.

“I have to keep moving forward.”

She understood that moving forward did not mean leaving Elena behind.

It meant carrying the love, the lessons, and the courage Elena had given her.

Maya also began repairing the parts of her life she had damaged.

She accepted responsibility for the betrayal in her former relationship.

Chapter 14 — The Next Morning After the Storm

The next morning after the storm arrived quietly.

Blackwood Cove was still recovering from the damage, but the sky had cleared and the sea had settled into a calm rhythm.

Maya woke early and found herself listening to the silence.

She knew Elena was gone, yet grief still came in strange waves.

Some moments felt almost ordinary until a memory suddenly reminded her that Elena would never walk through the door again.

Nikki found Maya near the harbor.

She did not ask Maya to stop grieving.

She simply stood beside her.

“You don’t have to be strong every minute,” Nikki said.

“I’m trying,” Maya replied.

“You don’t have to try with me.”

Maya looked at her childhood friend.

“Away?”

“A holiday.”

Chapter 15 — The Holiday Plan

Nikki spent the rest of the day planning their short holiday.

She wanted somewhere peaceful, somewhere far enough from Blackwood Cove to give Maya a change of scenery without making the journey overwhelming.

When Nikki told Maya she had chosen Granbury City Beach Park in Texas, Maya looked surprised.

“Texas?”

“Yes.

We can spend a few days there, walk by the water, eat good food, and forget the clock for a while.”

Maya hesitated.

“I’m not sure I know how to have fun right now.”

“Then don’t try to have fun,” Nikki said.

“Just come with me.”

That answer made Maya smile.

Chapter 16 — The Journey: Granbury City Beach Park

The afternoon sun rested gently over Granbury City Beach Park.

The water moved quietly toward the shore, and the warm breeze carried the sound of people enjoying the beach.

Maya and Nikki changed into their swimsuits before walking toward the water.

Maya wore a simple blue swimsuit, while Nikki wore a black one.

For once, Maya felt comfortable enough to laugh without immediately feeling guilty about it.

“Ready?” Nikki asked.

“I think so.”

They ran into the water.

Nikki splashed Maya first, and Maya immediately splashed her back.

“You did that on purpose!” Maya laughed.

“Maybe.”

For several minutes they were simply two friends enjoying a summer afternoon.

No storm.

No harbor.

No difficult questions.

Just water, sunlight, and laughter.

Later, they sat together on the sand.

Maya looked toward the horizon.

“I feel guilty when I enjoy myself,” she admitted.

Nikki turned toward her.

“You’re allowed to smile, Maya.

Chapter 17 — When Hearts Speak

That evening, Maya and Nikki walked along the quieter part of the beach.

The last sunlight stretched across the water.

Nikki had been carrying words inside her for years.

She had cared for Maya since childhood, but she had never known whether speaking honestly would bring them closer or push Maya away.

“Maya, there’s something I need to tell you.”

Maya stopped.

“What is it?”

“I’ve loved you for a long time.”

Maya was silent.

Nikki quickly added, “I’m not asking you to forget Elena.

I’m not asking you to decide anything because you’re grieving.”

Maya leaned closer and kissed Nikki gently.

Chapter 18 — The Wedding

Time passed, and Maya and Nikki continued building their relationship with patience.

Their love grew through ordinary days: shared breakfasts, long walks, difficult conversations, and quiet evenings when neither needed to speak.

Eventually, the day of their wedding arrived.

The ceremony was small and intimate.

Family and close friends gathered near the coast beneath a clear sky.

The sea moved gently in the distance.

Maya stood waiting, nervous and smiling.

When Nikki appeared, Maya felt the same warmth she had felt during their first real moment of honesty.

They exchanged rings.

Maya looked into Nikki’s eyes.

“I choose you, not because my past disappeared, but because I am ready to build a future with you.”

Nikki answered, “I choose you exactly as you are, with your memories, your strength, and your heart.”

They promised to support one another through ordinary days and difficult ones.

They were honest.

“Mrs.

Chapter 19 — A New Beginning

The days after the wedding felt surprisingly ordinary.

There were no dramatic changes in the outside world.

The sun still rose.

The sea still moved.

People still hurried through their mornings.

But for Maya and Nikki, everything had a new meaning.

They were building a life together.

Maya began discovering the small pleasures of married life.

Morning coffee became something they shared.

Grocery shopping became an excuse to tease each other.

Even deciding what to cook could become a long conversation.

One evening, Maya found the photograph of Elena she had kept safely stored away.

Nikki noticed the change in her expression.

“Do you want to talk?”

Maya nodded.

“You’re not.”

Maya looked at her wife.

“Thank you for understanding.”

Nikki kissed her forehead.

Chapter 20 — Beyond the Horizon

The final morning of their journey began quietly.

Maya and Nikki returned to the coast and stood together beside the water.

The horizon stretched endlessly before them.

Maya thought about how much had changed.

She had once believed she understood exactly what her life would be.

Then Elena had entered it and changed everything.

Then Elena’s death had broken the future Maya thought she would have.

Now Maya stood beside Nikki, her wife, carrying both love and loss inside the same heart.

“What are you thinking?” Nikki asked.

Maya smiled.

“About the journey.”

“The trip?”

“Everything.”

Maya looked toward the horizon.

“I used to think moving forward meant leaving things behind.

Now I think it means carrying what mattered and continuing anyway.”

Nikki took her hand.

“That sounds like you’ve learned something.”

“I have.”

Maya looked down at her wedding ring.

“Love can change us.

Loss can change us.

But neither one has to stop us from living.”

Nikki smiled.

The memories no longer felt like a storm.
