A is the ache that begins without warning
B is the body learning its own weight
C is the chaos behind calm
D is the distance between touch and meaning

E is the echo of what was almost said
F is the fatigue of feeling too much
G is the gravity that pulls even silence down
H is the hesitation before truth

I is the isolation that wears a smile
J is the journey that circles back home
K is the knowledge that love is never pure
L is the light that refuses to stay

M is the memory that rewrites itself nightly
N is the nothing that hums beneath everything
O is the opening that fear pretends to close
P is the pause that pretends to be peace

Q is the question that keeps the heart alive
R is the ruin we mistake for growth
S is the stillness after surrender
T is the tenderness that survives the storm

U is the universe folded into a gaze
V is the void that teaches us to see
W is the waiting that becomes wisdom
X is the crossroad between loss and becoming

Y is the yielding that feels like grace
Z is the moment we realize
we were the alphabet all along,
each letter a life, each breath a beginning.

My body is a circus,
a shimmering ruin of light and longing,
where bones juggle their tired weight
and the heart walks a trembling rope
between faith and despair.

The world comes to watch it falter,
to see the dancer twist through pain,
the clown smile through a secret ache,
the ringmaster pretend to be in control.

I am the whole performance,
the one who dances, the one who watches,
the applause and the silence that follows.
My flesh feels like a tent of betrayal,
yet it shelters me like a quiet cathedral.

This body does not always love me back,
this strange companion of skin and will.
Still, I tend to its broken mirrors,
kiss its unhealed corners,
teach it how to breathe through the spectacle.

Let the world call it a circus,
to me, it is sacred ground.
Every ache is a hymn,
every scar a whispered prayer.
And when the lights fade to dark,
I will love her still!

I forced the door that I had long denied,
its rusted claws too fiery, too wide.
Its frame was carved from sleepless years,
its lock still rusted with my tears.

The key cracked as I twisted the lock,
a nostalgic sound—half breath, half shock.
The air remembered what I’d lost,
still led me in, each step a cost.

The bed still held the shape of fear,
as if the dark had slept just near.
The hands of the clock had stopped at all,
and innocence hung right on the wall.

And there, my childhood on the floor,
a burnt diary trying to say more.
I touched the past, it touched me too,
some scars remained-just a few.

Between forgiving what was done
and letting go of what’s begun,
I learned some doors won’t choose a side,
they wait for truth, not peace, inside.

I turned the lock, the handle cried,
for all the selves I’ve left inside.
And somewhere deep beneath my skin,
that door still waits to let me in.
...Aqsa

title.stringValue: The Locked Room Between Forgiveness and Forgetting by Aqsa
The Last Lie Before the End —The lie that kept you warm by Aqsa

content.stringValue:
Your eyes begged me not to leave,
so I stitched a lie you’d believe.
I swallowed the agreement that death had signed,
kissed your forehead: “Yes, love, we still have time.”

With all the strength left in me,
I smiled brightly for you to see.
You cuddled close, not acknowledging the weight,
not knowing the hour, the weight, the fate.

I tucked the lie behind your ear.
“But you look weak,” you said with fear.
So I lifted you in my arms, maybe for the last time,
though for good, but lying to you felt like a crime.

My lungs were fire, my knees were ash;
it was the moment before my whole world collapsed.
Knowing well I’d not be here tomorrow,
I tried my best to vanish my sorrow.
I whispered dreams we’d never chase,
you were falling asleep under my embrace.

I never said, but I hoped you knew
that goodbye hid in every “I love you.”
For love, I lied one final time,
to leave you whole while I lost mine.

....Aqsa

It’s a Saturday night
and the room feels small.
I sit with the week replaying itself,
wondering when we began to fall.

The moment doesn’t arrive with sound,
it never announces its end.
It slips in quietly,
like distance pretending to be a friend.

Between unread messages
and replies that take too long,
I realise the bond we shared
does not feel as strong.

The late-night talks
don’t happen anymore,
the kind that felt like therapy,
the kind I still look for.

I am no longer
a part of your everyday life,
no longer the person you run to
when things don’t turn out right.

And the worst part
is not losing you,
it’s watching you give
what we once knew
to someone else.

What we had
didn’t break or fall apart,
it slowly grew distant.

Your chapter
in the book of my life came to an end.
I still turn the pages sometimes.

No happiness.
No grief.
Just a journey we took.

Why?
Because neither the person, nor the promise stayed.

Maybe in another universe
you are still my Chandler somehow,
and I am still your Rachel,

எனக்கு இந்த வாழ்க்கை கிடைச்சிச்சு நீ பண்ண உதவிக்கு உனக்கு இப்போ இந்த வேலை கிடைச்சி இருக்குமா போமா போய் சந்தோசமா வேலை பாருனு சொன்னார். ராதிகாவும் மிகவும் சந்தோசமா வேலை பாத்த நல்ல வேலை பாத்ததால அவருக்கு அடுத்து அடுத்து பதவி உயர்வு கிடைத்தது. அவள் நினைத்த மாதிரி மிகப்பெரிய வீடும் கட்டினால் அவள் அம்மா, அப்பா மிகவும் சந்தோசிம் பட்டன்கள், ஆனால் அந்த சந்தோசம் அவளுக்கு ரொம்பநாள் நீடிக்கல ஒருநாள் அவள் காரில் வந்து கொண்டிருக்கும் போது தீட்ரென்று ஒரு விபத்து நடந்தது அவள் மிகவும் உயிருக்கு போராடி கொண்டிருந்தாள். அவள் பெற்றோர்க்கு என்ன செய்யவேண்டும் என்று தெரியவில்லை அவளுடைய ஓனர்க்கு கால் செய்து சொன்னார்கள். அவர் உடனே மருத்துவமனைக்கு இந்து டாக்டரிடம் டாக்டர் எவ்வோ பணம் ஆனாலும் சரி ராதிகாவா காப்பாத்திடுங்க என்று வேண்டிகொண்டார். ஆனால் டாக்டர் சார் இவடுடைய இதயம் பாதிக்கபட்டு இருக்கும உடனே வேற இதயம் ஆப்ரேசன் செய்து மாதனும் ஆனால் இதயம் இதுவரைக்கு கிடைக்கல அவளுடைய இரத்தவகையிலனு சொன்னார் டாக்டர். இவருக்கு என்ன செய்யனும்னு தெரியல் சிலமணிநேரம் கழித்து தெரிந்தது அவளோட இரத்தவகையும், அவரோட இரத்தவகையும் ஒன்னு என்று. உடனே அவர் ஒரு முடிவு எடுத்து உறுப்புதானம் செய்தார். ஏனென்றால் அவருக்கு மூளையில் ஒருகட்டி அதனால் இன்னும் ஒரு சில மாதம் தான் உயிருடன் இருப்பார். அவருக்கு உறவினர் என்று யாரும் இல்லை அவரும் பலநாள் அந்த கம்பெனிய பாத்துகுறத்துக்கு ஒரு நல்ல திறமையான ஒரு நபரை தேடிக்கொண்டு இருந்தார். அப்போதுதான் ராதிகா அவர் கண்ணில் பட்டாள். அவளுக்கு வேலையும் கொடுத்தார். இப்போது இன்னும் சிலமாதத்தில் இறக்க இருப்பதால் ஒரு நல்லநாள் பார்த்து அவளிடம் இந்த கம்பெனிய ஒப்படைக்க பார்த்தார் அப்போது தான் அவருக்கு விபத்து நடந்தது. இப்போது அவர் உறுப்புதானம் செய்துவிட்டு அவர் துக்கமாத்திரையை சாப்பிட்டுவிட்டு கோமாவிற்கு சென்றுவிட்டார். அப்படியே ஒரு கடிதமும் எழுதி இருந்தார். அதில் அவர் உடைய இதயம் ராதிகாக்கு வைத்துவிடுங்கள் என்றும் நான் இன்னும் ஒடு சில மாதத்தில் இறந்து விடுவேன். என்னை காப்பாற்ற வேண்டாம். ஒரு சில மாதத்தில் இறந்தாள் என்ன இல்ல இப்போ இறந்தான் என்ன என்னால ராதிகா உயிர் பிழைக்கனும் அது மட்டுமின்றி என்னோட செர்த்து எல்லா அவள் பேரில் மாற்றிவிட்டேன் இனி ராதிகாதான் இந்த கம்பெனி ஒனர் என்று கூறிவிட்டு, எழுதி வைத்துவிட்டு தூக்கமாத்திரையை சாப்பிட்டுவிட்டு கோமாவிற்கு சென்றுவிட்டார். இதயொல்லாம் டாக்டரிடம் முன்னாடியே கூறிவிட்டு, மருத்துவமனையிலே தூக்கமாத்திரையே சாப்பிட்டுவிட்டார். அவர் கோமாவிற்கு சென்றதும், உடனே ஆப்ரேசன் நடத்தது ராதிகாவிற்கு அவரின் இதயம் வைக்கபட்டது. ராதிகாவும் உயிர் பிழைத்தாள். அவள் உயிர் பிழைத்ததும் அவர் கூறியபடி அந்த கம்பெனிக்கு அவள் ஓனர் ஆனாள். நல்லபடியாக அந்த கம்பெனிய நடத்தினாள் ராதிகா.

உதவியின் உயிர் மூச்சு ராதிகா!

Invisible threads weave through my mind,
A map of memories, forever left behind.
The scars that don't show, the wounds that don't heal,
A silent suffering, that only I can feel.

Like a ghostly presence, it haunts me still,
A pain that's hidden, but never standing still.
It echoes through time, a whispered refrain,
A reminder of hurt, that refuses to wane.

The world sees my smile, my laughter and glee,
But behind the mask, a different story's me.
The invisible scar, a weight I bear alone,
A secret pain, that I've yet to call home.

But in the silence, I'll find a voice,
A way to express, this hidden choice.
To let the world see, beyond the disguise,
And understand the depth, of my invisible cries."

 Each petal holds promise of your comeback to me soon .

title.stringValue: ऐसे लगा कि बचपन लौट आया

content.stringValue:
सालों बाद मेरी बहन का फोन आया
ऐसे लगा कि बचपन लौट आया

घंटो की हमने कई सारी बातें
दिल भर आया, आंखे हुई नम
थोड़ी देर में जीजा ऑफिस से आया
बच्चो की भूख ने ज़ोर से चिल्लाया,
सालों बाद मेरी बहन का फोन आया
ऐसे लगा कि बचपन लौट आया....

बच्चो को सोते हुए देखते ही
चाची का थपथपाना याद आया
उनके माथे को चूमते ही
नानी के स्पर्श का एहसास हुआ,
सालों बाद मेरी बहन का फोन आया
ऐसे लगा कि बचपन लौट आया....

स्कूल की छुट्टियों का अलग ही था मज़ा
खेलना, कूदना, सबको परेशान करना
रात में भैया की कहानियों का इंतज़ार होता था
मामा का लाड और मासी की खीर पे थपथपना
सालों बाद मेरी बहन का फोन आया
ऐसे लगा कि बचपन लौट आया....

होली हो, नवरात्रि हो, चाहे हो दीवाली
रिश्तों का मेला लगा रहता था
दीदी, भैया, चाचा चाची, चाहे हो मामा मामी
दिलों में प्यार और सिर्फ अपनापन था,
सालों बाद मेरी बहन का फोन आया
ऐसे लगा कि बचपन लौट आया....

बड़े हुए हम सब बच्चे
अपने सफ़र पे निकल पड़े
सब अपनी दुनिया में हैं
देश विदेश में बसे हैं,
सालों बाद मेरी बहन का फोन आया
ऐसे लगा कि बचपन लौट आया....

समय ने वो अपनापन छीन लिया
रिश्तों में केवल नाम की स्थायी रह गई
अब तो यादों में भी धुंधलापन आ गया
दूरी ने नज़दीकियां आ गई,
सालों बाद मेरी बहन का फोन आया
ऐसे लगा कि बचपन लौट आया....

Vrushalee

खुद को साबित करने की राह में
भटक जाता हूँ मैं,
चलते-चलते यूँ ही
अटक जाता हूँ मैं।

सहमा-सा है किरदार मेरा,
शमा-सा है किरदार मेरा,
इसलिए जंग-ए-ख़ौफ़ के दौर में
लटक जाता हूँ मैं।

मैं चाहता हूँ बताना
अपनी सारी परेशानियाँ मगर,
क्या वो सच में समझ पाएँगे मुझे —
यही सोचकर अटक जाता हूँ मैं,
जंग-ए-ख़ौफ़ के दौर में
लटक जाता हूँ मैं।

मैं देख सकता हूँ आँखों में
छुपे हुए राज उनके,
क्या वो समझ पाते हैं कभी
किरदार मेरा?

मैं संभाल लूँ पहाड़ सी
परेशानियाँ उनकी,
क्या वो संभाल पाएँगे
मेरा छोटा-सा सितारा — आँसू मेरा?

वो करते हैं दगा हरदम,
मैं फिर भी यक़ीन करता हूँ,
हाँ… मैं कुछ रिश्तों के खोने से
डरता हूँ।

टूटी साँसों के साथ
टूट जाएँगे सपने मेरे,
बीते वक़्त के साथ
छूट जाएँगे अपने मेरे।

ना हो तकलीफ़ उन्हें —
यही सोचकर रुक जाता हूँ मैं,
जंग-ए-ख़ौफ़ के दौर में
लटक जाता हूँ मैं।

खुद को साबित करने की राह में
भटक जाता हूँ मैं…
जंग-ए-ख़ौफ़ के दौर में
लटक जाता हूँ मैं।

title.stringValue: Jung-e-khoof ke dor me latak jata Hu main
Par ham ne v duniya dekhi hai

content.stringValue:
कभी बारिशों की बूंदों तले,
कभी ठंडी हवाओं के बीच,
कभी पेड़ों की छाँव में,
कभी नंगे पाँव की राहों में।

कभी चाँदनी की गोद में,
कभी तारों के शहर में,
मैं लिखता हूँ अपने जज़्बात,
स्याही की बहती लहर में।

ओ सरसराते खेतों की साँस,
ओ नाज़ुक पत्तों की छोटी सी जान,
इन सबके बीच बैठकर,
मैं लिखता हूँ इंसान की
बिगड़ी हुई पहचान।

सुबह की चाँदनी लेकर,
चमकते हैं लोग ज़माने में,
पर बात अगर दिल की उठे,
तो छुप जाते हैं सिरहाने में।

नीयत अच्छी है — सीना ठोककर कहते हैं,
पर ज़ुल्म सामने हो तो
चुपचाप खड़े रहते हैं।

कहते हैं — “हम पचास के हैं, हमने दुनिया देखी है”,
फिर अपनों पर ही ज़ुल्म करें —
क्या यही तुम्हारी नेकी है?

भले ही मैं हूँ सिर्फ बीस का, साहब,
पर हमने भी दुनिया देखी है…
हाँ, हमने भी दुनिया देखी है।

One day, before almost 68 years when I was 14 I met your grandma. She was so beautiful and passionate about her studies. We met first time on the first day of school after summer vacation. I still remember, she was wearing a red dress and white shawl. Her hair was tied-up in a simple pony tail. Her skin was fair and she was just looking amazing to blow my mind and in reality she did that only.

After few days, we both started talking to eachother and I daily used to drop near by her home through my bicycle. We became good friends within a short period of time and till then we both completed our high school studies. But we both used to promise one another everyday that we will be there for eachother until we got wrinkles on the face. Then, for further studies, I went to city and her parents didn't allow her to study further. We two were badly missing eachother but still, we couldn't talk as there was no any digital platform to talk. Nowadays, at your age..love has been so faster that if you didn't get reply in hours you get mad or starts doing doubts on one another.

Dear child, remember always that love has no boundaries but the one who's in love have must respect to their boundaries. Lemme tell you more about your grandma. 
The hours, days and years had been passed and finally after 8 years I came back and met her. She was about 25 years old beautiful and amazing girl and I was 26 at that time. I went village to take my parents with me and I met her for one last time. We both thought that it will be our last meet but it says that nobody can predict what your destiny has decided and the magic happend after 5 years.

I got my new job and frankly saying, I moved on from her and started focusing on my career. I was earning well enough and my father was searching a girl for me to make me settle. Her father was also doing the same. I said to dad that once, I loved a girl and then I moved on so you can search a girl for me. He agreed and started working on it.

One day, he asked me to come on the terrace and we talked about your grandma. He listened it carefully and next day he took me to our village. We went over there and saw that she is getting married to somebody.

My eyes was filled with tears and I had a huge fake smile and flowers with me. Seeing her again..one last time was the biggest grief of my life at that time. But as I said, no-one can predict the destiny..the magic happened.

As soon as she saw me, she ran towards me and hold me tightly that she really didn't wanted to do that marriage and asking me to God. I still remember, how her father scolded her while she ran from her marriage ritual.
She came to me, and then everybody got to know about us. Then my dad had silent tears on her face and later on her dad also agreed for this marriage.

And then, we called my mumma for marriage and that's how I got your grandma. But right now, the biggest grief I've is I couldn't keep her until we both had wrinkles on the face. I couldn't fulfill her promise that I'll be there until her and mine wrinkles. Now look at this face, I've wrinkles of her face also.

Grandson: Dadu, pls don't cry. Have some water.

~DIYA KI DICTIONARY

The room smelled of iron and sandalwood . Elias sat across from Him. His white shirt matched his eyes bloodshot, face unreadable, who stared right into his soul. The stillness between them thrummed like static behind some old theatre curtain.

Elias clicked his pen. "They said I could observe you. Just for a while."

The man tilted his head, "I see..." He then chuckled at his own answer amusingly.

Elias blinked, ignoring the mocking echo. "I need to understand... for the role."

A pause.

The man tilted his head. "Understand what?"

Elias hesitated. "Your hands. Why are they still bloody? Why not wash it off? And why a knife? It’s so...personal."

"Because it’s part of the scene. It ends with truth, messy. The knife doesn’t distance.....it reflects."



Elias scribbled something. "I’ve played killers before. But none of em looked like this. Your tears, your blank face....how does that even happen?"


"They're echoes. What’s left when the soul claws at the walls on its way out."



"How do I show that?" Elias leaned forward. "The audience needs to believe it."


“Then don’t show. Let it seep. Grief doesn’t perform. It stains.”



Elias nodded slowly. His hand wet, moved across the page, looping words like he'd written them before.

"Did you plan it....the act?"

“Every night. Every night I stopped at the edge. The real performance is restraint .”



"And when you finally let go?"

"It was quiet. My hands moved like they’d done it before."



Elias laughed under his breath. Familiar, almost fond. "It felt... choreographed?"

“No. It felt remembered.”



Elias swallowed. "Then why call the police yourself?"

"Because I wanted someone to see the scene exactly as I left it. No edits. No cuts."



"Did you love her?"

The man’s eyes flicked upward, then rested back on Elias like the spotlight on stage.

“Enough to do it real.”



Elias paused, a cold pressure behind his temples. A chill crept into Elias’s spine.
"You didn’t improvise. You followed something. An emotion? A beat?"

"Instinct. The moment I knew the third act had no redemption."

Elias dropped the pen.

His voice lowered, tentative now. "So… was it a fight? Is that what did it?"

"The fight just lit the fuse. The rest was already soaked in gasoline."



Elias swallowed. " But didn't you love her?."

"I did. Enough to keep her. Enough to stop her from walking out the door, the way she looked at me."

His own memories creeped up. He remembered the last time his wife touched him. How her smile was tired, not warm. How the lipstick she wore wasn’t the shade he liked. How she'd started to speak without waiting for him to listen.

Elias clenched his fists. Love isn’t always soft, he told himself. Sometimes it’s just... wanting someone to stay so badly, you can't let them leave. 

He shakes his head dismissively "You talk like an actor."

"You talk like someone pretending not to be, Elias".


A thin, deafening sound sliced through the air.The room closed in. 
Elias’s hands trembled. His knuckles were sticky.

"W-wait how do you know my name?",His voice trembled. 

"You told me. You’ve always told me. Every time."



Elias’s breath hitched. He looked down down at his lap...dark spots bloomed on his jeans, growing with every tear that slipped off his chin

The chair in front.... Vanished

In the mirror across the room, Elias saw himself,

Sitting alone....
And his Maria, ever so beautiful onthe floor in a deep slumber, her pale tone looking angelic against the dark crimson. His eyes crinkled.... they finally agreed on the same colours.

His chest rose like he'd reached the final cue. 
The silence applauded.
He had done it... Finally delivered the perfect scene. Every line precise. Every emotion calculated. The performance of a lifetime.



With sirens getting louder outside. Blue and red lights flickered against the flowing curtain, 


He whispered to the reflection, voice trembling with a tired yet dark satisfaction, the edges of his mouth twitching like a bow after the final note,


"Cut."

But this wasn’t a take,

It was the final scene...

1 day, 24 hours, 1440 minutes that will be
Carrying 7 years of us.
I cried, your hand caressing, whispering helpless comfort and lips in a trembling curve.
With nostalgic eyes and a glint of something you weren't ready to accept, you kissed away my tears coaxing me to surrender to the dawn.

We walked in that park which seemed to bloom as if it recognised our warmth,
The water shining diamonds that dulled in your light.
The thought of tomorrow sat deep within the cracks you once healed, refusing to breathe without you greeting the sun.

You gleamed at the laughing kids, dancing, as if... you denied what the world declared you to do,
I stood there, unblinking watery eyes, hopeless with the verdict i can't undo.
The world envied us two lucky souls,
The water flowed with a hurry unknown,
Yet,
Your pearly whites seemed in no rush, sipping the tea.

As the sun dimmed visibly, you shuddered so deep... as if your soul shook with something that finally caught up with time,
A feeble wobbling smile painted your face, 
I knew then,
Even the Sun cried for the day,
With a fading joy, Even your hidden pain slipped free.

Life's twisted humor laughed at the turn tables, as I held you just like you did, what felt moments ago,
Salty tears, the only reflection of our fleeting time,
I slowly brought us afoot, twirling you as I go,
Sniffing, you looked up with knowing eyes.

The bittersweet fate sang in the growing twilight, 
With no tomorrow and fading memories of the past.

We danced... two souls, with minds that kissed and hearts that vowed forever.

Blessed by the crying gods, wedded under the moon halo.
A bond they couldn't sever.

title.stringValue: Before We Knew It Was a Memory

content.stringValue:
Life and its moments are fleeting,
Still, we rarely pause what we are doing,
And the present keeps gently retreating.

We live in halves.
Half-listen, half-watch, half-feel,
We eat a meal while we scroll,
Empty a plate without letting the taste linger,
Talk to family while typing replies,
As if nothing in front of us deserves our full attention.

We live like life has drafts,
like we can come back later and do it better.
We listen while we plan,
Hug while reaching for the next task,
Do one thing with our hands,
Another with our minds,
Meanwhile time doesn’t pause,
And life’s most beautiful moments pass by unnoticed.

Moments never announce themselves,
We don’t know when one is happening for the last time.
The ones we cherish later,
Once looked like laughter, errands,
Goodbyes and ordinary conversations.

Years later, we call them beautiful,
Frame them and reminisce as memories,
As if beauty only exists in retrospect.

I learned that truth the hard way.

I used to believe I could always return,
to my favourite place, people and version of myself.
I did go back.
We laughed, we talked, we made new memories.
But the ones I miss,
belong to a time that no longer exists.

That’s when I understood:
You can revisit a place,
But you can’t relive a moment.
We have to learn to choose,
Because life doesn’t let us have it all.

The quiet wisdom is in learning to notice,
What is already ‘here’,
Before it turns into something we can only lose.

I say something, you hear something else

I say I value you, you focus on my past mistakes

I say I care about you, you remember the past misunderstanding we had

I say let us be in the present, you focus in the past

I talk about present issues we are facing, you remember my childhood vulnerabilities I shared with you

I'm walking on a path of life, you are walking on your own path of life, our paths never meeting

You have your own perception of right, wrong, good and bad, I have mine

You say God gave you this life and you need to live it whatever it takes, 
as if everything is fair in love and war

But is everything actually fair in love and war? 

I have my morals and values, you have yours

I have my beliefs, you have yours

I believe in honesty and truthfulness, you believe cheating and lying is fine to serve your purpose

I know you faced tough times in life , but what is a life lived without morals and values

I have a conscience, you seem to not have

 I feel all emotions deeply, and you feel everything at a very basic level or no emotion for others and feel emotion deeply only when it comes to you

When I care about you and you also care only about yourself, who is going to care about me? 

You say be human, yes, I am, but why do you forget to be human too

You say I'm lazy, but I keep getting achievements in life, 

What did you achieve.. 

It's easy to point fingers at others rather than looking at your own faults

I am human, you are human too

We all have our own faults, no one is perfect

Then why point fingers at me and magnify my faults when you have far more faults than me.. 

I ask you how are you doing, to know about your well being

You want to know how someone is doing, so you can rejoice in their mishaps

I feel happy seeing my friends doing well in life

You feel jealous seeing your friends doing well in life

I get happiness by sharing and giving

You get happiness by taking and receiving

I don't take advantage of people for my gains

You take advantage of people for your gains

I treat people as human, you treat people as objects to be used

I try so hard to explain my perception of things

You try so hard to argue with me

In the end I give up, you win! 

You may win the argument, but you lost the person

Then how can we ever be compatible

-वैश्यावृत्ति का काम तो यूं ही बदनाम हो जाता है। गुनहगार होता है कौन और सजा कोई और ले जाता है। 
उसने शरीर बेचा है माना,क्योंकि वहॉं  खरीदार आया है।
मर्जी नही थी उसकी, उस पर मजबूरियों का साया है।इस काम को न करने के लिए भी,  उसने शारीरिक कष्ट बहुत उठाया है। 
मानसिक प्रताड़ना तो ,जीवन भर का साया है ।
 पर हमारे समाज ने केवल ,नारी पर प्रश्न चिन्ह लगाया है। 
अगर सही था पुरुष ,तो रात के अंधेरे छिपकर क्यों आया है।
 पूरे समाज के सामने,रोशनी के साथ में, क्यों सिर उठाके और तनके नही आया है। 
जानता था वो समाज को, उसकी अर्द्ध अज्ञानता को। पलड़ा समाज की नजरों में नारी का हल्का रहेगा। हमेशा नारी को ही दोष दिया है, नारी को ही दोषी कहेगा।
 वो कुछ भी कर लें ,मर्द है और मर्द ही रहेगा। 
उसको अधिकार है घर में भी नारी का उपभोग करें, उस पर अधिकार धरे, अपनी बातों से अपनी लातों से उसकी भावनाओं पर वार करें। 
बाहर जाएं तो बाहर भी उसका उपभोग और शोषण करें। 
पूछो उस नारी से जो छल्ली हो चुकी है अन्दर तक । चल रही है जी रही है ,पर मर चुकी अन्दर तक ।
 क्या उसके दर्द को , कष्ट को कोई खरीदार समझ पाता है? 
अरे असल में तो वो भी मजबूरियों का फायदा उठाने ही आया है। 
और उसको भी ये अधिकार समाज द्वारा ने ही तो दिलाया है। 
इसलिए हर साल छोटी-छोटी लड़कियों को बहला-फुसलाकर बेचा और खरीदा जाता है। 
वरना ऐसा काम कौन खुशी से करना चाहता है। वेश्यावृत्ति का काम तो बस यूं ही बदनाम हो जाता है। झांककर तो देखो उनके दिलों में भी,भावनाओं का गहरा गम्भीर सागर मिल जाता है।
 सीपी से हृदय में भावनाओं का मोती कौन कहॉं ढूंढ पाता है। 
वहॉं पर पुरुष केवल शारीरिक सुख पाने को जाता है। उन भावनाओं से उसका क्या रिश्ता है उनको तो रोज कुचलकर आता है

In the hush of the morning routine,
In the race of the brewing dreams,
Before the world speaks loudly,
The siren of kettle alerts me smartly.

The waves of steam reminds the curves of life,
The confluence of milk and water is the toil,
Pinch of sugar reminds to cut the bitterness with smile,
Realising dream grows darker with every boil.

In between the turmoil of inner noise,
The aroma in the air holds the hope,
With the cluster of thoughts in the mind,
I stire the memories with high tide.

Every sip, every drop is a soft confession,
Things fall right when given appropriate time,
The emptiness of cup fills the freshness,
To rewrite the bucket list with full shine.

I opened the storeroom door.
Darkness held its breath;
dust clung to the air
like a second skin.

There he stood—
my childhood partner,
cobwebbed,
grease dried to a whisper
along the chain.

A silver gouge split his frame
where a curb once won.
Tires sagged, exhausted.
Every scar
knew my hands.

I had misplaced him for years.
He had not moved.

I took him
out.

The road answered.

Air threaded the spokes,
bit my eyes awake.
The bell cleared its throat.

My shoulders dropped.
My fingers forgot
to clench.

Each turn loosened
a knot I didn’t name.
No destination—
only balance.

For a moment
the ground felt farther away.

We didn’t ride long.

When I stopped,
my palms still hummed,
and the dust he wore for years
fell behind us.

My grandmother knows
the alphabet the way one knows
geometry—
by shape,
not by sound.

She recognizes an A
like a door:
meant to open,
even if it never did for her.

Words never nested
on her tongue.
They arrived as houseguests—
unsure,
then left before they thickened
into sentences.

English skipped her.
It reached me instead—
uniforms, notebooks,
assemblies where silence was
scrubbed into pronunciation.

I learned to explain.
She learned to listen.

At home,
I translate myself downward—
shorter sentences,
obedient verbs—
until meaning fits
between us.

Some characters
do not survive the journey.

I speak now with confidence,
with grammar—
doors in mind
that never opened for her.

Between us,
English rests—
not as theft,
not as gift—
something that learned my name
but forgot hers.

And when I thought of his favourite flower to gift,
With the confusion of which one he’d pick.
Roses, daisies, or tulips bright,
Orchid, sunflower, or jasmine white.
So without thinking much, I bought them all,
Just in case one among them would be his favourite call.

It wasn’t just the flowers, I suppose,
But the effort behind each petal I chose.
That maybe one of them gets to be seen,
And carries my whispers, hidden in between.
Even if one reaches his heart’s space,
He’d know — each reach of mine had softly traced his name.

GOSSIP CYCLE
One fine day, Sharada had finished her kitchen work and was just surfing through her whatsapp messages when her neighbour Lalita dropped in.

‘Hello Lalita. Please come in. How are you? These days you are so busy. I don’t get to see you in your balcony.’
‘Yes Sharada. I got busy with my son’s admission formalities to engineering. My husband is busy at his work. So I have to take care of all these things.’
‘Is it done now? Are you relieved of your duties?’
‘Yes. Now I am free. That is why I came here to talk to you.’
‘Did Lakshmi tell you?’
‘What?’
‘Her daughter-in-law Bina is pregnant, that too, five years after marriage.’
‘I thought they didn’t want to have kids. That is the trend among present generation couples.’
‘Okay Sharada. I just wanted to let you know.’

After Lalita left, Sharada couldn’t keep quiet. She had to share this information with Radha. She called her up and asked her to come so they can have a chat with for some time. When Radha arrived, after initial formalities, Sharada told Radha, ‘You know Lakshmi. Her son was married some five years back. After all these years, I believe her daughter-in-law Bina is pregnant.’ 
‘I see. I have a feeling Lakshmi’s son must have had some problem. Otherwise, why did they take so much time to get a child? Did the couple go through IVF?’
‘I don’t know. I just told you what I heard. I don’t have any details. I haven’t yet spoken to Lakshmi.’
‘Lakshmi is such a bore. She has an attitude. She always flaunts her wealth. I don’t like her.’
‘Leave it. What do we have to do about it?’

Radha returns home after speaking for an hour about all other matters with Sharada. When she reached home, she couldn’t contain herself. She had to share this information with her closest friend Parvati. She decided to drop into Parvati’s home after lunch when her husband will not be at home.
Radha came to Parvati’s home.

‘Hello Parvati. How are you? I was just passing by. I thought I will just meet you. It is more than a week since I saw you.’
‘Come in Radha, It is so nice to see you. Did you have lunch?’
‘Yes. I have finished lunch. I came to tell you. I am told Lakshmi’s daughter-in-law is pregnant now.’
‘You mean Bina. I know her very well. I keep meeting her in the market when I go to buy vegetables. She didn’t tell me anything.’
‘How will she tell you? They didn’t have a kid for the last five years. Her husband, that is Lakshmi’s son, must be having some problem. She went through IVF and got pregnant.’
‘I am told IVF process is very expensive.’
‘Yes. They have lot of money. They can afford it.’
‘I see. I will ask her when I meet her next time.’
‘No, no. Don’t ask her. She will be surprised how you came to know of that. And you don’t tell her I told you.’
‘Okay Parvati. I will see you later.’

After Radha left, Parvati was thinking why Bina didn’t tell her directly. ‘May be Radha is right. Bina doesn’t want to spread the information that she has gone through IVF to get pregnant.’ she thought to herself.

Parvati got busy with her household work. Next day she couldn’t keep quiet. She had to share this information to her neighbour Kusuma when she meets her in satsang that evening. When satsang discourse was over, Parvati called Kusuma to a side and told her, 
‘You know Kusuma. That Lakshmi performed her son’s marriage some five years back. Lakshmi was worried that she didn’t get her grandchild even after so many years. I believe Bina, her daughter-in-law, is now pregnant through IVF. That means her son Akash had a problem.’
‘I see. Whenever I saw Akash, I got a doubt. Somehow he doesn’t look manly. This proves it. Lakshmi was unnecessarily finding fault with Bina.’
‘I see.’

When Parvati left satsang and took leave of Kusuma, she couldn’t keep quiet. She went to her sister Sushma who lived nearby.  As she entered Sushma’s house. 
She called out: ‘Hello Sushma. Are you there?’
‘’What is it Akka? Is there some emergency? Is Jijaji alright?’
‘Ohho. All fine. You now. I just heard about Lakshmi’s family. Lakshmi got her son Akash married five years back. Is it not? And they haven’t had a child till now. Lakshmi was so proud of her son and daughter-in-law. She was vehemently saying Akash and Bina are purposely delaying having their first child. All that is false. They had a medical problem. That is why they didn’t get a child. In fact it is Akash who is having the problem. Anyway I believe they have undergone IVF and Bina is finally pregnant now.’
‘Yes, Akka. You were always doubting Akash’s manliness.’
‘That is right. Now it is proved that Akash is not able to get intimate with Bina and that is why they didn’t get a child till date.’
‘OK. But why are YOU so hyper about it?’
‘I just feel I am so right in my judgement. Ok. I will leave now. I just wanted to convey that to you. That is all.’

After Kusuma left, Sushma kept thinking about it. I her mind, she thanked God that she hasn’t had any problem like that. At night, she told her husband Suresh about it. Now Suresh got a chance to intimidate his colleague Kumar.

Next day when Suresh met Kumar during lunch break, he called out to him. Kumar couldn’t refuse his boss. While they were having lunch together, Suresh told Kumar.
‘You know Kumar. I was always telling you about that Akash, Lakshmi’s son’
‘Yes. What about him, Sir?’
‘I just heard yesterday that Akash is gay. That is why they have not had a child till now.’
‘Oh God! What a pity. I feel bad for Akash’s wife. She is so beautiful. She was so happy to marry the handsome man Akash. I am sure she wouldn’t have expected this, Sir.’

Later that evening, Kumar called up his friend Ravi in the US. 
‘How are you Ravi? You remember Akash, your classmate. You used to make fun of him in class. I just got to know that Akash has turned out to be gay.’
‘So what, Kumar? Here in the US, gays are so common. They are accepted as third gender’
‘But it is not so here in India Ravi. You know we are expected to get married and beget children and make our parents happy. If that doesn’t happen, it becomes a big issue.’

This put Ravi thinking. This is something he spread in India itself. There is no point talking to anyone in the US.
Ravi called up his other friend Prasad who still lives in India. 
‘Hello Prasad. Do you remember Akash?’
‘Yes. That weird guy? What happened to him?’
‘’I believe Akash has now declared himself as gay.’
‘I had guessed about him all this while. It has turned out to be true.’
‘My friend Kumar told me. He knows his whole family quite well.’

When Prasad came home, he couldn’t contain himself. He told his wife Priya about it. Priya was very surprised to hear that from her husband. 
‘Do you guys speak about these things in office?’
‘Ravi just now called me from the US. I don’t know who told him. But Akash is our mutual friend you now.’

That evening, when Priya was shopping for vegetables in the market, she met her long time friend Rama.
‘Hai Rama. How are you? Long time no see?’
‘I am fine. So nice to see you. So what is cooking?’
‘You know Bina who married Akash, Lakshmi aunty’s son.’
‘Yes. That was some five years back.’
‘Yes. Lakshmi aunty was worried they haven’t had a child since then.’
‘Some couples delay their child purposely.’
‘No Rama. I believe, that Akash has declared himself as gay now.’
‘Who told you this?’
‘My husband Prasad. His friend Ravi told him. Ravi’s friend is Kumar whose boss is Suresh. Suresh told Kumar in his office. I believe, Suresh sir is quite close to Lakshmi aunty’s family. So that should be reliable news.’
 ‘I feel very bad for Bina. Poor girl. She has so many aspirations.’

Rama’s neighbour Sushma was watering her plants. Rama caught her attention.
‘Hello Rama. How are you?’
‘You know aunty. Lakshmi’s aunty’ son Akash claims he is gay. I just came to know through one of my friends who know their family quite well.’
‘But I heard something else.’
‘But this is most reliable news aunty.’

After lunch, Sushma went to her sister Kusuma’s house.
‘Akka. The problem is with Akash himself. He has claimed himself to be gay in front of the doctor, I believe.’
‘So how did they get a child?’
‘They haven’t got one yet. They may adopt one in the doctor’s clinic and declare it as through IVF.’
‘I see.’

Kusuma called on Parvati next day.
‘Parvati. You know we are all being misled. Bina is not pregnant. Akash claims he is gay. So they must be adopting a child. To cover it up, Lakshmi is saying Bina is getting a child through IVF. Anyway it is unduly delayed. So people may believe it.’

Parvati also had to clarify the matter. So she met Radha.
‘I am sorry Radha. I think I conveyed wrong information. I believe Akash and Bina are adopting a child because Akash is gay and Bina can’t get pregnant. Lakhsmi must be covering up the matter by spreading information that Bina is pregnant through IVF.’

Radha met Sharada to clear up the matter.
‘Sharada. I think I gave you incorrect information. I believe Akash has claimed himself to be gay. So their doctor has advised them to adopt a child instead of any other procedure. Bina has accepted. But Lakshmi doesn’t want to say the child is adopted. Property litigations, you see, between Akash and his sister. So Lakshmi is spreading information that Bina is pregnant through IVF.’

Sharada met Lalita that evening.
‘Hello Lalita. What you told me about Bina is incorrect. She is not pregnant. I believe Akash is gay. So Akash and Bina are going to adopt a child. To cover up the matter, Lakshmi is making up news that Bina is pregnant through IVF. She doesn’t want to declare the child as an adopted one. And Lakshmi has to register the adoption process and make it authentic. Otherwise, there will be legal issues concerning property matters. Akash’s sister can oppose it. As it is, Akash doesn’t have good relations with his sister, you know.’
‘Wow! That is interesting.’

Lalita thought for a while. She decided to hear from the horse’s mouth. So she went straight to Lakshmi’s house. Everyone seemed to be busy. On seeing Lalita, Lakshmi met her and told her.
‘We are busy right now Lalita. You know, thankfully, Bina got pregnant in the normal course.  She has developed labour pains. It’s after such a long time. So we are taking her to Shanti nursing home. Doctor has said delivery can happen anytime soon. So please excuse us. I will talk to you later.’
Lalita was flabbergasted.

I was sitting in the library, staring at an open chat where it was always only me who had texted. The room was quiet, but my phone felt loud in my hands.

Then a notification appeared.

Panic rushed through me when I saw it said seen. For a moment, I waited, certain a reply would follow. But his love language, I had learned, was leaving things on read.

I scrolled up.
The last messages were mine.
Read. Never answered.

The familiar questions returned, pressing in on me, asking what I had done wrong. People had told me to leave him, to stop waiting. But how do you leave something that once gave your days a reason to begin?

I might have stopped talking about him, but that didn’t mean I had forgotten. Silence doesn’t erase attachment; it only hides it more carefully.

After sitting there for a long time, I deleted the chat.

The calm that followed surprised me. It was physical and steady, like setting down a weight I hadn’t realized I was still carrying. I should have done it earlier, I thought, instead of holding on to conversations that ended without answers.

Later, I noticed something else.

I wasn’t thinking about him anymore.

I had been forcing myself to revisit those thoughts, even when I no longer wanted to.

That was when I understood the truth.

The message was never meant for him.
It was for the version of me that kept hoping things would turn out differently - the version that needed explanations for every silence in her mind and heart.

I locked my phone and left it in the other room.

Some conversations don’t end when they are spoken.
They end when they are no longer needed.

Because sometimes, what feels mutual is only one person trying to make it work - and slowly losing herself in the process.

The cupboard still carries
the fragrance of her perfume,
faint and stubborn,
caught in the grain of wood
where his fingers pause.

The surface has worn smooth,
as if it learned his hand.
It opens with resistance,
remembering someone else.

Inside, letters lie flat,
stacked with careful order.
No envelopes.
No addresses.
Only dates,
aligned one after another.

He writes each evening
when the fan hums past midnight
and the bulb smells faintly burnt.
The pen hesitates, then moves,
recording anger, small victories,
things no report would ask for.

Sometimes the ink runs dry
before the sentence does.
He presses harder.
The paper scars.
He continues.

Old letters wait:
ink darker in training days,
lighter in the first posting.
Her handwriting curves,
but the voice remains.

He folds each page once
and buries it at the bottom,
where errors are kept, not destroyed.

The cupboard closes.
Tomorrow, it will open again.
Some routines survive absence
because ending them
would admit
no one is waiting anymore.

Deceiving the world with a faking smile.
Holding pierced blood all inside
Carrying layers of shuttered emotions 
We are blessed by eyes that don't lie.

🌱 The Seed That Woke Up

A story about science, patience, and Allah’s perfect timing

⸻

The morning after the rain felt different.

Not loud.
Not bright.
Just… different.

The air was cool and soft, like it had been washed. Tiny drops of water still clung to the leaves, shining like small diamonds. The soil smelled fresh and deep, the kind of smell that made you want to breathe slowly.

Abuzar stepped into the garden with his slippers half on.

“Ahh,” he said, stretching his arms. “I love the smell after rain.”

Aaisha followed him, holding her scarf carefully so it wouldn’t drag on the wet ground.

“Everything looks clean,” she said. “Even the sky looks new.”

Birds hopped near the fence, pecking at the ground. A butterfly rested on a flower, opening and closing its wings.

Abuzar was walking toward the guava tree when he suddenly stopped.

“Aaisha!” he called. “Come here. Quickly!”

Aaisha ran over.

Near the wooden fence, something tiny and green was pushing through the dark soil. Just a little curve. Just a small tip.

“It wasn’t here yesterday,” Abuzar said, eyes wide. “I was here before Maghrib. There was nothing.”

He bent closer.

“Did someone plant it at night?”

Aaisha knelt carefully and looked closely.

“No,” she said softly. “See the soil? It’s not disturbed.”

Just then, Ammi came into the garden, wiping her hands on her dupatta.

“What’s happening?” she asked.

Abuzar pointed excitedly.
“Ammi! Look! A plant appeared by itself!”

Ammi smiled and sat beside them.

“By itself?” she repeated.

“Yes!” Abuzar said. “No one planted it. No one watered it. It just… came!”

Ammi gently touched the soil.

“Let me ask you something,” she said.
“Was this soil always empty?”

Abuzar thought.
“I think… yes?”

Aaisha shook her head.
“No. Soil always has things inside it.”

Ammi nodded.
“That’s right.”

She scooped a little soil into her palm.

“Long before yesterday… long before the rain… a seed was resting here.”

Abuzar frowned.
“But we didn’t see it.”

Ammi smiled.
“Because not all work is visible.”

Aaisha whispered,
“So it was hidden.”

“Yes,” Ammi said. “It looked dry and lifeless. But Allah had placed life inside it.”

She continued, slowly, so they could imagine it.

“The rain softened the soil. The seed drank the water. Air entered the tiny spaces in the ground. The sun warmed the earth.”

Abuzar’s eyes grew bigger.
“And then?”

“And then,” Ammi said, “when the time was right… Allah allowed it to wake up.”

Aaisha leaned closer to the plant.

“So it was alive all along?”

“Yes,” Ammi said. “Just waiting for Allah’s command.”

⸻

🔬 A Curious Question

Abuzar sat back on his heels.

“But Ammi,” he asked, “how does a seed even know how to grow?”

Ammi chuckled.
“That’s a very good question.”

She pointed to the seedling.

“Inside every seed, Allah has placed a plan.”

“A plan?” Aaisha repeated.

“Yes,” Ammi said. “Like instructions.”

She held up Aaisha’s school notebook.

“When you write homework, you follow steps. Seeds also follow steps.”

Abuzar tilted his head.
“Seeds can’t read.”

Ammi laughed.
“They don’t need to. Allah has already written everything inside them.”

She explained,

“Scientists say seeds need three main things to grow:
	1.	Water – to wake the seed
	2.	Air – so it can breathe
	3.	Warmth – usually from the sun”

“This process is called germination.”

Abuzar repeated carefully,
“Ger…mi…na…tion.”

Aaisha giggled.
“It sounds like a big word for such a tiny seed.”

Ammi nodded.
“Big miracles often start small.”

⸻

🌧️ Why Rain Matters

That afternoon, clouds gathered again.

Aaisha looked at the sky.
“Ammi, why does rain make plants grow but not stones?”

Ammi smiled.
“Because stones have no life inside them.”

She continued,

“Rain is the same. Soil is the same. Sun is the same.”

She pointed to the garden.

“But only what Allah has placed life inside will grow.”

Abuzar whispered,
“So rain doesn’t create life.”

“No,” Ammi said gently.
“Rain is just a helper. Allah is the Creator.”

She recited:

“And you see the earth lifeless, but when We send down rain upon it, it stirs and grows.”
(Qur’an 22:5)

Aaisha closed her eyes.
“It’s like the earth is sleeping.”

“And rain is an alarm clock,” Abuzar added.

Ammi smiled.
“Yes. But Allah decides when to turn the alarm on.”

⸻

🧠 A Science Experiment

The next day, Abuzar had an idea.

“Ammi,” he said, “can we test this?”

Ammi raised an eyebrow.
“Test what?”

“The seed thing,” he said. “Science!”

Aaisha clapped.
“Experiment!”

They planted three pots.
	•	One with water + sunlight
	•	One with sunlight only
	•	One with water but kept in the dark

Every day, they checked.

After a week—

Only one seed sprouted.

Abuzar gasped.
“It worked!”

Aaisha looked thoughtful.
“But Ammi… all the seeds were the same.”

“Yes,” Ammi said.

“So why only one?”

Ammi looked at them carefully.

“Because even when all conditions are perfect… growth still happens by Allah’s will.”

Abuzar nodded slowly.
“So science explains how… but Allah decides when.”

Ammi smiled proudly.

⸻

🌿 Hidden Growth

Days passed.

The tiny plant grew taller.

But one day, Abuzar complained,
“It’s not growing anymore.”

Ammi took him to the plant.

“Are you sure?”

“Yes! Yesterday it was the same.”

Ammi knelt.

“Most growth happens under the soil first.”

“Under?” Aaisha asked.

“Yes,” Ammi said.
“Roots grow deep before leaves grow tall.”

She looked at Abuzar.
“Just like people.”

Abuzar blinked.
“Me?”

“Yes,” she said softly.
“Sometimes Allah is growing your patience, your strength, your faith — and you can’t see it yet.”

Aaisha smiled.
“So Allah works even when we don’t notice.”

“Exactly,” Ammi said.

⸻

🌍 Planting Is Worship

That evening, Abbu joined them.

Abuzar showed him the plant proudly.

Abbu smiled and said,

“The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ taught us something beautiful.”

He recited:

“If a Muslim plants a tree or sows seeds, and a bird, a person, or an animal eats from it, it is charity for him.”
(Bukhari & Muslim)

Aaisha’s eyes sparkled.
“So plants give rewards!”

“Yes,” Abbu said.
“Even after we are gone.”

Abuzar whispered,
“I want to plant many trees.”

⸻

🤲 A Dua from the Heart

As the sun set, Ammi raised her hands.

“Let’s make a dua.”

They stood quietly.

Ya Allah,
Just as You bring life to the earth,
bring goodness into our hearts.
Teach us patience like the seed,
and trust like the soil.

“Ameen,” they said together.

The tiny plant stood quietly in the fading light.

It didn’t rush.
It didn’t worry.

It trusted Allah.

Abuzar looked at the garden one last time.

“Even small things grow,” he said,
“when Allah is taking care of them.”

Aaisha nodded.

And the seed—
no longer asleep—
had begun its journey…

exactly on time. 🌱

⸻

🌟 What We Learn from This Story
	•	Allah places life where we cannot see
	•	Science explains process, not power
	•	Patience is part of growth
	•	Caring for nature is worship
	•	Allah’s timing is always perfect

I stepped out of my hut, just to see the villagers crying their hearts out.I looked over my flooded village, the people, the terrifying lightning sky, as if it was mother earth herself, describing her anger.My stomach growled with hunger, hands trembling,head throbbing,body weaker than it could ever be. It’s not easy being a woman,
in a nation where they are worshipped,
yet faces fall every time a daughter is born.

It’s not easy being a daughter—
Watching mothers cry, we pray not to end up like her.
But every son wants a wife like his mother, glorifying her sacrifice!

It's not easy being a woman,
in a land where daughters are killed— for honour. 
But has any father ever killed a son— for being a rapist?

It’s not easy being a sister,
witnessing your brother’s share of freedom—his being trust, ours a permission?

It’s not easy being a wife— 
When you eat last, from leftovers. 
When you are reminded, you came from elsewhere. 
Do women ever truly— have a place called to call "home"? 

It's not easy being a woman,
for the length of our clothes—becomes consent and verdict.

It's not easy being a woman,
going through different shades of biology— Menstruation, postpartum and menopause.
Yet, men decide for bodies, they do not live in!

It’s not easy being a woman,
when pregnant bellies are kicked, because there is a girl inside!
But how silly of men, the abusers, 
to remain unaware that it is their chromosome that decides!

It's not easy being a mother—
turning bricks and walls into "home".
Bringing life into the world,
and then asked to give up her own! 

Yet, the world questions—
What did she ever do?
She? She—
She was insulted like Draupadi,
She was tested like Hajar.
She was devoted like Rukmini,
She spent herself like Khadijah.
She was punished like Ahilya,
She lived the ache like Mary,
She sacrificed like Sati.

It's not easy to being a woman,
in a country that worships them,
because there she is punishment for being born a woman!

The sky looked undecided that morning,dark clouds gathered, yet the road still breathed dust. I was half-asleep when my mother asked me to fetch a litre of milk. She slipped some money into my pocket and said, “Go carefully. It seems Indra Dev is angry today.”

With slippers on my feet and sleep still clinging to my eyes, I stepped outside. The wind pushed hard against my weight, making every step a struggle, forcing me to lean forward just to keep moving. Soon, the rain followed, sudden and sharp. I ran toward a nearby shop to take shelter.

An old man sat there quietly. His kurta and dhoti hung loosely on his frail frame. Something about him reminded me of my late grandfather. I didn’t know why, but my chest felt heavy looking at him.

After collecting the milk from Ramu Kaka, I reached into my pocket, and my heart sank.
My fingers searched again, slower this time, pressing into the damp fabric as if the coin might appear if I wished hard enough. Rainwater had soaked my pocket through. Whatever hope I had left slipped away with the wind. Cold rain mixed with a sudden heat of fear inside me. I didn’t know what to say.

Ramu Kaka narrowed his eyes.
“You boys fool around all day,” he said sharply. “You must’ve eaten a samosa on the way. Now you’re acting innocent.”
“I—I didn’t,” I whispered. “Ma gave me the money. It must have flown away in the storm. I’ll return the money in the evening.”

He didn’t wait for my reply. He turned to another customer and shook his head, as if my guilt was already decided.
Before I could say anything else, the old man stood up. Without a word, he unfolded his fist slowly and placed ten rupees into my open palm, curling my fingers over it as if afraid the wind might steal this too. Then he pushed the earthen cup toward me, silently insisting.

I couldn’t speak. I lowered my head and took a sip of the tea. Its warmth spread through me, loosening the tight knot in my chest.

Milk in hand, I walked back home, the rain softer now. Along the way, a thought stayed with me: in a world full of people ready to question, sometimes all one needs is someone willing to understand, without asking anything at all.
That morning, ten rupees taught me what money alone never could.

It was a cold, lonely evening when Alex, 27, finally moved into his new house at the edge of a quiet suburb. The moving truck had just left, leaving behind silence and the faint rustle of winter wind against the windowpanes.

Boxes were scattered everywhere. Determined to make some progress, Alex decided to set up his bedroom first.

Hours passed as he unpacked and arranged his belongings — a 48-inch TV, a small sofa covered in cloth, a bed, and a window with drawn curtains. Through that window, the outline of an old storeroom was faintly visible.

By evening, Alex had also managed to organize his dining room and part of the kitchen. Exhausted, he sank onto his bed. The air felt heavy, the silence unnatural. His eyes wandered once again toward the storeroom.

Curiosity tugged at him.

Carrying a few boxes, he opened the storeroom door. A cloud of dust burst out, coating his shirt. The air smelled foul—like rust, mold, and something oddly metallic.

A single white bulb flickered, throwing uneasy shadows across the walls.

As he set the boxes down, his gaze landed on an object half-buried beneath old newspapers — an antique film projector. Cobwebs clung to it, but it looked strangely intact. Attached was a film reel labeled:

> “25th December, 2012.”



Just below the date was a symbol—a crude drawing of a smiling man with jagged teeth and hollow eyes.

“Weird,” Alex muttered, brushing it clean. He took the projector to his bedroom, set it up, and plugged it in.

When he pressed the power button, nothing happened. He tried again. Still dead.

“Too old, maybe,” he sighed, turning to leave.

Just then—click.

The projector came to life on its own.

Alex froze. Slowly, he turned back. Numbers flashed across the wall:

> 3... 2... 1...



A white flash filled the room. Then came the flickering footage of a family—a father, a mother, a boy, and a little girl—celebrating a birthday.

The date on the screen read:

> 25th December, 2012.



“Put the camera on the tripod and join us, brother!” the father said cheerfully.

The unseen cameraman obeyed, joining them. The room filled with laughter as the mother placed a cake on a round wooden table and said,

> “Come on, sweetheart, cut the cake!”



The family sang the birthday song. For a brief moment, the film seemed innocent.

Then — the screen glitched.

A face flashed for half a second — a pale man with zigzag teeth and black, hollow eyes. On his forehead was scrawled one word in blood-red letters:

> “BOOGYMAN.”



Alex jumped back, his heart hammering. The image cut to a new scene.

The same family.
But now… all dead.

The parents lay decapitated, their heads placed neatly beside their bodies. The girl’s face was buried in the wooden table, her small hands limp.

Only the boy stood, trembling, a knife clutched in his hand.

Behind him stood Boogyman, whispering into the boy’s ear.

And then, the boy stabbed himself.

Alex shouted and lunged for the projector, pressing the power button — but it wouldn’t turn off.

Instead, the speakers began to play a distorted version of “Jingle Bells.”

Slow. Off-key. Drenched in static.

> “Jingle bells... jingle bells... Boogy’s here to play...”



He struck the projector repeatedly until it shattered. Silence.

He grabbed his phone — 11:59 PM, December 24th, 2018.

Then, from the corner of his eye, he saw movement.

In the kitchen, under the faint light of the refrigerator, stood Boogyman — drinking water.

The creature turned its head toward him slowly, the corners of its mouth stretching unnaturally.

> “Jingle bells... jingle bells...”



Alex stumbled backward, hitting the broken projector. His head struck the sharp edge — blood oozed down his neck.

The lights flickered out.

He switched on his phone’s flashlight — and instantly, the beam illuminated Boogyman’s face, inches from his own.

Alex screamed.

He crawled back toward the window, yanked the curtains aside — and froze.

Boogyman was outside, staring in through the glass.

Panicked, Alex ran toward the storeroom again. A faint square of light glowed there. The projector was somehow on again.

This time, the label on the reel read:

> “25th December, 2015.”



The footage showed children playing “Ring Around the Rosies.” Their laughter echoed... then stopped.

The next frame showed them dead, their small bodies sprawled lifelessly.
Only one girl was alive, drenched in blood, clutching a handkerchief marked with Boogyman’s symbol.

Alex opened the box beside the projector — several more reels inside.
Each dated one year apart: 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, 2017...
And the final one:

> 25th December, 2018.



He turned around — Boogyman stood right behind him.

Alex screamed, fell backward, and hit his head hard. Blood pooled beneath him. The projector burst into flames, and again, that eerie carol filled the air.

> “Jingle bells... jingle bells... Boogy’s here to stay...”

Alex somehow manages to escape and enters inside his room and then suddenly Alex’s eyes drifted toward the storeroom.
Inside, under the flicker of the dying bulb, a shadow swayed unnaturally, as if dancing to some silent tune.
Then—without warning—the shadow’s neck twisted sharply with a sickening snap, though nothing was there to break it.



Staggering to his feet, Alex fled upstairs.

In the last room, he found a girl sitting on the floor, a cake before her, a knife in her hand. The only light came from the flickering candle.

She looked up slowly and began to sing in a childlike whisper:

> “Happy birthday to Boogy,
He was born on Christmas Day,
Boogy loves the children,
And the children love to play...
We work for Boogy,
Boogy eats us and we’re dead,
Happy birthday, Boogy,
Jingle bells...”



She cut the cake. The candle blew out.

The lights snapped on.

The girl was dead, her body limp, the symbol of Boogyman carved onto the cake beside her.

Alex looked down at his own trembling hand — the same symbol burned into his skin.

Screaming, he slashed his arm to remove it, blood streaming down.

He staggered downstairs. In the mirror, the reflection staring back wasn’t his.

It was Boogyman.

And behind him — lying motionless on the floor — were Alex’s body and a woman’s corpse beside him( his wife).

The projector flickered one last time.

> “25th December, 2018.”
