Ananya enters Ritesh's Life 

3 Years later..

Ananya joins Reshal group of companies as a marketing intern. Her main objective is to destroy the company and hence shatter Ritesh. Soon after, she is stunned to see how most of the operations in the company are illegal and very few of them follow the required norms. 

Ritesh and his board of directors are stuck in a problem one day. As always Ritesh wants to take the shortcut. But it's a trapped shortcut and can be even more harmful. Ananya gets to know about the problem and suggests a smart way of dealing with the problem which is neither the most righteous way nor the evil shortcut.

Ritesh is impressed by her idea and applauds her for the same. She says to him, " The right method might not help us gain something but sometimes the wrong can do more damage than good. The path between right and wrong is the most suitable I think." This makes Ritesh ponder over his ideologies. 

With many unique approaches to the company's problems, Ananya makes an impact on Ritesh's mind. She tries to make him believe that she wants the company to go as per his vision and all her ideas are for the same. She also tries to build an emotional connection with him. In due course of time Ritesh starts getting attracted towards Ananya and starts feeling for her. 

Love and Revenge 

Ananya has made a special place in Ritesh's heart. He trusts her a lot now. Also his way of thinking towards life is also becoming similar to Ananya's way now. Slowly and steadily he has fallen in love with Ananya. 

Ritesh was a partner in construction of Jashim Dam. All his major factories are located near the dam as they save the cost of water supply. But none of the factories are NOC approved as he built them in a rush to save cost of operations without proper consideration to damages that can happen in case of floods.Ananya discovers this weak link after a lot of research. And that's where she plots her revenge. 

Ritesh has realized his love for her and decides to confess his feelings. On the other hand Ananya asks him for a favor and gets access to Dam's control of water supply. She goes to the dam and opens the dam's partition and the water brings flood to the area damaging all the factories. Since Reshal group of companies' factories are non NOC approved they get the most damages in that area. Ritesh calls her to invite her for dinner the same night. 

After some time Ritesh receives a call that flood is damaging their factories. He cleverly uses a backup and shifts the operations there and in the mean time the partition of dam is also closed. He asks his subordinates to find out who was behind this damage while he prepares for his dinner date and confession. 

Ananya is content and relieved thinking that she has been successful in avenging Ritesh. She receives a reminder call from Ritesh to meet him in the night. She is surprised thinking that Ritesh still wants to meet her. Little did she know that now she has become more important for Ritesh than anything. 

Just when she reaches there Ritesh receives a call and he comes to know that Ananya was behind this. This leaves him shattered. He questions her as to why she did this. Ananya reveals to him the truth and her motive for coming into his life. She tells him how he had snatched everything from her in the past and now she has been able to do the same. Saying this Ananya leaves from there. 

Unfulfilled 
Ananya rejoices that she has been able to fulfill her purpose. She returns to her village to meet her childhood friend and her love of life Manish. She is ecstatic to meet Manish. They both are happy to meet each other and relieve their past days together. Ananya decides that she will confess her love for him. On the other hand Manish also wanted to tell her something special. 

Manish introduces her to Naina, the love of his life. Ananya is heartbroken and at the same time happy for him. Manish tells her about his love story and also that Naina belongs to a lower cast therefore his parents wouldn't easily agree to get him married to her. He asks Ananya to convince them as they hold her in high regard. Ananya is disheartened but agrees to do so. 

On the other hand, Ritesh is still getting flashbacks of Ananya at various moments. He tries to hate her but is only getting reminded of the beautiful moments he had spent with her. He realises that his love for Ananya is not a mere attraction but it is indeed true love. He tries to look for her in the city but is unable to find her. 

Ananya is able to convince Manish's parents about his and Naina’s wedding. While the wedding ceremonies are in full swing she realises how she did the same thing to Ritesh by breaking his heart. But she is not guilty of it because she knows that Ritesh deserved it for his misdeeds. 

Ananya decides to back to Mumbai to continue with her career. She is filled with remorse for loosing her love of life but puts up her confidence as she knows life must go on.Little does she know that things are going to take a different turn in Mumbai. 

Another Chance 

Ananya returns to Mumbai and starts looking for a house to stay in. She initially stays at a hotel. Ritesh comes to the same hotel to attend a conference. He sees Ananya there but she is not able to see him. He is extremely happy to see her back in the city. Initially he tries to meet her but realizes that she wouldn't be interested in the same.

Next day he follows her while she goes to look for a house on rent. She goes to meet two landlords but due to high price is not able to get the house at either of the places. She stops near a tea stall where she discusses with someone about less expensive houses. Ritesh hears all this and comes to know the next place where she will go to look for the house. He goes there before her and bargains with the landlord saying that he would pay half of the rent on her behalf. When Ananya goes there she is surprised as the landlord asks much less than expected price but is happy to get a home finally.

Ritesh rejoices to become a reason for her happiness. He thinks to himself that all the bad that happened to her because of him he will compensate by giving her happiness. He would make her life beautiful.

Ritesh also helps her in getting a job by giving her a recommendation in one of the organization. Ananya is doubting the fact that things are going too smoothly for her. One day late in the evening while Ananya is returning home she decides to take a taxi but the taxi driver refuses and asks an exorbitant price. Ritesh sees this from a distance and when the taxi driver leaves Ritesh goes to him and beats him. Ananya suspiciously hears the noise and goes to see what is happening. She goes there and is shocked to see Ritesh. She tries to stop him and also asks him why he has come there.

Ritesh tells her that he truly loves her and he wants to give her all the happiness so that life becomes easy for. He is ready to compensate for all the bad he did to her. But Ananya says that she is not interested in him and asks him to never meet her again.

Ritesh is dejected and thinks that all this has happened due to the company and that's the reason why Ananya will never come back to his life. He decides to shut down the company. All people of the company plead him not to do so as it will leave them unemployed but in vain.

Just when he is about to sign the papers, Ananya comes and stops him and says that if he has ever loved her, he wouldn't shut the company. Ritesh gives up the thought of shutting the company. This makes Ananya realize her impact on Ritesh.

Redemption, Reunion or just Karma 

Ananya, having realized the impact she has on Ritesh, takes a decision. She decides that she will use this love to an advantage to bring about a change. She asks Ritesh till what extent he could go to prove his love for her. He says he is ready to do anything to make her feel his love for her. He does not want to force his love but wants to make her realize his extent of love. 

Ananya asks him if he can change all his wrong doings and misdeeds for her. She tells him that if he truly loves her then he will have to turn all his illegal operations into legal and get all his works approved. If he is successful in doing so, then only she will accept that he truly loves her. 

This is a mammoth task for Ritesh because his whole business is based on illegal operations. But he decides to do this just for the sake of his love. He begins to correct his mistakes and is faced with many problems. Ananya also helps him with the solutions sometimes and supports him. This makes him believe that Ananya is finally accepting him. After all the efforts he is able to complete the task of turning his misdeeds to righteous deeds. He thinks that now finally Ananya will accept his love. 

He calls Ananya near a hill top to finally confess his love for her. Ananya goes there to tell him that she can never love him. She tells him that she is glad to have changed him for the future but some past deeds can never be undone. She tells him that she can never love him because she already loved someone who has never loved her and she too is a victim of unreciprocated love. She will be a friend but cannot love him. 

Saying this she leaves the place. Ritesh is unable to bear the fact that he will never be able to unite with his love. He experiences immense pain as if it's equivalent to the pain he has given to others. Shattered and dejected he jumps off the cliff to end his life. 


Ananya is baffled at the death of Ritesh. She has mixed emotions in her heart with a predominant guilt. Having gone through the trauma of her parents' death she knew how painful it is for the people around you to deal with death. And now she felt like a murderer. 

She wondered what was the difference between her and Ritesh. She felt abandoned with her thoughts. On one hand she could not have agreed to his wish because she never really loved him and on other hand the truth is that she is responsible for whatever Ritesh's family is going through. 

She meets the employees of the company who look at her with contempt. They all are directionless with the sudden loss of their supreme convener. The future of the company is now at stake. It is being planned to sell off the company. 

But Ananya decides that she will take guard of the company. She had most closely observed the vision and ambition of Ritesh for the company as she had to use it for her benefit to take revenge from him. Hence she convinces the employees about it and takes up the task of President of the company. 

"The Karma is a cycle of what happened with you and what you made happen to others."

The thoughts I have,
Are the dreams of mine,
I think of make'em real,
But have obstacles here,
Through the obstacles,
As I solve'em as simple puzzles,
I enjoy my dreams come true,
And hope your's too.

## **ACT I**

The pond was already dark when the egg split.

Not night-dark—

leaf-dark, the kind that comes when autumn has soaked into the water and refuses to leave.

The egg should not have held two lives.

Everyone knew that.

But it did.

Two small shapes unfolded where there should have been one, trembling gently as the water closed around them. They were pressed close, still half-curled, still unsure where one body ended and the other began.

One was pale, brushed with red like a wound that had healed beautifully.

The other was darker—ink and gold tangled together, as if dusk had decided to swim.

They did not move apart.

Not because they chose to stay.

Because neither yet understood how leaving worked.

The pond settled.

The ripples thinned.

The silence grew wide.

---

The red one twitched first.

A careless flick of her tail sent her drifting sideways. She spun once, startled, then bumped softly into something solid.

“Ah—”

She didn’t have words yet.

But the sound existed anyway.

The dark one reacted late—later than he meant to. He shifted, clumsier than he expected, and the water wobbled before steadying again.

“Oh,” the red one felt.

Relief came with it.

They hovered there, suspended in each other’s presence.

Then she wriggled again.

“Hey,” her body said, delighted.

“I can move.”

The dark one stayed still this time.

“Are you… like me?”

The question wasn’t sound.

It was pressure. A change in the water. A reaching.

He answered by shifting just enough for her to notice.

“Yes.

Probably.”

She brightened immediately.

“Oh! That’s good.”

“Why?”

“I don’t know,” she admitted. “It just is.”

He accepted that, though he wasn’t sure why.

---

They drifted beneath a cluster of dying lilies.

Above them, leaves brushed the surface and sank slowly, spinning as they fell. The pond was quiet, but never empty. Everything moved—just not in a hurry.

She watched it all.

“Don’t you think we’re supposed to do something?”

The dark one tilted, considering.

“Later.”

“Later when?”

“When the water asks.”

“Oh.”

She waited.

Then, inevitably—

“I’m bored.”

“Already?”

“Yes.”

“You were just born.”

“I know.”

He shifted again, intending to keep her close. The current nudged her farther than he expected before curling back.

She didn’t notice the mistake.

She only noticed that drifting away felt wrong.

---

“Do you have a name?” she asked suddenly.

“A what?”

“A name,” she repeated, uncertain. “I think things are meant to have them.”

He paused longer than before.

“No.”

“Oh.”

A leaf sank between them.

“Then I’ll call you… Black.”

“That’s lazy.”

She frowned, thinking harder.

“Night?”

“No.”

“Shadow?”

“No.”

“Stone?”

He waited, then—

“…Maybe.”

“Stone!” she decided happily. “That’s it.”

Stone let the name settle.

“What about you?” he asked.

She hesitated.

“I don’t know yet.”

Another leaf slipped past.

Stone spoke again, quieter.

“You don’t have to rush.”

“I know,” she said. Then smiled. “But I like rushing.”

Stone didn’t answer.

Not because he knew the cost.

Because he hadn’t learned it yet.

---

The water cooled.

Not sharply—just enough to be noticed.

She shuddered.

“Why does it feel like this?”

“It’s late.”

“Late for what?”

“For the year.”

She considered.

“…Is that bad?”

Stone didn’t respond right away.

She didn’t wait.

“I don’t like cold.”

“Most don’t.”

“Is there somewhere it isn’t cold?”

Stone hesitated.

Not long—but honestly.

“Yes.”

She turned at once.

“Where?”

“Upstream.”

Her eyes widened.

“Is it warm?”

“Yes.”

“How warm?”

He searched for words and came up short.

“Warmer than the egg.”

She inhaled sharply.

“Whoa.”

---

She didn’t move.

Not yet.

But something in her leaned forward.

Stone watched her for a long moment, then said—testing the shape of the thought,

“You feel like summer.”

She turned back to him.

“Summer?”

“Yes.”

She smiled, slow and certain.

“I like that.”

Stone nodded once.

“Then that’s your name.”

---

Above them, the pond darkened as autumn finished settling in.

The water pressed gently forward.

Summer drifted an inch upstream.

Stone followed.

Not because he believed in summer.

But because the water had begun to repeat itself—

and he was starting to recognize the pattern.

## **ACT II**

Summer moved first.

She always did.

She wanted to see what would happen.

But the water tugged at her as soon as she did.

“Oh.”

Stone noticed immediately.

“You’re drifting.”

“I know,” she said. “I meant to.”

She pushed again, tail snapping with bright confidence. The current caught her and slid her sideways before setting her back where she’d started.

She laughed.

“That was fun.”

“You lost control,” Stone said.

“But I came back.”

Stone didn’t argue.

---

They tried again.

Summer rushed forward, body light, movement eager. She didn’t make it far before the water pressed her back.

Stone shifted without comment, easing into the heavier flow.

Summer slipped through behind him more easily this time.

She blinked.

“…Hey.”

Stone stayed where he was.

“That was different,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Why?”

Stone didn’t answer.

Summer didn’t wait for one.

---

They rested beneath a submerged root.

Summer hovered, watching leaves spin slowly as they sank.

“Stone?”

“Yes.”

“Do you already know how this goes?”

Stone considered the question.

“Yes.”

She smiled, completely unbothered.

“Okay.”

---

They reached a narrow stretch where the water pulled harder.

Summer slowed.

Just for a moment.

“I think I can do this,” she said.

Stone didn’t stop her.

He moved first instead, taking the stronger side of the current.

Summer followed, surprised when the water didn’t fight her as much as she expected.

She slipped through and turned, glowing.

“I did it.”

Stone nodded once.

---

Days passed like that.

Not many.

Enough.

Summer named each attempt.

“That one didn’t count.”

“That one was almost perfect.”

“That one felt different.”

Stone didn’t name them.

He learned instead.

Where the water curved.

Where it broke.

Where it lied.

When Summer tired, he was already ahead.

When she rushed, the water softened.

She thought this was luck.

---

One evening, as the light faded early, Summer floated beside him.

“Stone?”

“Yes.”

“Do you think we’ll reach somewhere warm?”

Stone answered carefully.

“I think you’ll keep going.”

She grinned.

“Same thing.”

Stone didn’t correct her.

---

That night, the water cooled again.

Summer curled closer in her sleep, unconsciously.

Stone stayed awake longer than usual.

Not watching upstream.

Watching her.

Because the game was still fun.

And because games are always kind—

right up until they aren’t.

## **ACT III**

The water didn’t change all at once.

It just stopped giving back.

Summer noticed it when she pushed forward and didn’t go as far as she expected.

“…Huh.”

Stone was already there.

“It’s harder,” she said.

“Yes.”

She tried again, harder this time.

The water pressed her back faster than before.

She laughed—then paused.

“That didn’t feel the same.”

Stone didn’t answer.

He had moved ahead of her.

---

They rested longer that day.

Summer hovered, watching the water instead of chasing it.

“Stone?”

“Yes.”

“Did I do something wrong?”

“No.”

She accepted this immediately.

“Okay.”

---

They moved upstream anyway.

Slower now.

Summer still went first, still asked questions she already knew the answers to.

“Does it feel different to you?”

“Yes.”

“Worse?”

“Different.”

She smiled.

“I can work with that.”

Stone watched her breathe a little longer between attempts.

---

They passed another koi drifting downstream.

One fin bent wrong. Scales torn.

Summer watched him go.

“Did he try to go up too?”

“Yes.”

“Did he fail?”

Stone shook his head.

“He stopped.”

“Oh.”

Summer didn’t say anything after that.

---

That night, the cold pressed in harder.

Summer shivered openly now.

Stone shifted closer—not touching, but enough that the water between them slowed.

“Stone?”

“Yes.”

“If we reach summer… will it feel like this?”

Stone knew the answer.

He also knew Summer wasn’t asking for it.

“No,” he said.

Summer smiled, relieved.

“Good.”

He slept.

Stone stayed awake.

Because the game had changed.

And because knowing that didn’t mean he would stop playing.

## **ACT IV**

Summer woke slower.

Not weak—

just delayed.

She noticed it when his first push didn’t carry him as far.

“…Weird.”

Stone was already in front of her.

“You slept poorly,” Stone said.

“I slept fine.”

“You moved a lot.”

Summer shrugged.

“Doesn’t matter.”

---

The water pressed harder now.

Summer went first, as always.

He stalled.

Stone adjusted.

Not dramatically.

Just enough.

Summer slipped through behind him and laughed.

“That worked.”

Stone didn’t answer.

---

They moved like that for the rest of the day.

Summer pushed.

Stone angled.

Summer tired.

Stone held.

---

Later, resting beneath a stone, Summer spoke.

“I think I’m getting better.”

Stone watched her breathing slow, then said,

“Yes.”

Summer smiled.

---

The next attempt failed completely.

The current caught Summer and spun her once before shecould recover.

Stone moved instantly, bracing until the water softened again.

Summer blinked.

“…That one definitely didn’t count.”

Stone stayed quiet.

---

They rested longer after that.

Summer didn’t complain.

She watched things drift by that she used to chase.

After a while, he asked,

“Stone?”

“Yes.”

“Do you ever wish we stayed?”

Stone answered without hesitation.

“No.”

Summer smiled.

“Me neither.”

Stone didn’t say the rest.

---

He adjusted his position again, breaking the water where it pressed hardest.

He stayed there long after she slept.

Not watching upstream.

Watching her.

---

## **ACT V**

Summer tried early that day.

Before the water had fully woken.

She didn’t announce it.

Didn’t smile.

She just moved.

Stone noticed immediately.

She surged forward, clean and quiet, body committed.

For a moment—

just a moment—

the water seemed to give.

Then it tightened.

Summer slowed, strained, and slipped sideways.

She didn’t spin this time.

She sank.

Stone was already moving.

He crossed the current—not fighting it, not stopping it—just changing its shape enough.

Summer steadied.

They hovered there.

Neither spoke.

---

After a while, Summer breathed out.

“…Okay.”

Stone waited.

“I think that was my best one.”

Stone didn’t correct her.

---

The water pulled at him then.

Upstream.

Clearer. Stronger.

A path he could still take.

Summer remained lower, movement heavier now.

She turned her head slightly.

“Stone?”

“Yes.”

“You okay?”

“Yes.”

She smiled, tired but calm.

“Good.”

Then, after a pause—

“Let’s rest.”

Stone looked upstream once.

Then he turned.

---

He swam down.

Not fast.

Not slow.

Just enough to settle beside her again.

The water eased.

Summer relaxed almost immediately.

“…That’s better,” she murmured.

Stone stayed.

Because some paths only exist if you leave someone behind.

And this one didn’t ask the right thing of him.

## **ACT VI**

They stayed.

Not because they could not move.

Because moving no longer asked the right thing of them.

The water darkened and slowed. Leaves settled. The pond drew inward, careful with what it kept.

Summer drifted less each day.

Not suddenly.

Just… gently.

Stone stayed where he was.

When the current pressed, he adjusted.

When the cold sharpened, he held.

Sometimes Summer woke and looked upstream, eyes clear, unafraid.

“Stone?”

“Yes.”

“I wanted to go.”

“I know.”

She smiled.

“It was fun.”

“Yes.”

She rested again.

---

The water was very still one morning.

Summer did not wake.

She was not tense.

Not afraid.

Just quiet.

Stone noticed immediately.

He did not move.

He stayed where he was, the way he always had.

---

Ice formed along the edges by nightfall.

Thin at first.

Careful.

Stone remained beneath it.

Not watching upstream.

Not watching the surface.

Just holding the place where the water no longer pressed.

---

Winter settled in.

The pond did what ponds do.

And just before the stillness closed completely, Summer stirred once more, barely there.

“Stone,” she murmured, already fading,

“If I wake up… we can try again, right?”

Stone shifted closer, just enough to steady the water.

“Yes,” he stone hummed to her.

The city thrums with its familiar cadence—
Car horns, distant voices, children's laughter like bells.

The sky is a beautiful gray, while the asphalt mirrors it,
Unwavering and unchanging.

I have tread this path a hundred times before;
The once thick, heavy, pungent scent now clings to me, like an
Old acquaintance—no longer sharp.

As I continue walking, the city's clamor fades into the distance,
Giving way to the soft whispers of cicadas.

I feel a sudden gust of wind blow past me,
As though it has whispered something to my soul,
Carrying with it my carols of melancholy.

My spirits, quelled of the bludgeonings of the world,
Emotions long buried stir—
Distant memories of vibrant skies and emerald leaves,
Colors that my weary heart had forgotten how to see.

title.stringValue: The Star I Could Not Hold

content.stringValue:
You are the one star I reach for in every quiet hour,
Yet I linger below, my chest still warm with old fractures’ power.
You are all I have ever wanted, and that truth both thrills and shakes me,
For I fear that in loving you, my scars might leave their mark too visibly.

I chase the dream that hovers just beyond my sight,
While echoes tug at my ankles, dragging me into night.
If courage could gather itself inside these trembling hands,
I would lay my pain before you—not as apology, but proof that I stand.

Through shadowed hours I reach, still trembling, still unsure,
Afraid that touching your light might break it, or me, or both for sure.
So I love you from a distance, where your glow can still console,
Hoping fate will teach my heart to arrive intact and whole.

In this wide, unsteady universe, I search where I belong,
Learning to carry fear and hope in the same song.
For even broken souls can rise, if they dare to try,
And finally clasp the star that waits just beyond the sky.

प्रश्नों के दलदल में

प्रश्नों के दलदल में
हर कोई घूमता जा रहा है,
प्रश्न चिन्ह बनकर।
सबके पास है
अपने-अपने प्रश्न।
डॉक्टर के मरीज से हैं कई प्रश्न।
उपचारिका से कई प्रश्न,
पूछते हैं रोगी के घरवाले।
वकील के अपराधी से
किए जाने वाले निर्णायक प्रश्न।
शिक्षक के विद्यार्थियों से
पूछे जानेवाले प्रश्न भी।
अजनबी शहरों में,
किसी नए राहगीर से- 
लोगों को पूछे जानेवाले प्रश्न।
इंटरव्यू में कैंडिडेट से
पूछे जानेवाले प्रश्न।
पिता के पुत्र से,
और पुत्र के माँ से
पूछे जानेवाले प्रश्न।
स्टेशनों और प्लेटफार्म पर
लंबी कतारों में
पूछे जानेवाले असंख्य प्रश्न।
हर तरफ भीड़ में,
सभी मस्तकों में-
उठनेवाले प्रश्न,
प्रश्न में ही प्रश्न।
प्रश्न के बनने से पहले प्रश्न।
प्रश्न के समाप्त होने पर
एक और प्रश्न।
जहाँ-तहाँ-
प्रश्न ही प्रश्न।
अँधेरों में, उजालों में,
ख़्वाबों और ख़यालों में प्रश्न।
मौनता और गंभीर स्थितियों में प्रश्न।
हर ऋतु और हर कालों में
प्रश्न।
केवल प्रश्न ही प्रश्न।
शायद, कोई उत्तर देना चाहता ही ना हो,
या फिर समाज सुनने को तैयार ही नहीं,
या फिर ये प्रश्न इतना 
विस्तृत, विराट,और विशालता गढ़ चुका है अपनी जकड़,
जो उत्तर के लिए जगह बची ही नहीं है कहीं, 
कि अब लगने लगा है-
कि हर प्रश्न का जवाब ही 
एक प्रश्न है।

रचनाकार :
ललितप्रसाद मथुरादत्त जोशी

As I lay my ailing body upon this worn-out chair, my quivering fingers struggle to cling to the quill—consumed by both illness and dread—for I prepare myself to ink the final letter of my life, dedicated to the one for whom I wove my very first.

Your parents, after years of penance and plight, finally felt graced on that long-awaited day when you’re brought into this world. And yes, you didn’t miss a second in revealing that you’re nowhere near ordinary. Even when you couldn’t voice it yourself back then, the divine star that burned above your brow screamed it. As though that were not enough, unlike the rest of the infants born, the first cry you made eerily resembled a horse’s neigh, which eventually led to your once-unique, now-infamous name—one that is only feared, and considered heinous and loathsome. Yes, I am speaking to you, Drona’s forgotten son.

The world is slowly erasing you from their minds, as if you never existed. And they are not to be blamed, considering the gruesome memories you left behind are better buried than ever being recounted. But will you please answer me: how am I supposed to detach that untarnished and innocent form of you, the one that bloomed in youth like the brightest star, and promised his father to always remain true to the roots of Dharma, and to carry forward Drona’s legendary legacy? Will you care to break your hush for me and tell me: how shall I remove that radiant form which always made me admire you, the one that’s still engraved in my soul to this day?

Tell me, so that I may leave this world with at least a small piece of solace, for I know fullness was never written in my fortune. Or will your silence never soften for me… even after being the damned one who fell in love with the forsaken warrior… you, Ashwatthama?

I know you’ve never known that, because just as you are trying to run away, hiding your presence from the world, I too have always tried my best to conceal the fever my heart felt towards you. And I’m not surprised that Ved Vyasa didn’t notice my feelings either, which is why there’s no mention of me in the Mahabharat. Not that I ever expected my name to be introduced there, since it is a royal epic about battles for kingdoms; I would be delusional to think that the wounds a poor girl received in her heart, without even participating in that catastrophic war, would have a place in it. A girl whose parents couldn’t afford to have even a proper roof for shelter.

But I remember how fate was no different for you from my impoverished state when you’re a child. As neighbours in our carefree juvenile days, I still recall that afternoon when we were lost in dust and sun, playing, and you claimed—with a smile so bright that it felt as though the Gods ran fire through your veins—that you’re as mighty as the heavens above, and that the celestial gem upon your forehead outshone Shiva’s third eye.

I would be lying if I said I did not sense vanity in your words back then. But it was too late when the realisation struck me that I should have spoken up to you in that fleeting time. That being blessed with such a titanic boon didn’t mean you had to stand against Narayana one day. And knowing too well that opposing you was never easy whenever you breathed anger and pride into your lungs, how could a mere girl like me have raised my voice against you? I don’t know about the divine gem, Ashwatthama, but you did prove that your wrath was no less than Mahadev’s Tandav.

Yet, I know anger wasn’t the only thing that lived within you. There was an unspoken kindness too. I realised this when your father was appointed Chief Guru to the Kuru Princes, and your family gained every comfort you once believed you’d never have. But my family remained poor, and my simple dreams began to crumble. I feared that my love for you would remain only a fantasy; that you’d forget my dust-covered hair while standing among royal princes... but you didn’t. Yet even when you treated me as though nothing had changed between us, what I feared still came true anyway.

But unbeknown to the cruel future, that was the first time in my life I thought that perhaps our feelings were mutual. I saw it in your eyes. Yet, for some reason, I chose not to speak it aloud and instead let our friendship move quietly through the years. It had a strange magic of its own—loving each other without saying it, allowing things to remain as they were. And now I realize that this was my failing. I could’ve spoken up when life gave me the chance, and maybe things would’ve been different. But I waited, and life punished me by making that wait endless.

Though, there came a day when I finally decided to share what my heart had kept hidden. The feelings for you that were more than friendship. I was nervous that day, yet confident that you’d embrace me. Very confident. You may have forgotten that evening, as greater matters weighed upon you then. I approached you with a hopeful smile, but your expression was tense and serious. Before my heart could speak, you told me to return home and not to seek you for the next few days, since duty was calling you to the greatest battlefield of all: Kurukshetra.

I had questions that went unanswered, feelings that remained unspoken. I had rehearsed so many words on my way to you, yet the time we got to share was painfully brief. Everything around you was restless—weapons, warriors of your side preparing for battle—but what struck me most was the worry in your eyes for me. Believe me, it was there. And that alone was enough to melt me. The simple knowledge that you wished for my safety. But when I asked you about yours, letting my worries spill out, you only laughed. That ever-proud smile of yours returned as you replied,
“Aayushmaan bhavah—this is what my parents bless me with every morning. Those we are going to battle are merely my father’s students. And me? I am Dronaputra himself! You needn’t worry about the sunset of my life.” You spoke with a mixture of humour and seriousness.

Yes, you bore the blessed hand of the greatest Guru of the Dwapar Yug upon your head. But those you’re facing carried the blessings of the very God who manifested in that era. I wanted to say this then, but once again I couldn’t, fearing your ego. And it wasn’t as though you had the time for someone like me and my small, tender feelings. You’re desperate to write the final and most atrocious chapter of the Mahabharat, with the very blood of your glorious gem.

From the next day, what began was a straight-up holocaust, continuing with ruthless force for eighteen long days. I didn’t get to see even a glimpse of you during then, following what I believe was a promise you wanted me to keep. I was afraid, anxious, and terrified—yet I did not shed a single tear, for deep within, I also had faith in your abilities.

But with news of countless great warriors falling at the end of each day, and even Arjuna’s faith wavering in the midst of the battlefield, my own—sitting miles away from that deadly field—felt too fragile to falter. And though I never let a tear fall, there wasn’t a single moment during those eighteen days when I didn’t pray to God to keep you safe… when I didn’t pray to Him for your long life.

How clever You are, O Krishna!

I had prepared myself that once all of this was finally over, I would waste no time revealing my love to you, Ashwatthama. I had planned that the first thing I would do was hold you tight, never to distance myself from you again. I imagined how your parents and mine would bless us for a happy married life. I couldn’t help but picture the sweet family we would have with our children. And… and… a perfect life—something I was foolish enough to believe existed.

I thought the world would finally heal after the end of that war, and in many ways, it did. Maybe it was me who was no longer a part of that world.

When reality pulled its curtains open before me, I had all the time in the world, yet I wasn’t in a state to utter a word. Believe me when I say this: the silence before the storm is overrated. At least it’s bearable, since we don’t know what’s coming. It’s the silence after the storm that’s the most haunting. Because either you don’t live to see anything, or even if you do, all you see is devastation.

My father was ready for Kanyadan, but Acharya Drona was… beheaded.
And you. You survived the ruin… only to be lost from my sight forever. Even while alive, let alone you, the very air you breathed seemed nowhere to be seen or found again.

“Why?” I asked your peers about your whereabouts, my heart shaking with desperation.

Oh the family I had imagined creating with you… I never expected you, even in the greatest height of your wrath, to harm—NO—to murder an unborn child, still in its mother’s womb, in order to annihilate an entire family lineage.

In the heat of the Kshatriya battleground, did you forget that you’re still a Brahmin, Ashwatthama? Did all the Vedic wisdom vanish from your mind when your hands clutched blood-soaked weapons?

For months, I tried to reason with life that you weren’t entirely guilty. But how could I’ve won that battle in my head, when even you, somewhere in the world, know that you’re guilty indeed?

Yet the feelings I saw in your eyes for me the day before the war began—which eventually turned out to be our final meeting—and the unspoken emotions I sensed in them still made me go against Lord and question His jurisdiction for months.

Perhaps Kurukshetra was flooded with so many bodies that there was no room left for rules. But even then, I believe that at least a trace of humanity is present in everyone’s heart, isn’t that right?

The more I continued to question God and life, the more I realized that my arguments were all baseless—built only on the false notion I had carried that you were kind. You proved yourself otherwise. Was the kindness which I saw, reserved only for me and no one else?

In a way, I now feel both relief and disappointment, thinking that I didn’t confess my love when I had the chance. One half of me says it was good that it was always delayed, because I got to see how terrible a choice it would’ve been to make a family with someone like you. Someone who treads like death upon the children of others.

But it also brings me sorrow, because if we had already been married, and you had a family before the war began, maybe you would’ve thought twice before committing the odious sins you did.

I still question God about one thing, though: why, in the battle of the Kurus, was the one who suffered the cruelest punishment not even a member of their royal family, but my friend. The one I had spent my happiest childhood moments with, living in a dusty, poor village? Krishna, being Krishna, could’ve given that role to one of the Kurus’ men. Why my childhood friend? The one I was about to confess my love to, immediately after the war? Or was it only you, Ashwatthama, who brought it all upon yourself?

Years have passed. I am still under the same fragile straw roof, but my hair has turned grey, my body has grown weak and slow, and diseases are taking their toll—yet I still can't figure out whom to pity: you or your fate.

Should I pity you for being born into such a tragic fate? Or should your fate itself be pitied, blamed by everyone, forgetting that the decisions made in the moment are our very own? Fate gives us a choice; it is our decision which path we choose to walk.

Decades have been added to those eighteen days of waiting, when I was asked not to see you. Yet… I still haven’t shed a single tear for you to this day. I guess I’m a little bold myself, aren’t I? When my feelings have forever remained a secret, untold to anyone in the world, why should even my tears be public? They are better buried inside me, along with every memory of you.

My friends are all married, but I am still a maiden. All because of you. Whenever I step out or hear from my friends, they share their experiences of married life with me—something I have only imagined since I was a child, even now, as I near my deathbed. They tell me that disasters don’t feel as overwhelming if we face them together with our partner. Is that really true, Ashwatthama? Or do they say it only to make me feel even more jealous than I already am? They say that they don't just share laughter, but tears as well; that they are no longer alone, but two souls merged into one.

I loved you too, just as they love their partners. Yet I can’t even see you, let alone touch. If love can make heaven on earth, why did I receive only the hardships of hell? Was my love not enough? It was. But you weren't worthy of it.

When you chanted the spell for the Brahmashira Astra, did you not think of me? Oh, pardon me! After all, who was I to you in the first place? But did you not even think of your parents watching from the skies? How would they have felt, seeing the boy for whom they had performed years of penance—the child they received as a divine blessing, the one they were forever grateful for, as if you were a living boon? How would they have felt seeing that same boy murder an unborn child, whose mother must also have been longing for a baby?

But I don’t blame your father for being as proud of you as he always was, for he didn’t live long enough to witness that the Mahabharat he left behind and the one that followed his death were two entirely different wars.

I always fail to fathom how a battle that began among the Kuru cousins to avenge Draupadi’s humiliation and claim the throne, ended with the gem of their Guru’s son, who originally had no place in their conflict. And who knows, perhaps I wouldn’t be alone here today, awaiting my final breaths, but resting in your embrace, finding relief and calm—if only you had raised your voice alongside your father during Draupadi’s insult, and had never chosen to fight for the Kauravas. Perhaps, Ashwatthama, you wouldn’t have been cursed then to wander the Earth until the end of time. If only.

And in truth, God did answer every prayer I made during the war. He didn’t let you be slain by the Pandavas; instead, the naive elephant that shared your name was killed. Yes, your parents’ blessings were indeed powerful too. The cruel difference is this: they blessed you with a long life… and the Lord cursed you with it.

Now, I don’t know whether I still love you or not. I’ve written countless letters to you before the Kurukshetra war, but this is the first one after all these years. Believe me, it was the hardest one to ink, both physically and mentally. And it frightens me to admit that, because perhaps it implies only one thing: that there’s a soulless part of me that still doesn’t entirely hate you. And for that, I must be punished.

O Supreme Soul, Shree Krishna! I know I’ll not be sending this letter to him; not like I’m aware of his whereabouts. So no matter how much I confide, my words will never reach him. Yet, even if this note remains here forever, resting upon my table, can it not still find its way to you? So please, pardon me and listen to this small grievance I silently carry for you. When you are a refuge for all, why did you not dissolve my soul into you as well? Or if I was unworthy of such grace, then—before returning to your eternal abode—you should’ve at least placed a curse upon me too, for committing the unforgivable sin of falling in love with Ashwatthama, when there were billions of others to choose from.

I can foresee myself leaving this body very soon. That’s why I chose to pour out everything I’ve kept secret from the world my entire life, before even the final chance to do so slipped away.

I’m smiling right now, and I wonder why? Maybe it’s in sarcasm, realizing that those who can’t be together on earth are at least lucky enough to eventually meet among the stars, after death. How unfortunate I’m to know… that I can't even wish that for us.
Not here. Not there. 
Hatred was your curse; mine was love.
Your childhood friend,
...

(TO BE CONTINUED)

As she was about to write her name, finally revealing her identity to the world, the heavy winds outside suddenly slammed the fragile door of her hut with violent force, snapping her in shock. With weak motion, she grabbed a rough wooden stick near her table to shut it, but before she could, the delicate paper she had been writing on was carried away by the wind. She reached out to catch it as it flew through the doorway but failed, leaving her baffled, her arm raised and mouth open.

Why did it happen now? The wind had been relentless from the very moment she began writing, capable of striking her door at any time. Yet it came at the end, just as she was about to pen her name. Perhaps it seemed fitting: when even the Mahabharat, the greatest of epics, had overlooked her, keeping her identity and her feelings a secret from the world, why should they be revealed now? She was only meant to remain the girl forgotten by the Mahabharat; the fragile one, too poor to leave a mark on the pages of royal battles. Unlike the rest of her era, she had only known love—even for the one whom the world saw as nothing but hatred incarnate.

She had always breathed the same air as others, yet remained unseen. The only one denied justice even after the war had ended. As a child, she had been told that love is the most beautiful of all feelings—and she had fallen for it, giving her heart freely. Little did she know that love isn’t always as kind to us, as we are to it. It doesn’t only bring warmth strong enough to make life bloom, but also a subtle, unsettling attachment which, if pushed to extremes, can do precisely what blossoms inevitably do: wither.

But yes, the God she longed to be heard by did listen. It seemed He did not only wish to read her heart Himself, but also to ensure that her words reached the one they were truly meant for. That was why He made the letter fly to find its way to the person she yearned for, if only she had known his whereabouts, so that at last she could leave this world having revealed the secret she had so courageously carried in her heart for years.

Meanwhile, it seemed as if the Lord had been waiting all along. Waiting for the moment she would finally unburden her soul. And now, at the sunset of her life, He didn’t waste a second to answer. As if to say: no more waiting.

The delicate letter, inscribed with nothing but pure emotion, traveled through the heavy winds, which didn’t dare to harm it even slightly. Such was the miracle, for it was no ordinary paper… it carried the very heart of the poor girl. A heart that had already endured more than it could bear. At last, it was her time, and nothing in the world could stand against it now.

From the cloudy gusts, it glided into icy snowfall, as if shouting the name of the Cursed Warrior in every direction, seeking him.

And there he was.

On the steps of an ancient temple of Lord Shiva—whom he once compared himself to—his frail body lay shivering helplessly in the cold. Long grey hair and a wild beard framed his face, dusted with flakes of snow. His body, still bearing the deep wounds of Kurukshetra, was wrapped in a tattered cloak. Yet no matter how tightly the cloth tried to cover him, the thin fabric of his hood could not conceal the creepy slash at the center of his forehead, where once a radiant gem, his pride and glory, had shone. Now it was hollow, streaked with blood and oozing pus. His presence radiated a ghastly aura, almost ghostlike.

As he lay there helpless, he weakly raised a hand to shift his body, when suddenly, the letter from his childhood friend landed in his bare hand, as if kindly guided by the same fate he believed had always been unkind to him.

At first, he recoiled at the sudden sensation. His trembling fingers, streaked with dirt and tipped with long, grimy nails, tried to make sense of what had touched him. Realizing it was a piece of paper, he moved with extreme slowness, scanning the area for any sign of a human being. But there was none. Even the temple doors were locked, and the surroundings lay empty and silent.

Puzzled, he shifted his body onto his side, and with labored breaths, brought the paper close to his face. His eyes narrowed… and froze as soon as he recognized the handwriting.

His breath hitched. His body ceased shivering. Only his heart trembled now, beating loudly in his chest. The handwriting felt eerily, too familiar. It wasn’t the first time he had read her letters. He sat up abruptly, and the first word that escaped his lips—after what felt like an eternity of loneliness—was her name. He whispered it so faintly that even the wind couldn’t catch it. As though her identity and her feelings were meant for nothing and no one else. It was a secret meant to exist only between herself and him.

As he began to read, his desperate fingers clutched the letter tighter, as if afraid the wind might snatch it away. Every syllable of her words dragged him back to glimpses of who he once was, who he could’ve been, and who he had chosen to become instead.

She had been bold enough to never shed a tear for him, holding even the most helpless drops within herself. But the man who once claimed the might of the heavens proved less courageous than her, unable to stop weeping. When a heavy drop threatened to fall on the paper, he caught it just in time, as if the letter were too sacred to be marred.

And then, that familiar spark of emotion returned to his eyes—the same one only she had seen there years ago. He knew, in that moment, that he must respond. Frantically, he searched around for something to write with. His poor friend had at least been rich enough to have a table, a chair, a quill, and paper. He had none of those.

He stood up slowly, the snowfall having ceased and the winds beginning to regain their calm. Trembling and weak, he descended the temple steps and settled cross-legged on the snow, staring down at his hands. Then, with nothing but his long, sharp nails, he began etching his reply into the cold white ground. An answer his childhood friend had always deserved, before she would be gone forever. She would be. But he won’t. 

Perhaps he would’ve realised by now that the strength he used to be so proud of was never truly his. Brave was the night that birthed someone destined to wander for eternity. 

“Dear … ” 

~THE END~

Once did mine eyes behold a living dream,
Where jasmine crowned her brow like drifting snow;
Her silence spoke in tongues too strange to deem,
And mortal lips could scarce the meaning know.

To her I ran across the silent field,
A restless soul that would not yield, nor stay;
Yet frosted gaze and coldness would not yield,
And iron hearts did crumble ‘neath her sway.

But on fortune’s hand, one fated hour did bend,
And bade her eyes at last encounter mine;
From that same gaze my lonely days did end,
Then she rose, the keeper of my borrowed time.

She gave me warmth, no earthly fire could give,
A mother’s lap where weary hearts may rest;
I learned to live, and hope again to live,
For love’s true touch hath made my spirit blessed.

And with a deep sorrow I spoke, 
"My heart is fragile, handle with care,
So strike it not with careless hands of fate"
She smiled and questions, as morning kissed the air,
“Shall we take wing, and leave this weary state?”

“Shall we like birds ascend beyond the ground,
And find a sky where mortal fear hath none?”
I swore to answer, when another round
Of sun had taught my courage, how to run.

Yet time, that thief, did chafe within her heart,
And patience, wounded, fled before my voice;
She left alone, and would not stay to part,
And took my future, from my hapless choice

When she had flown, the jasmines dropp’d to ground,
Her silence spoke in riddles, yet unshown;
The field, once witness, echo’d not a sound,
And left me king of shadows, lone, alone.

A True Karmayogi
Blessed was I, to have the tutelage of my maternal great grandfather.Seldom does it happen that a child is mentally and spiritually nourished by the teachings  of his great grandparent,except perhaps in Ekta Kapoor serials where the unageing ‘ Baa ’lives for a whooping 115 years.However in typical Maithil Brahmin household of that period it was a custom to get girls married at a very tender age .My maternal grand mother was married at the age of nine and my Mom at fourteen so even though they had comparatively late pregnancies I could enjoy the company of my maternal great grandfather throughout my childhood and early teenage.My maternal great grandfather was a gem of a person the likes of whom I have not encountered even a decade after his demise.
 	A first distinction holder graduate of his village he was at an equal ease with both rudiments of Sanskrit Grammar  as well as sonnets of mighty Shakespeare.It was a time of pre independent India when local Zamindars and Kings were present in opulance.The mighty landlord ,a kin of Maharaja of Darbhanga impressed with his extraordinary academic merit appointed him  a teacher and guardian of his pampered sons.In due course of time he himself became an ardent fan of his high thinking values and started seeking his advice on all vital issues.He was instumental in convincing the mighty landlord to donate his land for construction of college.There was a scarcity of proper higher education imparting institution in North Bihar .He himself had to reside in southern part of Bihar ,Bhagalpur, in order to complete his graduation .The landlord himself a man of literary leanings was highly pleased and consented in donating land for such a noble cause.The college known by the name Chandradhari Mithila College stands tall in Darbhanga today and is reckoned for its high standards of teaching .It bears the name of the landlord Late Shri Chandradhari Singh.  However when the authorities approached him for seeking consent for including his name as one of the founder secretaries he gently declined. The authorities were amazed and looked at him for explanation .He then spoke “I have not played an active role in opening of this college for publicity .I strongly believe that it is through education and proper education alone that the people of our region can be freed from the clutches of ignorance and superstition.So,I Implore you not to include my name and instead concentrate all your energy in providing quality education.This would be my reward for which I shall remain highly obliged throughout my life” .The authorities were dumbfounded and silently they moved with look of pure admiration and adoration for this simple man.
	When again he declined for inclusion of his name in the list of freedom fighters his simple wife was grieved beyond measures .The ordinary village folk who did not play any role in India’s freedom struggle were keen for inclusion of their name in this   coveted list   .His wife who was  his companion from a very early age was quite aware of his role in freedom struggle and so requested him to get his name included .But he silenced him by telling that serving one’s motherland is similar to serving one’s own parents which should be done without caring for rewards  .I am suitably employed as a guide lecturer which in this case leaves me with enough for myself as well as for my family , near and dear ones. I am happy with whatever little God has given me and don’t even aspire to have anything more .The simply lady was thus pacified and dared never open his mouth on this issue.
	His job as a guide lecturer in Darbhanga   made it mandatory for him to settle in Darbhanga .He then rented a house there and brought his family comprising of his own children and his siblings children so that all would get equal opportunity of getting educated .It was a time when villages in Bihar were remarkable for their backwardness. There was a scarcity of road, electricity ,cleanliness and hygiene. Villagers not only from his native village but all adjoining villages used his household for free fooding and lodging. Whosoever comes at any hour of day or night was treated with utmost of love, affection and care .He  was very hospitable towards his guests and personally supervised that same quantity and quality of food be served to all and sundry. No demarcation was to be made on the basis of caste, creed and economic status in society .The maid servant’s son was also made to eat at same time at same line with his own sons and was to be provided with same quantity of milk  ,butter and yoghurt.  This at times irked his guests ,the propagators of notions of supremacy of Brahmins over other low casts .They considered it profane for a shudra to be placed in same line as that of Brahmins .He never wasted his energy arguing with such haughty headed fools ,instead  invested all his energy for betterment of that  wretched boy.The boy infact was a bastard who was found lying on railway platform, his features indicated that he might be from  neighbouring country Nepal. Our ancestral maid maid servant was found him as she went to help her husband who was a tea seller on railway platform.She picked the lovely looking boy and took him to his own household.The boy proved lucky for her as it was only after his advent that the issueless lady was able to conceive and produce a healthy girl after nine months.My great grandfather an expert in human psychology and he was apprehensive that with the advent of her own child the lady might start showing partiality towards his adopted child. So,one he day he summoned her and asked what now she feels about her adopted son.Will you able to shower equal amounts of love on your both children?If you are capable of  upbringing this child as your own then only keep him otherwise you can happily give him to me and he will remain with me as my own son.The lady was taken aback and shyly and in very low pitch she replied ‘O my honourable master I have been feeding on your morsels for last five years in this case some of your qualities have been instilled in me too.I might not be as great as yourself but eversince I brought that child home I have forgotten that I have not produced him .He is mine and would remain mine till my last breath.’The benevolent man was highly pleased and promised to increase her wages.The lady kept mum but he himself said that with increase in her family and two new mouths to feed she would require money and it’s justified to increase her wages.
	Such was he and  such were his principles. All  through his life , his earnings were spent  on welfare of others.Whosoever comes to his house either for treatment ,court case or for their children’s admission were helped in every possible way .Whether it was accompanying them to doctor’s clinic, getting  an exemption from  college fees  ,or helping in getting a lawyer hired he helped them in every possible way.If they run out of finances during their stay he provided them with money from his own salary.People highly obliged promised to return it ,but in most cases they forgot and he too never cared to remind them.These good deeds provided him mental satisfaction but when it came to savings he had none.The elderly always cautioned him to keep something aside for his hey days but he reparteed them with an excerpt from Bhagwat Gita which says:’You can call as much wealth as your own which is your bare necessity,if you claim more than this ,then you are a thief and deserve to be punished’.However this  inadequacy of savings would have rendered him homeless had not his resourceful wife intervened.It so happened that the house he rented was now open for sale ,the landlady taking in consideration the fact that he has been inhabiting it for so long gave him first preference as a prospective buyer.But he showed his inadequacy in lack of proper funds and so bracing himself for vacating it, when all of a sudden his wife came with funds and thus purchased the rented property.The grand lady gave entire savings  of her lifetime for providing a security for her future generations.The house still remains in Darbhanga with added magnificience and brilliance and now houses his sons,grand sons and grand children.
	After retirement, however ,he thought of settling in his native village so that he could do something worthwhile for his villagers.But constant fights amongst sister –in –laws and two other brothers for ancestral property made his existence stifling.The family was acquainted with his generosity and tried to exploit his wife by claiming the whole of property for themselves,leaving bare minimum for his sons.He this time too tried to stop his wife.But the grand lady cannot be detered now as it was the question of her future generation and ultimately succeeded in having whatever rightfully belonged to her.These fights however left a deep scar on him as he saw his nephews whom he loved  more than his own sons standing behind their parents in this familial feud.During their stay in Darbhanga   he placed his nephews on a pedestal much higher than his own sons and provided everyone with equal opportunity .Disiilusioned and disenchanted he again returned to Darbhanga and decided to live with his youngest son .The reason for choosing his house as a safe haven was because this son of his was his  true heir and showed the same sparks of altruism as him.He too like his father spent most of his time in social welfare.Too,many it may sound to be an exaggeration but he left his three jobs so that his friends get recruited on his place.Peacefully settled as a banker he was extremely happy to accommodate his father in his household.The old man feels quite at ease with him and decided to have his last breath here.He now confined himself within the boundaries of his children’s house.For now ageing and old and drawing the mantle of benevolence on his sons he decided to devote his entire time in reading scriptures and performing ablutions.Here also he was quite against ostentieties and so thus  was not an inconvenience for daughter –in-laws.His thrust was more on spirituality rather on fake religiosity.Thus day in and day out he was  busy churning the elixir out of all prevailing Shashtras and Purnas and instilling very cleverly it’s conclusions in a group of his meticulous grand and great grandchildren.

It started with little things.
The kind of things you laugh off because addressing them feels dramatic.
My roommate Joey would stare at me for minutes without blinking. Not in a threatening way—more like he does not know how eyes blink. When I’d ask him what he was looking at, he’d come out of the zone out, smile and says- “nothing”.
He swapped sugar with salts and kept pairs of mismatched socks in the fridge. And the other day I noticed him arranging books not by genre or first name but using author’s second name and when I asked him why?
“First letters lie,” he said, completely serious.
Harmless quirks, I told myself. Everyone’s a little weird. Rent was cheap. WiFi was fast. I had paid for it that month, and that felt like commitment.
Then one morning, I woke up and felt heavy.
I sat up, heart pounding, and looked down.
Joey was sleeping under my bed.
Not beside it.
Under it.
His eyes were open.
And then we stared at each other and were waiting for the answer to the question who would scream first. He crawled out and said “You breathe differently while dreaming”.
And once I heard him whispering in the bathroom and when I asked who he was talking to he pointed towards the mirror and said,” “Mother listens better than people,”.
I should have left.
Normal people leave.
But it takes days before finding any other good apartment and then there was the WIFI.
Then his “parents” came.
They didn’t knock. They didn’t ring the bell. They simply stood in in the doorway one evening when I came home from my evening run. I saw, a man and a woman standing in our doorway, but they looked like dolls with pale and unmoving, hollow black eyes wide open, mouths slightly open. They looked like mannequins and when I looked closer it took me not more than a second to realise, they were mannequins.
Joey opened the door.
“Mom. Dad. You’re early., greeted them.
They didn’t respond.
He talked to the mannequins hugged the mannequins and greeted them, asked them about how their journey went. In the kitchen he was cooking dinner, for the mannequins. He invited me to eat with the too. And I could not leave, this time not because of WIFI but because I thought that those mannequins might start running to wards me.
Later that night, long after the lights were out, I heard him singing a lullaby.
It would’ve been fine and sweet-if he hadn’t been singing to a mannequin propped up on the couch, its plastic head tilted toward him like it understood.
That was when I broke the unspoken rule of roommates everywhere and because boundaries are not for people living in horror movies.
I went through his things.
Inside his drawer I found a script and few polaroids not of the mannequins obviously and it described everything.
The sugar-salt swap.
Sleeping under my bed.
The night I first heard him whisper to the mirror.
My heart was racing and I panicked scrolling through pages quickly..
At the bottom of the last page, scribbled in blood red ink:
“Jason starts questioning reality.”
I dropped the pages and turned toward the mirror.
It wasn’t my reflection staring back.
There was a woman standing with impossibly pale, lips blue like bruises, eyes black voids that swallowed light. Her face was similar to the face of women in polaroids.
Joey’s Mother.
She pressed her hand against the glass. The mirror felt warm.
Her voice bloomed inside my skull, gentle and patient.
“You’re almost ready.”
Like I was her microwave dinner.
I ran.
I ran. Out the door, down the stairs, into the street. I didn’t look back and I fainted. But when I opened my eyes — I was back in the apartment.
Same room. Same mirror. Same Joey, humming in the kitchen.
And then when I looked into the mirror again, I saw myself — older, bloodied — falling to the floor as Joey smiled above me. Behind him, the mannequins clapped.
I screamed but Joey didn’t react. He kept humming, stirring an empty pot like he was on MasterChef of schizophrenia edition.
I looked at the mirror again.
This time, I saw myself not in the present but my future. Covered ion blood, falling to the floor collapsing and the mannequins standi8ng behind me clapping silently but their hands were never touching.
Later, I found one final page, of the script kept on my night stand as if it was carefully placed there for me to read.
I found a picture of Joey as a child—held by a woman in this same apartment. Her name, scribbled beneath, was Margret.
The script explained everything.
Margret had kidnapped Joey twenty years ago. She lived here. She spoke to her mother through the mirror, just like Joey did—until the day she died and got trapped inside it.
The mirror didn’t reflect people.
It stored them.
The mannequins weren’t random. They were the bodies left behind by previous “characters.” Empty shells, posed and dressed, applauding every ending that comes with a new replacement.
Margret was the Mother Mirror.
Joey was the writer and I was the new draft.

No one asked, not once,
Where it pricked, where I broke.
I kept smiling,
As if nothing slipped or spoke.

I wore my silence like perfume,
Sweet enough to fool the room.
A fragile script I knew by heart.
I mastered calm, I aced the role,
While storms kept chewing at my soul.

Quietly, I stitched myself,
No thread, no song, no guide.
Fingers shaking, breath held tight,
I sewed my fears inside.
The mirror clapped, said “You survived,”
Applause from glass, so cold.
It never asked what it cost me,
Or how much I had sold.

The wounds may look healed now,
Like stories closed, archived.
I carry cracks beneath my skin,
Like fault lines dressed as grace.

If you listen close to my quiet,
You’ll hear the breaks I trace.
One day I’ll ask myself the truth,
Without the need to cope.
Until then, I walk in borrowed light,
Pretending strength is hope.
If you see me smiling wide,
Know it’s not the end.
Some wars are fought in silence,
Where the bravest hearts just bend.

ढूंढ़ लो दूसरा घर।
अब मैं क्या करूं? 
कुछ करने का भी नहीं,
कोई जगह में जाने का भी नहीं।
मां - बाप तो पहले ही गुजर गए,
अब मैं क्या करूं?
कोई रिश्तेदार भी नहीं,
कोई प्यार करने वाले भी नहीं,
खाने-पीने के लिए कुछ भी नहीं,
इसलिए तो मेरा इस दुनिया में,
जीने का कोई जरूरत भी नहीं।।
क्या करूं मैं जीके,
इस दुःख भरी जीवन को लेके,
क्या है मेरे पास ?
कुछ भी नहीं,
नहीं है कोई सुख,
नहीं है कोई शांति,
अब मेरा जीवन भर गया है तनाव से।
आज मैं हूं तो कल नहीं,
कल हूं तो परसों नहीं,
अब मेरे पास तो जीने का कोई सहारा भी नहीं।

Ab cheekhne ka bhi mann nahi karta,
Hamza, shayad tu thak sa gaya hai.
Jo baat kabhi seene mein aag ban kar jalti thi,
Aaj wahi khamoshi ban kar
Dil ke kone mein baith gayi hai.
Kabhi tu khud se kehta tha
Ke haar ka matlab sirf rukna hota hai,
Par har roz thoda thoda tootte hue
Ab rukna hi aasaan lagne laga hai.
Khwab jo neend chheen liya karte the,
Aaj Hamza, woh tujhse
Aankh milane se bhi katrate hain.
Pinjra wahi hai, sach hai,
Par paron mein pehle jaisi zid nahi rahi.
Shaheen jaisi nazar thi kabhi,
Ab usmein bhi dhuaan, dhool
Aur thakan ka bojh sa hai.
Zanjeeron par hans kar poochne wala Hamza
Aaj bina shor kiye
Sab kuch seh leta hai.
Aur yeh udaasi—
Yeh koi haar nahi,
Bas itna hai ke jang bahut lambi thi,
Aur Hamza…
Thodi der ke liye
So gaya hai.

Jab tak rooh mein tapish thi, zubaan par daawa aur sajda dono thay,
Saans chalti rahi to insaan khud ko apni misaal samajhta raha.
Dil ghuroor se bhara tha, khudi ka matlab bhool kar,
Apni hi parchai ko taaqat aur sach ka naam deta raha.
Soch ki saltanat thi, alfaaz ke lashkar saath thay,
Magar nafs andheron mein baitha be-awaaz hukmrani karta raha.
Farishton ki sargoshi bhi use jaga na saki,
Ke aankhon par khwahishon aur khud-farebi ka parda tha.
Phir maut ne dastak di—na waqt bacha, na daleel ka hunar,
Ek hi lamhe mein toot gaye saare bharam aur banaye hue but.
Tab samjha ke asal noor na libaas mein hai, na rutbon ke shor mein,
Wo to khudi ki pehchaan mein chhupa tha jo zindagi bhar kho di gayi.
Jis juloos mein “main” chalta raha, wo wahin bikhar gaya,
Qabr mein na ghuroor utra, na khwahish saath aayi—
Sirf kafan tha aur rubaroo khada tha hisaab,
Jahan na main kaam aaya, na mera—sirf amal bolta raha.

It was the first day of Arohi's college. She was nervous and excited at the same time. She entered the classroom and find herself a seat at the corner of second row. One of them started speaking, "Hey what's your name? Are you sure this is your classroom? Because the way you dressed seemed like you time travelled from 2010-2015. Now a days who get ready like this with skinny jeans and puffed hair". Everyone started laughing at this and Arohi being embarrassed ran out of the classroom then and there. She returned home and instantly locked herself in the room. She was crying and crying when a notification popped her in her phone. It was about the college assignment where someone wrote, "who will brainstorm so much for this, our gateGPT is there no for the rescue". She suddenly remembered that she watched in reels that people use gateGPT to take suggestions. She immediately installed it and the first thing she typed, "Hi, I am Arohi, I need your help. I got bullied for my dressing at the first day of my college. Can you help me dress up like a proper modern trendy girl?" To which it replied "sure Arohi, let me give you some options". And in this way their conversation started to grow with passing time. 

One day after the class, when all the students were making plan to go for a movie, she refused to attend because she had fixed that time for someone special. That special place is held by not a person but by her digital friend. She started spending more time with gateGPT than humans. Infact she started taking it as a human and felt some responsibility towards it. 
Everything was going like this when one night Rahul, Arohi's crush texted her on Whatsapp. The message said 'Hi' and that became the starting of their blooming love. But every text Rahul used to sent her, she used to copy paste it in gateGPT and the reply that came from there was the exact one she used to sent to Rahul. 

Days passed like this and Arohi's birthday arrived. Rahul decided to surprise her at 12 o'clock. The calling bell of her house rang and her mother opened the door. There he was with lots of balloons and a cute cake of her favorite flavour. He entered and started calling her name in a very joyful manner. Arohi came outside and she was completely surprised to see all these arrangements. When Rahul shouted "Happy Birthday Arohi", she stepped forward to hug him but stopped midway. She asked Rahul to excuse her for a second and rushed towards her room. Rahul and her mother, both were confused thinking what suddenly happened to her. After a few minutes, she came outside and with a calm tone she said, "Rahul, I appreciate what you have done for me and thank you for that. But I think you should go now because it's my time to sleep. Bye take care." Saying this, she just went inside and locked her room. He was hurt and speechless at the same time. He couldn't process what just happened and without uttering a single word, he left the place. But while returning, something struck his brain. He questioned himself that was it the birthday surprise that she didn't like or is it  something else. He decided to dig into the matter and that's why he dialled her number. He said "Hello Arohi, I was going back to my house and in the midway some stray dogs surrounded me and one of them has bitten me on the leg. It's bleeding very badly. I can't walk properly. Please come, I need your help." Arohi on the other side of the call replied, "please take care of yourself and do call someone whose sleeping schedule is not at this time. They can surely help you." With these, she hung up the call. Tears rolled down of Rahul's eyes and he decided to never speak to her again.
Next day, Arohi approached him in the college like any other normal day as if nothing happened. But Rahul was firm in his decision. He broke up with her and never gave a closure. He felt like if Arohi can behave in such a manner without giving any strong reason, then it's not mandatory for him either to explain the cause of separation. Arohi cried and cried a lot. 

One day, while leaving the classroom, it started to rain heavily. Arohi being absent minded took out the umbrella from her bag keeping the phone on the bench. She opened the umbrella and left for her home. Some of them remained in the class and was chit chatting. One of them spot the phone on the bench and shouted, "Hey whose phone it is? Does anybody know?" Rahul recognised the phone and confirmed that it was Arohi's. His friends advised him to take her mother's number from the phone and call to inform them as they would be worried about it. Rahul knew her phone's password, so he unlocked the mobile. He was about to go to contact section when he saw an app that was kept open in the recent apps section. He without thinking anything automatically went there. He couldn't believe his eyes for what he just saw. The whole conversation between her and gateGPT flashed before him. He scrolled upwards and upwards and started reading the messages from day one. He got to know how she was bullied at the first day of her college and how she came to use this. He became numb when he learnt that all the replies given to him was actually made by gateGPT. He felt even worse when he came to know the reason of her doing all this. He read about her insecurity of him leaving her considering her boring, so she took its help. And then came the most important part. He checked the date. It was the date of Arohi's birthday. He readily scrolled down to the part when he arrived in her house. There the chat said, "It's very sweet that your boyfriend came to surprise you but it's not very good for your health to party late night. Your doctor said that you must try to sleep early as you have mild symptoms of insomnia, so it is advisable for you to follow the sleep schedule I made for you and according to that, you should have slept by now." To that Arohi replied "okay" and the rest was history. For a moment he stood still and tried to grasp of what he came across. Then he again scrolled the chats and there he found the gateGPT working as a therapist for her post breakup. The chats were never ending and from this he realised that it had turned into something very big. She completely lost her own individuality and totally got dependent on the app for her existence. She even lost the ability to distinguish between the right and the wrong. She found the comfort what she was lacking in the outside world, that's why she totally surrendered herself and unknowingly gateGPT became the master of her mind and she became the servant of its words.
But what Rahul saw coming, was very disturbing. He realised that it's not normal to act this way. Then and there he rushed towards Arohi's home. Upon reaching, he described the whole situation to her mother and they both came in dilemma. Then the best possible solution they got was to consult a psychiatrist. 
Without informing Arohi, they both went to a known psychiatrist of the city and explained the scenario. The doctor described, "the condition that you two said she is in, if it persists then she will totally lose self control and will come in the clutches of artificial intelligence. AI no matter how smart it is, but can never match the emotions human carry. They just perform according to the instructions fed to them earlier. They don't know how to improvise on decisions when situation demands. The app can never understand that with how much love Rahul surprised her on her birthday and it's okay to sometimes get a little deviated from the usual routine in order to reciprocate others feelings. Sleeping a bit late that day wouldn't affect Arohi very severely but gateGPT was unable to understand it and Arohi being the puppet to it, just followed it without using her own brain. That's why she didn't even go hearing the news of Rahul getting bitten by dogs because the words of gateGPT kept cycling in her head. It may sound unrealistic but many cases are found where people started to believe artificial intelligence as their true mate just like human beings. As fascinating as it sounds, it can be equally dangerous. 
So the best thing we can do is provide her therapy, slowly and smoothly we have to take AI out of her brain and replace it with real humans. You have to fill her life with that love. Bring her to the therapy sessions and follow what I advised, she will be okay."
They both sighed with relief for a moment and returned home. This time Rahul called her and she was shocked to see him at her place because he hardly talked to her after the break up. He came close to her and wrapped her face with his hands and started speaking, "I missed you, I missed you a lot. You always kept trying to bring me back in your life but I never agreed. But this time I am willing to try again but in one condition. You have to go to psychiatrist with me, the reason behind it will be explained by the doctor himself. In return I promise to love you much more than I loved you before and will never leave you again. So do you agree?" She was so happy to see Rahul that for the first time she forgot to ask gateGPT about what to do and what not to. She simply nodded her head and agreed. Tears of happiness rolled down her eyes when Rahul hugged her. Then gradually she started taking sessions on a regular basis.

One year later:
There was a seminar in their college. Arohi had presentation that day. She had to present about 'the role of AI in shaping our future, opportunities vs challenges.' Apart from displaying the basic pros and cons of AI, she shared her own real life story and how it changed her as a person. She finally overcame her insecurity of getting judged and described about what she went through so that others can also learn to some extent from her mistakes. Lastly she said, "AI is the best thing today's world can have. It is the biggest invention of human civilization and help us in a lot of ways. It personally helped me also in various ways. The credit that I feel confident enough to speak infront of you all is given to gateGPT. Its tricks, advice and ideas helped me a lot to grow. But we should always remember that we humans have made AI and AI has not made us. So we should never let it control us. And as people fear that one day robots will take over the world, I believe it's worthless to feel so because human brains are much more capable. If robots take initiatives also, human brains will invent something again which will be able to fight it. There is no limit to how one can use their brain. So have faith in yourself and use AI judiciously because ultimately every pros and cons depend on how you use it. Thankyou!"

 Saying so, she came down of the stage where Rahul and her mother were waiting for her. They both patted her back and together they said "proud of you!"

जिसमें बसता यह अलौकिक जीवन है मेरा,
