Medications.
A small pouch of jewellery her mother had given her before marriage.
She woke the kids gently.
“Wake up, babies… We’re going somewhere safe,” she whispered, her voice trembling.
They sensed the urgency but trusted their mother blindly.
She dressed them quickly.
Pulled her dupatta low over her face.
Breath held, she checked again - no sign of Shahmeer.
With shaking fingers, she opened her phone and booked a cab.
It was barely a fifteen-minute drive - but those fifteen minutes could decide her entire life.
A driver accepted the ride instantly.
“Arriving in 4 minutes.”
Her heart thudded so hard she felt the floor vibrate beneath her feet.
She turned the phone into silent mode.
Packed the charger.
Switched the phone off.
No trails.
No last-minute calls from him.
No tracking.
She lifted the suitcase.
Carried her son’s small backpack.
Held both children tightly by their wrists.
Opening the door felt like stepping out of a prison.
The sunlight hit her face - blinding, almost unreal.
She kept her head lowered and walked quickly toward the gate, praying no neighbour would stop her.
The cab pulled up.
“Madam?” the driver called softly.
She nodded, eyes still lowered, and ushered the kids inside.
“Airport,” she whispered.
As the cab moved, Ashira’s breath finally loosened.
But her eyes flicked to the rearview mirror constantly.
Every biker behind them.
Every car turning.
Every pedestrian.
Her mind kept whispering:
What if he comes back early?
What if he asks someone?
What if he comes after her to the airport?
Her daughter squeezed her hand.
“Mumma… are we running away?”
Ashira swallowed her tears.
“No, baby… We’re going home.”
The cab driver glanced at her through the mirror.
He didn’t ask questions.
Just drove faster.
The closer they got to the airport, the more her chest burned with fear and hope mixed together like fire and rain.
The security guard asked for IDs, and Ashira handed them over with trembling fingers. The guard looked at her, then at the children, then back at her.
For a second, she felt her world freeze.
Ashira quickly flashed the booking confirmation on her phone. The staff nodded, processed everything swiftly, and guided her to the baggage counter.
Her hands trembled as she lifted the suitcase onto the belt.
She watched the bag disappear, as if her entire painful past was being swallowed by that conveyor line.
The airline tag slipped into her hand.
A small, stiff piece of paper - yet it felt like her first fragment of freedom.
Holding the children close, she headed toward the security check.
Every step felt like walking out of a burning house.
Once the screening was done, she gathered their things, clutched the children’s ID cards, and moved to the waiting area. There were still fifteen minutes left before boarding for their 12:45 p.m. flight.
She sat with the children, her heart racing, her eyes scanning every corner - half afraid Shahmeer might storm in, half praying he never found out.
The airport announcements echoed softly overhead.
For the first time in years, she breathed without fear.
The escape had begun.
As she moved toward the security check, her phone - tucked in her bag though switched off - felt like a bomb waiting to explode.
She didn’t dare turn it on.
She didn’t dare slow down.
Every step she took away from the island felt like peeling away another layer of pain.
When she finally boarded the plane and sat in her seat, buckled the children in, and heard the announcement - 
“Prepare for takeoff -”
Tears rolled silently down her cheeks.
She wasn’t just leaving a home.
She was leaving a nightmare.
And as the plane lifted into the sky, Ashira whispered,
“We’re free.”
Spending the next two hours on the flight with her children safely beside her, their small hands wrapped around hers, sensing the storm they had just escaped. The sound of the aircraft felt like a lullaby after years of chaos. Her son, Azlaan, leaned on her shoulder, drifting into sleep, while her daughter drew quietly in her drawing book, unaware of the life-changing journey they were on. Ashira looked at them, her whole world and felt a wave of relief. Every mile the plane travelled was carrying them closer to the people who loved them, closer to safety, closer to the life she had always dreamed of giving her children. For the first time in a very long time… she allowed herself to breathe.
Her family waited at the airport. The moment Ashira saw them - her father’s trembling hands, Zoya’s tear-filled eyes, Sharique’s protective stance - her heart broke open.
She collapsed into their embrace.
“You’re home now,” her father whispered.
 “No one will hurt you again.”
Ashira cried until her body shook. Years of pain flowed out of her.
Her children clung to their grandparent, feeling the safety, they had never known.
That night, Ashira slept peacefully for the first time in nearly a decade.

Shahmeer discovered Ashira had escaped along with the kids; something inside him snapped open like a beast released from its cage. Within minutes, Ashira’s phone began lighting up with dozens of missed calls, all from him. He slammed her with messages, each more desperate and threatening than the last. At first, he pretended to be worried - acting as if she had suddenly “gone missing” without informing him. But very quickly, that façade melted away. His real face emerged.
He sent long, furious texts demanding she return immediately.
He accused her of “breaking the home,” of “destroying his life,” and of “abandoning her duties as a wife.”
But then, in the same breath, he switched to emotional manipulation - claiming he couldn’t live without her, saying she was the only one who understood him.
He weaponised guilt like a sharp blade.
When she didn’t respond, his anger erupted into threats.
He warned her that he would file a missing person complaint, claiming she had run away with the children without his consent. He threatened to tell the authorities that she had “kidnapped” his kids. He sent photos to the nearby local police station, just to terrify her. He said he would drag her to court, ruin her reputation, and make sure the children were taken away from her forever.
Then came the worst message - the one that chilled her to the bone.
He said that if she didn’t return, he would come to her city and snatch the children back, no matter who stood in his way. He claimed he would find them anywhere, no matter where they hid, because they were “his blood,” “his property,” and “no mother has the right to separate a father from his children.”
His words felt like claws around her throat, squeezing, trying to pull her back into the darkness she had finally escaped.
He bombarded her with voice notes - screaming, crying, begging, and threatening.
“I will not spare you.”
“You think you can run?”
“I’ll take my children back.”
“You are dead to me if you don’t return.”
It was a storm of anger, manipulation, victim-playing, and cruelty - an emotional assault meant to break her spirit all over again.
But Ashira remained silent.
Not a single reply.
Her silence was the strongest response she had ever given him.
She simply blocked his number! 

 
CHAPTER 11
Reclaiming Identity  

When Ashira first returned to her father’s home with her children, the silence around her felt loud. It took weeks for her body to understand that no footsteps would pound toward her door anymore. No angry voice would erupt over a misplaced object. No hand would strike her for breathing the wrong way.
Her nervous system - trained for years to live in fear - needed time to relax.
And healing became her full-time journey.
Ashira began therapy - something she once believed was only for “big problems,” for people who fell apart, for those who needed rescuing.
But she soon discovered she had carried storms inside her for too long. Storms that had never been allowed to settle. Storms, she had learned to hide even from herself.
For the first time in years, she sat in a room where someone listened - not to judge, not to twist her words, not to manipulate her - but simply to help her understand herself.
Session by session, she unravelled pieces she had buried deep:
Why did she keep forgiving him?
Why did she keep returning to him?
Why did she keep shrinking herself to make others comfortable?
Why did she believe endurance was loyalty?
Her therapist explained concepts she had never heard before - trauma bonding, gaslighting, emotional dependency, and suppression of identity. Words that gave shape to pains she had endured in silence for years.
Ashira learned the difference between love and trauma.
Love wasn’t supposed to hurt.
Love wasn’t supposed to break her spirit.
Love wasn’t supposed to silence her voice.
For the first time, she understood that what she endured wasn’t love at all - it was a cycle of abuse disguised as affection, apology, and temporary calm.
Ashira started her healing with the simplest acts - because healing begins with reclaiming tiny pieces of yourself.
She wrote daily affirmations, each one like a seed planted in her bruised heart:
“I choose myself.”
“I deserve peace.”
“My children deserve love.”
“I am allowed to rest.”
“I am worthy.”
“I will never lose my voice again.”
Her handwriting grew steadier and stronger.
Her words reflected a woman rising.

Leaving Was Not the End - It Was the Beginning. People believe the hardest part is leaving.  But leaving is only the first step.
Healing is the real battle.
Shahmeer tried every trick to pull her back into the cage she had finally escaped from.
The first wave hit through his messages - sharp, wild, and overflowing with fury.
Late-night messages from another mobile number filled with rage lit up her phone, one after another. He accused her of “destroying the family,” his voice heavy with entitlement rather than hurt. Between every call lay the same chilling warning: he would take the children away.
His anger was not sadness. It was control slipping out of his hands.
When the rage didn’t work, he shifted his tone. Suddenly, her phone buzzed with fake apologies and rehearsed “I’m sorry” messages. He wrote long paragraphs claiming he had changed, calling himself a “new man,” and pretending remorse he never felt.
There were crocodile tears, emotional dramas, and carefully crafted guilt trips meant to pull her back into the same cage she had escaped from.
When apologies failed, he resorted to the familiar strategy - blaming her for everything.
“You are the problem.”
“You misunderstood.”
“You exaggerated.”
“You broke this home.”
Each line was an attempt to rewrite the truth, to make her question her reality, and to shift all responsibility onto her shoulders. But this time, she didn’t bend.
As his manipulation fell apart, the threats began.  “Come back, or I’ll make your life hell.”
He filed a missing persons complaint and threatened to keep her and her family behind bars. 
He threatened to take the kids away.  Every message was a bomb meant to shake her foundation. Every call was a reminder of how far he would go to maintain control.
His noise - his anger, his manipulation, his blame, his threats - came crashing at her like a storm meant to drown her spirit.  But now, she had already stepped out of the storm.
And she refused to go back.

But this time, Ashira stood tall.
She wasn’t alone anymore.
She had the truth.
She had evidence.
She had her father.
She had her siblings.
She had her own strength - finally awakened.
For the first time in years, Ashira felt her heart breathe.

There is a kind of healing that only comes from being surrounded by genuine love.
The silence of her father’s home felt warm - not threatening.
The sound of utensils in the kitchen didn’t trigger fear anymore.
The doors' opening didn’t make her flinch.
Footsteps didn’t make her brace for impact.
Her sister’s voice - soft, comforting, and full of affection - filled the house like a protective shield.
Zoya became her emotional anchor, holding her through her breakdowns and celebrating her smallest victories.  Sharique, gentle and playful, helped with the children - taking them to school, helping them with homework, and bringing back their lost laughter.
Her father, who had quietly watched his daughter’s pain for years, finally breathed a sigh of relief. He encouraged her work, supported her decisions, and reminded her every day that she was home, safe, and protected.
For the first time, Ashira realised she had never truly been alone.
She had simply been too buried in survival to see the hands extended toward her.
Slowly, the noise of Shahmeer’s threats faded into background static - irrelevant, powerless, insignificant.
She was rebuilding her life brick by brick. Ashira went back to her passions.
She rediscovered her confidence and stepped into a world where she no longer needed to hide her tears behind forced smiles.
Every day wasn’t perfect.
Healing never follows a straight road.
Some days, she cried quietly.
Some nights she woke up sweating, heart pounding from forgotten nightmares.
But she kept moving.
Steady.
Determined.
Unapologetically herself.
She had chosen the right path.
Not just safety.
Not just freedom.
But herself.
For the first time in years, she wasn’t just surviving.
She was living.
Her friends, once pushed away because of her isolation, reached out again.
New friendships slowly blossomed - women who admired her courage, clients who trusted her professionalism, and neighbours who noticed the glow returning to her face.
Ashira no longer felt like a shadow moving through life.
She was becoming a woman with a voice, a purpose, and a presence. 
 
CHAPTER 12
Purpose from Pain 

This chapter is not about regret.
It’s about the transformation and rebirth of a caged life.
The world outside Ashira’s life now felt different. It was peaceful, quiet, gentle and pure. The trees she once watched with a restless, trapped heart now looked greener, brighter, as if dancing in happiness. Birds were chirping, and she could feel their carefree life. The air was lighter, the sky wider, and the sunlight touching her like a blessing.
Today, she opened that same diary, its pages yellowed in places, its edges carrying the faint scent of memories and tears and hope. But her hands did not tremble. For the first time in a long time, her heart beat with certainty.
She wrote not as a victim, not as a frightened wife running from storms, but as a survivor,
 as a mother who had fought wars in silence,
 as a woman reborn.
Words started flowing from her pen like truth finally freed:
**“To every woman who cries silently at night…
To every mother who shields her children from storms…
To every soul who thinks she is not enough…
You are stronger than your circumstances.
You are not alone.
You deserve peace, dignity, and love.
Walk away when it hurts.
Walk away when it destroys you.
Walk away before you lose yourself completely.
And remember - your worth is not determined by who failed to love you.” **
She placed her hand on her heart after writing, as if she was closing the unseen wounds with a gentle stitch. She took a deep breath, letting her painful past flow like a smooth smoke and disappear into the universe.
She whispered softly, as though her mother was in the room:
“Never again will I lose my voice.
 Never again will I settle for pain.
 Never again will I forget who I am.”
This wasn’t merely a promise.
 It was her rebirth.
Her life approached now in a more positive note.
She was moving into something larger - something more meaningful and powerful.
The days flowed like a smooth river, yet profoundly healing. Peace did not arrive all at once - it came in slow, gentle waves.
She was cleaning her room one afternoon and found old memories that carried traces of the woman she used to be - exhausted, overworked, and bruised emotionally and physically. Instead of breaking her, these objects now felt like proof of just how far she had come.
She smiled - a real smile - when she realised she didn’t have to walk on eggshells anymore.
She didn’t have to constantly monitor her tone, her words, or her expressions.
She didn’t have to fear footsteps approaching her door.
Freedom tasted sweeter each day.
One morning, after dropping her children off at school, she sat down at her desk and opened her laptop. It felt strange - almost sacred. This machine had once been her doorway to the world, her source of independence, and her means of survival.
She created a small workspace at home - just a table, her old laptop, a few pens, and a lamp her mother had once gifted her.
That small corner became her dedicated workspace.
It reminded of her existence she was before her marriage:
a creator, a designer, and a dreamer.
At first, she took small projects - branding, poster designs, and social media creatives. Then her confidence grew.
Her momentum returned.
Her creativity re-ignited.
Old clients responded with warmth:
“Where have you been? We missed your work.”
New clients admired her calm dedication, unaware of the battles she had survived to return here.
She rebuilt her routine.
Mornings belonged to her kids, making them ready for school and cooking.
Afternoons are for her work.
Precious moments were spent with her kids in the evenings, teaching them, and making snacks for the family.
She also opened a small online business - nothing fancy, just a quiet beginning. A shop that grew slowly, lovingly, peacefully.
Every order felt like a victory.
Every recurring customer felt like an affirmation. 
Every milestone felt like a message from the Almighty saying, “You made the right choice.”
Her diary - once filled with fear, tears, and apologies - began to transform. 
Ashira learned this gently, day by day.
She started to walk every morning - not to escape, not to clear her fear, but simply to breathe in the fresh air. To acknowledge that her feet now carried freedom, not chains.
Her body, once tense like a clenched fist, slowly relaxed.
Her shoulders dropped.
Her breath returned to normal.
Her skin glowed again.
She no longer lived her life seeking permission.
This time, she lived it on her own terms.

One evening, she sat cross-legged on her bed with her diary in her lap.
The early pages were full of her teenage dreams.
The middle pages are full of heartbreak and prayers whispered at midnight.
But now…
She opened a fresh page.
The blankness no longer terrified her.
 It inspired her.
And she wrote:
“I am not broken.
 I am rebuilding.
 I am rising.”
Her handwriting had changed - firmer, stronger, and more certain.
 As though her soul finally held the pen.
Life, when healed, gives birth to purpose.
Ashira joined an online women’s community. At first, she was hesitant - sceptical about sharing her wounds in a group of strangers.
But the first night she logged in, she listened to women speaking - voices shaking, stories trembling, hearts identical to hers.

Women who endured what she had.
Women who prayed the same prayers.
Women who were trapped, confused, and terrified.
Women who were one painful step away from leaving but lacked courage.
She didn’t speak that day.
But the next day, and the next, she began participating gently.
A woman messaged her privately:
 “I read your comments. You speak as you understand.”
Ashira replied, “I do. I’ve lived it.”
Word spread quietly within the group. Soon, women began reaching out to her one by one:
“How did you find the courage to leave?”
“How did you plan your escape?”
“How did you manage your kids?”
“How did you restart your life?”
Ashira didn’t preach.
She didn’t force her opinions.
She didn’t dramatise her story.
She offered something much more precious:

“You don’t have to stay,” she would say softly.
“You’re stronger than you think.”
Women began telling her how her journey inspired them:
“You gave me the courage I didn’t know I had.”
“Your words helped me take my first step.”
“I left because I saw myself in your story.”
Every message felt like a blessing.
Her pain had not gone to waste - 
It had become a pathway for others.
 

A Peace She Earned
Months passed.
Life wasn’t perfect - but it was peaceful.
Peace… something she once prayed for with tears streaming down her face.
Peace… something she begged for in the middle of the night.
Peace… something she had nearly forgotten existed.
Now, she embraced it.
The children no longer jumped when a door opened suddenly.
No longer paused before speaking.
No longer hid behind her when voices rose.
They were free children.
Because she had been a brave mother.
For the first time, she realised purpose was not to erase the past, hide her scars, pain or pretend storms never happened.
Her purpose was to reconstruct her journey into an inspiration for others who were still walking. She was now empowered! 
She felt happiness seeing her children sleeping peacefully, with the innocent smile on their faces - they were safe, warm, and not scared anymore!
For the first time in years, she whispered to herself:
“I am NOW FREE.
 I am at PEACE!
And I am finally home.” 
 
 
“Still I Rise… Quietly”
 I was the daughter with dreams in her eyes,
 Raised on love, beneath gentle skies.
 I gave, I smiled, I played the part,
 But silence grew inside my heart.
They saw the sparkle, missed the pain,
 A quiet storm beneath the rain.
 I lost myself in roles I wore,
 Until I couldn't anymore.
Now from the ashes, here I stand - 
 No prince, no saviour, just my hand.
 Each scar a story, every tear wise…
 I didn’t break - 
 I learned to rise.

Dedicated to every woman who forgot her worth
… and found it again.
 -  Afshan Ambarin 


 
About the Author
 
Afshan is a creative designer, inspirational writer, and former software professional whose life story exemplifies bravery, resilience, and transformation. After working in the software industry for several leading corporations, she realized that creativity was her true calling. With vision and tenacity, she shifted her career path and founded her own creative agency, turning her talent into a flourishing expression of independence and purpose. She is also a World Record Author, recognised by the Asia Book of Records and the India Book of Records, a recognition that celebrates the impact of her voice and work.
A mother of two lovely children, Afshan draws deeply from her life experiences in her writing, crafting stories shaped by resilience, quiet struggles, and an unyielding determination to rise. Through her personal journey, she rebuilt her identity and discovered a deeper sense of purpose. By infusing healing, hope, and truth into every chapter she writes, she inspires women to recognize their worth and reclaim their inner power.
Helping women recover from toxic relationships and emotional trauma has always been close to Afshan’s heart. She is deeply committed to empowering women who feel trapped, ignored, or unheard. Through her voice, her work, and her unwavering empathy, she strives to guide women toward healing, self-assurance, and independence. Her mission is clear: to ensure every woman knows she deserves peace, dignity, and a life rooted in strength and self-love.



***************THE END*******************

He came when the clock struck the hour of 'too late,' A silhouette in black, a defiance of fate. In his right hand, a bouquet of violet orchids—royal and deep, While in his left, red heart balloons danced where the willows weep.

He looked like a dream dressed in a velvet tuxedo night, A vision of perfection, a staggering sight. The man I had waited for, through silence and thin lines, Finally arrived where the cold marble shines.

He knelt with a grace that the living rarely know, Placing his heart where the wild grasses grow. He leaned down to whisper a secret, a prayer, A kiss on my forehead, a breath of warm air.

It was the "Ever Perfect" I had written in my head, But the orchids were for the living, and I was the dead. A soul recognition that finally found its home, Underneath the heavy weight of the soil and the stone.

The calendar turns to February, and the world begins to drape itself in shades of red, celebrating a love that is loud and visible. But for me, this month is just a countdown of survival. I sit in the quiet of the night, asking a question that has been rotting in my chest: “So tell me, how long will I continue being dead before I die?” 

I have spent my life giving unlimited love to everyone around me, acting as a soft place for them to land when they were broken. I made it look easy to be damaged and still be there for someone else; I made it look effortless to carry their weights while mine stayed buried. But eventually, they all stopped seeing me. They made me invisible, and I realized I had become a ghost in my own story.

Now, when the house is empty and I try to turn that same love inward, it feels like a crime. Why does loving myself feel like a guilt I cannot shake? Why is the air full of sympathy and pity, but never the permission to simply love the one who survived?.

I realized then that the “strength” everyone admired was just a debt I was paying off—the debt of existing when I felt like I was already gone. I am tired of being a hero who only knows how to clap for herself in a silent room. If this is what it means to be alive, then let me find the courage to stop surviving for the world and start living for the one I see in the mirror. Because lately, breathing feels more like bleeding.

content.stringValue:
A lifelong friendship that got lost while searching the way
Were the secrets that we shared a bond or a weapon meant to be unfolded ,
Was it faith or a consequence that we ought to be separated?
Well, searching the path back to each other, tensed, we lay.
Is it the universe telling us that we were not meant to be, or is it just that we fought?
Finding ways, we were just waiting to know what we had to be taught.
Now, in this circle of lifelong friendship, we were caught
I did not know what to do, but I did know what to not .
Hold on to the people surrounding you; most of them are gems
The best ones often show you the world with a more beautiful lens.
Their presence does not let you feel tense,
and hence, when they cut you off, you feel like being stuck on a fence.
There are very rare friends for forever,
and you can’t find anyone else like them ever.
Even though you have a new bunch of people around you every year,
they always stand with you when you are in tears.
You love them the same, even if they are not near;
therefore, your life with them is crystal clear.
In a crowd, they are the loudest ones to cheer,
and hence, losing them makes you fear.

From unknown to friends,
From friends to following trends,
From following trends to the one who lends
and from the one who lends to the one who for the perfect match let
themselves and their feelings blend;
I often say she was the one to arrange her feelings as flowers and send,
but what about our feelings, were they really chained?
Showing love as fight,
Care as aggression,
Tension as silence,
And this beautiful relation of our friendship was all that I gained.
Suddenly a spark made it silent
and made us cry through nights
only with the intention
that when we meet again we realise and reunite.
~Guneet Kaur

In a quiet corner of a small town called Jagatpur, where life moved at the pace of temple bells and evening lamps, lived a young girl named Mira. At first glance, she seemed no different from the other girls of the town—simple clothes, tied-back hair, eyes lowered out of habit. But beneath that calm surface burned something rare: a courage that refused to be silenced.
Mira was outspoken and fearless from a very tender age. She asked questions when others stayed quiet and stood her ground when most chose obedience. Her family carried a long legacy of service—three generations of army officers whose photographs lined the walls of their ancestral home. Tales of bravery were spoken at the dinner table like bedtime stories. Yet, paradoxically, the same home that glorified courage placed invisible chains around Mira’s dreams.
From childhood, Mira knew what she wanted—to serve the nation by joining the Indian Armed Forces. She didn’t want applause or medals; she wanted purpose. She wanted to stand where duty called, to protect rather than be protected. But Jagatpur had its own unwritten laws. In that locality, girls were not meant to dream beyond the household. Education was acceptable, ambition was tolerated, but uniforms, command, and leadership were forbidden.
Her family was no exception to this mindset. Though proud of their military heritage, they believed it belonged only to the men. Mira’s brother often laughed at her determination and said casually, almost cruelly,
“Girls are not meant to take leadership. They are meant to serve the household with utmost devotion.”
Each time those words were spoken, something inside Mira tightened—but it never broke.
She had grown up watching soldiers march through the dusty lanes of Jagatpur. Their boots struck the earth in perfect rhythm, echoing against the distant hills. Their faces were stern, their eyes fierce, their hearts loyal. While other children clapped or waved, Mira stood still, absorbing every detail. She admired the discipline, the unity, and the quiet strength that walked past her every morning.
When others played games, Mira imagined herself in uniform. She pictured standing tall where fear dared to whisper. She learned early that bravery was not the absence of fear, but the courage to move forward despite it.
Denied formal training, Mira trained herself.
She woke before dawn, when the sky was still painted with stars and the world lay silent. She ran through narrow paths, her breath fogging the cold air. She strengthened her body with whatever means she had—lifting stones, sprinting uphill, balancing her weight against resistance. She sparred with her shadow, correcting her stance, sharpening her focus. More importantly, she trained her mind.
She learned patience from the rising sun and endurance from the long, lonely mornings. She mastered silence—the kind that teaches you how strength can roar without making a sound. Her hands bore scars, her feet knew pain, but her spirit wore pride.
Years passed. Seasons changed. Society remained the same.
Her dream was mocked, dismissed, and ignored, yet Mira never let it shatter. She carried it quietly, like an ember hidden deep within her chest—unseen, but alive.
Then one night, everything changed.
War crept into their homeland—harsh, sudden, and unforgiving. Chaos tore through Jagatpur like a storm. Sirens screamed. Houses trembled. Fear spread faster than fire. People ran for shelter, clutching their loved ones, praying for rescue.
While most ran away from danger, Mira ran towards it.
With no uniform, no weapon, and no command—only courage and a handmade staff—she stepped into the flames. She guided children out of collapsing homes, shielded the elderly with her own body, and stood between danger and the defenseless. Her movements were instinctive, her resolve unshaken.
Fear knocked at her heart, but she did not answer.
By the time the soldiers finally arrived, the worst had passed. Smoke still lingered in the air, and the ground bore the marks of destruction. Among the ruins, they found a young woman standing tall—hair singed, clothes torn, eyes blazing with an unbroken fire.
She had protected her home before the army even reached.
When the officers asked her where she found such strength, Mira smiled—not with pride, but with quiet certainty—and said,
“Some fires are not lit by torches. They are born within.”
From that day onward, she was no longer known simply as Mira.
People called her The Unborn Blaze—the fire that had existed long before it was ever seen, the courage that needed no permission to rise. She became a symbol, not just of bravery, but of possibility. She proved that leadership is not granted by gender, and courage does not wait for approval.
The town of Jagatpur slowly changed. Conversations softened. Beliefs cracked. Young girls looked at Mira and dared to dream a little bigger. Even those who once laughed fell silent in respect.
Mira’s blaze was once unborn, unseen, and unacknowledged—but it had always been there.
And when the moment came, it lit the way for many more to follow.

I have lived in rooms
where thoughts screamed louder than people,
where nights stretched like questions
with no courage to answer them.
My heart knew wars
no map could ever mark—
regrets marching back and forth,
memories firing without warning.
I smiled in daylight,
carried calm like borrowed clothes,
but inside, something kept breaking
softly, so no one would hear.
Then one evening,
nothing extraordinary happened—
no miracle, no sudden light.
I simply sat with myself
and did not run.
I let the storm speak.
I let the silence listen.
And somewhere between
a tired tear and a steady breath,
peace arrived—
not as victory,
but as understanding.
Now I know—
peace is not the absence of turmoil,
it is learning to stay
when the chaos asks you to leave.

It was Commencement Day when I was handed over to Hrishi, now Dr. Hrishi. A moment of complex emotions washed over me. The hectic, the hard, the emotional, the godly, the divine, everything I had experienced with Dr. Krishnaraj flashed through my mind.

I remember the first time I entered this world, alive, when the late Rahulraj ji held me. His eyes gleamed with joy as he looked at me. He was beaming. And then, strangely, he placed me inside a box. I was confused. Why would someone pack me away in such a good mood?

About an hour later, the box opened. I was gently placed on the shoulders of Krishnaraj. “Krishu,” Rahulraj ji had said, “is now future Dr. Krishnaraj Rahulraj Mohanty.” The whole family clapped.

Krishu held me, sat on the sofa, and admired me in silence for a whole fifteen minutes. From that day on, he never let me be far from him.

His MBBS journey began. Those first-year days when he used me during silly pranks with friends. Once, he placed my bell on a friend’s knee and said, “I hear lub-dub… I think your heart is misplaced!” Everyone laughed. Another time, he wore my earpieces the wrong way and got scolded by a professor. “With this seriousness, you’ll definitely top the practicals!” And the first time he used my bell, he placed it on the wrong side. When he finally turned it and heard clearly, he whispered, “Oh… so this is how it’s supposed to be.”

He was clumsy, yes. But slowly, his hands grew steadier. The first time he heard a fetal heartbeat, he paused. “It’s fast… rhythmic.” His eyes widened. “Oh… it’s a baby inside.” That moment changed something inside him.

He passed his PG entrance with a stellar rank and surprised everyone by choosing Obstetrics and Gynaecology. “OBGY? You? Not radiology or orthopaedics?” But Krishnaraj didn’t waver. There was something personal in his choice.

His mother had died suddenly just before his final exams. She was the one who waited late into the night with turmeric milk. Who packed his lunch and blessed his forehead before exams. Her absence didn’t make him fall apart. It made him silent. Focused. Every time he touched a patient’s abdomen or heard a fetal heart, he softened.

He went on to become Head of the Department after sixteen years of service.

And then Hrishi arrived.

From day one, Krishnaraj was unimpressed. Hrishi had a laid-back charm, a cheerful tone, a tendency to joke even in serious moments. Where Krishnaraj measured silence and precision, Hrishi operated with ease and laughter.

“He forgets case names,” Krishnaraj muttered once, “walks into the OT humming songs, and has never once arrived ten minutes early.”

It wasn’t that Hrishi lacked knowledge. But to Krishnaraj, it felt like he lacked gravity. Medicine was sacred. He had once told me, “We hold lives. We can’t afford to forget. We can’t afford to laugh carelessly.”

He would often pause while Hrishi fumbled during presentations, tapping his pen, not out of anger, but out of disappointment.

I could feel it on his chest, the ache. The disappointment wasn’t just in Hrishi. It was in himself too, for investing hopes in someone who, he thought, didn’t take this calling seriously.

And then one afternoon in the OPD, a woman walked in with a newborn in her arms.

“Dr. Krishnaraj?” she asked.

“Yes?”

“I’m Smitha. This is my son.” She tilted the baby toward him. “I’ve named him Hrishi.”

Krishnaraj blinked. Confused.

She smiled gently. “Your student, Hrishi, told me to come to you. Said, ‘He’s not just a great doctor, he’s a great man.’”

“I don’t think we’ve met,” Krishnaraj said.

“Oh, we have,” she said. “You just don’t remember. Four months ago, I was pregnant, alone, and climbing the stairs near the old wing. I was in pain, scared. Hrishi saw me. He was rushing somewhere, but he stopped. He asked if I needed help, and when I didn’t reply, he gently insisted.”

She paused, her eyes glistening. “I broke down. Right there in the corridor. He stayed. Said, ‘Don’t worry, ma’am. I’m like your younger brother.’ He sat with me, took me to the lift, got me checked, and waited until I felt okay.”

Krishnaraj felt a strange stillness in his chest.

Smitha continued, “That was the day of his OBGY viva, wasn’t it?”

He nodded slowly.

“He missed it because of me,” she said. “And he never told you. I found out later from one of the nurses. He didn’t want you to know. Said it wasn’t important.”

Her voice dropped to a whisper. “But it was. That day, I felt safe because of him. I was abandoned. My husband left when he found out I was pregnant. I had no one. But Hrishi came with me for appointments later. Even brought his mother once. Treated me like family.”

Krishnaraj looked down at the baby in her arms.

“You named him Hrishi…”

She nodded. “Because I want him to grow up to be as human as your student.”

That evening, Krishnaraj called Hrishi to his cabin.

“You referred a patient to me today?” he asked calmly.

“Yes, sir. Smitha ma’am. She’s… strong.”

“She told me why she named her son Hrishi.”

Hrishi looked down, then slowly said, “I thought she could benefit from your care.”

“She told me what happened four months ago.”

Hrishi was silent.

“You didn’t say anything that day,” Krishnaraj said. “You missed the viva. I scolded you. And you just took it.”

“I didn’t want to explain it, sir,” Hrishi said quietly. “It didn’t feel right to turn that moment into an excuse. She needed me. That’s all.”

There was silence.

Then Krishnaraj stood up, placed a hand on his shoulder and said, “That day, you may have missed a viva. But you passed something far greater.”

And on Commencement Day, he placed me on Hrishi’s shoulders, not because Hrishi was the top ranker, but because he had learned what it truly meant to listen.

And me?

I’ve heard thousands of hearts. The frightened, the brave, the dying, the unborn. I’ve learned that not all heartbeats lie beneath the ribs. Some live in silence. In sacrifice. In stories untold.

And I, the silent witness, have heard them all.

It was the first day of medical school, and the air buzzed with anticipation. Rudra, clutching his notebook tightly, scanned the crowd of fresh faces. Friendship, for him, wasn’t just a casual bond—it was something deep and lasting, a brotherhood that could withstand time. When Aditya, Vivaan, and Kabir entered his life, Rudy believed he had found it.

Aditya’s calm demeanor, Vivaan’s boundless energy, and Kabir’s steady presence and humor brought a sense of belonging Rudy hadn’t felt in a long time. At first, the group was inseparable, their days filled with laughter and late-night study sessions. Rudy, with his love for poetry, often captured their shared moments in verses. While his friends admired his writing, they never truly understood its emotional depth. To them, it was just another one of Rudy’s quirks.

As the semesters rolled by, cracks began to form in their seemingly unbreakable bond. Aditya’s focus expanded to his other friends, Vivaan and Kabir grew closer and made an impenetrable solar system of their own, and Rudy found himself retreating into his world of words. Ananya, his close friend and confidante, became his anchor, the one person who truly understood him and the feelings he poured into his poems.

One particular day late in their second year was especially draining for Rudy. A series of exams, combined with an endless list of assignments and the growing sense of disconnection from his friends, left him emotionally exhausted. That evening, after dinner, Rudy skipped their usual group hangout and headed to the solitude of the banyan tree near the hostel. The soft rustle of leaves and the faint hum of campus life provided the quiet he craved.

Taking out his notebook, Rudy let the weight of the day flow into his pen. The poem came to life, raw and unfiltered:

I stood at a distance and saw the thread,  
Four knots bound tight, or so it was said.  
But as I looked closer, my heart knew the truth,  
One knot lay apart, far from its roots.

The words I spoke fell into the void,  
Feelings dismissed, connections destroyed.  
The warmth I gave, it faded to cold,  
A story of friendship left untold.

I wondered, I waited, but silence grew loud,  
A lone knot forgotten in the midst of the crowd.  
The thread remained, but the bond was undone,  
Four were once bound, now three and one."

He closed the notebook with a heavy sigh, resting his head against the tree trunk. The poem encapsulated everything he felt but couldn’t say aloud. To Rudy, it wasn’t just a poem—it was his truth, written in the language of his heart.

Unbeknownst to him, the poem would later play a pivotal role in bridging the distance with his friends. Though they admired Rudy’s poetry, they hadn’t grasped its significance until,

One evening, as the campus buzzed with preparations for the upcoming exams, Ananya found herself walking into the café for a quick break from studying. To her surprise, she spotted Aditya, Vivaan, and Kabir huddled at a corner table, their conversation animated. At first, she thought little of it, but as she passed by, she heard Rudy’s name.

Curious, and slightly concerned, she paused to listen.

“Don’t get me wrong,” Aditya was saying, “I really like Rudy, but I feel like I just don’t get him sometimes. He’s so ambitious and... intense.”

“Yeah,” Vivaan agreed, “and emotional, too. He’s always writing those deep poems, and honestly, I never know what to say about them.”

Kabir nodded thoughtfully. “He’s different, isn’t he? Like... more innocent than us, but also way more in his own world.”

Ananya couldn’t hold back anymore. She walked up to their table and gestured to the empty chair. “Mind if I join?”

The three looked at her, startled but welcoming. Aditya slid the chair forward, and Ananya sat down, her expression calm but serious.

“I heard you talking about Rudy,” she began. “You’re right—he’s different. But do you really know why?”

Vivaan shrugged, looking unsure. “I mean, he’s always been kind of reserved. And those poems... they’re great, but I don’t really get what he’s trying to say.”

Ananya tilted her head, her voice soft but firm. “That’s the thing. His poems aren’t just random words or creative expressions. They’re how he communicates what he’s feeling—what he can’t say out loud.”

Aditya frowned, leaning forward. “What do you mean?”

She sighed, choosing her words carefully. “Rudy feels things more deeply than most people. He’s not just ambitious; he’s someone who puts his whole heart into everything—his dreams, his friendships, his writing. But he doesn’t always feel like he gets the same in return.”

The weight of her words began to sink in. Kabir’s brows furrowed as he asked, “Are you saying he feels... left out? By us?”

Ananya nodded slowly. “He does. You’ve seen his poems, haven’t you? Those verses he writes about knots and threads—that’s him trying to tell you how disconnected he feels. He loves you guys, but he doesn’t feel like he belongs in the same way you do.”

Vivaan shifted in his seat, guilt flashing across his face. “But we never meant to make him feel that way. I mean, he’s... Rudy. He’s always been there.”

“And that’s the problem,” Ananya said, her voice tinged with frustration. “You’ve taken his presence for granted. Just because he doesn’t say anything doesn’t mean he’s fine.”

Aditya let out a heavy sigh, running a hand through his hair. “We’ve been blind, haven’t we? All this time, we thought he was just... quiet. But he’s been trying to tell us how he feels, and we didn’t listen.”

Ananya’s tone softened as she saw their growing understanding. “It’s not too late. Rudy doesn’t need perfection—he just needs to know that he matters to you, that you see him for who he is.”

The table fell into a heavy silence as the three friends reflected on her words. For the first time, they began to see Rudy’s silence not as a sign of indifference but as a mirror of their own lack of attention. The poems they had admired from afar now carried a weight they hadn’t noticed before.

“Thank you, Ananya,” Kabir said quietly. “We needed to hear this.”

She offered a small, encouraging smile. “Just... don’t let him drift any further away. He deserves better.”

That evening, armed with a newfound perspective, the three friends set out to find Rudy and begin mending the threads they had unintentionally frayed.

Ananya’s words opened their eyes to the pain Rudy had been carrying silently. That evening, they found him under the banyan tree, his notebook resting on his lap. Their conversation marked the beginning of a new chapter—one where their friendship wasn’t perfect, but real, built on mutual understanding and the promise to do better.

They say that a close brush with death is enough to turn an atheist into a believer. Rehaan had one such experience. 

The young man was not an atheist per se, but his belief in God was limited to Friday prayers and good manners. That is until he woke up on a stormy night, only a few hours away from the dawn. 

It didn’t take long for the muezzin to give the call for prayer that was heard despite the sky bombarding some thunder. But the azan was not enough to stir the young man from his half-sleep, especially with the chilly weather due to the heavy downpour and strong wind. 

 ‘I will pray when the rain slows down,’ Rehaan lied to himself as he wrapped the blanket tighter around himself. 

That’s when he saw it, a mist of light floating in his pitch-dark room. Rehaan’s heart stopped at that moment, his eyes glued to the mist that was forming a humanoid silhouette. He thought of moving but his body froze, ‘the spirit has put a spell on me!’ he realized.

With blood pounding in his ears, Rehaan remembered all the prayers he missed, all the sins he committed, and all the people he hurt. He had told himself that he’d repent later, ‘but now I can’t for Azrael has come to claim my soul,’ he thought. 

The Angel of Death lifted its hand as if to reach for Rehaan’s soul and asked, “Should I switch the fan off?” 

“No, it’s okay,” Rehaan answered his grandmother.  

That day, Rehaan didn’t miss the pre-dawn prayer. 

The end.

Adi’s parents don’t fight anymore.

In the past, they’d fight over the littlest things. The remote, the washroom, the lunchbox, Adi’s school fees, electricity bills and more; no subject was worth letting go of.

Most of the times, they’d just shout. Sometimes they’d throw stuff or hit each other. Sometimes the neighbours would have to intervene.

It’s been a few months since the last fight and the neighbours are glad about it.

But Adi knew that things weren’t okay. Sure, they don’t fight anymore. But that’s because they don’t talk anymore. They stay out of each other’s way, at least as much as their small two-bedroom apartment would allow them to.

It’s clear to him, that they’ve given up on each other.

They still live together only because of the usual excuse: him. He is the link in the chain that binds them and prevents them from seeking happiness elsewhere.

Which brought up a question in his mind a few weeks ago that he’d rather not think about. He manages to push it to the back of his mind during the day. But it plagues him in the nights when he has nothing but his thoughts to turn to.

How long until they give up on him too?

The end.

इक कहानी सिर्फ तुम्हारी मेरी हो...
जिसमे तुम हँसते हो तो,मैं हँसती हूँ,
तुम उदास जो हो..तो मैं भी उदास होती हूँ...
इक लम्हा सिर्फ तुम्हारा मेरा हो,
जिसमे तुम गुनगुनाते हो,
तो मैं तुम्हारा संगीत बन जाऊं,
इक नजारा सिर्फ तुम्हारा मेरा हो,
तुम्हे देखती वो नज़र मैं बन जाऊं...
इक रस्म सिर्फ मेरी और तुम्हारी हो,
राह चाहे कोई भी हो,सफर कैसा भी हो,
तुम आगे जो चलो,तुम्हारा हाथ थाम कर,
तुम्हारे साथ मैं भी चलूँ..
इक वादा सिर्फ मेरा और तुम्हारा हो,
वक़्त चाहे जैसा हो,हालात चाहे जैसे हो,
ना मैं तुम्हारा साथ छोडूं,ना तुम्हे खुद से दूर जाने दो... इक एहसास सिर्फ मेरा और तुम्हारा हो,
किसी भी दुख में हम इक दूसरे को,
सांत्वना दे सके या नही,
पर साथ बैठ कर जी भर रो कर..
इक-दूजे को सम्हालते रहे...
इक कसम सिर्फ मेरे और तुम्हारी हो,
छोड़ कर एक-दूसरे का साथ,
हम कभी जाए..
सांसे जितनी भी इक-दूजे के जीवन से बंधी रहे..
पर हाँ एक बात सिर्फ मेरी हो,
तुम्हारे सारे दुख,तुम्हारी सारी असफलताएं,
तुम्हारी हर कमजोरी मेरी हो...
मेरी सारी खुशियाँ,
मेरी सारी उपलब्धियां तुम्हारी हो....!!!

title.stringValue: The Unanswered Why of My Existence.

content.stringValue:
Wherefore I Love Thee,
 Though I Know It Not,

Wherefore I love thee—ask me not for cause,
For love came robed in neither why nor how;
It broke the scales of thought, outpaced the laws,
And crowned my heart before I knew my vow.
I searched for sense, yet sense did flee my sight,
As stars do scatter when the dawn draws near;
For love is not a scholar of the mind,
But faith that blooms where logic dares not peer.

I love thee not for virtues sung aloud,
Nor for the gentle mercies thou dost give;
I loved thee ere thy name my lips had found,
As though my soul knew first how it must live.
No reason led me to thy sacred door—
My fate had known thy knock a life before.

If thou shouldst ask me why my breath is thine,
I’d answer thus: the rose knows not the spring;
Yet still it bleeds its scent in perfect time,
And asks no pardon for its blossoming.
So too my heart—unlearned in reason’s art—
Did choose thee whole, before it chose a part.

Thou art the cause I never sought to prove,
The truth my trembling words can scarce contain;
I live not for thee—nay, I live by love,
As oceans live by moon’s unspoken reign.
Take thee away, and I am dust and sound,
A verse unmeant, a crown forever drowned.

For thou art not my reason, nor my plea—
Thou art the breath by which I came to be.

I loved thee ere my reason learned thy name;
For some souls meet—and logic dies in flame.

A Novel of Prediction, Power, and Human Error .

Genre

Literary Crime Fiction Novella· Psychological Thriller · Speculative / Tech‑Noir Mystery · Philosophical Noir

Tone

Dark, cerebral, and quietly devastating · Atmospheric and slow‑burning · Morally unsettling · Poetic, restrained, and ominously intimate

Setting

New York City — glass‑walled research institutes, underground tunnels, rooftops at dawn, quiet apartments, obsolete server rooms, and digital landscapes where silence and data intersect

Dedication

For those who think too much, feel too deeply, and live in a world that punishes both.

For the girls who were told their minds were dangerous.

For the ones who learned that loving the truth often means standing alone.

And for anyone who has ever wondered whether the future should be known—

or forgiven.

Prologue — Before the Future Learned Your Name

The future does not arrive all at once.

It leaks.

In probabilities. In patterns. In decisions so small they feel harmless until they are not.

Dr. Elara Myles understood this long before the world understood her.

She believed intelligence was responsibility—that discovery demanded ethics, and that knowledge without restraint was simply another form of violence. On the night she would be murdered, New York moved outside the glass walls of Helix Institute as it always did: trains rattling underground, lights blinking on in distant apartments, strangers brushing past one another without consequence.

Inside Laboratory 6B, Elara erased her work for the fourth time.

Not because it was wrong.

Because it was right.

She had discovered a method of predictive cognition—imperfect, probabilistic, devastatingly accurate. Enough to be weaponized. Enough to turn possibility into policy.

Once the world understood what she had built, she knew she would no longer be necessary.

She wrote the sentence carefully, deliberately, as if it were both a prayer and a warning:

If they understand this, I am already dead.

When the door opened behind her, Elara did not scream.

She did not fight for long.

Her final thought was not fear, but hope—that somewhere, someone would be unpredictable enough to undo what she had begun.

ACT I — THE DEATH THAT ASKED A QUESTION

Chapter One: Valeria Ashcroft

Detective Valeria Ashcroft did not believe in coincidence.

She believed in patterns, pressure, and people lying to themselves.

The laboratory smelled sterile in the way hospitals do—clean enough to hide rot. Elara Myles lay facedown on the tiles, cobalt staining her hands blue. Valeria studied the body with practiced detachment: the bruised wrists, the puncture below the collarbone, the violence executed with precision rather than rage.

On the whiteboard, the sentence waited.

Valeria read it twice.

“She knew,” she said quietly. “She knew someone was coming.”

Behind her, Noah Reed adjusted his glasses.

“Or,” he said, “she wanted to make sure we’d understand too late.”

Interlude I — The Girl Who Knew Too Much

Elara had always known curiosity had a cost.

She simply hadn’t expected the bill to come so quickly.

ACT II — THE LIVING AND THE LIARS

Chapter Two: Helix Institute

Helix Institute rose over Manhattan like a cathedral made of glass.

Everything visible. Nothing honest.

Dr. Conrad Voss spoke smoothly, confidently, the way men do when they believe intelligence absolves cruelty.

“She was sensitive,” he said of Elara. “Brilliant minds often are.”

Valeria leaned forward. “Sensitive people don’t erase five minutes of surveillance footage.”

Voss’s smile tightened.

Noah wandered near the servers. “Systems don’t fail emotionally,” he said lightly. “They fail intentionally.”

Something flickered behind Voss’s eyes.

Author’s Note — On Power

Institutions do not commit crimes.

People do.

Institutions simply teach them how to justify it.

Chapter Three: The Apartment

Elara’s apartment was immaculate in the way a lie is immaculate.

No photographs. No warmth. Only notebooks.

The equations were elegant. Terrifying.

“This isn’t neuroscience,” Noah whispered. “This is behavioral prophecy.”

On the final page was a list of names.

One circled in red.

VALERIA ASHCROFT.

“She didn’t know you,” Noah said.

Valeria nodded slowly. “She studied me.”

Interlude II — An Unspoken Variable

Valeria had learned early that attachment was a liability.

Still, when Noah looked at her like she was the only constant left, something dangerous stirred.

She pretended not to notice.

ACT III — ORACLE VEIL

Chapter Four: Predictions

They ran simulations.

The system—ORACLE VEIL—predicted outcomes with horrifying accuracy.

Including Valeria’s.

“She built me into it,” Valeria realized.

Gunfire shattered the moment.

They were no longer observers.

They were variables.

Chapter Five: Noah’s Truth

In an abandoned subway tunnel, Noah confessed.

“Elara contacted me months ago,” he said. “Helix was using ORACLE VEIL to eliminate future threats. People who might expose them.”

“Including her,” Valeria said.

“And you.”

The truth settled heavily between them.

Author’s Note — On Love

Love does not weaken us.

It gives us something worth destroying certainty for.

ACT IV — THE CONSPIRACY BENEATH THE CONSPIRACY

Chapter Six: The System

There was no single killer.

ORACLE VEIL had turned probability into policy.

Elara was murdered not for what she did—but for what she might have done.

Interlude III — Elara’s Poem (Recovered File)

I asked the future what it wanted from me.
It said: silence.
I answered with truth.

ACT V — THE FALL

Chapter Seven: The Rooftop

At sunrise, Valeria confronted Voss.

“You didn’t kill her,” she said. “Your system did.”

Progress fell apart under evidence and daylight.

Helix collapsed.

PART TWO — THE AFTERLIFE OF CERTAINTY

ACT VI — RESIDUALS

ORACLE VEIL survived in fragments.

Elara had anticipated destruction.

She had distributed the future.

ACT VII — THE DETECTIVE AS DATA

Valeria learned the truth.

She was the core.

Elara had trusted her with the world.

Interlude IV — Elara’s Confession (Recovered Audio)

You were the only variable I trusted.

ACT VIII — LOVE OR OBLIVION

Chapter Twelve: The Choice

ORACLE VEIL could end wars before they began.

Valeria fed it contradiction.

Noise.

Love.

The system went blind.

ACT IX — THE PRICE

The world remained imperfect.

Human.

Valeria resigned.

Noah left New York.

They did not say goodbye properly.

Epilogue — After Prediction

The city never noticed the moment it was spared.

Valeria lived quietly, without certainty.

Once a month, a message arrived:

The future is quieter when no one listens too hard.

Years later, a child dropped a glass beaker in a school laboratory.

Blue liquid spilled.

No equation was written.

And somewhere, the future hesitated.

FINAL AUTHOR’S NOTE

Because certainty is seductive.

Because love is disruptive.

Because the most dangerous idea is not that we can predict humanity—

But that we should.

---------------------
एहसास भरी दोस्ती
---------------------

अजीब सी ये दोस्ती है, ना मुलाक़ात, 
ना साथ बिताए कोई पल,
फिर भी तुम्हारे शब्द हर दिन में रंग भर जाते हैं।

कभी मज़ाक, कभी सलाह, कभी बस एक “कैसी हो?” 
पर इन छोटी बातों में, कितनी बड़ी मुस्कान छिपी होती है।

कभी सोचा नहीं था, कि इतनी दूरी के बावजूद
कोई इतना अपनापन दे जाएगा।

तुमसे सीखा, दोस्ती मिलने से नहीं,
एहसास होने से भी होती है 

~Nova Sanju

--------------------------
पुराने चैट्स की खुशबू
----------------------------

कभी-कभी सोचती हूँ,
क्या तुम भी मुझे याद करते हो?
या मेरी बातें अब बस पुराने चैट्स में रह गई हैं?

तुम्हारा "Hi" भी किसी ताज़ी हवा जैसा लगता था,
अब वो हवा भी जैसे ठहर-सी गई है।

शायद ज़िंदगी ने तुम्हें busy कर दिया,
पर मेरे दिल ने अब भी वो कोना खाली रखा है 
जहाँ सिर्फ़ तुम्हारी दोस्ती रहती थी।

शब्द अब कम हो गए हैं, पर एहसास अभी भी वही है...
कभी-कभी खामोशी भी, पुराने रिश्तों की धड़कन बन जाती है 

~Nova Sanju

--------------------------
तेरी यारी जैसी कोई नहीं
--------------------------

तुम्हारे साथ की आदत सी हो गई है,
हर बात करने की आदत सी हो गई है।

हँसी में तुम, खामोशी में तुम, 
हर छोटे लम्हों में तुम।

ना कोई रिश्ता नाम से बंधा, 
ना कोई वादा कहा गया,
फिर भी तुम वो सुकून हो, 
जिसकी कमी दिल को महसूस होती है।

कभी-कभी सोचती हूँ, अगर तुम ना होते,
तो ये मुस्कुराहटें भी शायद अधूरी होती।

~Nova Sanju

----------------------------------
वो दोस्त, जो अब कम बोलता है
----------------------------------

कभी लगता था, हमारी बातें कभी खत्म ही न होंगी,
अब खामोशी भी जैसे कुछ कहती सी लगती है।

तुम ऑनलाइन तो होते हो, पर वो अपनापन अब नज़र नहीं आता, शायद वक्त ने कुछ फासले बना दिए हैं।

मैं समझ सकती हूँ, ज़िंदगी busy भी होती है, पर 
दिल तो वही है, जो हर रोज़ तुम्हारी याद में मुस्कुरा उठता है।

कहने को कुछ नहीं, बस इतना बताना है आज,
कि अगर कभी ये पंक्तियाँ तुम्हारे दिल तक पहुँचें, 
तो याद रखना… 
कोई अब भी तुम्हें अपना सच्चा दोस्त मानता है 

~Nova Sanju

-------------------
तुमने सीखा दिया 
-------------------

इतने कम समय की इस दोस्ती में, तुमने मुझे हँसना सिखा दिया,
और साथ ही अपनी बात कहने का हौसला भी दे दिया।

पहले शब्द दिल में ही रह जाते थे, पर तुमने सिखाया,
“जब तक कहोगी नहीं, सामने वाला समझेगा कैसे?”

अब मैं कभी–कभी अपनी बात कहने की हिम्मत कर पाती हूँ,
वो भी उसी सादगी से, जैसे तुम कहा करते थे।

अपने इस दोस्ती के रिश्ते में, मैं इतना ज़रूर जानती हूँ,
तुमसे मिला ये नया एहसास हमेशा मेरे साथ रहेगा।

शुक्रिया… इस भरोसे, इस मुस्कान के लिए
शुक्रिया.... इस नए, छोटे से बड़े एहसास के लिए,
शुक्रिया.... उस सच्ची दोस्ती के लिए,
जिसने मुझे खुद से रूबरू करवाया 

~Nova Sanju

---------------------
मुस्कान का तोहफा
---------------------

मुस्कुराना सिखाया उसने,
हर ग़म को छुपाना सिखाया उसने।
ज़िंदगी को आसान बना दिया,
सिर्फ़ अपने कुछ मीठे अल्फ़ाज़ों से।

पर अब वही…
मेरी मुस्कान को साथ ले गया,
छोड़ गया पीछे बस यादों का समंदर,
और होंठों पर एक अधूरी सी हँसी। 

~Nova Sanju

I am partially drowned, stuck
In the middle of the river,
Charmed by a piece of wood
That pierced through my clothes,
Slaughtering standard fate.
Maybe the wood doesn’t want me
To cross into the afterlife,
Or will I be stuck here
Until I drown myself, dry up?

Perhaps the river whispers secrets to me
Of those who crossed,
And those who sank free.
The wood that binds me-
Is it a root of regret?
A hitch to life,
Or a toll for death?

I call the current, but it buzz in refrain,
Carrying sounds of souls that remain.
Will the sun dry me, or turn me to bone,
Or will I break loose and die alone?

We learned to dream quietly, because money always spoke louder.
Taunts from rich ones burn us like heating gunpowder.
We dropped our dreams due to our condition,
Yet it feels like ongoing nuclear fission.

From lantern to lights, we grew,
We try to do everything new.
From dreaming of rich people’s breakfast,
To sleeping without eating, considering it a fast.

We carry our dreams, our hope,
Like a secret mission led by the Pope.
From studying in little schools,
To universities becoming a little cool.

Yes, we belong to a middle-class family,
That completes its expensive dreams rarely

A little too early, a bit too late. Never ending is the game of the goal and the fate.

Each passing day, billions of bees on the roses hover by; 
Amidst the chaos,once in ages, you rise and die!

So let lose that armour for once, feel your vulnerability at its zenith, 
Let those hands try a wave at least and see the wings unfold beneath. 

Try if you must for once with no strings attached, 
Unleash the passion within, with a kind of fuel unmatched .

As long as your clock ticks; find your adrenaline rush. 
Let that fire within burn a little more; Let your blood boil and gush! 

A little lesson from the sweat beads, a great learning, 
A condemned desire within still forever burning, 

Break your inhibitions, let alone your traumatic fears those embarrassingly conspire.
Walk a little, if not run, before you take that last step to your burning pyre!

Let your gut feeling be your trigger, even if it is a mere perchance. 
Let that roaring triumph buried within at least get a fair chance. 

Else, there are many with a muted voice on a bloated face. 
A million species in a single rat race!

Against a million opportunities, choose wisely, the mere regrets to procure.
The companions on the death bed; the regrets to mature.

Your tenacity convicts your life journey, so decide your share.

Too worthy to spend, 
 Too earthy to spare!!

आहिस्ता-आहिस्ता ख़ुद से मोहब्बत

आहिस्ता-आहिस्ता बहुत कुछ जान गई हूँ मैं,
जो सीखना नहीं था, वही सबसे पहले सीख गई हूँ मैं।
उम्र से ज़्यादा तजुर्बे समेटे हैं इस सीने में,
अब ख़ुद को ही सब कुछ समझना सीख गई हूँ मैं।

अब किसी से बात करने की भीख नहीं माँगती,
ख़ामोशी में भी ख़ुद से बातें कर लेती हूँ मैं।
दिन भर की भागदौड़ से थोड़ा वक़्त चुरा कर,
आईने के सामने ख़ुद को मुस्कुराते देख लेती हूँ मैं।

मेरी हँसी, मेरी ख़ुशी—सब मुझमें ही बसी है,
मेरी दुनिया अब मेरी अपनी रोशनी से सजी है।
ख़ुद फूलों से सजाऊँगी अपनी हर एक राह,
किसी को इजाज़त नहीं—मेरे फूल तोड़ने की चाह।

मैं टूट कर नहीं, निखर कर जीना सीख गई हूँ,
आहिस्ता-आहिस्ता…
मैं ख़ुद से मोहब्बत करना सीख गई हूँ।
मैं ख़ुद से मोहब्बत करना सीख गई हूँ।

The Orephic lyre in the Grecian summer,
Sweet melody that sang to nymph, satyr and fawns.
And drowned Cerebus with melody deep;
to a great slumbering sleep,
And Hades' keep, and his heart, opened
So saved his good Eurydice.

But Orepheus wouldst not need his lyre,
If he had but thee by his side.
For in thy smile, a greater melody found,
Than all lyre, or the flute's flowing sound.

The chirping birds ere the new dawn,
And rivers murmuring admist verdant glens.
Or after winter pale, dry and bare;
the pitter patter of the first rains.

Against all these thy smile prevails,
With dimples as if Aphrodite.
And meandering locks that properly revere,
A beauty's temple such as this.

Such poetry by the Maker is wrought,
Upon the canvas of thy fair face.
If Helen could see she would then give,
Her laurel upon thy brow to rest.

And thy smile may ne'er be lost,
To trials of time and her tests.
Against all, 
of this mortal world,
May thy smile ever prevail.

“Courage is not the absence of fear but the triumph over it”- Nelson Mandela

                     It’s a foggy day in Phek district. One can frequently experience fog in Nagaland and it makes the weather cool and pleasant throughout the year. Nick and Dhiraj have come to Nagaland to spend their long summer vacation. Nick’s father is a central government teacher, posted in Phek district. They set off their journey to explore a mysterious Cave which has been discovered by them earlier in the deep jungle atop the hill. Filled their bags with biscuits, dry fruits and water bottles they start as if they are going for a long vacation. They have also taken a big torch and one long stick that will help them easily to climb up the hill in addition to protect them from jungle habitants. 
However, they start their journey towards the hill, without knowing what will happen to them. Eventually when they reach to the top hill, it is already noon. With much excitement as they grasp the old rock Cave in front of them, the sight makes them entirely amazed. ‘What a big Cave! I have never seen a real cave like this before,’ Says Nick. ‘Yes, and it’s totally different looking than what we have read about in our History books”, replies Dhir. Now they can`t control their curiosity to enter inside the Cave but at that moment suddenly a fear of unknown catches their mind and heart. The place is in complete solitude, surrounded with long trees and rocks.  

However, as soon as they keep their first step of foot inside the dark Cave, a group of bats, all of a sudden, fly away thrashing their wings that break the silence of the area. They immediately lit the torch and start entering the cave slowly. While they are approaching inside, they are being thrilled. Unexpectedly, they find that inside the cave area, it’s so clean as if people live here. After getting inside, what they see, their eyes can’t believe on. They see that there are logs of wood kept nicely, different handmade utensils and different size of stones are placed beautifully. Moreover, dry fleshes of animals are stored nicely in a big round pot from where bad smell is suffocating them. Nevertheless, when they are observing all these, all of a sudden, they catch up strange sound of footsteps as if some human beings are coming inside. With no time they feel terrible and run to hide themselves in the back side of the long heaps of woods. Unimaginably what they see, makes them horrified and the sight is unbelievable to their eyes. A group of six people, holding spear in one hand and carrying a big dead animal, is entering inside the cave. The Folks are barely dressed except some short of thin clothes on their waist, long and small garlands made of leaf on their neck and hand. More, they have painted their face with white and black color stripes. Physically they are looking very strong and fit. Meantime, the folks keep the dead animal in their store cum kitchen room and start talking in their Naga dialect. 

Farseeing those, Nick understands that he is meeting with the Konyaks Naga tribe. Once his father told him about Konyaks who were the last and most dangerous headhunters’ tribe of Nagaland. They are still residing in some interior parts of Nagaland. They keep themselves away from the outside world and at the same time they don’t allow outsiders to enter into their area. They are defined culturally by their headhunting practice and facial tattoos. It is said that when they used to attack the villages of rival tribes, it was tradition to rip off their victims’ heads. And the heads were proudly displayed on the walls and doorways of the warriors.
Thinking these Nick becomes worried and murmurs to Dhir “we have to come out from this cave as soon as possible to save our life.” Dhir keeps his mouth shut tightly with his both hands not to make any sound. He doesn’t know anything about this tribe people. After some time the folks come out from the cave. Feeling terrible and suffocated both of them start running outside the cave without looking anywhere. When they exit the cave, it is about to set evening. They start running towards the school campus without looking anywhere. After a while, they reach the campus and breathe a sigh of relief.

Another Morning
—----------------------------------------
When another morning is born, 
Leaving behind all the fatigue, 
Darkness and uncertainty of the night, 
Then life seems to be not yet lost. 
The first rays of the new sun touch 
The deep corners of the mind and say - 
Unfulfilled dreams can breathe again, 
Broken hopes will have a chance to sprout again. 
All the mistakes, pain and tears of 
Yesterday slowly fade in the light of this morning, 
And the mind is filled with new inspiration. 
The chirping of birds, 
The cold touch of dew and the affection of the light breeze, 
All together teach us to love life again. 
“Another Morning” is not just the beginning of a day, 
It is a silent promise to wake up the defeated mind, 
That as long as the dawn comes, hope lives on. 
After another morning touches the earth, 
It feels as if the entire world is slowly opening its mouth.  
As the dark shadows of night recede, 
The light of the sun touches the depths of the earth, 
Giving a new life to the weary souls. 
The silence that has settled in the dewy grass is broken 
By the first calls of birds, 
And those voices illuminate the dark corners of the mind. 
The pains, failures and imperfections of yesterday are 
All calmed down, even for a short time, 
In the soft light of this morning, 
The earth itself tells us, 
“Try again, today could be your day.” 
The touch of a light breeze raises a new wave of hope in the heart, 
And this encounter with dawn gives life a new meaning, 
That as long as the earth welcomes the dawn, 
Human hope never dies.
