title.stringValue: We Were Meant To Find Each Other

content.stringValue:
We Were Meant To Find Each Other.

Chapter 1 - When It All Began 

My life had always been simple — painfully simple. The kind of simplicity that almost felt repetitive. Every day felt the same: wake up, scroll through my phone, attend online classes, talk to a few friends, listen to some music, and go to bed thinking the next day would be different, but it never really was. I had people around, but no one who truly stayed. Days went by quietly, and somewhere inside, I had already made peace with the idea that maybe this is how my life was meant to be — calm, uneventful, and ordinary.

Sometimes, I think about those days and smile. Not because they were good, but because they were the kind of days that make you crave a little chaos. And then, one day, that chaos came wrapped in the form of a name — Vibha. It wasn’t planned, it wasn’t expected, and definitely not something I was looking for. But somehow, life decided to surprise me when I least expected it.

It wasn’t some cinematic entrance where violins played or time slowed down. No. She just came into my life like a quiet breeze — unnoticed at first, but strong enough to change everything later. I didn’t even know that one casual evening would turn into something I’d remember for years.

I still remember that evening clearly. I was lying on my bed, phone in my hand, tired of the same old routine. That’s when my friend Ashu sent me a number and said, “Bhai, ye ladki bahut achi hai, baat karle.” I laughed, thinking it was just one of his random suggestions. But I don’t know what made me save that number. Maybe curiosity, maybe boredom, or maybe destiny was already at work.

Before texting her, I stared at her number for a long time. You know that weird hesitation before you talk to someone new? That fear of sounding stupid or creepy? Yeah, that. I kept typing and deleting, trying to sound normal, casual, not too eager. And after thinking too much, I finally sent the most basic message ever — “Hii.”

I remember staring at the screen, waiting for the double tick to turn blue. Every second felt longer than usual. And then, after what felt like forever, she replied. Just one word. “Kon?” She asked.

I chuckled. Not because it was funny, but because I didn’t even know what to say next. I didn’t have an introduction ready. So, without thinking much, I replied, “Insaan.” Yeah, I know, lame reply — but that’s what came to my mind. And honestly, that one silly word started something that I never imagined.

Now, as I sit here, looking at the smoke curling up from my cigarette, I still smile thinking about that reply. “Insaan.” Who knew something so small, so random, would begin something that would mean so much someday? It’s funny how life hides its biggest moments behind ordinary ones.

She saw my reply and laughed. That “Haha” from her changed the tone completely. From that moment, the awkwardness faded a little. The conversation didn’t flow like magic — it stumbled, paused, and picked itself up again. But somehow, it didn’t stop.

We talked about random things — like school, college, music, and sometimes just nonsense. But every word started building a small comfort. Slowly, she wasn’t just “that girl Ashu told me about.” She was Vibha.

And Vibha had this strange calmness in her words. Even through text, she had a way of making things feel lighter. Sometimes she would send a random meme or a line like “You’re weird, but kinda funny.” And I would smile at my screen like an idiot.

I think that’s how connection begins — not through big talks or long confessions, but in small, meaningless exchanges that start meaning everything later.

I take another drag from my cigarette, staring at my phone’s blank screen now. The same phone where it all began. It’s strange, you know — the same device that connected us is now just a reminder of how far things have changed.

Back then, every notification made my heart race. Every “typing…” moment felt like a heartbeat waiting to land. I didn’t know her face properly, didn’t know her voice, but somehow, I started knowing her.

Sometimes I wonder, what if I hadn’t messaged that day? What if I had ignored Ashu’s text and just kept scrolling through my playlist? Maybe my life would have stayed simple — and maybe I wouldn’t be sitting here tonight, writing about her.

Life is weird that way — you never realize which moment is changing you while it’s happening. It’s only later, when everything’s over, that you look back and say, “That was it. That’s where everything began.”

As I flip through my old chats now, I can still see that first message — “Hii.” It looks so ordinary, yet it carries the weight of an entire story. Sometimes, the smallest words carry the biggest meanings.

And maybe that’s what destiny really is — a collection of simple, random moments that somehow make perfect sense in the end.

I lean back, exhaling the last puff of smoke, and smile faintly to myself. Maybe it wasn’t a grand beginning. Maybe it wasn’t love at first sight. But it was real. And that’s what made it special.

Some stories don’t need a perfect start. They just need two people, a little courage, and one simple “Hii.”

“Not all beginnings are magical. Some just happen, quietly — and still change everything.”

Chapter 2 - Without Asking, Without Permission 

Some nights feel heavier than others. I don’t know if it’s the silence, or the memories that fill it, but tonight feels like one of those nights. The cigarette in my hand burns slowly, its smoke twisting upward like the thoughts in my head. I still remember those late-night conversations with Vibha — how they started with nothing and slowly became everything.

At first, we talked like strangers trying to find a reason to keep the chat going. “So, what’s the weirdest thing you’ve ever done?” she asked once, probably expecting a funny story. I remember smiling at my phone and replying, “Talking to you.” She sent a laughing emoji, followed by, “That’s such a lame answer.” But even through that teasing, something about her felt… real. The kind of real I didn’t come across often.

Those conversations became the rhythm of my nights. We would talk about random things — movies, songs, childhood memories, our worst fears, and even about people who had once broken us. I found comfort in her words, in the way she listened like she actually cared. I told her about my past — things I hadn’t shared with anyone before — and she didn’t judge me; she just listened, sometimes replying with a soft “That must’ve hurt.” And I don’t know why, but that made me feel lighter.

Sometimes I’d be lying on my bed, phone in hand, and she’d send a message like, “Aaj bhi soya nahi kya?” And I’d reply, “Nahi, neend toh tabhi aati hai jab tum goodnight bolo.” She’d respond with a simple “Pagal ho tum,” and yet, that single line would make my entire night. It’s strange how someone you’ve never met can make you feel seen in ways people around you never could.

I remember one night she asked, “Why do you always stay up so late?” I typed back, “Because these are the hours when the world is quiet and I can think about you without distraction.” I didn’t send it though. I just deleted it and wrote, “Because I can’t sleep.” Maybe love had already started building up inside me then, but I wasn’t ready to admit it yet — not even to myself.

Now, when I look back, I realize how easily she slipped into my life. It wasn’t forced; it wasn’t planned. She was just there — at the right time, in the right way. Every message she sent, every “good morning” and “good night,” started meaning more than it should have. I started checking my phone too often, waiting for her name to light up my screen.

I take another drag from my cigarette now, staring out of the window. The night sky looks endless — much like our conversations used to. It’s crazy how two people who had never met could talk about everything and still never run out of things to say.

There were times when she’d tell me about her day — how her mom scolded her for waking up late or how her best friend didn’t text back. And I’d listen like those were the most important details in the world. Because to me, they were. Every small thing about her felt precious.

She once said, “You know, I feel like I can tell you anything.” That line stayed with me. Because I felt the same. Somewhere between our endless chats and random calls, she became the person I trusted the most.

One evening, she sent me a voice note of her laughing. I still remember replaying it over and over, like some addict who couldn’t get enough. That laugh — it wasn’t perfect, but it was mine in some quiet, invisible way.

And then came the feelings. Not all at once, not like a movie scene, but slowly — like rain building up before the first drop falls. One day I just realized that I had started missing her before our conversations even ended.

She’d ask me, “What do you think about love?” and I’d reply, “It’s dangerous.” She’d laugh and say, “Then don’t fall for me.” But deep inside, I think both of us already had. We just didn’t want to say it yet.

Now, sitting here, I wonder how love can creep in so quietly — without asking, without permission. One moment you’re talking to someone like a friend, and the next, they’re all you can think about.

I remember one night, I told her, “If I ever write a book, you’ll be in it.” She said, “Haha, why me?” And I said, “Because you make ordinary things sound like poetry.” She didn’t reply for a few seconds. Then she said, “You’re crazy, Aditya.” And maybe I was — crazy for her.

Days turned into weeks, and weeks into months. The bond kept growing, untitled, undefined, but real. I didn’t need a label for it. Her presence was enough. Her messages were enough. She was enough.

Sometimes, I scroll through those old chats now — random jokes, silly goodnights, small fights, quick apologies. It all feels like a different world, one I still live in even though she doesn’t.

Maybe that’s what love is — not grand gestures or promises, but quiet consistency. The way someone becomes your habit before you realize they’ve become your heart.

As I stub out my cigarette and watch the smoke fade away, I whisper her name softly — Vibha. It still feels like home.

Some loves don’t begin with fireworks. They begin with “What’s the weirdest thing you’ve done?” and end with silence that never really leaves.

“Sometimes, love doesn’t knock. It just walks in — quietly, without asking, without permission.”

Chapter 3 - The Day Everything Changed 

There are some days that don’t leave you, no matter how many years pass. 2nd July 2021 — that date still feels fresh in my mind, like it happened yesterday. I don’t even know why I remember it so clearly, but maybe it’s because that was the day my heart first learned how it feels to hope. Even now, as I sit here staring at that same old image on my phone — the one she sent me that evening — I can still hear her voice in my head, “Chalo ye drawing banao ab, aur muje bhejo photo.”

At that time, I smiled at her message like a fool. I didn’t even know how to draw properly, but still, I took out a page and tried. The picture she had sent was simple — a heart with “I love you” written inside it. It should have been just another random thing, but it wasn’t. That small heart started beating somewhere deep inside me too. I didn’t even realize when a silly drawing started meaning something more.

I took my time making that drawing, erasing, redoing, trying to make it look perfect. I remember thinking, why am I even putting so much effort into this? But somewhere inside, I already knew the answer. When you like someone, even their smallest request feels like a purpose. I finished it, clicked a photo, and sent it to her.

Within seconds, she replied — “I love you too.” Just those four words. And I swear, for a moment, I forgot how to breathe. My heart was racing so fast it felt unreal. I just sat there, staring at the screen, smiling like a madman. It felt like the world had suddenly paused for me — like everything I had ever wanted was finally in front of me.

But then, a few seconds later, her next message came. “Haha, prank kar rahi hu.”

And just like that, everything inside me froze. The excitement in my chest turned into silence. I didn’t even know how to react. My smile faded, but I somehow typed, “Nice prank.” Pretending like it didn’t matter, even though my heart had already started believing that one moment of magic was real.

I look at that same photo now, the one she told me to draw. The lines are uneven, the handwriting messy, but that image still holds a story — the story of the first time I felt something real for her. I take a slow drag from my cigarette and watch the smoke blur my sight. Maybe that’s how love begins — blurry, confusing, yet beautiful.

Days passed after that prank, but something had changed inside me. I didn’t stop talking to her, but every time she texted, I could feel that small pull in my chest. That feeling of wanting her to mean what she said that day. I told myself it was just a crush, just friendship — but my heart knew better.

And then came 4th July 2021 — the day I had decided to tell her. I remember sitting with my phone in hand for hours, typing and deleting a hundred times, scared of what might happen. The fear of losing her was real, but so was the need to finally say it.

That evening, we were on a call. The conversation was normal — random talks, laughter, teasing — until I finally gathered the courage. I said softly, “Vibha… mujhe tumse kuch kehna hai.” There was a pause. I could hear her smile through the phone when she said, “Kya bolna hai, bolo.”

My hands were sweating. My heart was beating louder than my thoughts. I took a deep breath and said it — “Vibha, I love you.”

For a moment, there was silence. A long, unbearable silence. I could hear my own breathing, the static sound of the call, and nothing else. And then… click. She disconnected.

I just sat there, staring at my phone, the word “Call Ended” glowing on the screen. My heart sank. Maybe I had ruined everything. Maybe she didn’t feel the same. Or maybe… I shouldn’t have said it at all. A thousand thoughts hit me at once, and I couldn’t stop replaying that silence in my head.

I remember pacing in my room, feeling that heaviness inside. I was scared — scared that I had lost something I hadn’t even fully gotten yet. I thought about deleting her number, but my heart refused. I just sat there, hoping, praying for her to call back.

And then, after what felt like forever, my phone rang. It was her. I remember my hands shaking as I picked up. Before I could say anything, she said softly, “I love you too, Aditya.”

That moment — that one sentence — changed everything. My entire world shifted in those five words. I didn’t even realize I was smiling with tears in my eyes. It felt unreal, like something I had only imagined was now happening for real.

You know, everyone used to call me Sonu, except in college where people knew me as Aditya. I never really liked that name much. It always felt too serious, too formal. But that night, when she said, “I love you too, Aditya,” I fell in love with my own name for the first time. It sounded softer, warmer — because it came from her.

Now, as I sit here, scrolling through those old messages, I can still feel that moment. I can still hear her voice in my head, still see that smile I never saw in person but could always imagine. It’s strange how some moments can live forever inside you.

Maybe love isn’t always grand or poetic. Sometimes, it’s just two people sitting miles apart, saying “I love you” over a phone call, and still feeling like they’re sitting next to each other.

I take another drag from my cigarette, watching the smoke dissolve into the quiet night. The same night that once carried her laughter through the phone now carries my silence. But somewhere deep inside, I still whisper those words she once said — “I love you too, Aditya.”

And that’s how everything changed — quietly, beautifully, and maybe… permanently.

“Some words are not just spoken; they’re felt — deep enough to stay, even when the voice that said them is gone.”

Chapter 4 - The Days Felt Like Forever 

There are days in life that feel like they were never meant to end — days that hold a softness you can still feel years later. Those July days were like that. Everything around me felt ordinary, yet something about that time made it all feel more alive, more real. Maybe it was her, maybe it was love — or maybe it was the peace that came from finally finding someone who understood me without me having to explain. Even now, when I close my eyes, I can still feel that calmness — like her presence still lingers somewhere inside me.

After the night she said “I love you too,” I couldn’t sleep. I remember lying on my bed, staring at the ceiling, smiling for no reason. I wasn’t used to feeling this way. For the first time, I didn’t need music to feel something — her words were enough. The next morning, everything felt different. My phone wasn’t just a device anymore; it was a doorway to her. I kept waiting for her text, and when it finally came, “Good morning, Aditya,” I couldn’t stop smiling.

We started talking more after that. Small talks turned into long conversations, and long conversations turned into confessions of thoughts we’d never shared with anyone else. I remember one night she asked me, “What’s the weirdest thing you’ve ever done?” I laughed and said, “Probably falling for someone I’ve never met.” There was a pause. Then she replied, “Then we’re both weird.” I didn’t know what to say after that — I just knew I was already too deep into something beautiful.

Those days, our calls used to last for hours. I’d sit near the window, listening to her talk about her college, her friends, her silly fights with her mom. Sometimes she would hum a song softly, and I’d just listen. I didn’t care what the song was — I just liked the sound of her voice. When she used to say, “You’re so quiet on calls, say something na,” I’d reply, “I’m listening. That’s my favorite thing to do when it’s you.” She used to laugh, that soft laugh that felt like it could heal every tired part of me.

Every night, before sleeping, I’d scroll up our chat just to read her messages again. “Did you eat?” “Are you still awake?” “Don’t overthink too much.” She cared in the smallest ways — ways that didn’t look grand but meant everything. And even now, when I look back, I realize that love doesn’t need to be loud to be real. Sometimes, it’s just quiet concern in a message you get at 2 a.m.

There were nights when she couldn’t sleep, so she’d call me and say, “Tell me something random.” And I’d start talking nonsense — stories, memories, random dreams. She’d listen, laugh softly, and say, “You talk like you write — slowly, but it stays with me.” I still remember that line. It’s funny how one sentence can stay in your heart forever.

Sometimes, while we were talking, she’d suddenly ask something deep — “Do you believe in soul connections?” I’d say, “I didn’t… until now.” There would be silence after that — not the awkward kind, but the peaceful one. The kind that makes you realize that words aren’t always needed.

Even now, when I sit outside at night, a cigarette between my fingers, the smoke curling up into the air, I think of those moments. I remember how my heart used to race just hearing her name appear on my screen. I still have that one chat pinned — the one where she wrote, “Promise me we’ll never stop talking.” I didn’t reply with words then; I just sent a heart. I really believed we never would.

Days started blending into nights. My phone became my favorite thing because somewhere on the other side of that screen, she existed. We hadn’t met, hadn’t even seen each other properly on a video call, but I could still picture her. I could imagine her expressions, her smile, her laugh. It’s strange how imagination can make someone feel more real than reality itself.

One night, I told her, “You’ve become my habit.” She laughed and said, “That’s dangerous.” I asked, “Why?” and she whispered, “Because habits are hard to break.” I didn’t know then that her words would someday feel like a prophecy.

She used to tell me stories about her school days — how she hated maths, how she got caught bunking classes once, how she once painted a wall in her room and ruined it completely. I’d just listen, smiling to myself, and say, “You talk like you’re still that little girl who never stopped dreaming.” She said, “Maybe that’s why you like me.” I didn’t deny it.

Our conversations weren’t perfect; sometimes we argued over small things — who texted first, who ignored whom, who was busy. But even those fights felt precious. Because at the end of every argument, we always found our way back. She’d say, “You’ll talk to me tomorrow, right?” and I’d reply, “I don’t think I can go a day without it.”

Some nights, when the city was asleep, I’d lie on my bed with my earphones on, listening to the songs she sent me. “Listen to this one, it’s my favorite,” she used to say. I didn’t even like half those songs, but when I played them, they felt different. Maybe because her voice was attached to them somehow.

It’s strange, isn’t it? How someone miles away can make you feel closer than anyone sitting next to you. How someone you’ve never met can become the only person who feels like home. I didn’t know what we were — lovers, friends, something in between — but whatever it was, I didn’t want it to end.

Sometimes, I still think of how she said my name — “Aditya” — slowly, softly, as if she was saying something sacred. I never liked my name before, but when she said it, it sounded like the most beautiful word in the world.

Even now, when I sit quietly, my mind drifts back to those nights — the laughter, the confessions, the “don’t hang up yet” calls. I miss that version of us — the one untouched by distance, by overthinking, by reality.

Maybe that’s what love is supposed to feel like — soft, uncertain, yet warm. Like something you can’t explain but can’t deny either.

Every time I exhale smoke into the night air, I wonder where she is, what she’s doing, if she still remembers that boy who once drew a heart because she asked him to. I don’t know if she does. But I still remember. And maybe, that’s enough.

“Some people don’t leave your life. They just live quietly inside your memories, where every goodbye still echoes as love.”

Chapter 5 - When Every “Good night” Felt Like Forever

Some memories never really fade; they just wait quietly inside your heart, waiting for nights like these — when you’re alone with your thoughts, a cigarette half-burned between your fingers, and the city outside is as quiet as your mind used to be before she came. I look at the smoke rising slowly, and I can still hear her voice echoing somewhere deep inside — soft, innocent, almost like she’s still there on the other end of the call saying, “You’re not sleepy yet, right?”

Those were the days when everything felt like magic — not the dramatic kind you see in movies, but the quiet kind that hides in ordinary moments. Like her “Hi” after a long day. Like her sending a random meme just to make me smile. Like us talking about absolutely nothing, but somehow those nothings meant everything. Every “goodnight” from her carried the warmth of a thousand unsaid things. I didn’t even realize when her absence started to feel heavier than her presence.

We used to talk about everything — from dreams to fears, from random questions to deep thoughts that even we didn’t have answers to. I remember once she asked, “What’s the first thing you notice in people?” I replied, “Their eyes.” She laughed and said, “You haven’t even seen mine yet.” I smiled and said, “Maybe that’s why I’m still here — trying to imagine them.” There was silence after that — not awkward, just peaceful. That silence was our favorite part.

Sometimes, she’d say something simple that would stay with me for days. Like the night she said, “You know, I like the way you listen. It feels like you actually care.” And I did. More than I should have. I never told her how her voice made everything else in my head go quiet. How just hearing her say my name felt like coming home after a long, lonely day.

Days were slow, but they never felt empty. She filled them with her random stories, her laughter, her thoughts about life. She’d talk about how she wanted to travel alone someday, how she loved sunsets but not more then rain, how she never liked her handwriting but still wrote pages of quotes in her diary. I’d just sit there, listening, smiling at every small thing she said. And somewhere between her stories, I started dreaming — of a life where distance didn’t matter, where maybe one day I’d actually see her smile for real.

One night, while we were on call, she said, “Close your eyes.” I did. “Now imagine me sitting beside you,” she continued, “and we’re just… quiet.” I didn’t say anything. Because in that silence, I could almost feel it — her presence, her calmness, her warmth. And then she whispered, “Do you think we’d still be this close if we ever met?” I replied softly, “Maybe even closer.” I didn’t know if she smiled at that, but I like to believe she did.

There was something about her that made me honest. I didn’t have to pretend to be strong around her. I could talk about my fears, my insecurities, the things I usually hide. And she never judged — she just listened. Sometimes she’d say, “I wish I could hug you right now.” And I’d whisper, “You just did.”

Every little thing she said stayed with me — the way she’d say “Sonu” in that teasing tone, the way she’d send random voice notes saying, “Don’t miss me too much,” knowing I already was. It wasn’t love that hit me suddenly; it was the kind that quietly built itself inside me, piece by piece, until one day I realized — she wasn’t just someone I talked to; she had become a part of me.

Even now, when I scroll through those old messages, I stop at her “Take care, okay?” because I know how much emotion she hide behind those words. She never said, “I’m worried about you,” but I could always feel it. That’s the thing about real connections — they don’t need constant words; they just need presence.

Sometimes I wish I could go back to those nights when I’d wait for her text, when time zones and distances didn’t matter because hearts were closer than cities. I wish I could relive the simplicity of it — the comfort, the care, the innocent way she made everything feel light.

Now, when I look at the moon, I think of how we used to send pictures of it to each other saying, “Look, we’re under the same sky.” Maybe that’s why I still look up sometimes — not to find her, but to feel her somewhere in the quiet light that touches everything she once did.

I miss that version of us — the one untouched by fear, by doubt, by time. The version where every goodnight felt like forever, and every morning began with her name on my screen.

Maybe love doesn’t always need to end beautifully. Maybe sometimes, it just needs to be remembered beautifully.

“Some nights, I still wait for her goodnight, not because I expect it — but because a part of me still believes she’ll send it.”

Chapter 6 - The Distance Between Hearts

It’s strange how love grows — not through touch or presence, but through words, through silence, through the comfort of being understood. I still remember those nights, the ones that stretched endlessly, where every heartbeat felt like it carried her name. The world outside kept moving, but for me, time stood still between her “hi” and her “goodnight.”

Now, sitting on my balcony with the city asleep beneath me, I light another cigarette. The smoke rises slowly, curling into shapes I can’t name, and I find myself smiling — the same way I used to when she said something silly just to make me laugh. The night feels colder now, but her warmth still lingers somewhere in my chest.

Back then, every conversation with her felt like a story being written in real-time. We talked about everything — from our favorite movies to our deepest fears. She once asked, “If we ever meet, what’s the first thing you’ll do?” I laughed and said, “Probably stare at you for a few minutes just to believe you’re real.” She replied softly, “Then I’d probably look away, because I’d be smiling too much.” That conversation stayed with me longer than I expected.

We started sharing dreams too. She’d say, “One day, I’ll visit Mumbai.” And I’d reply, “Then I’ll finally show you my world.” We both knew it might not happen soon, maybe not ever, but it didn’t matter. The thought itself was enough — it gave us hope.

Sometimes, she’d get quiet suddenly. When I asked what happened, she’d say, “Nothing. Just thinking.” But I could always tell when something was wrong. “You can tell me,” I’d say. She’d reply, “You always say that in such a calm way, it feels like everything will be okay.” That’s when I realized — maybe love isn’t about big promises; it’s about small reassurances.

Our calls became longer, softer. There were moments where neither of us said anything for minutes, just breathing on the line, knowing the other was still there. She once whispered, “You know, I talk to you more than anyone else.” And I smiled in the dark, whispering back, “Then I guess I’m lucky.”

“Hmm?”
“I’m sorry. For everything.”

I smiled, though my eyes were burning. “Don’t be. Just… take care of yourself.”
Before she could reply, I ended the call.

For a few minutes, I just sat there, staring at the screen, waiting for her to call back — but she didn’t.
Then her message popped up.
“Sorry for everything.”

I read it again and again until the words blurred. My hands were trembling, but I typed back, “It’s okay, Vibha.”
And then, I put my phone aside, pretending to be fine — like I always did.

But deep down, I knew…
I wasn’t fine.
I had lost not just her, but a part of myself that only existed when she was around.

That night, I looked at the sky one last time and whispered,
“Maybe love doesn’t end, it just changes its form — from presence to memory.”

The Message That Changed The Night 

It’s 2:47 AM.
The world is asleep, but my mind isn’t. I’m sitting in my balcony with a half-empty glass of alcohol in one hand and a cigarette slowly burning between my fingers. The smoke rises slowly, almost like it’s trying to touch the stars that look too far tonight. Maybe that’s how we were — close enough to see each other, but too far to ever reach.

The night feels familiar — quiet, heavy, full of thoughts that refuse to leave. I look at my phone screen again, not because I’m expecting anything, but because old habits die hard. It’s been months, maybe more, since we last spoke. Vibha’s name still sits there in my chats, somewhere between “goodbyes” and “almosts.”

I take another sip, staring into the dark sky. I wonder how she’s doing now.
Is she still awake late at night like she used to be? Does she still listen to those slow songs we once shared? Has someone else taken my place in her heart — the way I once took someone else’s without meaning to? I don’t know. I’ll probably never know.

And maybe that’s okay. Maybe some questions are meant to remain unanswered. Because sometimes, peace doesn’t come from knowing — it comes from accepting that you never will.

I exhale slowly, watching the smoke fade into the air. It’s all over now, I whisper to myself.
Everything we had, everything we were — it’s all gone.

But just when I’m about to put my phone down, the screen lights up.
A message.

For a moment, my heart stops.
And there it is — her name.
Vibha.

I stare at it for a second, afraid to open it, afraid it might disappear if I blink. My hands tremble slightly as I unlock the phone.

The message reads:
“Can we sort out? Mujhse bhi raha nahi jaa raha tumhare bina.”

I don’t move. I just sit there, staring at the screen, feeling something heavy inside me melt for the first time in months. I don’t know if this is another beginning or just a memory trying to come back one last time. But in that single moment, everything I’d buried starts breathing again.

The cigarette burns down between my fingers, but I don’t notice. The alcohol glass sits untouched. All I can feel is my heartbeat — faster, louder, alive again.

I smile faintly, the kind that hides both relief and fear.
Because sometimes, love doesn’t really end — it just takes a pause, waiting for the right moment to return.

I put the glass down, take a deep breath, and whisper to the night —
“She’s back.”

And somewhere in the silence, it feels like the universe smiles too.

"Timeless moral-stories reimagined for today’s children growing-up with screens, speed, and choices"

Panchtantra Reboot – The Fun Tales

Author: Aayansh Kumar
Category: Novel (Contemporary Moral Novel-in-Episodes | Children’s Fiction)

Overview and Conceptual Framework

Panchtantra Reboot – The Fun Tales is a contemporary moral novel that draws inspiration from the ancient Indian Panchatantra while deliberately reshaping its narrative form for a modern, digitally oriented generation. The novel is conceived as a unified literary work, not as a loose anthology, and presents a coherent moral universe in which animal characters confront ethical dilemmas rooted in present-day realities such as technology dependence, social media influence, misinformation, consumer culture, declining attention spans, and the erosion of patience and empathy.

At its heart, the novel explores a central question: How do timeless values survive and adapt in a world driven by speed, screens, and instant gratification? Each chapter contributes to this inquiry, forming a progressive moral journey that moves from personal discipline to social responsibility, and finally to ethical maturity.

The work consciously positions itself as a novel-in-episodes, a form historically used to convey philosophical and moral development through interconnected narratives. While each episode is self-contained and accessible, together they form a continuous ethical arc, offering readers a cumulative understanding that deepens with progression.

Narrative Structure and Unity

The novel is structured into sixteen chapters, each functioning as a narrative episode within a shared worldview. The setting shifts across villages, schools, parks, digital spaces, and symbolic environments, yet remains unified by tone, theme, and moral logic. The animal characters are not random figures but recurring archetypes—embodiments of human tendencies such as ambition, laziness, curiosity, vanity, wisdom, fear, and compassion.

The narrative progression is deliberate:

Foundation of Discipline and Effort

Formation of Ethical Identity and Relationships

Confrontation with Digital-Age Moral Challenges

Reassertion of Balance, Community, and Wisdom

This structural movement allows the novel to function as a cohesive literary experience rather than a collection of unrelated stories.

Thematic Development and Key Episodes
Effort versus Instant Gratification

The novel opens with The Gamer Lizard and the Hard-Working Ant, which establishes the ethical backbone of the entire work. Gecko, the lizard, is immersed in virtual rewards and entertainment, believing convenience can replace preparation. The ant, by contrast, represents foresight, discipline, and sustained effort. When winter arrives, the consequences of these opposing choices become clear.

This opening episode introduces a recurring motif: virtual reward versus real consequence. The tension established here echoes throughout the novel, reappearing in different forms—online validation, shortcuts to success, impulsive decisions, and avoidance of responsibility.

Moral Identity and Relationships

As the novel progresses, the focus expands from individual behavior to interpersonal ethics. In True Friends vs Fair-Weather Friends, loyalty is tested under the pressure of success and failure. Characters abandon integrity for advantage, only to discover that achievement without trust is hollow.

The Wi-Fi Lion and the Smart Mouse reframes traditional power dynamics. Strength and authority fail where intelligence, humility, and courage succeed. This episode challenges inherited hierarchies and introduces the novel’s recurring assertion that moral authority is earned, not imposed.

Together, these chapters explore how character is formed not in isolation, but through relationships, choices, and accountability.

Digital Ethics and Illusion

A central section of the novel addresses the moral complexities of the digital age. In The Monkey, the Crocodile, and the Fake Selfie, deception is modernized into online manipulation. The predator no longer lurks openly; it hides behind friendly appearances and curated images. The story transforms abstract concerns about online safety into a concrete narrative, encouraging discernment without fear.

The Fox with a Fake YouTube Channel critiques misinformation and viral culture. Popularity is shown to be an unreliable measure of truth, and the pursuit of attention is exposed as a moral risk. These episodes collectively form a sustained examination of truth, influence, and responsibility in a world shaped by algorithms rather than wisdom.

Health, Balance, and Self-Care

Another thematic arc focuses on the neglect of physical and emotional well-being in the pursuit of convenience and validation. In The Lazy Dog Who Ordered Pizza Online, indulgence replaces effort, leading to decline rather than comfort. The TikTok Crow and the Cool Water Bottle presents perhaps the most symbolic moment in the novel: a character prioritizes online attention over survival itself.

These stories argue that self-care is not merely personal preference but a moral obligation. The novel positions balance—not excess—as the true measure of progress.

Community, Cooperation, and Humility

Midway through the narrative, the focus shifts toward collective ethics. The Pizza Pigeons and the Hungry Hawk demonstrates how unity transforms vulnerability into strength, reinforcing cooperation over individual bravado. The Shy Donkey and the Rock Concert dismantles glamour culture, revealing that sincerity and quiet competence often surpass loud confidence.

These episodes critique modern performance culture and reassert the value of humility, teamwork, and mutual respect.

Wisdom, Patience, and Ethical Maturity

The later chapters deepen the moral tone. The Young Skateboarder Goat and the Wise Old Cow highlights generational wisdom and the cost of ignoring experience. The Little Kite & the Trapped Balloon elevates compassion and service, arguing that talent gains meaning only when used for others.

In Eagle, Nightingale & Viral Symphony, rivalry in the age of virality gives way to collaboration. The episode suggests that ethical leadership is measured not by dominance, but by the ability to uplift others.

Conclusion and Moral Resolution

The novel concludes with The TikTok Crow and the Cool Water Bottle, a chapter that synthesizes the work’s central concerns. The pursuit of virtual approval nearly results in physical collapse, forcing a reckoning between illusion and reality. The resolution is reflective rather than punitive, emphasizing learning, renewal, and awareness.

This ending brings the novel full circle, returning to its opening tension between convenience and responsibility, and affirming its core message: progress without ethics is empty, and pleasure without effort is unsustainable.

Language, Style, and Accessibility

The novel employs simple, rhythmic language enriched with humor, rhyme, repetition, and symbolic imagery. While accessible to younger readers, the narrative maintains philosophical coherence and thematic depth. The animal characters function as moral mirrors, allowing complex ideas to be explored without didacticism.

The episodic structure encourages both sequential reading and reflective pause, making the novel suitable for individual readers, shared reading, and educational settings.

Justification for Novel Classification (Integrated)

Panchtantra Reboot – The Fun Tales qualifies as a novel by structure, intent, and execution. It presents:

A single moral universe governed by consistent ethical principles

A progressive thematic arc across chapters

A deliberate narrative beginning, development, and conclusion

A unified authorial voice and worldview

The work aligns with established novel forms such as the moral novel, picaresque narrative, and novel-in-episodes, all recognized within global literary tradition. While inspired by Panchatantra storytelling, it consciously modernizes and integrates that tradition into a cohesive novelistic framework.

Conclusion

Panchtantra Reboot – The Fun Tales stands as a contemporary moral novel that honors ancient wisdom while engaging with the ethical complexities of modern life. It asserts that storytelling remains one of humanity’s most powerful tools for moral reflection and that even in a digital age, values such as effort, empathy, balance, and wisdom remain essential.

As a submission to the Indian Writers’ League – Novel Category, the work represents a confident fusion of tradition and innovation, offering a unified literary vision that speaks meaningfully to both present and future generations.

The Story of Us, the Mountain Dwellers.
Nestled in the lap of the mountains was a village called Chiragpur. It was a tiny haven hidden in the foothills of the Himalayas, where the first rays of the morning sun pierced through the clouds and fell straight onto the fields. We, the people of Chiragpur, were the true inhabitants of the mountains. Our story isn't one of royal palaces' glamour or city hustle-bustle. It's a tale of simplicity, struggle, and that priceless beauty spread before our eyes every day.My name is Karim. I was born and raised right here in Chiragpur. My father was a farmer who grew rice and millet on the hilly slopes. My mother managed the home and grazed the sheep and goats. Our house was made of wood and stone, with a thatched grass roof. City folk called it poverty, but we knew it was part of our life. Every morning, the mountain peaks called out to us. Lush green forests, the tinkling of waterfalls, and those flowers that bloom only here—red rhododendrons, white clusters of brahmakamal. These were our treasures.But living in the mountains isn't easy. Basic facilities? Oh dear! Electricity came and went. Fine in summer, but in winter, snowfall shut everything down. Our village was ten kilometers up from the main road. Road? It was just a dirt path that turned to mud in the rains. No vehicles came. We had to carry everything on our shoulders—rice, oil, medicines. There was a school in the village, but the teacher showed up only twice a month. Kids studied, but with old books and a broken blackboard. Water? A stream flowed from the hill above. Women woke at 4 a.m., walked for hours with filled buckets. Tap? A dream. Hospital? Even farther. Fall sick, and it was herbal remedies, grandma's potions. Helicopters came sometimes, but for the rich.Still, we don't complain. Why? Because the beauty we have can't be bought for any price. Imagine—sunrise when the mountains turn golden. Sky so blue and clear, stars seem visible even by day. Stroll in the forest and spot deer, langurs, peacocks. Air so crisp and pure, breathing feels like heaven. Fruits? Wild mangoes, apricots—free for the picking. Rivers so clean you could drink straight. We kids bathed naked in the streams, caught fish. Evenings by the firewood stove, mom baking rotis, grandma telling stories—of mountain kings and queens, ghosts, and warriors who lived here.Once, in the summer heat, the village faced a severe water shortage. The stream dried up. Fields withered. Dad said, "Karim, there's a big waterfall on the peak above. We'll pipe it down." But the peak was 2,000 meters high. The path treacherous—cliffs, wild animals. Still, villagers gathered. Ten or fifteen men. Ropes, shovels, old pipes. It took three days. A bear roared en route. One uncle slipped off a rock but survived. Finally, water flowed. Fields turned green. That night, the whole village danced. Drums beat, folk songs rang out—"O mountains, our eternal guardians, you sustain our lives."Childhood passed like that. Grown up, I thought, time to do something. Went to the city to study. Saw Delhi's dazzle—highways, malls, 24/7 power. But breathing there was hard. Pollution, noise, crowds. Missed the mountains. Returned. Installed solar panels in the village. Formed an NGO with friends. Got a road built under a government scheme. Now vehicles come. Computers in school. Water tank installed. But not perfect yet. Power still cuts in snow. Weak mobile signal. No doctors. COVID was chaos. Medicines airlifted. Many lost lives.Our women are the strongest. My brother Prakash's wife, Radha. Up at 4 a.m. for water. Then fields, grazing buffaloes, housework. Baskets on arms, wood loads on heads. But smile never fades. She says, "Mountains made us strong." Yes, strong. Tourists come now. Call our village a 'homestay.' They snap mountain pics, sip our tea, watch folk dances. Money flows in. But we protect the environment. No plastic. Save the forests. Once, big hoteliers came to chop woods. We refused. "This is our life," we said.Winter's joy is unique. Snow falls, blanketing the village white. Kids make snowballs. We elders chat by the fire. Knit woolens. But dangers too. Blizzards bury homes. Landslides. Villagers die sometimes. Yet, we mountain folk fight on.Now I have a daughter, Seema. She goes to school. Dreams of becoming an engineer. Says, "Dad, I'll make the village like a city—power, water, hospital." I laugh. "Daughter, don't make it a city. Keep it mountains. Don't lose the beauty." Because that's our strength. Basic facilities are coming slowly—solar lights, satellite internet, heli-services. But that beauty? Eternal. Moonlit nights when peaks gleam silver. Fog draping forests. Birdsong waking us. Can't buy these with money.One day, tourists arrived. A rich man said, "Your life is so tough. Come to the city." I replied, "Sir, your city is so empty. Here, every breath is life." They left, thoughtful. Our story is this—struggle blended with beauty. Lack of basics doesn't weaken us; it strengthens. We are the mountains' children. Us, the mountain dwellers. Our roots are here, and they'll stay.Tired of city life? Come to Chiragpur. We'll serve tea, share stories. Show you the mountains. And tell you true life is here.

Respected Sir,
I am taking an opportunity to introduce my new book titled "Unspoken Wounds: A Saga of Communal Turbulences." It is an English novel based on inter-communal relations during three eras of tension in various parts of Punjab. This novel not only refreshes our memories of the freedom struggle and freedom gained by India from the British in 1947 and the birth of Pakistan following partition, but also recalls the tragedy endured by the people of Punjab during militancy and Operation Blue Star in 1984. More importantly, it conveys the clear-cut lesson learned from those dark days: that neither is every individual wrong in any community, nor is every individual entirely right in any community. Furthermore, it reveals that those with a perverted mentality who exploit tense situations across all communities hold no regard for even their blood relations.
While this novel chronicles the story of inter-communal tensions, it also presents examples of communal harmony through various characters. The narrative attempts to portray the mindset of riot-affected families enduring repeated displacement, as well as their companions, relatives, and attackers during migration. This novel demonstrates how passionately many Hindu and Sikh families were helping riot-affected Muslim families in India, despite the tensions between Hindu-Sikh and Muslim communities during partition. It shows how a Hindu family aided a Muslim family even in a refugee camp established at the Indo-Pak border and later brought them back to settle in Punjab.
Similarly, many Muslim families were helping riot-affected Hindu and Sikh families with complete warmth and affection. On the other hand, there were Hindu, Sikh, and Muslim looters too, who, considering these tensions as an opportunity for looting, became bloodthirsty not only towards other communities but even towards their own blood relations.
The novel also depicts how, during the tension that spread across Punjab in the 1980s, militants shed innocent blood, while some corrupt officers in the Punjab police and Central security forces accused many innocent Sikh youth of being militants and targeted them in fake encounters for promotion.
During that period, journalism—the fourth pillar of democracy—also faced a big crisis. Major newspapers like Punjab Kesari had to sacrifice many journalists and non-journalist employees, including two chief editors, while maintaining fearless journalism. Additionally, through the story of a small-town-based journalist, the novel illustrates how the journalist community became a target not only of militants but also of the police and administration during that tense atmosphere.
The novel also makes symbolic reference to the assassination of Prime Minister Mrs. Indira Gandhi following the army's Operation Blue Star at the Golden Temple—the holiest site of the Sikh community—in June 1984, and then the infamous events that occurred in the national capital, Delhi, during the subsequent anti-Sikh riots of 1984.
In the novel's third phase, it mentions the unfortunate events of 2005 in a town in Punjab bordering Pakistan, where the local administration, under the influence of the land mafia, played an inhuman game of atrocities against some Muslim families. After media exposure, the Chief Minister intervened, which finally ended this series of torture, and the wall that had become a symbol of destruction for these Muslim families was demolished.
Friends, I acknowledge that my command of English is not so good, but some of my seniors encouraged me to write this novel in English. I once again express my heartfelt gratitude to the organizers of the event.
Thank you. Jai Hind. Jai Bharat.

title.stringValue: A HEART OF RAFI - UMESH MAKHIJA's UNWAVERING PASSION

content.stringValue:
A Heart for Rafi - Umesh Makhija's Unwavering Passion
The immortal melody of Mohammed Rafi still echoes in our hearts, and his legacy continues to inspire generations. The song "Mein Zindagi kaa saath nibhaata chalaa gaya" is a poignant reminder of the legendary singer's timeless impact. Mohammed Rafi left the world on 31st July 1980, but his love still lives on in the hearts of his fans.
In Ahmedabad, a devoted fan, Umesh Makhija, has taken his admiration to an extraordinary level by building a temple in his house dedicated to Mohammed Rafi. Makhija's love story with Rafi's music began more than 60 years ago, and since then, he's collected over 4,000 songs sung by the maestro, including rare tracks in various languages. His treasure trove of memorabilia includes Rafi's glasses, pocket watch, shaving blades, ties, blankets, and even visiting cards.
Makhija's devotion is not just about collecting rare items; it's about celebrating Rafi's legacy and sharing it with others. He says, "There are many fans of Mohammed Rafi Sahab, but I am his devotee. I consider myself very fortunate that Rafi Sahab entered my life." Every day, people visit his temple, and on Rafi's birthday, the celebration is a grand affair. Makhija's temple is a testament to Rafi's enduring impact on Indian music and culture. 
The temple is a treasure trove of Rafi's memorabilia, with a room filled with his songs, photos, and rare items. As you enter, you'll see a bed with Rafi's songs written on it, and on the pillows, the first song he sang and the last song he recorded are inscribed, along with his date of passing. The clock in the room is stopped at 10:29, the exact time Rafi Sahab passed away on July 31, 1980. Makhija's mobile numbers end with Rafi's birth (24 12 24) and death (31 7 80) dates. His i10 carries the numberplate '1067', matching Rafi's iconic black Fiat.
Rafi's impact goes beyond his music; he was a humanitarian, a kind soul, and a true legend. His versatility, command over different genres, and modulating techniques have assured him an immortal place in South Asia's music history and worldwide. He sang for numerous films, including 'Ganga Jumna', 'Chaudhvin Ka Chand', and 'Sasural'. His duets with Lata Mangeshkar are still widely popular, and his solo tracks like 'Babumoshai Zindagi Ke Mat Phool' remain timeless classics.
Makhija's dedication to Rafi's legacy is inspiring, and his efforts to keep the singer's memory alive are commendable. He has made it his life's mission to share Rafi's music with the world and to ensure that his legacy continues to inspire future generations. Makhija's love for Rafi is contagious, and his temple has become a pilgrimage site for fans who want to pay homage to the legendary singer.
Umesh Makhija has turned one of the rooms of his three-bedroom house into a Mohammed Rafi Mandir, or temple. It's the world's first temple dedicated to Rafi. Every morning, Makhija burns incense sticks in front of Rafi's photo and offers prayers. The temple attracts many film and non-film personalities. Indian and foreign news media have covered the temple.

Like Rafi, Makhija also preaches a message of peace, unity, and brotherhood. Rafi's contribution to music is immense, so the demands made by his fans in the comment sections of online sites that play Rafi's songs are understandable. Fans are also involved in writing letters to editors and appearing in the news media, putting pressure wherever they can to urge the government to give Rafi a Bharat Ratna posthumous award.

But most awards given these days are not to appreciate the work of the recipients, but to gain political mileage for officials giving them or for undeserving people wanting the award to profit from it. Rafi's talents, humanity, humility, and honesty are pristine compared to the stained Bharat Ratna. Rafi's real Bharat Ratnas are people like Makhija who are keeping Rafi's name and art alive.

Umesh, a cloth merchant from Ahmedabad, has no limits to his devotion for Rafi Sahab. Every item in the temple is connected to Rafi. The only temple dedicated to Mohammed Rafi in the country is located in Umesh Makhija's home in Ahmedabad. Umesh has dedicated an entire room to Rafi, and every year, he celebrates Rafi's birthday in grand style, attracting fans from all over the country.

The Rafi Temple Makhija has transformed a 3-BHK apartment into a shrine devoted to Rafi, featuring walls covered in photos of the singer, specialized bedsheets and pillow covers printed with lyrics of unforgettable songs, and a collection of personal items. His collection includes personal items associated with the singer, such as a necktie, a blanket, a muffler, a wallet, spectacles, and even a shaving blade.
Makhija and his family perform a "Rafi Aarti" every morning, and he begins his day listening to and singing Rafi's songs. As a businessman in Ahmedabad, Makhija has incorporated his devotion into his work, printing lyrics from Rafi's songs on the packaging of the clothing items he manufactures. His dedication is well-known within the film industry, and he has been visited by Fuzail Rafi, grandson of Mohammed Rafi.
One would say that “If Rafi Sahab was alive today, he would have been an inspiration for today’s generation and he would surely have made himself available for social events.”

Songs like "Jaane Walon Zara" from Dosti, "Suhani Raat Dhal Chuki" from Dulari, "Ae Mohabbat Zindabad" from Mughal-e-Azam, "Badi Door Se Aaye Hain" from Samjhauta, and "Tujhe Kya Sunaoon Main Dilruba" from Aakhri Daao are just a few examples. Similarly, his famous qawwalis and songs for children like "Nanhe Munne Bachche", "Chun Chun Karti Aayi Chidiya", and "Na Hindu Banega" are still the hallmark of good songs with a message. When Umesh Makhija's customers open the women's lingerie he manufactures at his Ahmedabad unit, the box's printed inlays greet them with: "Ae phoolon ki rani, bahaaron ki mallika, tera muskurana gazab ho gaya." Anyone associated with Makhija knows they will have to accept the Mohammad Rafi hangover. Even Rafi's family endorses his passion. When they stayed at his home during his daughter's wedding in January, they were overwhelmed by how Rafi was stamped on every facet of Makhija's life and home.
Being a 'devotee' means he must make time for Rafi fans visiting the temple for two hours every Sunday and host a party for around 500 people on the legend's birth and death anniversaries each year. Rafi's songs play on a loop; many attempt karaoke, and bowls of kheer, Rafi's favourite sweet, are served all evening.
As we remember Mohammed Rafi on his passing anniversary, let's celebrate his life, his music, and the love he shared with the world. Let's also acknowledge the efforts of fans like Umesh Makhija, who are working tirelessly to keep his legacy alive. Rafi's music is a treasure that we'll cherish forever, and his life was a symphony of kindness, humility, and passion.  His dedication is known to Mohammed Rafi's family members who have visited his home and endorsed his passion. 
Umesh Makhija, a true devotee of Mohammed Rafi, has shown us what it means to love and cherish the legacy of a legend. His temple, filled with Rafi's memorabilia, is a testament to the enduring impact of the singer's music. As we remember Mohammed Rafi, let's pledge to keep his music alive, just like Umesh Makhija continues to do so with unwavering dedication.

title.stringValue: ASLAM KHAN – THE LAME SOLDIER (LANGRA FOUZI)

content.stringValue:
A SOLDIER LEFT BEHIND

Snow fell softly over the village, as if the mountains were trying to cover their own scars. The houses crouched low against the cold wind, smoke rising from chimneys like tired breaths. Beyond the last row of homes, the land rose sharply—dark forests, jagged ridges, and somewhere beyond them, the invisible line that divided nations and destinies.

Aslam Khan sat outside his house on a wooden stool, adjusting the strap of his prosthetic leg.
The metal clicked faintly, an unforgiving sound that reminded him, every single day, of what he had lost.
Five years ago, in Dras, the wind had cut like knives and the air had smelled of cordite and blood. His unit had been surrounded. The militants kept coming, wave after wave, screaming slogans that echoed off the rocks. Aslam had fired until the barrel burned his palms. When the shell hit, there was no pain at first, only a violent force throwing him backward, the sky spinning, and then darkness.

When he woke up, his left leg was gone.
The Army gave him medals. The village gave him a nickname. The lame soldier. 'Langra fouzi'.
Children whispered it. Men said it half-jokingly, half-cruelly. Aslam never corrected them. Discipline had taught him restraint; loss had taught him endurance. Still, every word landed like a slap.

Inside the house, life continued because Farah insisted it must. She moved with quiet strength, hiding her worries behind routine. Zoya and Amina, fourteen and sixteen, were his sunlight. They treated his limp as if it didn’t exist. When he struggled up the slope behind the house, they slowed their steps so he would never feel left behind.

FARAH, ZOYA, AMINA, PILLARS OF ASLAM’S STRENGTH

Farah was not a woman who feared hardship. Life in the border villages had taught her to endure shortages, winters, and uncertainty. What she feared was silence, the kind that followed gunfire.

She loved Aslam without a pity. When he came home with one leg missing and eyes that no longer slept, she did not ask why fate had been cruel. She simply made space for his pain. At night, when phantom pain seized him, and his jaw clenched to stop himself from crying out, Farah would press his head against her chest and whisper stories of their early days, those before uniforms and wars.

Zoya was sharp-tongued, fiercely protective of her father. She hated the boys who mocked him. Once, she broke a stick on a boy’s back and said coldly, “He lost his leg saving cowards like you.”

Amina was gentler. She braided Aslam’s beard when he sat in the sun. She believed her father was still a soldier, just fighting a quieter war.

BEGINNING OF THE FATAL DAY

That morning, Aslam wrapped his shawl tighter over his jacket and pull-over.
“I’ll go to the township,” he said. “We’re out of salt and kerosene.”
Farah nodded. “Come back early. Snow may worsen.”
Amina teased, “Don’t forget the sweets this time.”
Aslam smiled, a rare, fragile thing.
“I won’t,” he promised.
It was the last promise he ever made.

THE SLAUGHTER

The terrorists were already being hunted.
Eight of them, battle-hardened, trained beyond mercy. Their radios crackled with panic as the Indian Army closed in from two sides, bullets snapping through the trees, helicopters thundering overhead. Retreat was their only option.
They chose the village because villages bleed silently.
They entered firing.
Bullets tore through walls made of mud and stone. Windows exploded. People ran and fell. Mothers screamed names that would never be answered. Children dropped where they stood, school bags still slung over their shoulders.
Farah heard the first shots and pulled her daughters close.
“Stay behind me,” she whispered.
The door burst open.
The men were faceless under beards and scarves, eyes cold, fingers twitching on triggers. They saw fear—and mistook it for weakness.
Farah stood tall, like a wall
She did not beg.
Zoya tried to step forward.
Amina closed her eyes and whispered her father’s name.
The gunfire was deafening as bullets pierced them.
When the terrorists left, the village lay broken, blood darkening the snow, silence pressing down like a shroud.

RETURN TO HELL

Aslam returned in the afternoon. He already came to know about the terror attack on his village while in the town. He was praying for a miraculous escape of the three women he had in the world.
The village did not greet him.
No voices. No movement. Only the wind.
He sensed it before he saw it.
A slipper near the well.
A bloodied scarf tangled in a fence.
A door hanging from one hinge.
His steps quickened, pain forgotten, breath burning.
“Farah?” he called.
No answer.
‘Zoya? Amina?”
A sheer silence was prevailing across the house.
He entered his house.
Time stopped.
Farah lay near the doorway, her eyes open, staring at nothing. Zoya was beside her, one hand stretched toward her mother. Amina lay against the wall, as if trying to make herself invisible.
Aslam dropped to his knees.
The world narrowed to a ringing silence.
He touched their faces, absolutely cold.
There was no scream.
No tears.
Only a sound deep in his chest, like something tearing apart.
Aslam stood in the ruins of his home for long, his breath shallow, his ears ringing. His fingers brushed Zoya’s hair, still warm from the fire that had just passed through the village. Amina’s bangles were broken, scattered like small, useless prayers on the floor.
“I was trained to protect”, his mind whispered.
“I was trained to kill the enemies like terrorists”.
He pressed his forehead to the ground.
“I’m sorry,” he said, not to God, but to them.
When he finally rose, the man who stood was no longer the same. The soldier woke fully.
From an old trunk, he took out a large, thick corrugated dagger—steel dulled by time, memory sharpened by grief. He tied it tightly to his waist.
Then he stepped into the snow.
Chase began to eliminate the fleeing rats.

THE CHASE

The tracks were clear, eight sets of boots, careless, hurried. Blood drops marked their path where one of them had been grazed. Aslam followed with grim patience, his limp slowing but never stopping him.
Night fell.
The cold bit through his bones. His prosthetic chafed his skin raw. Every step sent fire through his body. Still, he moved.
Across the invisible line.
Into hostile land.
Into the mountains he knew better than his own scars.
By the second night, he saw the light.
A hut.
Smoke.
Voices laughing. Bantering aloud.
They thought they were safe outside Indian territory without having an iota of idea of the presence of a lame, undaunted soldier of the Indian Army.
Aslam waited, with patience in mind and revenge in heart.

THE FINAL ENCOUNTER AND REVENGE FOR THE FAMILY AND NATION

THE FIRST KILL -THE SHADOW

The mountain night was alive, wind howling, snow whispering secrets. Aslam crouched behind a boulder near the terrorists’ hideout, his breath measured, his pain catalogued like a battlefield injury.
Eight of them, he counted.
Eight breaths stolen from my world.
The first man stepped out, careless, laughing softly.
Aslam moved.
He grabbed the man from behind, clamping a hand over his mouth. The terrorist struggled, strong but panic weakens even trained men. Aslam felt his own heartbeat in his skull.
This is for Farah, he thought.
He whispered into the man’s ear, voice shaking with control,
“This is for my family.”
The dagger moved once.
When the body stilled, Aslam lowered it gently into the snow—not mercy, but discipline.
One.

THE SECOND AND THIRD - PAIN RETURNS

The second terrorist sensed something wrong.
“Did you hear?”
Aslam charged.
They collided hard, rolling downhill. The terrorist punched him in the ribs. Pain exploded. Aslam felt his prosthetic leg twist awkwardly.
You took my pain, his mind snarled.
You don’t get to use it.
He headbutted the man, feeling teeth crack. As the terrorist reached for his rifle, Aslam pinned the arm with his knee and drove the dagger down.
Breathing hard, Aslam stood, just as the third man fired.
The bullet tore into Aslam’s shoulder.
He staggered, screamed despite himself.
So this is how it ends?
No.
He rushed forward.
They fought barehanded, fists, elbows, desperation. The terrorist was younger. Faster.
Aslam was angrier.
He slammed the man into a tree, again and again, until resistance faded.
Aslam leaned against the trunk, gasping.
You shot me, he thought.
I was shot before. I lived.
He whispered,
“This is for my village.”
Three.

THE FOURTH AND FIFTH - THE SLOPE

Two terrorists ran into the open snowfield.
Aslam chased them, his limp carving agony through his body. His lungs burned. His vision blurred.
Stop, his body begged.
Walk, his soul ordered.
One slipped and vanished into the ravine, screaming.
The other turned, firing wildly.
Aslam lunged.
They fell together, rolling, snow filling mouths and eyes. The terrorist clawed at Aslam’s wound. Aslam roared and bit into the man’s shoulder, raw, animal fury. He seized the man’s head and smashed it against the frozen ground until the struggle ended.
Aslam lay there for a moment, staring at the sky.
Farah… I’m still moving.

THE SIXTH - THE BLADE DANCE

The sixth terrorist waited, knife swiftly drawn, and flashed in the snow.
They circled.
The man slashed cutting Aslam’s ribs. Warmth spread.
Aslam countered, moving with training drilled into muscle memory. He disarmed the man, twisted his wrist, slammed him down.
The terrorist spat blood. “You’re nothing,” he hissed.
Aslam leaned close, eyes blazing.
“I am what you couldn’t break.”
He ended it swiftly.

THE SEVENTH - THE BEGGAR

The seventh dropped his weapon and fell to his knees.
“Please,” he sobbed. “I have children.”
Aslam froze.
Zoya’s face flashed.
Amina’s laugh.
Farah’s voice.
Aslam’s hands shook.
You had children, his mind screamed.
You still pulled the trigger.
He spoke aloud, voice low, breaking,
“This is for my daughters.”
The dagger fell.
Tears followed.

THE EIGHTH -THE FINAL WORD

The last man ran until his lungs failed him.
At the ridge, cornered, he turned.
Aslam stood before him, blood-soaked, shaking, unbroken.
The terrorist raised trembling hands.
Aslam lifted his dagger.
“This,” he said, voice steady at last,
“is for my family.”
A step forward.
“This is for my village.”
Another step.
“And this—”
His voice rose, echoing through the mountains.
“—THIS IS FOR MY COUNTRY.”
The blade flashed.
The mountains fell silent.

THE FINAL SALUTE

Aslam collapsed near the border at dawn.
When Indian soldiers found him, they raised rifles, then froze.
He was still conscious, smiling faintly, with repetitive whispers that surprised them utmost.
“Bharat Mata Ki Jay!” 
One junior officer recognized him instantly.
“Sir, he is Aslam Khan, one of the toughest cookies of my previous unit in Dras.”
The limp.
The medals.
The name.
They carried him with every bit of care and reverence.
Later, in the hospital, an officer stood by his bed and saluted, not out of protocol, but out of awe.
Aslam silently stared at the ceiling.
His eyes were dry. 
Mind was vacant.

His family was gone.
His body was broken.
But his soul had not bent.

The Langra Fouzi had walked where even the bravest feared to tread.

And the mountains remembered each of his footsteps to glorify our beloved motherland.


A short-story by Dr (Mr) Sugata Mukhopadhyay, as a sincere tribute to the Indian Army

Mother mother, will you calm me down?
I think I'm losing my mind.
Mother mother, will you stay with me?
I think I'm running out of time.

Our house is on fire; 
Everything is burning down.
The garden has been the first to burn; 
All the elements are following it now.
The clock in the dining room, 
The pictures on the wall.
All are set to burn.
Will i be able to save them now?

Why are my legs frozen in the spot?
Why can't i move my hands to save it all?
While the house keeps burning; 
My burning eyes just wander around.
My mouth stitched shut;
Mother mother, why can't I scream or howl?

As the house burns to flame; 
Why can't I extinguish the fire of my soul?
Why am I just standing here frozen, 
Watching my life unravel in smoke?

Is this how it ends?
Or Is this something I did on my own?
Mother mother, 
Will you still be okay,
If I can't save our house?

The clock in the dining room,

Memories made of time;

Is this what life is? 
Leaving things behind?
Is this what life is? 
Pretending everything's fine?

Will i be able to save this time now?

Before there's anything left around?

“Hey Reyansh, going home early today,” said Tedd with a sarcastic smile at 8:00 pm.


The office was almost empty, and the coffee machines had also stopped buzzing. Some of the lights were already switched off, and the peons were impatiently waiting for the last few members to leave the office and call it a day.


“Yes boss, thought of taking a half-day today,” said Reyansh with equal humour.


In the chilly winters of London, January has a different story to tell altogether. All Reyansh wanted at this point in time was his warm bed in his cozy apartment, with a hot bowl of soup and chicken momos by his bedside, watching the thriller web series which he had left mid-way yesterday.


He had already ordered the soup and his favourite chicken momos. They were on their way to delivery. Everything was well-planned, and nothing was to go wrong.  


“Aa ha, I thought I could give you the pleasure of dropping me home. You see, my car is in the garage”, said Tedd, looking at Reyansh dead in the eyes, daring him to say no.


“Actually, I was…………………” words stuck in Reyansh’s mouth, even though every inch of his body screamed for him to deny.


It would take another one hour to be back home and start with the cozy plan of his. Tedd lived in the outskirts of the city.


Before Reyansh could muster up the courage to refuse or find a plan B, he was already driving towards Tedd’s house.


The grumpiness was visible on his face, but did his boss care anyway? With eerie silence, the drive was getting unbearable when the car came to a halt behind a lane of cars….. Damn! 


Traffic Jam!


“I know a shortcut”, said Tedd. Just follow my directions, and they turned into a godforsaken lane.


After 30 mins
They were still driving, wherein the night was getting darker and the roads were getting longer.


“For Heaven’s sake, you mind taking out your phone, for the assistance of Google Maps,” said Reyansh, with all his patience evaporating in thin air.


This was the perfect opportunity and the perfect reason for burying his boss alive.


“OHHH… my soup might have already gone cold”, thought Reyansh.  


“My phone is out of battery; you mind if I borrow yours?” said Tedd not missing out on the impatience on Reyansh’s face.


That’s the time, Reyansh realised that he had left his phone on his office desk in a hurry.
“Holy God…. “ said Reyansh, almost crying.


With not even a single person to be seen in the furthest corner, the cold becoming colder, the dark becoming darker, and the suffocation of his Boss’s presence was taking a toll on Reyansh.


After driving for almost 2 hours, he knew for sure that this was going to be a long night, in the company of the man whom he could not stand.


“There is a Winter Cabin on the right. We could spend the night there,” said Tedd unexpectedly.


Looking towards the source of direction, it seemed the best plan as of now. Parking his car to the side, both entered the Cabin to get some help, only to find it deserted.


Looking around, there was nothing- no electricity, no phone, no internet, no furniture, and most importantly- No people. Suddenly, the car felt like a more comfortable option.


Or, killing Tedd seemed an even better option. At least that would relax Reyansh’s throbbing blood pressure, which was on the rise.


“Finally, we found a place to spend the night,” said Tedd humorously, trying to sound a bit positive.


“We are in this shit because of you,” screamed Reyansh. With all the patience gone and with no intentions of being polite for no reason, his boss definitely deserved his piece of mind. 


"If you cannot remember lanes, then why do you need to act smart?”


“Hold it Reyansh, I hope you remember you are talking to your boss”, said Tedd.


“Of course, I know I am talking to my Boss. Not only lanes, but you are also good for nothing. You are lucky to have staff who work for you. Had it been you, running the office on your own, you would have been bankrupt by now” blurted out Reyansh all frustrated. 


The chill of the night was boring holes into his skin.


He was not sure, whether they will make it till the morning or not. At least he could tell his boss how much he hated him.


“Oh really, I’ll remember that Reyansh. Now hope that you do not get through this night. Or else things will be difficult for you in the approaching days” said Tedd coming dangerously close to Reyansh.


Reyansh pushed him back with all his force. “I am not scared of you any longer, and I am sure either this chilling night is going to kill me, or the suffocation of your presence. That is how toxic you are”, said Reyansh with equal vigour.


“Aa ha, why not I make your fear come to life right this instant, and I kill you with my bare hands?” said Tedd, emphasising on each word.


With that, they both stared at each other for some time. 


After half an hour:


“Let’s get a hold of ourselves. It's high time we realize that it's only the two of us here. Don’t you think it will be easier to pass through the night if we act more civilized with each other?” said Tedd, breaking the ice and trying to sound reasonable.


Reyansh said nothing. He was just listening. He knew what Tedd was saying was indeed right.


With nothing else to do,, they sat down on the cold ground staring at nothing.


The silence was deafening. The shrilling sound of the wind blowing and hitting their skin was painful. The moon had hidden behind the clouds, hence with no light, they could not even see each other’s faces clearly.


It was creepy and dreadful, to say the least.

For the first time in life, both knew that they needed each other’s support to survive, and the unexpected happened. They held each other’s hands, the only assurance both felt at that point in time, was that they had each other.


A guarantee that they were not alone.


Then Reyansh heard a S.C.R.E.A.M.


A scream, so chilling that it sent shivers down his spine. It was as if frozen metal was being dragged across glass.

He looked up at Tedd, and his fingers tightened around Tedd’s hand instantly. Tedd didn’t pull away.
For the first time that night, Reyansh felt Tedd’s palm trembling.

“Did you………” Reyansh whispered.

Tedd didn’t reply.

He was staring straight ahead. Reyansh slowly followed his gaze.

There stood a white-colored statue in thick winter fog, clearly visible in the dark night, with no hands and no legs, only a face and its mid-body, smiling widely at him.


Thereafter, Complete Black Out.


Next-Day Newspaper Headlines- Two dead bodies found in the Outskirts of London.


ALERT: Never go to a lane you are not sure of, especially at night. You never know how chilly the winter might get.

The Dream
The dream where it will all begin,
The start of a journey unfolding within.
A path through spirals of feeling and trials,
Guiding your spirit across countless miles.
The moment you glimpse your finest self,
Will be a treasure beyond all wealth.
Yet that very vision, pure and true,
Will humble the ego, dissolving you.
It marks the beginning of an end,
The end of a wasted life, my friend.
A call to live as sages teach,
To walk the truth within your reach.
A love will rise, unbound, untamed,
Shattering borders the world has named.
Like metal forged in fire’s embrace,
You’ll be renewed with holy grace.
At times you’ll feel you’re drowning deep,
In childhood wounds that never sleep.
But each descent is meant to free,
The tangled knots you made for me,
For I, your higher self, must guide,
And bring you through the storms inside.
These dreams are not a fleeting play,
But visions shown in God’s own way.
They free you from the past’s regret,
And worldly chains you’ve not broken yet.
What are you seeking? Nothing at all,
The path is here, you’ve heard the call.
Trust the process, do not stray,
You’re already walking the Higher Way.
So, doubt not the truths that unfold,
For dreams are mirrors, bright and bold.
Not fantasy, but light made clear,
Revealing the strength already here.

Whispers of the Higher Self

Child of eternity, in the silence I speak,

a current of light, unbroken, unique.

Beyond the noise, beyond the veil,

my truth within you will never fail.

I am the spark in your hidden flame,

the ancient song that calls your name.

Through shifting shadows, through paths unknown,

you walk with me you are never alone.

The world may dazzle with fleeting sound,

yet your deepest truth is silence profound.

There, in the stillness, your essence shines,

woven eternal with all that is divine.

Fear not the mystery, nor what lies ahead,

each step is guided, each tear is shed.

For destiny bends to the love you are,

your soul a mirror of the brightest star.

So, listen, beloved, with open heart,

I was with you always, from the start.

Follow my whispers, rise when you fall,

for you are sacred, eternal, all.
