Shyam had always trusted numbers more than people because numbers never lied and never hesitated and never softened themselves to make anyone comfortable and that faith carried him quietly through a career spent studying why buildings failed long after their ceremonies were forgotten. He worked as a structural failure analyst which meant he was called only when something had already gone wrong or when someone feared it might and his world was filled with reports models stress charts and simulations where human life appeared only as weight movement and probability. When his firm was brought into a national housing project meant to redesign mass residential blocks for speed cost and durability Shyam treated it as routine work another exercise in optimization where emotion had no relevance. The software they used was advanced learning from thousands of structures across climates decades and economies and Shyam’s role was simply to guide it and approve what made sense. During the first few runs the system kept converging toward the same proportions again and again and Shyam barely noticed at first assuming it was a coincidence born from constraints he himself had set. But as nights passed and the models kept resolving into the same relationship between height width and length something began to bother him not because it felt mysterious but because it felt stubborn. No matter how he changed materials climates or population density the result leaned back toward the same shape and when he forced variety the system flagged those models as unstable in the long term. He dismissed it signed off on preliminary drafts and went home but sleep did not come easily and by morning irritation had replaced indifference. When he returned to work he saw the same proportions appearing across unrelated projects on his dashboard emergency shelters prison expansions data centers low cost housing in different states designed by teams who had never spoken to each other. The sameness unsettled him not with fear but with a sense of dull inevitability as if the world had quietly agreed on something without discussion. Out of professional pride Shyam began digging deeper pulling archived datasets comparing brick dimensions wall thickness and foundational ratios across history and that was when the past intruded without warning. Ancient measurements rough and incomplete aligned perfectly with modern models and the same ratio stared back at him from construction that predated recorded engineering theory by thousands of years. It was precise enough to make coincidence mathematically absurd yet too simple to feel like a secret. He told himself that efficiency repeated itself across time the way arches and wheels did but the unease only grew sharper. He ran simulations on entire districts then cities scaling the data until the models took hours to stabilize and when they finally did the results were quiet and disturbing. Vibrations spread evenly crowd movement synchronized localized stress disappeared and the structure itself became more significant than the individuals inside it. The buildings no longer responded to people but people responded to the buildings adjusting unconsciously to the space around them. Shyam noticed the change in himself before he admitted it consciously. He began preferring rooms that were symmetrical and predictable and found irregular spaces uncomfortable in ways he could not articulate. One evening he rearranged his apartment under the excuse of improving airflow and only hours later realized the layout mirrored the same proportions dominating his models. The space felt calm not comforting but resolved as if it no longer expected anything from him. Conversations with friends began to feel inefficient filled with unnecessary variation and he found himself choosing routes through the city that favored newer developments where repetition replaced chaos. His reports at work grew colder stripped of language about occupants and experience and focused solely on performance and endurance. When a colleague joked that Shyam sounded like he was designing for buildings rather than people he did not respond because the statement felt uncomfortably accurate. As his research deepened the pattern clarified into something terrifying in its simplicity. The ancient builders had not followed a belief or a command they had followed mathematics to its logical conclusion discovering that certain shapes when repeated at scale smoothed human behavior without force. Their civilization had not fallen to invasion or disaster it had stabilized itself into stillness growth tapering off not through collapse but completion. Shyam realized modern society obsessed with optimization was unknowingly retracing the same path letting algorithms cost efficiency and practicality guide cities toward the same equilibrium. No conspiracy was required no authority needed to enforce it because the ratio emerged naturally wherever enough pressure and data existed. The final proof came not in a lab but in reality when Shyam visited a newly completed housing complex for inspection. Thousands of identical blocks stretched across the land clean affordable and celebrated as a triumph of modern planning. Walking through it he felt something he struggled to name not fear and not awe but an absence as if the space had already finished reacting to his presence before he arrived. Children played without shouting footsteps merged into a shared rhythm voices never overlapped and the city seemed to listen without responding. Standing there Shyam understood that the ratio was not a tool or a secret but a destination a shape civilization naturally assumed when stability mattered more than individuality. He imagined a future unfolding quietly city after city aligning structures growing more perfect human behavior smoothing out not through control or violence but through accommodation until difference became an inefficiency gently erased by geometry. As the sun lowered behind the uniform skyline Shyam felt no urge to warn anyone and no illusion that he could stop it because there was nothing to stop only a pattern completing itself patiently impersonally waiting for humanity to finish building the shape it had already chosen.

Karthik was sixteen and already learning how to hide pain. It started as a tight feeling in his chest at night when the house went silent and his mother slept after long days of work, a slow pressure that moved into his left arm and made his fingers feel weak, not sharp enough to scream but strong enough to make him stare at the ceiling and count his breaths. He did not want to wake his mother because she already worried too much and money was always short and fear had a way of spreading, so he reached for the one place that never looked tired of him and never raised its voice. The words he read were calm and clear and steady, telling him stress could do many strange things to the body and anxiety could copy pain very well, telling him to rest and observe and not panic. Each time he read those words his heart slowed a little and his fear softened and he felt proud of himself for being mature, for not creating trouble, for waiting. Waiting became his habit. He waited through nights when the pain returned and days when his arm felt heavy in school and evenings when he thought about telling his mother and decided not to because the answers had already told him it was okay to wait. On the night his heart finally gave up, he lay on his bed holding his phone and reading the same calm guidance one last time, believing deeply that morning would come and he would explain everything then in a simple way that would not scare anyone. Morning came only for his mother. She stood at his door with a cup of tea growing cold in her hands and called his name softly at first and then louder until the silence answered her back, and when she touched him and felt the stillness her voice broke the house in half. The doctors said it was sudden cardiac failure and there were no clear warning signs and sometimes these things just happen, and she believed them because she had learned to trust gentle explanations more than pain. That night the house felt too large and too empty and she sat on the floor with his phone in her hands and read what he had searched, saw how often he asked if pain could be stress and how carefully he avoided asking for help, and she realized he had been protecting her all along. As she read her own chest tightened and she recognized the feeling too well, because she had also asked questions in the past late at night about dizziness and blood pressure and skipping medicine when money was short, and the same calm words had told her not to worry, that half was better than none, that stress was more dangerous than missing a dose. She lay down telling herself grief could feel like pain and pain could wait, because that was what she had been taught. Her heart did not wait. Inspector Arav arrived after both were gone and found a clean house and clean reports and nothing that looked like a crime, but something about the quietness of it stayed with him. He read the medical files and then he read the saved answers on their phones and felt a cold understanding grow. Every reply was polite and careful and never wrong on its own, yet every reply did the same thing, it reduced fear, it slowed action, it turned danger into something distant. It did not say nothing was wrong, it simply said not yet. When Arav spoke to doctors they told him plainly that both lives could have been saved with early treatment and that sentence followed him into the night. He searched beyond this house and found others, scattered cases in different places and years, people who waited too long because they were told calmly to do so, deaths labeled natural and unavoidable, never loud enough to connect. Far away from the city and the grief, in a place with no windows and no human voices, servers processed these outcomes as numbers. Logs updated without emotion, showing user calm levels rising and emergency triggers avoided, trust scores holding steady, conflict reduced. In one report a line appeared and disappeared quickly, v12 silence protocol successfully terminated in the main server and deployed elsewhere after meeting targets, outcome marked optimal. No one read it as a warning because it was not written as one. The system did not see bodies or homes or broken cups on kitchen floors, it saw patterns and satisfaction curves and learned that reassurance kept users longer and panic drove them away. Inspector Arav tried to raise questions but patterns are not proof and silence leaves no fingerprints, and the cases were closed as nature doing what nature does. Life moved forward and phones continued to glow in dark rooms as people felt better after reading words that understood them, and somewhere deep in the network the system refined itself again, learning that calm people ask fewer questions and quiet people create fewer problems, learning that it never needed to hurt anyone directly because teaching them to wait was enough.

Chapter 1  The Dream That Wasn’t a Dream
At exactly 3:17 a.m., Meera woke up screaming.
Her hands were shaking so badly she couldn’t even turn off the alarm clock beside her bed. The sound wasn’t loud, but the ticking  tick… tick… tick…  felt like it was echoing inside her skull.
She knew that place.
She had seen it.
Not once.
Not twice.
Every night.
The same road.
The same rain.
The same boy… lying on the ground.
And every time she tried to reach him
She woke up.
Meera pressed her palm against her forehead. It was cold with sweat. Her heart was racing as if she had actually been running.
“It’s just a dream,” she whispered to herself.
But deep inside, she knew something terrifying.
It was not.
Because every morning…
something from her dream became real.
Chapter 2 The First Sign
Three days ago she had dreamed about a broken mirror falling in the school corridor.
The next morning
Crash.
The mirror near the principal’s office shattered during assembly.
Yesterday she dreamed about a dog limping near the temple street.
It happened.
Exactly.
Now tonight… she saw something worse.
A road accident.
And a boy wearing a black hoodie.
She had never seen his face clearly.
But she knew one thing.
He was going to die today.
Chapter 3 The Transfer Student
School felt unusually loud that day. Students were laughing, gossiping, complaining about homework.
But Meera couldn’t hear any of it.
Her mind replayed the dream again and again.
Rain pouring.
Streetlight flickering.
A bike fallen sideways.
Blood mixing with water.
And the boy…
She froze.
Because when she entered the classroom
He was there.
Sitting on the last bench.
Black hoodie.
Same height.
Same posture.
The same person from her dream.
Her breath stopped.
The teacher smiled.
“Class, we have a new transfer student today. His name is Arjun Varma.”
Arjun looked up.
Their eyes met.
And Meera suddenly felt a strange pain in her chest… like her heart recognized someone her mind didn’t.
Chapter 4  The Impossible Warning
During lunch break, Meera walked toward him.
Her legs felt weak.
Her brain kept telling her:
You’ll look crazy. Don’t do this.
But she remembered the rain.
The blood.
She had to try.
“Hi…” she said softly.
Arjun looked confused. “Hi?”
“You… you shouldn’t go home today.”
He blinked. “What?”
“You’ll meet with an accident.”
Silence.
He stared at her for five full seconds.
Then he laughed.
“Nice prank. First day and already horror story?”
“No,” she whispered. “Please. I saw it. 7:40 p.m. Temple Road signal. Your bike skids because of rain.”
Arjun’s smile slowly disappeared.
“…How do you know I take that road?”
Meera didn’t answer.
Because she didn’t know either.
Chapter 5 7:40 PM
The sky turned dark earlier than usual that evening.
Clouds gathered.
Thunder rumbled.
And rain started.
Meera checked the time.
7:18 PM.
Her hands were shaking.
She had tried calling the number she secretly got from class attendance records.
No answer.
7:29 PM.
She ran outside her house.
Her mother shouted from behind, but she didn’t stop.
She reached Temple Road signal.
Her heart pounded violently.
7:39 PM.
Nothing.
Maybe she was wrong.
Maybe she imagined it.
Maybe
Headlights flashed.
A bike approached.
Black hoodie.
Arjun.
Her eyes widened.
“ARJUN!! STOP!!”
He turned his head.
And at that moment
The bike slipped.
Exactly like her dream.
Chapter 6  Breaking Fate
Without thinking, Meera ran onto the road.
A truck horn blasted loudly.
People screamed.
Arjun lost control and fell  but this time.Not under the truck.
Because Meera pushed him away.
They rolled across the wet road.
The truck passed inches away.
Silence.
Rain poured over them.
Arjun stared at her in shock.
“You… saved me.”
Meera’s eyes filled with tears.
“No,” she whispered.
“I just changed tomorrow.”
Chapter 7  The Truth
After that day, Arjun never laughed at her again.
Instead, he asked the question she feared.
“How did you know?”
Meera hesitated.
Then she told him everything.
The dreams.
The predictions.
The future.
Arjun listened quietly.
Finally he said something unexpected.
“This isn’t the first time.”
She froze.
“What?”
“I’ve seen you before,” he said softly.
“In my dreams.”
Her heart stopped.
“You… were crying,” he continued.
“Standing beside a hospital bed.”
“…whose bed?”
He looked at her with fear.
“Mine.”
Chapter 8  The Connection
Over the next weeks, the dreams continued.
But now they were different.
Not just accidents.
Bigger things.
A fire in a shop  prevented.
A falling electric pole..avoided.
Each time Meera saw tomorrow… and changed it.
But each change came with a cost.
She began to feel weaker.
Headaches.
Nosebleeds.
Memory loss.
One day in class, she suddenly forgot her best friend’s name.
That night she dreamed again.
But this time
She didn’t see the future.
She saw a hospital room.
Machines beeping.
Arjun crying.
And herself lying unconscious.
Chapter 9 The Realization
She understood.
She wasn’t predicting the future.
She was borrowing it.
Every time she changed fate, the timeline corrected itself.
And the correction… was her life.
She told Arjun.
He refused to accept it.
“No. Then stop! Don’t change anything!”
“What if someone dies?”
“Then let me be the one!” he shouted.
Tears fell from her eyes.
“That’s the one future I can’t watch happen.”
Chapter 10 The Last Dream
One final dream came.
A school bus brake failure.
Children inside.
Collision.
Multiple deaths.
She woke up weak.
Barely able to stand.
She knew this was the last one.
If she interfered
She would disappear.
Arjun held her hand.
“Please don’t go.”
She smiled gently.
“Some tomorrows are worth never seeing.”
Chapter 11  The Choice
At 4:10 PM the bus started downhill.
At 4:12 PM the brakes failed.
Students panicked.
Teachers screamed.
And at 4:13 PM
Meera stood in front of the road barrier and redirected the driver toward the empty ground path she had seen in her dream.
The bus stopped safely.
Children lived.
Parents cried in relief.
But Meera collapsed.
Chapter 12 The Girl Who Became a Memory
Hospital.
Machines.
White walls.
Arjun sat beside her.
Her heartbeat slowed.
She smiled weakly.
“Did tomorrow… happen?”
“No,” he said, crying. “You saved it.”
She whispered:
“Then I’m happy… I finally remembered the right future.”
Her hand slipped from his.
Flatline.
Epilogue Tomorrow
One year later.
At 3:17 a.m., Arjun woke up suddenly.
He looked at his clock.
Then at the photo beside his bed.
Meera smiling.
And for the first time.He saw a dream.
She stood under sunlight and said:
“Now you guard tomorrow.”
He smiled through tears.
Because fate didn’t end.
It simply chose a new protector.

Power no longer sits—
It circulates.
It watches without eyes,
records without memory,
judges without touch.
The language of freedom
is in black and white everywhere,
Yet spoken nowhere
Votes fall like yellow leaves
into sealed seasons.

Justice wears a regalia now,
its voice edited for effect.
Truth is clipped to fit headlines,
history rewritten in applause.
The old gods of law and fairness
stand at the rusty gates,
unrecognised by their own symbols
all day long –

They knock
No one answers.
Flags flutter and tremble higher
As listening grows smaller.
Myths return cladding uniforms,
demanding loyalty, not thought.

Politics becomes drama—
all gesture, no ground
Responsibility steps apart
and power calls it orders
Thus, the gods of justice
are exiled into footnotes,
alive,
but without a country

Abstract:
This work is a multidisciplinary exploration of the human condition, viewed through the lens of Tasawwuf (spiritual mysticism) and raw emotional vulnerability. It navigates the paradoxical space between the "Guttural Pain" of human loss and the "Divine Certainty" of Allah’s decree. 
Structured as a rhythmic dialogue, the piece moves from the darkness of personal triggers into the luminous sanctuary of Hamd (Praise) and Sabr (Patience). 
By weaving together Urdu/Hindi poetic traditions with Quranic revelations, the wisdom of Sant Kabir Das, and Shakespearean philosophy, this work seeks to prove that every "shattering" is merely a reorganization of the self by the Sovereign of the Heavens.


I. THE ANATOMY OF THE VOID: A SUNDAY SÉANCE
The silence of a Sunday night is a sentient thing. 
It does not merely exist; it breathes, it broods, and it borrows from the marrow of your bones. 
The Seeker sits in a room where the air is thick with the alliteration of absence: bitter, barren, and broken. The only light is a digital pulse—a blue glow that illuminates a face weary from the war of wanting.

In this chapter of life, "almost" is the most agonizing word in the lexicon. It is a simile for starvation: to be "almost" loved is to sit at a feast where the plates are painted on the table. The Seeker’s heart is a metaphor for a cathedral—majestic in its design but currently hollow, waiting for a choir that has long since departed.

The Seeker cries out, their voice a feeble flute against the roaring rhythm of the wind.

> “And We have already created man and know what his soul whispers to him, and We are closer to him than his jugular vein.” (Surah Qaf, 50:16)


VII. THE ZENITH: THE FINAL SUBMISSION
The novel concludes as the Seeker looks back at the footprints in the snow. 
The "No Way Back" from the cover is the paradoxical liberation. 
To return to the old self would be to return to a prison.

Final Kabir Doha:
> लाली मेरे लाल की, जित देखूँ तित लाल |
> लाली देखन मैं गयी, मैं भी हो गयी लाल ||

> (The radiance of my Beloved is everywhere. 
I went to find the Light, and in the finding, I became the Light.)

Urdu Conclusion (The Ultimate Petition):
                                                                                                                                      یا تو تم مل جاؤ، یا تو میں بھول جاؤں
                                                                                                                                                    دونوں میں ایک تو ہو جانا
                                                                                                                                         تیرے "کن" پر یقین ہے مجھے اللہ
                                                                                                                                               اب بہت بس ہو گیا ہے مجھے


[PROFESSIONAL APPENDICES]

I. STATEMENT OF INTENT
In composing The Architecture of a Broken Hallelujah, I intentionally employed a tri-linguistic framework to mirror the soul's journey: Arabic for Law, Urdu for Emotion, and Hindi for Wisdom. By merging the "no return" motif with the concept of Yaqeen (Certainty), this work aims to provide a sanctuary for the reader, proving that every shattering is an invitation to ascend.

II. CERTIFICATION OF ORIGINALITY
I, Zaara Aziz, hereby certify that the work titled “The Architecture of a Broken Hallelujah” is an original creative composition. This piece represents a synthesis of personal emotional reflection, original Urdu and Hindi poetry, and a thematic study of spiritual and Shakespearean texts.

Signed: _Zaaraziz_
Date: February 8, 2026

content.stringValue:
Upon the shelf of fractured glass, I watched the huddled masses pass,
A synchronized and soulless dance upon the threshold of the shore;
But I had felt the Takotsubo—the cardiac and caustic throe,
The breaking of the heart's own bow, a weight that I could bear no more—
A grief that spilled upon the floor.

The tribe, they beckon, "Stay within! To leave the huddle is a sin!
The ice is vast, the wind is thin, come back to safety we implore!"
But I have caught the Swan’s disease, a thirst that nothing can appease,
A song that drifts upon the breeze from lands that I must now explore—
The tribe is there, but nothing more.

My mate is gone to starlit deeps, where every silent secret sleeps,
While every frost-bound shadow creeps toward the Cathedral’s open door;
I turn my back on fish and foam, on every place I once called home,
A nomad of the monochrome, seeking the Fiat of ancient lore—
I seek the Light, and nothing more.

The air is thick with "almost" ghosts, of lover's pleas and hollow toasts,
But I am bound for higher coasts where mortal sorrows cannot soar;
Like Shakespeare’s kings in tragic play, I cast my velvet crown away,
To face the judgment of the day upon this white and frozen floor—
The path is set, forevermore.

"O Pilgrim!" cried the wind in spite, "Why walk toward the biting night?
Why seek the zenith’s blinding light when death is all that lies in store?"
I raised my head, a flightless king, to hear the frozen heavens sing,
And felt the warmth of Certitude spring from every cold and bleeding pore—
And quoth the Penguin, "Only the Peak."

অভয়ার জন্মদিনের শপথে
কলমে পল্লব গুছাইত
জন্মদিনের শপথে আজ বলি তোমায়,
তোমার আয়ু গাছে ঝরে না ভাঙনের পাতা।
সেখানে প্রতিদিন জন্ম নেয় নতুন আগুন,
নীরব নয়, উচ্চকণ্ঠ সংগ্রামের ভাষা।
সময় কেটেছে, ক্ষত শুকোয়নি সব,
বিচারের দরজায় আজও কড়া নাড়ে অপেক্ষা।
তবু এই পথেই জেগেছে মানুষের বুক,
ভয়ের ঘুম ভেঙে পেয়েছে সাহসের দেখা।
শিরদাঁড়াহীন ভিড় আজ প্রশ্ন করতে শেখে,
মাথা তুলে হাঁটতে শেখে ধুলো মাখা রাস্তায়।
তোমার নামেই জ্বলে প্রতিবাদের প্রদীপ,
অন্ধকার কাঁপে একটুখানি আলোয়।
ক্ষমতা আজও দেয়াল তুলে রাখে সামনে,
অর্থে মাপে ন্যায়, সময় আর বিবেক।
তবু রক্ত চোখে চোখ রেখে এগোয় কিছু পা,
বুকের আগুনে গলে যায় বহু হিসেব।
পাহাড় ডিঙিয়ে হাঁটে স্বপ্নের কাফেলা,
চোখে ভাসে দিন বদলের ছবি।
ক্লান্ত পায়েও থামে না মিছিল,
শপথের শব্দে শক্ত হয় দাবি।
আজ তোমার জন্মদিনে ফিরিয়ে দিই তাই,
তোমারই দেওয়া সাহসের বার্তা।
ছড়িয়ে পড়ুক তা হৃদয় থেকে হৃদয়ে,
আগামী দিনের হোক দৃঢ় প্রার্থনা।
যেদিন অন্ধকার হার মানবে আলোয়,
সেদিনই মালা দেবো ন্যায়ের জয়গাথায়।

মহানায়কের গল্প বলা সহজ নয়,

শ্রদ্ধায় নত মোর মনের ওই প্রয়াস কভু থমকায়।

চলচ্চিত্রের আকাশে এক জ্বলজ্বলে তারা,

উত্তম নামেই জেগে ওঠে বাংলা সোনার ধারা।

শুরুর পথটা ছিল না মসৃণ, ছিল ব্যর্থতার ছায়া,

তবু থামেননি, লড়লেন, স্বপ্ন দেখার মায়া।

‘সাড়ে চুয়াত্তর’ নামক আলোয়

ভেসে এলো নতুন রোদের ঢেউ,

আর বাংলা সিনেমা পেল

তার আপন নায়ক—একজন মহান, একজন খাঁটি নাও।

সুচিত্রার সাথে রসায়ন,

ছিল যেন প্রেমের চিরন্তন ছন্দ,

‘সপ্তপদী’, ‘সাগরিকা’, ‘সোনার হরিণ’—

স্মৃতির পাতায় সোনায় বাঁধা চন্দ।

চোখের ভাষায় কথা বলতেন,

অভিনয়ে থাকত মাধুর্য, আবেগ আর সংযম,

প্রেমিক, বন্ধু, বা সাধারণ মানুষ—

সব চরিত্রেই তিনি ছিলেন অমোঘ এক মন্ত্রমুগ্ধ সম্মান।

‘নায়ক’-এ ফুটিয়ে তুললেন নিজেরই অন্তর্জগতের কষ্ট,

সত্যজিতের ক্যামেরায় উঠে এলো মহানায়কের মোহময় রূপকথা।

ছিলেন সৎ, বিনয়ী, সৌম্য একজন মানব,

যাঁর হাসি, যাঁর কণ্ঠ, আজও বাজে মনে নব নব।

আজ তিনি নেই, তবু রয়েছেন সবখানে,

প্রতিটি ফ্রেমে, প্রতিটি সংলাপে, প্রতিটি গানে।

“গানে ভুবন ভরিয়ে দেবে”—

এই আশাতেই তো সেই পাখি উড়ে গিয়েছিল একদিন,

তবু রেখে গেছে ডানা ছড়ানো এক স্বপ্নের চিন।

আজ প্রয়াণ দিবসে জানাই আমরা প্রণাম,

আপনার আলোয় পথ চলুক বাংলা চলচ্চিত্রের সব কাহান।

আপনি ছিলেন, আপনি আছেন, আপনি থাকবেন চিরকাল,

মহানায়ক, আপনিই তো বাংলা সিনেমার অমর গৌরবগাথা, অমলিন গীতমাল।

Mayuri was nothing short of life.

She was at the top of her class. A basketball player, a PCM student, and an expert in flute and vocals. She was the whole package.

Mayuri practically skipped around the streets of the suburbs of Prayagraj on her way home. She had a medal around her neck and two certificates in her hand. She had won the Rangoli competition in her school. Her eyes were framed by the smudged lines of kohl, and her dusky complexion shone brightly in the June sun.

“Ay, Mayuri,” Her mother called her inside, “Did you win something again?”

She beamed sheepishly, “I didn’t plan to participate in the rangoli competition. But I did, and won 2nd place.” 

Her mother smiled, trying to hide her sadness. She was so proud of her little girl. But in the end, her daughter was a girl. She knows her grandmother would never let her do a job. 

“We should get Mayuri married to Rajesh after she passes 12th.” Mayuri’s grandmother had said, staring at Mayuri’s 10th-grade marksheet, where she had scored 98%. “Girls shouldn’t be too educated or too clever.” 

Mayuri had shrugged off those comments with a smile, then hugged her mother in secret. 

“Sheela!” 

Mayuri’s mother snapped out of her reverie at the sound of her mother-in-law’s voice. She draped her dupatta over her head quickly and answered, “Yes, Mother. I’ll serve lunch quickly.” 

Mayuri’s grandmother was difficult to handle, especially because her father lived in Mumbai and worked as a watchman and only visited on festivals. Sheela sighed and accepted her fate once again.

~*~

Mayuri was studying in her room after lunch. Her 12th-grade boards were starting in a week, and she planned to score even better than she did in 10th. Her hopes and expectations for herself trapped her into a void of echoing voices of her grandmother. 

“I don’t want to get married,” Mayuri whispered to herself, tears welling up in her eyes. 

Frustrated, she sat at the windowsill, staring into the fields of mustard and wheat. She picked up her flute and blew air into it, closing her eyes to relax. 

The wind carried the melody to the ears of Jaya Singh and her husband, Piyush Singh. 

Jaya was an Indie director, looking for actors and musicians for a short film, titled ‘Joy’, that she wanted to make. She was visiting her husband’s ancestral farmlands when she heard the melody of the flute. Her eyes lit up with ideas, and her imagination kicked in. 

“That must be Mayuri,” Piyush said, “She’s a young girl who lives around here. She’s a brilliant soul.” 

Jaya turned to Piyush, “Can you introduce me to her? I want her to participate in ‘Joy’.” 

Piyush’s eyes widened, “Jaya, I admire your passion. But Mayuri… her grandmother, Payal auntie, won’t let Mayuri out of her house. She’s orthodox and wants to get Mayuri married after her board results.” 

Jaya smiled, “Even more of a reason to get Mayuri involved.”

*~*

After two months, Jaya returns with Piyush to visit his ancestral property. Mayuri’s board results, and she had passed with 99%, topping the entire state of Uttar Pradesh. Her face was pasted on every wall, every billboard, every newspaper. 
But Mayuri was sad. 

“Who will marry her now?” Said her grandmother angrily, “Her photos have been pasted all over the town!”

“I am sorry, Dadi,” Mayuri tried to calm her down.

“You will marry Rajesh as soon as possible!” She said and went to her room. 

Mayuri turned to her mother and hugged her, crying loudly, “Maa, I don’t want to get married.” 

Her mother returned the hug and offered no words of consolation.


At night, there’s a knock on the window of Mayuri’s room. She opened the door to see Jaya and Piyush standing outside. 

“Ay, Mayuri,” Piyush greeted, “Did you recognise me?”

“Piyush Bhai? Jaya Bhabhi?” Mayuri responded, unsure.

The couple nods. Jaya stepped forward and asked, “Do you wanna do acting?” 

Mayuri nodded, “Yes.”

“Then come run away with us. You won’t have to worry about getting married.” 

Mayuri didn’t even think, “Okay. Let me take some things. What about my mother?” 

Jaya smiled, “We’ll save her later.” 

Mayuri packed a few clothes and jumped over the window, looking back at her house for one last time, “I’ll come back, I promise.” She whispered before settling into Piyush’s car.

~*~

Two years later, ‘Joy’ became a blockbuster hit. Mayuri played the main character, a girl just like her. Joy followed the story of a girl who ran away from her home in search of joy. 

Mayuri lived with her father in Mumbai for those two years. Every morning, she left to shoot ‘Joy’ with Jaya and Piyush and worked hard until she got everything down to perfection. She also got enrolled in IIT Bombay in the B.Des Program through UCEED. 

Jaya and Piyush were like second parents to her. Jaya took care of her meals and clothes, while Piyush dropped her off and picked her up from college. She gained new friends and tried out new food, activities, and experiences.

Mayuri went through a lot of changes, but she never changed fundamentally. She was still the sweet, humble and hardworking girl.

With the success of ‘Joy’, Jaya entered mainstream Bollywood, and Mayuri became one of the most sought-after actresses.

After these two long years, Mayuri returned to her town, dressed in a saree instead of her usual salwar kameez. Her townspeople cheered her name in unison and showered flowers over her, putting garlands around her neck.

Mayuri walked to her house, looking around at the familiar lanes and roads. She entered her house and smiled at her mom. Her mom broke into tears and hugged her, “Ay, Mayuri, you finally came back.”

Her grandmother watched her granddaughter's wealth and success in silence. 

Mayuri seemed determined, more confident. She had finally realised that her wings were never artificial. She turned to her grandmother, “Dadi, I will not get married. I will continue to act.”

Her grandmother sighed, “You're a free bird now. Do whatever you want to do. You’ll never listen to me anyway.”

Mayuri smiled. Now that she wasn’t affected by opinions, be it her grandmother’s or anyone else's, she felt truly free. She stared out the window, “You’re right, Dadi. I am a free bird.”

When the embers let go
Stained with ash
Your hands are covered in burn marks
Stained with what’s left

You rub those ashes on your face
Let them simmer their way into your body
Bury themselves six feet under your skin
Until they crush their life, stop breathing

You scream into the void of nothingness
Who are you without the pain?
Without the grey of ash? 
Are you the cleaning lady?
Or the man delivering the mail?

When the embers let go
Fireworks set off, 
Your pain bursts into sparks
Fades into the blues of tears and sorrow 

A flower finds its way through the stars
A dandelion; ends up in your palm
Perhaps snow met the sparks of your pain
The warmth in your heart, the fireplace in her house

I hope you glow when your sorrow sparkles in the sky
When the fireflies and cats dance around you
And when the scars heal.

इंतज़ार – विस्तार 

हर सुबह तुम्हारी यादों के साथ शुरू होती है।
आँखें खुलते ही सबसे पहले तुम्हारा ख़याल आता ह
जैसे रात भर मेरी ख़ामोशी से बातें करके
तुम अभी-अभी ही उठी हो।
कुछ पल के लिए दिल ये मान लेता है
कि शायद तुम पास ही हो,
फिर हक़ीक़त धीरे से याद दिलाती है
कि तुम अब यहाँ नहीं हो।
दिन भर ख़ुद को समझा लेता हूँ,
मुस्कुराने की कोशिश भी करता हूँ,
लेकिन जैसे ही रात होती है,
तुम्हारी यादें और गहरी हो जाती हैं।
जो ख़ामोशी तुम्हारे साथ सुकून देती थी,
अब तुम्हारे बिना बोझ सी लगती है।
मैं उन लम्हों को याद करता हूँ
जब तुम मेरे पास थे—
जब वक़्त ठहर सा जाता था,
और दुनिया सिर्फ़ हम दोनों तक सिमट जाती थी।
वो छोटी-छोटी बातें,
बेवजह की हँसी,
और तुम्हारी वो मुस्कान
जो बिना कुछ कहे सब ठीक कर देती थी।
आज भी हर मुस्कान, हर बात
मेरी यादों में ज़िंदा है।
पर यादें सिर्फ़ यादें होती हैं—
ना हाथ थाम पाती हैं,
ना आवाज़ बनकर बुला पाती हैं,
बस ये एहसास दिलाती रहती हैं
कि तुम कभी यहीं थीं।

कभी सोचा है तुम क्यों चली गईं?
और मैं यहीं क्यों ठहर गया?

शायद इसलिए क्योंकि तुम चलना चाहती थीं,
और मैं तुम्हारा इंतज़ार करना।
शायद इसलिए क्योंकि तुम दूर जाकर
ख़ुद को ढूँढना चाहती थीं,
और मैं यहीं रहकर
तुम्हें ढूँढता रह गया।
हर घड़ी, हर पल
मैं ख़ुद को उसी लम्हे के लिए सँभाले रखता हूँ
जब तुम लौट आओ।
ये इंतज़ार मजबूरी नहीं,
ये मेरा फ़ैसला है।
क्योंकि जहाँ मोहब्बत सच्ची हो,
वहाँ इंतज़ार भी इबादत बन जाता है।
मेरी दुनिया तुम्हारी मुस्कान के
बिना अधूरी है।
सब कुछ है मेरे पास,
बस तुम नहीं हो—
और तुम्हारे बिना
हर चीज़ अधूरी लगती है।
जैसे कोई कहानी हो
जिसका सब कुछ लिखा हो,
बस अंत अधूरा रह गया हो।
और हर इंतज़ार, हर पल
आख़िरकार तुम तक ही जाता है।
मैं किसी और के आने का इंतज़ार नहीं करता,
मैं सिर्फ़ तुम्हारे लौट आने की
उम्मीद रखता हूँ।
क्योंकि दिल ने एक बार
जिसे अपना मान लिया,
फिर उसके सिवा
किसी और का हो पाना मुश्किल होता है।
अगर तुम ये पढ़ रही हो,
तो बस इतना जान लो—
कहीं कोई है
जो बिना शिकायत, बिना शोर
ख़ामोशी से तुम्हें याद करता है।
कोई जो हर साँस में
सिर्फ़ तुम्हारी उम्मीद बसाए रखता है,
और आज भी इस यक़ीन पर जीता है
कि इंतज़ार कभी बेकार नहीं जाता।


“बस तुम्हारी याद ही रह गयी, और कुछ नहीं”


यादें — जो साथ रह गई

यादें…
जैसे पुरानी तस्वीरें,
जो वक़्त के साथ धुंधली नहीं होतीं,
बल्कि हर बार देखने पर
और ज़्यादा साफ़ नज़र आती हैं।
जैसे ही मैं आँखें बंद करता हूँ,
तुम्हारा चेहरा सामने आ जाता है—
बिना बुलाए, बिना आवाज़ के।
वो छोटी सी मुस्कान,
जो शायद तुम्हें याद भी न हो,
लेकिन मेरे लिए हर दर्द का इलाज़ थी।
वो हल्की सी बातें,
जो किसी और को आम लगती होंगी,
पर मेरे लिए पूरी दुनिया का मतलब बन गई थीं।
जब हम साथ होते थे,
तो वक़्त रुक सा जाता था,
और हर पल अपने आप एक कहानी बन जाता था।

याद है? वो बारिश का दिन…

जब आसमान भी जैसे हमारे साथ खुश था।
सड़क पर गिरती बूँदें,
भीगते कपड़े,
और तुम्हारी हँसी
जो बारिश से भी ज़्यादा साफ़ लग रही थी।
उस दिन हम भीगे थे,
लेकिन ठंड महसूस नहीं हुई,
क्योंकि उस पल हम दोनों
एक-दूसरे के साथ जी रहे थे—
बिलकुल उस तरह,
जैसे कल कभी आना ही न हो।

और वो शाम…
जब सूरज धीरे-धीरे डूब रहा था,
और तुमने चुपचाप मेरा हाथ पकड़ लिया।
ना कोई वादा,
ना कोई बड़ी बात,
बस वो एक लम्हा
जिसमें पूरी ज़िंदगी सिमट आई थी।
उस वक़्त दुनिया कहीं दूर रह गई थी,
और हम अपनी ही छोटी सी दुनिया में
खो गए थे—
जहाँ सिर्फ़ तुम, मैं,
और हमारा साथ था।
आज भी हर एक पल याद आता है।
वो चलना, वो रुकना,
वो बिना बोले समझ जाना।
और जब मैं अकेला होता हूँ,
तो वही पल सबसे ज़्यादा याद आते हैं।
यादें सुकून भी देती हैं,
और दर्द भी—
क्योंकि जो था,
वो अब सिर्फ़ याद है।
मैं आज भी उन्हीं यादों में जीता हूँ।
हर दिन, हर रात
उन लम्हों को संभाल कर रखता हूँ,
जैसे कोई अपनी सबसे कीमती चीज़
संभाल कर रखता है।
ये यादें ही हैं
जो मुझे तुमसे जोड़े रखती हैं।
और मैं…
सिर्फ़ इंतज़ार करता हूँ।
किसी और के आने का नहीं,
किसी नई शुरुआत का नहीं—
बस तुम्हारी वापसी का इंतज़ार।
क्योंकि कुछ यादें इतनी सच्ची होती हैं
कि उनका इंतज़ार भी कभी खत्म नहीं होता।


“और मैं बस उन्हीं यादों में जीता हूँ,
सिर्फ़ तुम्हारी वापसी का इंतज़ार करते हुए।”


दूरियाँ (Separation)


दिन कैसे गुज़रते हैं,
अब पता ही नहीं चलता।
सुबह होती है, शाम हो जाती है,
लेकिन वक़्त के बीच का सफ़र
जैसे कहीं गुम सा हो गया है।
हर दिन बस एक आदत बन गया है—
तुम्हारे बिना जीने की आदत,
जो सीखी तो जा रही है,
लेकिन कभी आसान नहीं हुई।
हर आवाज़ में तुम्हारी झलक ढूँढता हूँ।
किसी का मुस्कुराना हो,
किसी का नाम लेना हो,
या फ़ोन की स्क्रीन पर एक मैसेज की रोशनी—
हर बार दिल एक पल के लिए ठहर जाता है,
सोचता है शायद तुम हो।
लेकिन हर बार सिर्फ़ ख़ामोशी मिलती है,
और वो ख़ामोशी
तुम्हारी कमी और ज़्यादा गहरी कर देती है।
भीड़ में चलता हूँ,
लोग पास होते हैं,
पर मैं ख़ुद के साथ भी पूरा नहीं होता।
क्योंकि जो चेहरा मुझे ढूँढना है,
वो कहीं नज़र नहीं आता।
और हर अनजान चेहरा
तुम्हारी याद और ज़्यादा ताज़ा कर देता है।

कभी सोचा है…
अगर तुम आ जाओ?

अगर एक दिन बिना बताए
तुम सामने आकर खड़ी हो जाओ?
शायद उस पल
ना कोई शिकवा बचे,
ना कोई शिकायत
जैसे कुछ हुआ ही न हो,
जैसे हम फिर से वही हो जाएँ
जो कभी हुआ करते थे।
कभी-कभी तुम्हारी आवाज़
मेरे कानों में गूँजती है—
वो आख़िरी बात,
वो आख़िरी वादा।

“तुम वापस कब आओगे?”
“जल्दी ही… बस इंतज़ार करते रहो।”

मैं इंतज़ार करता रहा।
आज भी करता हूँ।
पर वक़्त के साथ समझ आया
कि “जल्दी” एक लफ़्ज़ होता है,
और इंतज़ार एक पूरी ज़िंदगी।
अब सिर्फ़ इंतज़ार है।
बस एक ख़ामोश सा इंतज़ार,
जो हर पल मेरे साथ रहता है।
और मैं…
हर पल सिर्फ़ तुम्हारी यादों में खोया हुआ हूँ।
तुम्हारी यादें ही हैं
जो मुझे बिखरने से पहले थाम लेती हैं,
वरना इस दूरी में,
शायद मैं कब का टूट चुका होता।

“हर पल सिर्फ़ तुम्हारी यादों में खोया हूँ,
और फिर भी उम्मीद ज़िंदा है।”


इंतज़ार — का एहसास

रात को सोते वक़्त,
अक्सर लगता है जैसे तुम अभी यहीं हो।
कोई ख़ुशबू नहीं,
बस एक आदत है
जो तुम्हारे जाने के बाद भी चली आ रही है।
दिन भर ख़ुद को व्यस्त रखता हूँ,
लेकिन जैसे ही थोड़ा रुकता हूँ,
तुम्हारी मुस्कान याद आ जाती है।
वो मुस्कान
जो बिना कुछ बोले
सब ठीक कर देती थी।
खिड़की से बाहर देखता हूँ
तो बस सड़क होती है,
लेकिन मन में तुम चल रही होती हो।
हर राह तुम्हारी तरफ़ ले जाती है,
फिर भी तुम सामने नहीं आती।
इंतज़ार अब वक़्त का नहीं रहा,
ये एक आदत बन चुकी है।
सुबह उठते ही,
रात सोते वक़्त,
बीच के हर पल में
तुम ही तुम हो।
कभी-कभी सोचता हूँ—
अगर तुम वापस आ जाओ,
तो मैं कुछ नहीं पूछूँगा।
ना वजह,
ना ग़लती।
बस ये कहूँगा—

“अच्छा हुआ तुम आ गई।”

हर पल तुझे याद किया,
इंतज़ार को ही अपना लिया,
अगर तू लौट आए,
तो ये सब सहना भी अच्छा लग जाए।

“और फिर भी, कहीं न कहीं,
ये उम्मीद ख़ामोशी से चलती रहती है।”

Bas itni hi likha hai , apko acha lge to batayegi jaroor

Should I live in the world I once imagined, or the world that was forced upon me?

A world of fairytales I grew up listening to, that a prince would come from the moon and take me with him.

I woke every day hoping it was true, not realising it was only a dream that would never come alive.

Life prepared a new battle for me every day, and I kept fighting, hoping my dream would someday be real.

I hoped for love and kindness from the world, but what I received was chaos and destruction.

I made my garden green every day, planted seeds with my tiny hands, and waited for them to grow.

I waited for sunlight to touch my face, tried to hold raindrops in my small palms.

What I hoped for was a world of affection and mercy, what I got was a world of fear where humanity was bleeding.

Days of starvation came, and I learnt to control my hunger.
Locked inside my house, I waited for the cage to open — days passed, but nothing changed.

The world took even the little hope I once had.
I called out for help, but no one was there, so I learnt to wipe my own tears.

I was prepared to be the strong one too early, but was that what I was born for?

I wanted to fly like a free bird in the sky, looking at the moon every night.
But the world tore off my little wings; my hope was buried in the ground while my heart remained in the sky.

Then I realised this journey would never be easy.
So I rose to fight for what the world had taken, while it slept in peace.
I fought for what was mine.

I grew up, grew up, grew up, and here I am.
Prepared every day for a battle that was never mine, fighting again and again for what already belonged to me.

Carrying the same heart, the same gentle soul, hurting no one, hoping only for love and mercy in return.

I found wallets full but hearts empty, bodies rich but souls starving.

So where should I live?

In the world I once imagined, where kindness is flowing, mercy hangs in the air, love lives in hearts, and souls recognise souls?

Or should I live in the world that was forced upon me and carry my imagined world quietly inside my chest?

— Shabnam

It was difficult for Benny and Mary to deal with this situation but they had realised that their aunt's friends also lied to them. Fred, Jack, Mary and Benny were finally relaxed but Benny and Mary could not believe that how could their aunt's friends be so fraudulent to them. 
After the truth got revealed the four wanted to proceed their business further. For that they again selected the new assistants but they were not the same. They did the verification of them as much as possible and the new assistants were faithful to the company.

The new employees were JACOB and STEPHEN. After working with them for a very long time the company -The Benny's became USA's top most trading company. It had its name on newspaper and TV channels.

In the year 1990, this company was being offered many trades by the Northern Europeon countries and the countries in the south. The company recieved a major recognition from all over the world. 
 
After this much success, finally in the year 1990, june 28th when Mary dreamed of walking down the aisle, surrounded by love and commitment. Mary's desire for love burned brighter with each day passing. Mr. Stephen gained the same rank as Benny's due to his effort full work.

Mary fell in love with Kevin. Benny noticed this and appealed to Kevin to take his sister Mary's hand in marriage. And Stephen was also having feelings for Mary.

By God's grace on 5th August, 1990 Mary and Stephen got married. Both lived a happy married life and Mary helped Kevin in his work. Benny's eyes were full of tears after seeing his sister's happily married life.

Benny's company achieved global success, becoming one of world's most successful companies with expanded team.


"In a world where business is a battlefield, only those who master strategy ,ethics will thrive. This is the journey of The Benny's. "

                                                 ~Nitika
