Kuhu, a seven-year-old bubbly girl, buys a chocolate every day—not just to eat it, but for
the excitement of scratching the wrapper from inside and winning tiny gifts. A
sharpener, an eraser, a fancy clip, or any cute little surprise is enough to make her day.
Another part of Kuhu’s daily routine, however, marks the most annoying beginning of
the day for Mr. Bagchi, the tenant who lives downstairs. During the summer vacations,
when schools are shut, Bagchi finds the days especially traumatic. Without fail, every
morning Kuhu eats her chocolate, scratches the wrapper, celebrates her win—and
throws the wrapper from the balcony.
It lands on Mr. Bagchi’s clean, freshly mopped veranda, where he likes to sit on his
rocking chair. The sight of that small piece of litter burns him from inside. Before Bagchi
could even think of reacting, Mrs. Bagchi would gently place a cup of tea in his hands.
She would then bend down, collect the wrapper, and drop it into the bin. A soft giggle
escaped her as she walked away to her chores, as though the incident belonged to the
rhythm of the day—ordinary and unimportant. Days passed in the same pattern, playing
on repeat every morning. Bagchi finally decided to speak about it to Kuhu’s father while
paying his rent—and he did. However, Kuhu’s father seemed far more concerned about
his daughter’s dental health than about Bagchi’s mental peace, which was exactly how
the complaint had been carefully crafted, as suggested by Mrs. Bagchi.
On his way back from his favourite daily green-grocery shopping, Bagchi decided to take
a halt at the same grocer from where Kuhu bought her chocolates. Feeling visibly
uncomfortable, he picked up a packet of biscuits and, almost hesitantly, asked—rather
inquisitively— “Ganesh,” he asked, turning the wrapper over in his hands, “what is it
about this chocolate that children love so much?”
“Arey saab, this is all company strategy,” Ganesh laughed. “Small gifts
inside, that’s how they increase sales. Children fall for it.”
He went on about how the company timed it carefully—summer vacations, when
children were most vulnerable to temptation.
Ganesh leaned closer to the counter. “Last year, saab, in some place they even kept a
jackpot prize—a car!”
He chuckled and went on, explaining how this weekend the company was announcing
another jackpot round. Children, he said with certainty, would buy them in
plenty. Bagchi was flabbergasted learning all these. Just then few kids came
running over to the store to buy ‘The Chocolate’
.
Just as he was about to enter the main gate, Bagchi noticed Kuhu standing there
with her father.
“Kuhu, this will be your last chocolate,” her father said firmly. “If you don’t stop
eating them, your teeth will decay.”
“Greetings, Mr Bagchi. How are you?” he added apologetically. “These children
today have become so stubborn—dragging us to buy such junk unnecessarily.”
Kuhu, however, was least bothered. Her eyes were fixed on the shop across the
road, her feet impatient. She only wanted to scratch the jackpot coupon inside the
wrapper.
Bagchi stood there, listening. The words last chocolate echoed in his head, filling
him with an inexplicable delight. He smiled—almost giggled to himself—and
walked inside.
Asking for a glass of water, he realised that some endings came disguised as
discipline, and some joys arrived without warning.
Mrs. Bagchi looked a little unpleasant today. Their thirtieth anniversary was only a
few days away, yet—like every year—it would pass as just another ordinary day.
The thought disturbed her more than she cared to admit.
Bagchi noticed the swing in her mood and asked what the matter was.
“My co-sister has travelled almost the whole world,” she said, her voice thick with
agony. “And I have never even sat in an aeroplane.”
“Oh, come on,” Bagchi smiled gently, trying to pacify her. “Don’t be upset. This
time I’ll take you to your favourite South Indian restaurant.”
The next morning, Mr. and Mrs. Bagchi left for his brother’s house, planning to stay
for a couple of days.
Kuhu, after finishing her homework, stepped out onto the balcony to play. How
could she resist her favourite chocolate bar? She tore open the wrapper even
before scratching it. The wrapper slipped from her hand and fluttered down to the
veranda below.
She glanced around—no one seemed to be watching. Quickly, she took out another
bar. This time, eager to eat it at once, she barely took a bite before her mother
called her to get ready, asthey have to catch a flight in the evening to USA to visit
her grandparents.
Kuhu ran up to her mother. The wrapper fell from her hand, landing at the same
spot below.
Two days later, when the Bagchi couple returned and entered the house, the
littered veranda blew Bagchi’s mind. Torn wrappers lay scattered below the
balcony. A wave of panic rose in him.
Mrs. Bagchi noticed his unease and gently asked him to go inside first and relax. He
tried to steady himself, recalling what Kuhu’s father had said that
evening. Probably this really was the last, he thought, forcing himself to stay calm.
A little later, Mrs. Bagchi learned from the neighbours that Kuhu had gone to her
grandmother’s place.
“That poor girl is suffering from cavities also, as told by Malti(neighbour),” she
informed Bagchi quietly.
“She deserves it, huh,” he muttered—then paused, unsure whether he truly
believed what he had just said.
That night, as they were retiring to bed, Mrs. Bagchi spoke in a low voice—hopeful,
yet careful not to sound demanding.
“It’s our thirty-fifth anniversary day after tomorrow,” she said. “Are you excited?”
“Of course I am,” Bagchi replied. “It’s a milestone in a relationship.”
After a pause, Mrs. Bagchi asked if they could travel somewhere.
“Hmm… I shall see,” he said—the same answer he always gave.
Kuhu’s absence was, in a strange way, enjoyed by Bagchi. Yet a quiet worry
lingered in him about her well-being.
That morning, he pulled up his socks and stepped out to clean the veranda, hoping
not to find any more litter. He began watering the plants when, near the cactus
planter, he noticed two chocolate wrappers stuck to the damp floor—the ones
Kuhu had dropped on the last day.
Bagchi picked them up, muttering, “Uff… these useless pieces of paper.”
But just then, an old thought stirred his inquisitive mind. Ganesh’s voice echoedany.
Almost against his will, Bagchi unfolded one of the wrappers.
He pulled a coin from his pocket and scratched the inner film that Kuhu had left
untouched this time. A small pack of pencils emerged as the surprise gift.
He smiled faintly.
The second wrapper was opened with even less interest.
“Must be another petty gift by the company,” Bagchi muttered as he began
scratching.
Halfway through, his hand froze.
He leaned closer, scratched a little more, then stopped altogether. His eyes
widened. For a moment, he simply stared, unsure if what he was reading was real.
AIR TICKETS FOR TWO
BOMBAY TO GOA
The surprise left him stunned—it was more shock than joy. His thoughts spiralled,
neurons boggled his mind.
Was it ethical to keep the prize? Should he hand it over to Kuhu instead?
And yet—what about his wife’s unfulfilled dream of travelling? Destiny, it seemed,
had finally offered him a chance to make her happy. Perhaps it was meant for them
after all. After all, it was his veranda where the wrappers had landed.
After much struggle within himself, Bagchi finally decided to encash the jackpot
prize and turn it into a special anniversary gift for his wife.
The next day, he went to claim the prize and returned home with the air tickets
folded carefully in his pocket. That evening, placing them softly in her hands, he
said with a rare sweetness,
“Happy anniversary, Mrs. Bagchi. Pack your bags—let’s fly to Goa.”
She was completely taken aback. Disbelief flickered across her face until she read
through the ticketing details herself. Only then did she look up at him, eyes shining,
still unsure if it was real.
Bagchi smiled, but somewhere deep inside, the question of ethics still stirred. He
decided he would confess the truth to his wife after the trip.
Before leaving for their trip, Bagchi handed Kuhu’s father a small packet—a few
reading books and a folded note.
“Have fun, Mr. and Mrs. Bagchi,” he smiled. “I’ll give these to Kuhu once she’s
back,” her father said, then paused. “But… why this thank-you note?”
Bagchi smiled and said, “For being such a caring landlady to us.”
Some secrets, he realised, were necessary for life to flow gently

THE UNCERTANITY OF LIFE
The next moment of our life,
No assurance whether dead or alive!!
Suddenly it makes me feel,
We are in the squid game for real.
 
I fail to understand the suspense stories of the almighty,
Lord! We bow down to your supremacy,
But not ready for the uncertainty.
 
Yes, you are the creator and destruction also
In your power and control.
But God, if strong ‘coping mechanism’ of the bereaved be made a protocol!!
 
All the beautiful moments turn into memories,
All the golden times turn into past theories.
The separation, the loss, the emotional turmoil,
It hurts!!
Rolling tears, the fatigued mind and the pain in heart always bursts.
 
I wonder what is in fate -love, life, grief, gaiety or delusion?
Why are we all rushing to struggle, win battles?
Why do we thrive to win those high-end competitions?
It is beyond our capacity to earn the fact of destiny
And dive into the universe full of illusion.

She lies on her back as if the mattress has learned her outline.
The room is dim, not dark. Afternoon light slips through the curtain in tired strips, turning the ceiling into something unfinished. Above her, the fan rotates with slow indifference, as though it has been doing this for years and will continue long after today decides what it is.
Her phone rests face down beside her pillow.
She has stopped checking it.
Time is strange now. It does not move in minutes. It moves in sensations.
A warmth sits low in her abdomen, not quite pain yet more like the body clearing its throat before speaking. Every few breaths, something tightens and releases, a quiet rehearsal. Her hand rests there instinctively, palm flat, as though touch could translate what is happening inside.
The bedsheet smells faintly of detergent and something older her own skin, her own life.
Outside, Bangalore continues.
A scooter coughs awake somewhere below. A vendor’s voice stretches down the street. The city does not know what is happening in this room, and even if it did, it would not pause.
Waiting, she realizes, is not empty.
Waiting is full.
Full of thoughts that do not ask permission.
The pill had been small.
That is what surprises her most. How something so small can rearrange an entire day, an entire future, an entire version of herself.
She remembers the steel tumbler at the clinic, the water tasting faintly metallic. The way her throat tightened around the swallow like it understood before her mind did.
Now there is only this.
The bed.
The fan.
The slow gathering of inevitability.
She turns her head slightly. A patch of sunlight trembles near the floor, as if even light is unsure where to settle.
Somewhere in the apartment, the refrigerator clicks.
Life continues its small duties.
Inside her, something is ending.
She closes her eyes.
Images arrive without order.
A clinic wall painted an optimistic green. A nurse’s hands moving quickly, professionally, as though this was just another Tuesday. A form with her name printed neatly at the top, letters too clean for what they contained.
Her signature at the bottom.
Steady enough to pass as certainty.
She thinks about the word choice.
How heavy people make it sound.
As if choice is always freedom.
Sometimes choice is simply the least unbearable option.
A cramp blooms, holds.
She exhales through it.
Pain, she realizes, is not always an emergency. Sometimes it is only a passage.
She wonders if she should cry.
Films have trained women to break apart in the exact right places. Stories insist grief must look a certain way.
But what she feels is quieter.
A numbness with soft edges.
A strange, almost clinical awareness of her own body doing what it must.
Her phone vibrates once, muffled against the mattress.
She does not turn it over.
Some part of her cannot bear language right now. Messages would make this real in a way blood has not yet.
She shifts onto her side, curling slightly, knees drawn up, as though becoming smaller might make the day less heavy.
The next wave comes deeper, unmistakable.
Her fingers grip the sheet.
For a moment she is only sensation.
Only body.
Only breath.
When it passes, she lies still again, as if she has survived something private and ancient.
Outside, a horn blares. Someone laughs.
The world does not pause.
She stares at the blank wall and thinks, suddenly, of all the versions of herself that existed yesterday.
The girl who didn’t know.
The girl who hoped.
The girl who delayed.
The girl who made an appointment.
The girl who walked into a clinic pretending her legs were not shaking.
And now
This girl.
In bed.
Waiting.
As if waiting is the last responsibility before becoming someone else.
She presses her palm again to her lower stomach, gentle, not apologizing, not blessing, just acknowledging.
“I’m here,” she whispers, though she does not know to whom.
The room does not answer.
But her body, slowly, begins to speak.


It had not been love.
That is what she tells herself, because love would give this a shape people recognize. Love would make it heavier in a different way.
This was not that.
It was a night that happened the way nights happen in cities like Bangalore half-planned, half-drifting.
A rooftop gathering in Indiranagar where the music was too loud and everyone pretended, they were not lonely. The air smelled of smoke and perfume and rain trapped in concrete.
He had made her laugh.
He had leaned close to say something, and his breath had been warm against her ear, casual as if closeness meant nothing.
Later, when the Uber dropped her home, he texted:
Text me when you reach.
She did.
He replied with a thumbs-up.
The next day, the city moved on.
So did he.
It was not cruelty. It was just ease. The ease with which men stepped out of consequences.
Weeks later, when the line appeared on the test thin, undeniable she sat on the bathroom floor staring at it as if staring could unmake it.
Her first thought had not been motherhood.
Her first thought had been disbelief.
Her second thought had been logistics.
Her third thought, strangely, had been a kind of quiet mourning for the simplicity of her life before her body began something without consulting her plans.
She considered telling him.
She even typed the message.
Then deleted it.
What would she say?
Hello. Remember that night? My body remembered it more than you did.
She could already imagine his panic disguised as concern, his concern disguised as distance.
So she told no one.
Not her mother, who would hear shame before she heard her daughter.
Not her friends, who would try to comfort her with opinions.
Not him.
She told a clinic receptionist her name and age. She nodded at the right moments. She signed the form.
She told herself this was enough.


The cramps return stronger.
She sits up slowly, blinking at the room as though waking from a dream she did not choose.
The afternoon has shifted. The sun is moving, even if she is not.
She wonders, briefly, what people are doing right now.
Office workers in Koramangala complaining about meetings. College students laughing outside a café. Someone ordering biryani. Someone falling in love.
Life is full of ordinary continuations.
Her body tightens again, sharper this time, and she bends forward instinctively, breathing through it.
She remembers the nurse’s voice:
“It will feel like a heavy period. You will be safe. If you have severe pain, call.”
Heavy period.
As if language could soften biology.
She stands when the pressure becomes undeniable, moving slowly toward the bathroom.
The tiles are cold under her feet.
The light is too honest.
She sits, breathing, counting without meaning to.
One.
Two.
Three.
Outside the small window, the sky is pale, Bangalore’s winter pretending it is gentle.
Her body contracts.
Releases.
Again.
Time becomes small. Reduced to breath and waiting and the quiet insistence of muscle.
There is blood.
Not shocking.
Not new.
But today it carries a different gravity, like a sentence ending with a period she did not expect.
She wipes carefully, methodically, as though carefulness can make this cleaner in ways that matter.
Her hands move automatically.
And then she feels it.
A smallness.
A soft resistance.
Not pain.
Just presence.
She pauses.
The world narrows.
For a second she cannot tell if she is imagining it, if her mind is inventing weight where there is only biology, if guilt has learned how to take shape.
She swallows.
Her throat is dry.
She reaches again, slower, and there is something —something small, indistinct, not a baby, not a person, not what anyone in a comment section would name.
Just the physical remainder of a possibility.
Her stomach turns, not with disgust, but with recognition.
This is what no one tells you.
Not the politics.
Not the arguments.
Not the simplified stories.
Just this quiet, private confrontation with the fact that her body was building something without asking if her life was ready to hold it.
She stands too quickly, dizzy, and grips the sink.
Her reflection looks the same.
That is almost unbearable.
She expects to look different. Marked. Transformed.
But she is only a woman in an oversized T-shirt, hair slightly tangled, eyes a little hollow.
The tap runs.
Clear.
Indifferent.
She washes her hands longer than necessary, watching the red dilute into pale pink, then into nothing, as if disappearance is something the world does easily.
Her fingers tremble.
She turns off the water.
Silence returns.
In her room, the bed is still unmade, the sheet creased where her body tried to find comfort.
She sits down slowly.
Her legs feel unfamiliar, like they belong to someone who has walked through something irreversible.
She thinks, briefly, of him.
Not with romance.
Not with hatred.
Just with the strange emptiness of remembering how easily he had left.
A night.
A few messages.
A softness that did not come with responsibility.
She wonders if he is eating dinner right now.
Laughing.
Scrolling.
Living.
She does not want revenge.
She does not want an apology.
She only wants acknowledgment of the asymmetry.
How one body can move on while another must process.
How consequence is not evenly distributed.
She lies back again.
The ceiling is the same unfinished color.
The fan continues its slow rotation.
Her body aches in a low, ongoing way, like grief that has nowhere to sit properly.
She places her hand on her stomach once more.
The space feels both empty and full.
She thinks of the word nurture.
How it lives inside her even now, inconvenient and stubborn, even when she has chosen otherwise.
She does not regret.
She does not celebrate.
She simply is.
Outside, someone calls out to someone else.
Life continues, careless in its continuity.
She closes her eyes.
Not to sleep.
Just to stop looking.
The heaviness does not lift.
It settles.
And she stays there, breathing, while the day moves forward without asking what it has taken from her.

The first time she orders, she tells herself it is hunger.

Chennai is bright in the way it always is, sunlight pressing down like a hand. Even inside the apartment, the air feels warm, held. The ceiling fan moves, but it does not change anything. It only rearranges the heat.

She stands in the kitchen scrolling through menus she does not read.

Biryani. Fried rice. Something called comfort food.

The word makes her pause.

Comfort.

She taps Order Now.

The app gives her a name, a scooter icon crawling across a map.

She watches it move like it matters.

When the doorbell rings, she startles too quickly, as if she has been waiting for a different sound.

She opens the door.

A boy stands there with the bag held out, eyes already drifting away.

“Ma’am.”

“Thank you.”

He nods once and leaves.

The corridor empties.

She closes the door and eats standing up.

The taste is fine.

That is not the point.

The second time, she tells herself it is convenience.

Work has been relentless. Calls, deadlines, the endless polite exhaustion of being competent. Her apartment feels like an extension of her office-quiet, functional, indifferent.

She orders again.

Another boy.

“OTP, ma’am.”

She gives it.

He hands her the food.

Gone before she can feel embarrassed about wanting something so small.

Later, she throws half of it away.

The plastic rustles like accusation.

By the third time, she does not pretend.

It is not hunger.

It is not convenience.

It is the doorbell.

It is the possibility that someone will stand at her threshold and see her as more than an address.

The afternoon is hot enough to feel personal. The street outside shimmers. Somewhere nearby, a bus groans. The air smells faintly of dust and sun-warmed concrete.

She orders something cheap.

Then changes it.

Then orders anyway.

The scooter icon appears.

She watches it crawl.

When the bell rings, she is already standing.

She opens the door.

And stops.

The delivery person is not a boy.

It is a girl.

Young, hair pulled back tightly, face flushed from heat. Sweat gathers at her temples and slides down slowly, as if even her body is working too hard to exist in this weather. The branded jacket clings slightly at the shoulder.

For a second, both of them look surprised, as if they have stepped into the wrong expectation.

“Ma’am,” the girl says, voice steady. “OTP?”

The woman gives it automatically.

The girl hands her the bag.

Her fingers are warm.

“Thank you,” the woman says.

The girl nods, already preparing to turn.

Then the woman sees it—one drop of sweat slipping from the girl’s jawline, disappearing into the collar of her jacket.

Something in her moves before she can stop it.

“Do you want water?”

The girl pauses.

“It’s okay, ma’am. I have more orders.”

“It will take one minute,” the woman says, softer now. “Please.”

The girl hesitates. Time is money. Stopping is loss.

But heat is heat.

She nods once.

“Okay.”

Inside, the apartment feels suddenly too quiet, too personal.

The woman brings a steel tumbler filled with cool water.

The girl takes it with both hands.

She drinks slowly, like someone who has been moving too long.

The pause is almost audible.

“Thank you,” the girl says, wiping her forehead with the back of her wrist. Her right shoulder is damp.

“Hard day?” the woman asks, and immediately hears how small the question is.

The girl gives a brief laugh.

“Every day is hard, ma’am.”

Not complaint. Fact.

The woman swallows.

“I don’t know why I keep ordering,” she says suddenly.

The girl looks up.

The woman’s voice is quieter.

“I’m not even hungry half the time.”

Silence stretches.

Then the girl nods, as if understanding something without being told.

“Quiet can be heavy,” she says.

The words land.

The woman exhales shakily, surprised by the relief of being seen by a stranger.

The girl drinks again, slower.

“You live alone?” she asks.

“Yes,” the woman says. “For work. Two years now.”

The girl nods.

The woman does not add unmarried. The word hangs in the air anyway, implied by the silence around it.

The girl’s gaze flicks down the corridor, then back.

“My mother will be waiting,” she says simply. “And my brother. I help at home.”

The simplicity of it is heavier than a tragedy.

Just life.

The woman looks at her own hands, clean, unmarked.

Her loneliness does not disappear, but it rearranges itself.

The girl hands the tumbler back, then takes it again for one last sip, as if reluctant to return to motion.

“You are not stupid for ordering,” she says, almost gently.

The woman’s throat tightens.

“It’s hard,” the girl adds, searching for words, “to sit with silence. Sometimes you need a bell. Proof that the world still comes to your door.”

For a moment, the woman forgets to breathe.

Then the girl’s phone vibrates.

A new order.

The world calling her back.

The girl glances down, shoulders already shifting into work.

“I should go,” she says.

Of course she should.

She cannot afford pauses.

The woman nods, too slowly.

“Thank you,” she manages.

The girl hesitates, as if she wants to say something else, something truer.

But truth takes time.

And time costs money.

So she only says, “Take care, ma’am,” the way people say it when they cannot stay long enough to mean it properly.

Then she turns and walks away, footsteps fading down the corridor.

The woman closes the door.

The lock clicks.

Final.

She stands with the food bag still warm in her hands.

The fan continues its lazy rotation.

The apartment returns to itself.

Nothing has been solved.

The silence has only been interrupted long enough for her to understand it was never hers alone.

Somewhere in the city, a scooter moves through heat.

A girl delivers food.

A woman sits down in her own life again.

Outside, another doorbell rings.

गुज़ारते  वक्त ने मुझे सब कुछ सीखा दिया,पर तेरी याद ने वक्त को भी कम्बख़्त अपना बना लिया।

क्या कहा था तुमने की होंगे ना जुदा हम किसी हाल में ,
वो किस हाल से गुज़रे तुम की मुहे ही बेहाल बना दिया।

वादे करना, जीने मरने की क़समे खाना और इश्क़  में मुझे खुदा बनाना ,वो यकायक कौन आया जिसको तुमने अपना खुदा बना लिया।

और गए भी तो मुझे ही बेवफ़ा  करार कर,  वो किसने तामील दी तुझे कि उसने तुझे साजिशी बना दिया।

अब हम भी गुमनाम किसी शहर में बसर करते हैं, पर लोग आज भी पूछते है वो कौन थी जिसने तुझे बेजुबान बना दिया।

अब हम भी क्या कहें किसी से किसी, एक शक्स ने मेरी नज़रो में इश्क़ को ही खाईंन बना दिया।

ज़माने वालो अब इश्क़ ना करना तुम भी मेरी हालत देख कर , गलती से इश्क़ में हमने भी इंसान को खुदा बना दिया।

इक वो चांद है जिसे निहारती है दुनिया,
इक मिरा चांद है जिसे देखता हूं मैं।

चांद में दाग है ऐसा कहते हैं दुनिया वाले, अपने चांद को बेदाग लिखता हूं मैं।


पाने की होड़ में चांद को दिन रात लगी रहती है दुनिया,
बाजू में देखता हूं तो अपने चांद को पास पाता हूं मैं।

वो इक चांद है जो शायद आम है और है सारी दुनिया का,
इक मेरा चांद है जिसे खास लिखता हूं मैं।


लोगों से उस चांद को कभी ईद का और कभी चौदहवीं का कहते सुनता हूं मैं,

अपनी तो हर रात ईद है और हर रात चौदहवीं, आंगन में अपने चांद को हर रोज खिलता हुआ देखता हूं मैं।


जरा सी मौसम बिगड़े तो उस चांद की बादल में छिपने की शिकायत होती है, 
इधर तो मौसम का हाल भी एक है और चांद की फितरत भी मगर फिर अगर कुछ ऊंच नीच हुई तो अपने चांद को अपने कांधों से लिपटा हुआ पाता हूं मैं।

ऐ दुनिया वालों चाहे लाख जतन कर लो चाहे लाख मिन्नतें कर लो, वो इक चांद है और ना जाने उसमें कितनों की मिल्कियत की होड़ देखता हूं मैं,
इक मेरा चांद है जिसपे सिर्फ खुद की मिल्कियत रखता हूं मैं।

पुलवामा एक सुंदर भूमि का टुकडा है,
जम्मू कश्मीर के
 एक सुंदर भूमि का टुकडा है।

जम्मू श्रीनगर हाइवे में
 आतंकवादियों द्वारा 
किये गये हमले में 
जीवन नष्ट हो गया 
सैनिकों को, चालीस सैनिकों को।

राष्ट्र सुरक्षा केलिए 
जीवन नष्ट हो गया 
मातृभूमि को जीवन 
समझाता है वह।

बदलाव में दिया भारत 
उन आतंकवादियों के घर पर
बिजली की तरह नाश
शत्रु कभी नहीं भूलेंगे।



चौदह फरवरी हम नहीं भूलेंगे 
उन वीरों को हम नमन करेंगे 
मातृभूमि की शीश पर वह याद
शोभित है अभी सूरज के समान।

आपरेशन सिन्दूर 

आपरेशन सिन्दूर, आपरेशन सिन्दूर 

शुरू किया भारत के सशस्त्र सेना द्वारा,
भारत की बेटियों के सिन्दूर के बदलाव,
शत्रुओं को अंत करने केलिए हमने,
लेलिया इस प्रतिज्ञा आपरेशन सिन्दूर।

भारत एक अनूठा राज्य है विश्व में,
भारत एक स्वाभिमान राज्य है विश्व में,
हर भारतवासी शांति का दूत भी बन गया,
भारतीय नामक धर्म फैलाता है यहां।

कश्मीर के पहलगाम में आतंकवादियों से,
जीवन नष्ट हो गया हिन्दू पुरुषों को,
हिन्दू धर्म होने से जीवन लेलिया,
नारियों के माथे की सिन्दूर छीन लिया।

अधर्म को खत्म किया कृष्ण का देश है,
वसुधैव कुटुम्बकम अपनाया देश है, 
भारतीय नारी की अभिमान सिन्दूर छीनते तो,
वह दुश्मन का अंत की प्रतिज्ञाबद्ध है।

सुवर्ण रेखा में हम चरित्र रचते हैं,
पाकिस्तान को दिया बदलाव आपरेशन सिन्दूर,
भारत माता की माथे के सिन्दूर लगाकर,
शोभित है यह संरंभ आपरेशन सिन्दूर।

title.stringValue: A SAGA  OF  DAWN  AND  DUSK Volume I — The Ignition

content.stringValue:
PROLOGUE
WHEN THE SKY FIRST CRACKED

Before there were halls.

Before there were thrones.

Before men learned to kneel

The sky broke.

It did not shatter like glass. It opened.

And from that opening, something fell.

The Divine was not worshipped. It did not demand names. It did not ask for prayer. It existed the way fire exists without needing permission.

From its presence came the first beings of power.

The Old Gods.

They were not born in harmony. They were fragments each carrying a portion of something greater. Storm without mercy. Flame without restraint. Growth without limit. Silence without end. None were whole. Each believed they should be.

They shaped the early world violently. Mountains rose overnight. Seas swallowed land and retreated just as suddenly. Life formed, collapsed, and formed again. Creation was not guidedit was tested.

Then something unexpected happened.

Mortals began to fear.

And from fear came belief.

And from belief 

Came the New Gods.

They were not fragments of the Divine. They were shaped by human need. Structured by prayer. Strengthened by repetition. They understood something the Old Gods did not:

Control grows faster than chaos.

The Old Gods dismissed them as echoes.

But echoes multiply.

As suffering spread from divine conflict, mortals prayed harder. And the more they prayed, the stronger the New Gods became.

War followed.

Not a war of armies.

A war of existence.

Storms clashed against structured heavens. Fire rained against pillars of ordered light. The world trembled beneath powers it could not survive.

The Divine watched.

It did not intervene.

Until it was too late.

In desperationor jealousythe Old Gods struck the source itself.

The blow did not erase the Divine.

It split it.

Half fell from the sky.

When it struck the earth, continents shifted. Oceans recoiled. Mountains folded inward. The impact did not create a crater.

It created a wound.

And from that wound, something grew.

A tree.

Not sacred.

Not cursed.

Something else.

Its roots reached deeper than stone. Its branches pierced through clouds. It did not bloom with life.

It held residue.

Memory.

Power without direction.

The Old Gods weakened after the fall. Some faded into elements. Some vanished entirely. Some slept.

The New Gods claimed the silence.

They built order.

They built thrones.

One among them declared himself All Fathernot creator, but ruler. Not origin, but authority.

Mortals preferred that story.

It was easier to follow a throne than to understand a fracture.

Temples rose.

Institutions formed.

Systems hardened.

And beneath all of it

The Tree remained.

It did not speak.

It did not command.

It watched.

Ages passed.

Generations forgot the sky had ever cracked.

Forgot that the highest throne was not the first.

Forgot that something older still lay buried beneath the world.

But memory does not disappear.

It waits.

And when pressure builds long enough

It answers.

The era does not yet understand what has begun.

But dawn and dusk have started to overlap.

And something that once fell

Is beginning to remember.


I. Before the Breaking
Hope survived here on conditions.
Bread was given if you knelt.
Mercy was granted if you obeyed.
Faith was required if you wished to eat again tomorrow.
The Hall stood at the center of town like a monument to controlled hunger. Its stone walls reflected no warmth, only structure. Beneath its steps, the poor lined up each Sunday to register their names, bow their heads, and pray to the All Father in exchange for rationed survival.
Beyond the Hall walked the God Handenforcers of curfew, guardians of “peace.” Their boots did not need to strike loudly. Authority moved with them.
And far west, past the river and pressed against the forest’s edge, stood a shack that smelled of death.
Inside, a boy sat between two bodies and waited for answers that never came.
________________________________________
II. The Smell of Death
Rain hammered the forest roof without mercy. Water slipped through cracks in the rotting wood and tapped steadily against dirt.
Aren did not cry anymore. His throat had burned itself empty days ago.
Two forms lay beneath torn cloth on the floor. His father’s calloused hands. His mother’s sunken cheeks.
“Was I a good son?” he asked quietly.
No answer.
“You starved so I could eat.”
His fists clenched. Nails bit skin.
“I’ll make them pay.”
A knock came at the door.
He ignored it.
Another knock. Steady.
When he opened it, rain washed in. Two figures stood therean older girl with watchful eyes, and a younger one clutching her arm.
“I’m Radha,” the child said brightly. “This is my sister, Mera.”
They asked for food.
He told them about the bodies inside.
They did not run.
Mera studied him carefully.
“Someone who looks at the dead like that isn’t their killer,” she said.
She handed him bread instead.
Before leaving, she mentioned the Hall. Weekly rations. Pray to the All Father.
“My grandfather said this era won’t stay broken forever,” she added. “A Savior will come.”
Aren watched them disappear into rain.
People who wait for saviors are devoured first.
________________________________________
III. Eyes That Do Not Lie
Mera returned the next day with warm food.
She did not interrogate him. She did not pity him. She simply sat across from him in silence.
“You look like you’re carrying something alone,” she said eventually.
“I am.”
“Would it help if someone stood beside you?”
“No.”
She hesitated.
“Can I hug you?”
“Stay away from me.”
Yet when she stepped forward and embraced him carefully, his body frozenot from hatred, but from unfamiliarity.
He felt her heartbeat. Fast. Uneven.
She was not fearless. She was choosing.
“You look angry,” she said. “But not cruel.”
That unsettled him more than comfort would have.
Before leaving, she said softly, “Don’t shut yourself away completely.”
The silence after she left felt different.
Not empty.
Aware.
________________________________________
IV. A Child Who Isn’t Afraid
Radha arrived two days later with rice and lentils.
She called him “big brother.”
The word lodged in his chest like something fragile.
She dragged him outside. Forced him to race her to trees. To throw stones. To breathe open air.
For the first time since the shack filled with decay, Aren laughed.
Not fully. But enough.
When Mera returned and saw them playing, relief softened her face.
“You’re not broken,” she told him later beneath the trees.
He didn’t believe her.
But he remembered the way Radha hadn’t looked at him with fear.
________________________________________
V. The Man Who Is Faster
An old man named Kael approached them near town, asking for a swordsmith.
Thin wrists. Hunched posture. Faded clothes.
He challenged Aren to a race.
“If you win, I’ll train you.”
Aren accepted without hesitation.
He exploded forward. For half the distance, victory felt certain.
Then the air thickened.
His limbs grew heavy, breath strained unnaturally.
Kael passed him without visible effort.
Not sprinting.
Just moving.
At the finish, Kael stood relaxed.
“I’ll give you another chance,” he said calmly. “Come when you’re ready.”
Aren had lost before. But never like that.
Something unseen had interfered.
He felt it.
________________________________________
VI. The Grave Beneath the Trees
Training began immediately.
Push-ups until arms trembled. Chopping wood beyond necessity.
Mera noticed.
“So this is about more than a race,” she said.
She suggested a funeral.
They dug graves behind the shack together.
Hard soil. Blistered palms. No priest. No ceremony.
He carried his father. Then his mother.
When he lowered her into the earth, his jaw trembled.
He did not cry.
Afterward, he stood staring at the fresh soil.
“I can’t afford to be weak,” he said.
“You’re not weak.”
“Not strong enough.”
The difference mattered.
________________________________________
VII. The Dream That Watched
Sleep fractured that night.
He stood before a burning house.
He knew it.
He saw himself younger, screaming.
Behind him stood a massive tree.
It burned standing.
Above it, clouds split.
Two enormous eyes formed in the sky.
Watching.
Not judging.
Just witnessing.
A voice folded through darkness:
“Only when the time is right…”
And then
“Perun.”
He woke shaking.
“That wasn’t just a dream.”
________________________________________
VIII. The Price of a Bangle
In the marketplace, Mera paused at a jewelry stall.
Simple bangles. Inexpensive.
Aren had twenty-five coins. The price was thirty-two.
The seller eyed the black iron bangle on Aren’s wrist.
“I’ll take that.”
The iron had never come off before.
He pulled.
Veins rose. Skin reddened.
Mera whispered, “Stop. It’s not worth it.”
It slid free.
His wrist felt strangely exposed.
He handed it over.
“I’ll buy it back someday.”
Behind them, Kael retrieved the bangle from the seller with quiet satisfaction.
The game was moving exactly as intended.
________________________________________
IX. High Crest
Far above the lower districts, in a chamber of glass and stone, Adam Kraen listened to Amanda Ren’s report.
The orb reconstruction was nearing completion.
The first had been stolen.
The thief supposedly killed.
No body recovered.
“If this fails again,” Adam said calmly, “you will be erased.”
No anger. Only certainty.
“He is watching,” Adam added.
Below, something was stirring.
________________________________________
X. What Mera Carries
Cristina asked Radha who she loved moreAren or her sister.
“My sister,” Radha answered without hesitation.
She spoke of bruises she had seen. Of nights she heard Mera cry.
“She chose that so I wouldn’t have to beg.”
Later, atop the mountain overlooking town, Mera kissed Aren.
“I love you,” she admitted.
Then she confessed the truth.
“I work in a brothel.”
She expected disgust.
Instead, Aren said quietly:
“You’re strong. Not because you’re untouched. Because you endure.”
“But I don’t feel the same way.”
The words hurt, but they were honest.
“I have something I have to do,” he said. “And if I let myself feel too much, it will break that focus.”
“You want revenge,” she said.
He did not deny it.
________________________________________
XI. The God Hand
On their descent, three God Hand members blocked their path.
They mocked Mera.
They laughed.
Aren’s fists split open.
He did not speak.
He memorized.
Scars. Limps. Insignia placement.
Breathing steady.
Cold anger is patient.
That night, a sound echoed through their billet.
Gronk.
Layered. Bone-deep.
An ash-black tree burst through the floor of their dream. Roots coiled. Flames burned from within.
Above them
An eye.
Watching.
They woke screaming.
Elsewhere, Kael placed the black iron bangle into a furnace.
It glowed.
From within, a thin black mist seeped outalive, writhing.
“It’s working,” he murmured.
The raven tilted its head.
Somewhere beyond sight, something ancient answered.
Not loudly.
But decisively.
________________________________________
Epilogue  Ignition
Aren lay awake while the town slept.
The God Hand trembled.
The Hall prepared sermons.
High Crest secured its projects.
Kael smiled in his workshop.
And somewhere between dawn and dusk
A fracture widened.
This was not the story of triumph.
It was the story of pressure.
Of grief becoming memory.
Of anger becoming intention.
Of something watching.
And something waking.
The era did not yet know it.
But foundations had begun to crack.
And when dawn and dusk finally overlapped
Nothing built on fear would stand.

title.stringValue: The Shadowed Box: Forces of Fate

content.stringValue:
Chapter 1 – Discovery in Darkness
Arin had always been drawn to the forgotten corners of his grandfather’s sprawling estate. Dust floated like tiny specters in shafts of weak sunlight, and the floorboards groaned under his weight as if warning him to turn back. His fingers traced along splintered wood, and then he saw it: a small, chained wooden box, etched with cryptic symbols that pulsed faintly, almost like a heartbeat.

The moment his skin brushed the wood, a cold rush slid up his arm. Goosebumps pricked every nerve. His shadow, normally limp and predictable, stretched unnaturally, twisting around him like liquid smoke. A whisper—not words, but a sensation—pressed against his chest, a presence that was both alien and intimate. The room seemed alive, inhaling and exhaling with him.

The box creaked open, revealing a note:

“Every touch awakens forces. Some guide, some tempt, all demand balance.”

The air thickened, oppressive yet intoxicating. That night, Arin’s room seemed to breathe. Shadows swirled like living entities. Two instincts stirred within him: dark, chaotic, seductive; and serene, guiding, resolute. Fear collided with curiosity. The game had begun.

Chapter 2 – The First Choice
The next day, the narrow alley behind his estate felt unnaturally tight. A man struggled with a heavy crate. Arin’s shadow whispered:

Demonic: “Step aside. Let him fall. Not your concern.”

Godly: “Help. One act could tip the balance.”

His chest tightened, pulse pounding. He helped the man, and the shadow quivered, half approval, half mockery. Returning home, the box glimmered faintly, revealing:

“Small waves make tides. Watch them rise.”

Sleep that night was impossible. Every creak, every sigh of wind, every distant cough felt magnified. The forces were alive, waiting, testing.

Chapter 3 – Ripples Across Life
Days blurred. Every kind word, every act of help, carried consequences Arin could not predict. Shadows no longer followed him passively—they slithered, stretched, and occasionally touched his mind with hints of warning or temptation.

A note appeared:

“Every action echoes. Every hesitation feeds the unseen web.”

The thrill of power clashed with terror. He was observer, player, prey. Forces did not care for morality—only for ripples.

Chapter 4 – The Major Test
One evening, a woman stepped into the street, unaware of a speeding car. The box shuddered violently. A note:

“Intervene, and another will pay. Do nothing, and disaster strikes her.”

The shadow swelled, colossal, sentient.

Demonic instinct: “Ignore her. Let fate choose.”

Godly instinct: “Act. Courage defines consequence.”

Arin pulled her back. The car screeched past. Across the street, a cyclist crashed. The box pulsed:

“Every salvation demands sacrifice. Witness the ripple.”

Goosebumps prickled his skin. The forces were watching, judging, alive.

Chapter 5 – Rising Tension
Sleep became impossible. Shadows twisted unnaturally, lights flickered, whispers seeped from corners. The box glimmered with thought unspoken.

“You are never free. Every choice awakens threads you cannot see.”

Even mundane acts became perilous. Each step, word, glance could awaken the shadow’s wrath—or divine guidance’s demand. Reality itself felt fragile.

Chapter 6 – Visions of Consequence
The box revealed a mirror inside. Not an ordinary reflection—countless potential outcomes shimmered, branching like fractals.

The shadow split:

Demonic: jagged, chaotic, feeding on fear

Godly: radiant, calm, exuding patience and clarity

A note appeared:

“Behold what you have done, what you could yet do. Every act awakens forces beyond comprehension.”

Arin saw his life in infinite variations, every choice fracturing reality. The thrill of understanding intertwined with terror.

Chapter 7 – Breaking Point
Days bled into sleepless nights. Arin confronted the shadow:

“Enough! I cannot live like this, constantly tested!”

The shadow erupted, wall to wall, chaos and luminous light colliding, demonic and divine forces intertwining. Arin smashed the box. Splinters flew, mirror cracked, silence fell.

Yet, even in silence, the presence lingered. Consequences never vanish—they wait, eternal, patient, observing.

Chapter 8 – Mastery and Thrill
Weeks later, the alley where he found the box was empty. Yet the shadow lingered, subtle, patient.

“Every choice ripples unseen. Every act awakens forces. Your life is now your own… but the stakes never end.”

Arin smiled faintly. Mastery, awareness, thrill intertwined. Within him, mystic, demonic, and divine forces danced. Every heartbeat, every step, every choice—a gamble.

“The shadow watches. I walk forward. Every heartbeat, every decision, a thrilling risk.”

The woman's radiance is the pause in war, serene and beautiful.
She rises with a roar, regardless of the outcome.
You are Radha, Sita, and Gandhari, renowned.
Why is the Gita, the victory of truth over falsehood, maligned?

You are not just tears, but a conch shell's mighty sound.
Removing the darkness of time, you are a brave warrior, unconventional yet powerful.
You write history with the flame of victory, a beacon of valor and struggle.
Your steps never falter, beautiful and unwavering.
You are the half of the Ardhanarishwar, a unique name among many.

Like the Veerangna, 
you challenge, a painter of truth.
Like the new Sindhu, a new creation, you are a salute.
You flow like the Ganga and Yamuna, a hidden gust of wind.
Sometimes a queen, sometimes a mistress, you are a painter in yourself.

Every turn changes the course, the woman's form is creation itself.
She fights for the nation's honor, like the Rani of Jhansi, a roar.
The feminine history is written in eternity, fearless and accepting.
With two arms,
 a powerful mind, and anger, 
she is formidable.
You are the beginning
 and the end, now a massacre of men.
The fearless start of the end,
 dying for the motherland.

नारी का तेज 
युद्ध का विराम हो 
बस अभिराम हो 
ललकार कर उठे 
चाहे जो अंजाम हो.

तुम बनी राधा सीता 
तुम गांधारी विख्यात हो 
सत्य असत्य क़ी विजय 
गीता क्यूँ बदनाम हो.

अश्रु जलधार नहीं नीर 
तुम एक शंख नाद हो 
काल क़ो हटा कटा मिटा 
तुम वीर योद्धा वाम हो.

अलख जीत क़ी लहरा के 
इतिहास लिख़ वो नाम हो 
जला कर दीप तेज का 
तुम शौर्य संग्राम हो.

झुके नहीं रुके नहीं कभी 
तेरे कदम अभिराम हो 
नर नारी अर्धनारेश्वर सी 
तुम अनेक में एक नाम हो.

वीरगांना सी ललकार करो 
सत्य का तुम चित्रकार हो 
नव सिंधु नव निर्माण सी

बहे जो गंगा यमुना बनकर 
पवन वेग क़ी छिपी बयार हो,
कभी मल्लिका कभी स्वामीनी 
तुम स्वंय में एक चित्तकार हो.

हर मोड़ क़ी धारा बदल दे जो

सम क्रोध में ये विकराल हो.

आरम्भ तुम अंत तुम 
अब बस नरसंहार हो.

ख़ुशी झा 
मुंबई 
महाराष्ट्र

They had the office decorated in such a way that it looked like a fancy place for a special occasion. There were balloons tied to the glass wall, and on the central desk was a cake with frosting melting under the slow turning of the ceiling fan. It had his name written in blue icing, as if neat handwriting could compensate for absence. But he wasn't there. He was in the mountains. Not the kind that appear on postcards, and not the kind that forgive noise. These mountains didn’t care. They were enormous and so still that a person could hear their heartbeat echoing back to them.

Back at the office, though, they all clapped for him anyway. They cut the cake. 
Someone laughed louder than necessary.
Someone said he always wanted to travel.
Another said he needed a break.
They celebrated him without him. It felt appropriate, because sometimes presence is more uncomfortable than absence. Just a simple leave application and a small bag. People prefer departures that sound temporary.

He had, in fact, been tired for a long time. Not tired of his job. This man could work all day long. Not tired of the people either. He understood them too well to hate them. That was the challenge for him.
Emotional intelligence is praised in meetings and punished in solitude. Over time, he had learned something troubling.
Confusion never goes away. It simply changes form. Most of us spend our lives moving from one form of confusion to another.

He no longer needed answers. Instead, he wanted to experience a kind of peace that did not compete for his attention.
The mountains were neutral toward him.
They neither welcomed nor rejected him.
They simply were.

He walked through the mountains without music, notifications, or applause. The sky above him was larger than any ambition he had carried for years.
At first, he spent a great deal of time in his head, thinking about everything.
Politics at work.
Unfinished conversations.
Betrayals.
No one was truly bad. They were simply trying to protect themselves from their own insecurities.
The mind became worn out from life's day-to-day ups and downs.

 He began to focus on the little things.
The texture of stone.
The discipline of trees growing on the steepest of cliffs,
and the clouds that existed without needing anyone to pay attention to them.
Mountains do not compete. They simply endure.

He thought he came here to escape everyone. Instead, he learned he had actually escaped from the part of himself that thought he needed everyone to behave properly. This upset him. Being sensitive had always felt like a good thing. And it had value. However, being sensitive without detachment creates fatigue. To forgive first is the most powerful act of all in any unspoken battle. Not because the other has earned it, but because the mind has earned rest.

The staff shared his photo. Many common responses were posted.
Enjoy your trip.
Come back soon.
The tension that existed prior to his departure went unspoken. For comfort, memory makes changes on its own. Celebrating the concept of a person is simpler than facing their actual existence. Symbols are preferred above people.

He laughed one evening while standing close to a ridge where the wind was blowing hard at him. Despite all of this ascending, the mountain was unaware of his presence. He was humbled by that. People compete for attention in spaces that will forget them in a matter of months. Names are lost on the mountain. However, those who ascend it are not diminished by it. This is what gave him the shivers.

Most people are not fake. They are afraid.
Afraid of irrelevance.
Afraid of losing status.
Afraid of silence.
So they create noise.
Meetings.
Celebrations.
Conflicts.
He had done it everywhere.

Peace did not come in a flash. Instead, it was the urge to respond that had changed. He thought of the office collective praising him. He did not feel superior. He did not feel isolated. He felt clear.
They were choosing their version of happiness. He was above doing that.
Mountains are not more righteous than the office building. Just simple. People in offices believe everything lasts forever. In the mountains, though, nothing purports to stay.
All are illusions.

There were missed messages.
A video, a clip of them singing.
He saw it once and did not see it again.
He smiled again. Yet this time it was more of a nod to himself than any real expression. Not out of longing or repentance, in fact, but from knowing rationally that they were mistaken.
They were not his enemies. They were dancing under club lights and loud music, with no direction, only momentary order.
His place was one where silence reveals what noise covers up.
Neither side is wrong. 

But every man must choose his altitude.
He did not decide to resign.
He did not decide to return.
For the first time in years, he refused to rush toward meaning.
The office will replace him if he does not come back. The mountains will not notice if he stays. The world moves forward without consulting the confused.
Between applause and silence, somewhere in the middle, a man stands, realizing that neither offers real meaning.

And maybe that is the true altitude.

Everyday I see you 
Snuggling into sheets,
Finally trying to sleep
Your gaze is softer than the duvet,
Smile warmer than the day,
Slowly drifting into dreamland.
Everything i wish is to hold you,feel you and console you.
You are the rays of dawn in my dusky days,
Warmth I need for my frozen heart,
I wish you were here
Atleast like the air or the light.
Even when I reach the stars you will always be in my thoughts 
Maybe  in a parallel verse my warmth will be  with you through 
out the night
Maybe in another life may be we never be apart.

I’m not the lighthouse.
I’m the guy who once mistook a vending machine for a confessional
and still walked out lighter.

I’ve written entire manifestos
in the steam on bathroom mirrors
and lost them to conditioner.

You’re waiting for a sign.
I am the typo on it.

See, I have built empires out of maybe.
I’ve studied the art of almost-knowing
like it’s a religion that never asks for tithes.
My gods?
Mostly socks that vanished in the wash.
And doubt—she’s a lovely dinner guest. Never leaves.

I once tried to rescue someone
with a stick of gum and a speech about metaphors.
They survived. Out of spite, I think.
I called it love. They called it Wednesday.
Fair.

But look—
if you ever need a laugh
at someone who thought brooding was a skill,
I’m your man.
I’ve worn existential dread like cologne.
Spritzed twice. Wondered why no one stayed.

Still.
If your knees get tired from kneeling
to someone else's idea of you—
I’ll be over here
tripping on my own shoelaces,
offering a hand.
Or a snack. Or sarcasm.
Whichever keeps you moving.

And when you walk past—
strong, clear, half-smiling—
don’t look back.
I’ll be busy writing sonnets
to my inbox spam folder.

As it should be.

Voice Command House
Characters:
Murugan – tech-loving hubby
Lalitha – smart, witty wife
Kid – little mischief maker
Story:
One day, Murugan got a big idea while watching YouTube:
“Let’s make our house a smart home… everything  controlled by voice!”
He ordered speakers, smart bulbs, smart fans, smart  cooker… basically everything online.

Day One:
Murugan: “Fan on!” → Fan turns on 
Lalitha: “Light off!” → Light turns off 
Everything seemed fine… until their kid tried a little trick:
Kid: “Robot, dance!” → Speaker blasts music at full volume 
Murugan, frustrated, said:
“Set it to recognize only my voice!”

Next morning wake-up:
Murugan, sleepy: “AC off!” → AC off 
Later, Lalitha: “AC on!” → AC on 
The battle continued:
Murugan: “TV on, cricket!”
Lalitha: “TV off, soap time!”
Speaker: “Voice conflict detected… turning everything off!”
In the end:
They both sat down and laughed:
“Looks like our voice command house… also detects life conflicts!” 
Moral:
A smart house is great…
But in real life, the real conflict detector is husband vs wife

I roamed about — a vulnerable storm,
the calm of death on cover.
Along the beat of an open wood
the scent: a cozy, blood-warm.
The night devoured by its own stillness, 
like the kisses of a lover
for whom it wasn’t yet over.

Soon faded the thick mist,
carving out the lullaby of a river nearby.
Coldness crept in like snowfall on a summer night,
whenas a graveyard came in sight,
dressed with red spider lilies — the blessing of death.

The mists glowed red with enchanting dread,
stealing away my breath.
Amid the sorcery came the cry of a cicada — shrill,
eerie enough to leave goosebumps in its wake.

Left it to me an untold voice-
a reminder to snap out the gaze
before it’s too late, cross not the soul bridge-
the one-way path where all choices ache.

They pleaded with a silent voice —
a velvet whisper across the woods.
A serenity as warm as snow that still remembers the sun,
while ever-burning souls roamed
the blood-red, gorgeous mess.

O Higanbana, thou art a growth of poison-
carved into moonlight and mists.
O higanbana, from whither comes thy venom?
Perhaps 'tis the regrets —
The regrets ere death.

The regrets wrapped
in the silk of undying wishes and lingering emotions,
the faint lines of bittersweet memories
one carries into the afterlife.

O those dreamy memories —
how they linger in the solitude
of a dark night beneath the soil,
whenas one dissolves into the place
from which they emerged.
O human life, full of mistakes-
thou always leavest regrets.

If I were a thing,
I’d like to be a cloud, I said.
Someone asked, “Why? There are a plethora of things to be!”

I sat quietly on my couch, watching the flawless sky above,
And simply replied, “Why not?”

It floats wherever the winds may blow—
No stress, no burdens, no heavy load.
Just freedom to move in its own way,
Drifting gently, day by day.

Clouds don’t judge, but calmly observe,
They gather where the air has nerves.
They bring the rain, they cool the heat,
They make the world feel calm and sweet.

Yes, if I were a thing,
I’d choose to be a cloud—
Peaceful, free, and proud.

Gaon ki garmiyon ki shaam hamesha se thodi si udaas hoti hai.
Jaise suraj doobte waqt kisi purani kahani ko saath le jaata ho.
Rahul tab 12 saal ka tha.
Patla sa, gehri aankhon wala, aur itna shararti ki poora gaon uski shikayatein karta rehta tha.
“Yeh ladka kab sudhrega?” log kehte.
Kabhi aam tod kar bhaag jana.
Kabhi school ke master ji ki cycle ki hawa nikaal dena.
Kabhi doston ko dara kar hansna.
Par sach yeh tha —
Rahul shararti zaroor tha, par bura nahi tha.
Uska dil mitti ki tarah saaf tha.
Us saal garmiyon me gaon me ek nayi ladki aayi.
Shehar se.
Apni Nani ke ghar.
Naam — Anjali.
Safed frock, baalon me choti si clip, aur aankhon me ajeeb si shaanti.
Rahul ne use pehli baar talab ke paas dekha.
Woh mitti me pair se gol bana rahi thi.
Shayad paani me apni parchai dekh rahi thi.
Rahul apne doston ke saath tha.
“Dekho shehar wali,” kisi ne kaha.
Rahul ne bas dekha.
Anjali ne bhi dekha.
Us nazar me na darr tha, na hansi.
Bas seedha sa dekhna.
Rahul ko pehli baar laga —
Kisi ne use bina judge kiye dekha hai.
Agli subah Rahul jaan-bujh kar Nani ke ghar ke paas se guzra.
Anjali aangan me baithi aam ka tukda kha rahi thi.
“Tum kal talab pe thi?” Rahul ne pucha.
Anjali ne haan me sir hila diya.
“Tum wahi ho jo ped pe chadh kar aam tod rahe the?”
Rahul thoda sharmaya.
“Main girta nahi hoon kabhi.”
Anjali hans padi.
“Par pakde jaate ho.”
Wahi se dosti shuru hui.
Rahul use gaon dikhata.
“Yeh mera favourite ped hai.”
“Yeh rasta sirf mujhe pata hai.”
“Yaha se suraj sabse sundar dikhta hai.”
Anjali har cheez me khush ho jaati.
Ek din Rahul ne use kheton me le jaakar kaha,
“Jab hawa chalti hai na, lagta hai poora gaon saans le raha ho.”
Anjali ne aankhein band karke mehsoos kiya.
“Tum itne bure nahi ho jitna sab kehte hain.”
Rahul ne pehli baar chup rehna seekha.
Dheere-dheere Rahul ki shararatein kam hone lagi.
Master ji ne ek din kaha,
“Rahul sudhar raha hai.”
Uske dost hans kar kehte,
“Shehar wali ka asar hai.”
Rahul gussa karta…
Par andar se use achha lagta.
Shaam ko dono talab ke paas baithte.
Rahul pathar paani me fenkta, Anjali daire ginne lagti.
“Tum bade hoke kya banoge?” Anjali ne pucha.
Rahul ne kaha,
“Pata nahi… par main yahi rahunga.”
“Kyoon?”
“Kyuki agar tum kabhi wapas aayi… to tumhe koi to milna chahiye.”
Anjali ne uski taraf dekha.
Woh baat mazaak me nahi thi.
Phir woh shaam aayi jab tez baarish ho rahi thi.
Dono chhat ke neeche khade the.
Anjali ne dheere se kaha,
“Main kal wapas shehar ja rahi hoon.”
Rahul ka dil achanak bhaari ho gaya.
“Mat jao,” usne bina soche bol diya.
Anjali ne halka sa muskura kar kaha,
“Har saal aungi. Pakka.”
Rahul ne haath aage badhaya.
“Vaada?”
Anjali ne uska haath pakda.
“Vaada.”
Us pal Rahul ko laga jaise duniya ruk gayi ho.
Saal beetne lage.
Anjali har garmi me aati.
Ab dono bade ho rahe the.
Ab baatein badal gayi thi.
School, exams, shehar, sapne.
Ek din Anjali ne kaha,
“Rahul, tumhare sapne kya hain?”
Rahul ne kaha,
“Bas ek cheez ka darr hai.”
“Kya?”
“Ki kahin tum aana band na kar do.”
Anjali chup ho gayi.
Phir ek saal Anjali nahi aayi.
Rahul ne pehle din intezar kiya.
Dusre din bhi.
Teesre din usne talab par baith kar sirf paani dekha.
Nani ne kaha,
“Ab woh shehar me padh rahi hai beta. Busy rehti hai.”
Rahul ne sir hila diya.
Us raat woh pehli baar roya.
Chup-chaap.
Waqt badhta gaya.
Rahul 22 saal ka ho gaya.
Shararti ladka ab ek shaant jawaan ban chuka tha.
Par garmiyon ki shaam aate hi dil fir 12 saal ka ho jaata.
Ek shaam suraj doob raha tha.
Rahul talab ke paas baitha tha.
Peeche se awaaz aayi—
“Ab bhi pathar phekte ho?”
Rahul ne mud kar dekha.
Anjali.
Safed suit.
Thodi si zyada samajhdaar aankhein.
Dono kuch pal chup rahe.
“Kaise ho?” Anjali ne pucha.
“Sudhar gaya hoon,” Rahul ne halka sa hans kar kaha.
Dono baith gaye.
Hawa chal rahi thi.
Rahul ne himmat karke pucha,
“Tum kyun nahi aayi thi pichle saal?”
Anjali ne dheere se kaha,
“Zindagi kabhi-kabhi rok leti hai.”
Rahul ne uski taraf seedha dekha.
“Main ruk gaya tha.”
Anjali ne samjha nahi.
“Kya matlab?”
Rahul ne pehli baar bina mazaak ke bola—
“Main ruk gaya tha wahi. 12 saal ki umar me. Jab tumne haath pakad kar vaada kiya tha.”
Hawa thodi tez ho gayi.
“Rahul…” Anjali ne dheere se kaha.
“Main janta hoon,” Rahul ne beech me rokte hue kaha,
“Zindagi sirf gaon ke talab tak nahi hoti. Shehar, sapne, career… sab zaroori hai. Par mere liye tum sirf ek dost nahi thi.”
Anjali ki aankhon me nami aa gayi.
Rahul ne aage kaha—
“Main har saal isliye rukta tha kyunki mujhe lagta tha tum aogi. Aur agar nahi aayi… to bhi koi to hona chahiye jo tumhare liye yaha ruk kar kahe — main yahi hoon.”
Anjali ne dheere se pucha,
“Tum mujhse pyaar karte ho?”
Rahul ne halka sa muskurakar kaha—
“Bachpan se.”
Chup.
Sirf hawa ki awaaz.
Anjali ne aankhen band kar li.
“Rahul… mujhe nahi pata zindagi mujhe kahan le jaayegi. Main tumhari feelings ko ignore nahi kar sakti. Par main promise nahi kar sakti ki main ruk paungi.”
Rahul ne sir hila diya.
“Main tumse rukne ko nahi keh raha. Bas itna keh raha hoon… ki agar kabhi thak jao, ya bhatak jao… to yeh talab, yeh gaon, aur main — yahi milenge.”
Anjali ki aankhon se ek aansu gir gaya.
“Tum pehle se zyada ache ho gaye ho,” usne kaha.
Rahul hans pada.
“Tumhari wajah se.”
Suraj poori tarah doob chuka tha.
Anjali khadi ho gayi.
“Rahul… har vaada poora karna zaroori nahi hota. Kabhi-kabhi bas yaad rehna bhi kaafi hota hai.”
Rahul ne kaha,
“Par kuch log sirf yaad ban kar nahi rehna chahte.”
Anjali ne peeche mud kar dekha.
Us nazar me sab kuch tha —
Pyaar bhi.
Darr bhi.
Aur doori bhi.
Woh chal di.
Rahul ne use roka nahi.
Bas dheere se kaha—
“Main yahi rahunga.”
Is baar Anjali ne mud kar dekha.
Do pal ke liye.
Phir woh andhere me gaayab ho gayi.
Rahul ne ek pathar uthaya.
Paani me pheka.
Daire bane.
Is baar bade.
Phir dheere-dheere mit gaye.
Jaise bachpan ka pyaar —
Jo khatam nahi hota.
Bas waqt ke saath gehra ho jaata hai.

Dhool ka har zarra seene mein jalta tha us garmi mein,
Mera bachpan khamoshi se pighalta tha us garmi mein.
Talab ka paani aadha, aadhi si parchhaaiyaan thi,
Ek chehra phir bhi poora sa sambhalta tha us garmi mein.
Main shaakh pe chadh kar duniya ko hans kar chhedta tha,
Dil ka ek kona chup-chaap machalta tha us garmi mein.
Loo ki lahron se jab saansein bojhal si ho jaati thin,
Uska ek jumla mausam sa badalta tha us garmi mein.
Pathar paani mein gira to daire ban kar toot gaye,
Jaise har vaada khud se hi nikalta tha us garmi mein.
Uski aankhon mein sheheron ki thandak baqi si thi,
Mera har shor wahin aa kar theharta tha us garmi mein.
“Kabhi gir jaoge,” hans kar usne mujh se keh daala,
Main pehli baar haqeeqat se sambhalta tha us garmi mein.
Chhat ki deewar bhi haathon ko jala deti thi aksar,
Par uska naam hi jaise phool sa khilta tha us garmi mein.
Pehli baarish ki boond ne jab mitti ko chhua tha,
Ek khushboo ka dariya sa ubalta tha us garmi mein.
Phir saal badalte gaye, dhoop wahi rehti thi lekin,
Mera intezaar andar hi andar jalta tha us garmi mein.
Ek saal woh aayi hi nahi… aur tab ehsaas hua,
Koi rishta be-awaaz bhi bikhar-ta tha us garmi mein.
Das baras baad jab woh phir saamne aakar thehri,
Waqt aankhon ke kinare se fisalta tha us garmi mein.
“Ab bhi yahin ho?” usne pucha narmi se muskura kar,
Main khud se door kahin ja kar milta tha us garmi mein.
Mohabbat shor nahin karti, mitti si rehti hai bas,
Jo barsaat ki pehli boond se mehakta tha us garmi mein.
Aaj bhi jab hawa tez ho, aur yaadein gard udayen,
Ek lamha dil ke andar hi dhadakta tha us garmi mein.
Vaada shayad mukammal na hua ho taqdeer se,
Par umeed ka suraj roz nikalta tha us garmi mein.

Part I: The Spark in the Static
Before the stars whispered to the night, there was a silence so deep the world held its breath. Out of the formless Void came the first crack—a wound that spilled the Whisper, awakening the bones of mountains and the veins of rivers. It was a song of uncounted time, a signal that Orienna, the living land, had heard the call once more. Change was coming; an age would end, and a war would rise. At the center of this prophecy stood a name carved in shadow: Kai Ashen.  
Kai was born in the heart of a lightning storm, a boy followed by tempests. At thirteen, living in a city of gray metal and flickering neon, the static in the air began to pull at his bones. The hum led him to a forgotten storage locker where an impossible circle of white chalk etched with ancient symbols clicked open at his touch. When he brushed the edge of the glyph, the world flared white, and he was transported to a field of ash under a bleeding orange sky, where tall, cloaked figures with burning mirror-eyes spoke his name.  
He woke with a mark—a circle of flame shimmering on his palm. He was no longer a normal boy; technology glitched at his touch, and the city seemed to bend around him. Guided by a mysterious coordinate on an arcane forum, Kai found a building wedged between towers that time had forgotten. Inside, he met Elira, a woman with silver hair that floated like smoke and eyes that flickered with stars. She welcomed him to Academia Nocturne, the school that breathed, where staircases twisted mid-step and the walls listened.  

Part II: The Ashen Reclaimer
At Nocturne, Kai was inducted into the "Flame-class" after the induction thread exploded into sparks above his head. He met his circle: Myra, a sharp-tongued illusionist; Jax, a mechanical spell genius; and Lune, a pale-eyed Seer whose shadows moved incorrectly. Kai struggled with the curriculum of Rune Calligraphy and Spell Combat, finding that his magic only snapped into shape when his emotions surged.  
The peace was shattered by a Veilbreach in the Hall of Shadows. A creature seven feet tall, cloaked in ragged voidlight and wearing a mask of flame, emerged: Zar’ Thul. The demon claimed Kai as his own, but Kai, acting on instinct, completed a complex containment sigil used only by Archive Masters to seal the breach. Elira later revealed the terrifying truth: Kai’s blood remembered Zar’ Thul, and the demon remembered him.  
In the Duelcraft Hall, Kai’s rivalry with the elegant and cruel Varin Dros turned deadly when Varin used a banned Binding Sigil. The pain triggered the flame within Kai, causing his glyph to burn white-hot and shatter the platform. In the aftermath, Lune whispered a chilling observation: she had seen something inhuman wearing Varin like skin.  
Kai was soon led to the Whisper Archives, a library of captured memories and the lies the Academy had buried. There, he learned of his ancestors—rebels who carried the Ashen Flame and were erased from history after nearly ending Zar’ Thul’s first rise. He discovered the Moon-Bleed Prophecy, which foretold the rise of the Ashen Reclaimer when the moon turned to blood. As the moon shimmered and bled over the towers of Nocturne, Kai’s glyph evolved into a starburst, and he realized he was the prophecy’s turning point.  

Part III: The Fractured Circle
The awakening of the Reclaimer triggered Flamelock, a state of total school lockdown. Academia Nocturne became a prison of eye-orbs and silence. A mysterious "Ashen fever" began to spread, causing students to collapse as black smoke seeped from their veins. The Tribunal, the school’s masked governors, accused Kai of unsettling the balance.  
However, Kai discovered he was not the only one. Deep in the catacombs, he found Callen, a thirteen-year-old boy bearing a raw, jagged Ashen mark. When their palms met, a bond was forged—a resonance of fire that allowed them to share dreams and power. Zar’ Thul began to use this bond, haunting their shared sleep with a human smile, waiting for Kai to break himself.  
The tension between Kai and Jax reached a breaking point. Jax, feeling abandoned and fearing the destructive nature of the flame, grew resentful. "Friends don't survive fire," the masked whispers told Jax in his dreams, "they burn in it". During a Tribunal-ordered expedition to reinforce the wards in the Deep Catacombs, the group was ambushed by wraiths. In the heat of battle, Jax turned his back on Kai, revealing he had been the one informing the Tribunal of Kai's movements. They dueled—brother against brother—until Jax drove his blade into Kai’s ribs. Jax spared his life, but left with a haunting promise: "When he comes... you'll thank me".  

Part IV: The Heir of Ash
The Tribunal’s tyranny peaked with the public execution of a first-year student, turning the Academy into a powder keg of terror and rage. But a quiet rebellion was stirring; students began scratching the "split circle" symbol of the Ashen oath into the very stones of the school.  
The final confrontation began in the Depth Cells, where the ancient seals of reality tore open. A Hybrid being—part flesh, part spectral shadow—emerged and knelt before Kai, hailing him as the "returning flame". Kai was pulled into the Ember Hall, the birthplace of his line, where he met the spirit of Solara Ashen, the First Fire. She offered him the throne, but warned of the cost: to bind his flame to his friends, he would lose his freedom, becoming a ruler whose life was no longer his own.  
"My choice isn’t chains," Kai declared, "it’s responsibility". He stepped into the white fire, emerging as the Ashen King. He returned to the surface to find the Academy in open war. The High Inquisitor attempted an Annulment to erase the chamber and everyone in it, but Kai’s power, now fully unsealed, shattered the Tribunal's magic.  
As the sky split, a new force arrived: The Order of the Crownless, ancient warriors who had waited centuries for the Heir of Ash to rise. Their leader knelt before Kai as the world realized that the war had not just begun—it had finally fallen back into motion.

The Unforgettable Spice of Life
Consider a story titled "The Juice and the Chilli," which offers a reflection on life experiences.
Imagine a glass of thick pomegranate juice. If someone adds chilli powder and mixes it thoroughly, it becomes impossible to separate the two substances again. No one in the world can undo that mixture.
Application to Life
This concept can be applied to human experiences. A sweet, serene, and cherished life is represented by the pomegranate juice. Unexpectedly, a deep hurt or a painful experience may occur—this is represented by the chilli powder.
Just as the chilli powder cannot be removed from the juice, it is often difficult to remove the memory of a hurt from one's heart. Dwelling on these moments can lead to significant emotional distress.
However, a different perspective suggests not worrying excessively about pain and focusing on success instead. While accepting hurt is difficult, facing challenges and opposition is a natural part of growth. If every experience were supportive and easy, life might lack the contrast necessary for development.
The most productive path is to save time, move toward personal goals, and strive for success despite the "spice" of past hurts. This approach allows for achieving more in life rather than being held back by the actions of others.

The Old palm tree blessed the pair,
While the chirpy-cheers of nightingales;
Overlooked the pain.
The bornfire raised for its warmth.
And the couple lived happily ever after again.
