Tears silently rolled down his cheeks, refusing to stay hidden in his eyes. He wasn’t ashamed of crying. Not today.
He had always been the funny one, but right now, there was nothing left to laugh about. The life he had envisioned with Ananya, the battles they had fought, the years of waiting, the countless promises, they all came crashing down in that very instant. And, he couldn’t control the flood of emotions.

After Siddu left her home, Anu sat in silence. The walls around her didn’t echo anymore , they simply pressed in, heavy and still. But within her, there was noise, not of the world outside, but of memories of Siddu. His voice, his laughter, and his undying optimism filled her mind. His words, those playful, clever, heart-tugging lines, began to loop in her mind like a reel that refused to stop. They weren’t just memories anymore, they became her thoughts, her rhythm, her breath.

He would say, “If I can turn a boring lecture into a comedy show, you think I can’t turn our dreams into reality?” “You think I’ll just sit and wait? No, I’ll build the road, pave it, and put up a sign that says ‘Siddharth and Ananya’s Destination!’”

He never failed to say, “Anu, I was born to find solutions. You were born to be my biggest adventure. And, the day I stop finding solutions is the day I stop being Siddu!”

Those words clung to her like air she couldn't stop breathing. All his promises? They weren’t broken, they just evaporated into reality. And now, there’s just her, with all those 365 dreams they once shared, with echoes of “march forward” that only she can hear, and with a name she no longer says aloud, but never forgets.
Then she understood that love alone wasn’t enough to shatter walls built by generations. Every morning, she woke up hoping it had just been a dream, that he would call or walk in like he always did. But all she had now were echoes.

Siddu, who had always been Ananya’s steadfast support, had become a void that even time might never fill. Her life had already been a storm of emotions, and now she had to move forward without the one person who made everything feel right.

For the entire year that followed, those echoes of Siddu became her only companion. He was not there. Not physically. Not in her days. Not in her nights. Yet, he was everywhere, in her heart, in her sketches, in her silence. Like a rhythm that never fades, even when the music stops.

THE LAST SKETCH
Ananya's world had changed dramatically. The walls of her home no longer felt like a cage, nor did they provide the comfort they once had. She had fought battles within her mind, against the shadows of her past, and with the pain that had left her breathless. But she had survived. Siddu had disappeared from her daily life, yet he never left her thoughts.

Siddu, too, grappled with his own demons, but his heart was no longer in the blueprints he designed. His mind traced a different outline, one he would never complete. Success came knocking, but it never delivered the joy he had anticipated. Late nights at the office, countless hours spent designing structures for people who would call them home, all while his own dream home, imagined with Ananya, remained unfinished. There were nights when he would stare at his phone, scrolling through old messages, replaying conversations, and lingering over unsent texts. But he never pressed send. He couldn’t.

On the other hand, Ananya transformed into someone she had never imagined she would be. She found solace in books, in words that offered clarity, and in work that provided purpose. Slowly, she built a new version of herself, one that didn’t wait for love to rescue her, but instead learned to save herself. As the fog began to lift, Ananya could breathe again. She started smiling at sunrises. Yet, on some nights, especially during rainy ones, she still cried without understanding why. She eventually realised that Siddu had never left her life, he had simply transformed from a person into a memory. From a presence into a prayer. From a love story to a lesson of the soul. Some love stories don’t end, they

simply become silent chapters in our journey of becoming. She travelled, learned new things, and met new people, but she never allowed anyone too close. Love was a chapter she had closed, yet part of her still clung to the smudged and blurred ink of the past, never completely erasing it.

Siddu's love for her had not diminished, it had only changed shape, from loud, goofy energy to a quiet, enduring ache. But nothing could replace her. Some nights, he lay on his bedroom looking at the ceiling, asking himself the same question over and over, “Would it have been different if I were from the same caste?” The thought burned, but he refused to let it turn into hatred. He still respected her parents, knowing they were motivated by fear rather than cruelty. Every piece of art he created at work contained something that reminded him of her, a warm shade of purple, a little scribble of jasmine flowers, a quote she once said. He was building his career, but a part of him always whispered, “This is for you, Anu. Just in case you ever come back.”

Siddu was now known as the dependable, kind-hearted architect on his team. Always smiling, always polite. But no one knew what he had lost. He still didn’t date anyone, not because he was waiting, but because his heart never really felt vacant. He often visited that old spot in NeoVista where they had once sat after school, eating chips and teasing each other endlessly.

He didn’t cry anymore, but his eyes always looked tired, not from work, but from holding too much hope. Some days he thought, “Maybe she’s happy now. Maybe she healed. Maybe forgetting me was her way of surviving. And if so, I’ll take that pain gladly.” But there were still nights when he clutched his pillow and whispered, “Anu, if you still remember me, I’m still the same guy.

Just quieter. Just more patient. Just, still in love.” He would add, “If life gave me a hundred chances to live again, I’d still choose you every time, even if I had to lose you in every single one.” In his heart, Ananya still lived, not as someone he would hold hands with again, but as someone who taught him what it means to truly care, even in silence.

Two months later, out of the blue, Siddu came back on one unexpected day. He stood in front of Anu, looking nothing like the boy she once knew, yet everything like the man she always believed he could be. They sat opposite each other, time stretching between them like an invisible thread, fragile yet unbroken. The air around them trembled with the weight of unsaid years.
Somewhere at the edges of her memory, an image stirred: Siddu, laughing under the banyan tree after winning a cycle race, his messy hair, his eyes shining. That boy and this young man before her were so different, and yet unmistakably the same.

For once, the easy jokes and careless smiles Siddu usually wore around her had no strength to rise. “You look good, Anu,” he finally said, breaking the silence. She smiled faintly. “So do you.”

There was no anger left, no resentment, just a quiet acceptance of the pain they had carried alone. “I wanted to see you one last time,” he confessed. “Not to ask you to change anything, but just to leave behind something.” She nodded, waiting.
Siddu took a deep breath and spoke words that would etch themselves into her soul forever. “Anu, life is not about waiting for the pain to go away. It never fully does. We just learn how to carry it better. Some losses are permanent, but that doesn’t mean we stop living. I want you to promise me something, not for me, but for yourself. “Promise me that you will live, not just exist, that you will chase dreams, not memories, that you will love again, even if it terrifies you, because pain will always be a part of you, but so will hope. And if you ever find yourself lost in the past, remember that the future awaits you. Walk towards it.” A single tear slid down her cheek, but she did not wipe it away. For the first time, it did not feel like sadness. It felt like a release. She nodded, unable to say a word.

Then Siddu asked Ananya if she could come with him somewhere. His voice was calm, yet there was an unfamiliar heaviness in it. She didn’t ask where. She gave a small, silent acknowledgment. They walked side by side, the air between them filled with unspoken words and unshed tears. For the first time, there was no playful teasing, no silly arguments, just silence. As they reached their destination, Ananya looked up.

“A temple.” The very place she had always wanted to visit with him, the place he never really cared for. And yet, today, he was the one who had brought her here.

She turned to him, eyes searching. “Siddu...” she
whispered, her voice uncertain.
He smiled, a soft, tired smile. “Not to pray for us,
Anu,” he said gently. “Not for our love.”
Her heart clenched.

“We came here to pray for each other,” he continued. “For our lives. For our futures. So that no matter where we are, no matter how far we go, we both find happiness, even if it’s not together.”
A lump formed in her throat, her eyes stinging with tears.

Siddu turned toward the temple, folded his hands, and closed his eyes. “May Ananya’s life be filled with joy. May she never feel alone. May she find everything she ever dreamed of,” he prayed silently.
After he finished, he turned to Anu, only to see that she had already closed her eyes. A thousand thoughts raced through his mind in that moment, thoughts he could never bring himself to share with her. Tears filled his eyes, and his hands trembled. “I thought love could move mountains, Anu, but I guess, it couldn’t even cross the doorstep of your home.”

“They say time heals everything, but why does every second without you feel like a fresh wound?” “If loving you was a mistake, then I wish I had never learned to be right. I don’t regret loving you, but I regret believing that love alone would be enough.” Just before Anu turned to look at him, he swiftly wiped away his tears and masked his pain behind a familiar smile, as if nothing had happened. For the first time, they wished for each other's happiness, knowing they would not be part of it.

They both stepped out of the temple gates, the fading sunset casting long shadows ahead of them. Ananya walked in silence, her mind still caught in the goodbye she wasn’t ready for. Siddu walked beside her, not too close and not too far. The space between them felt like a memory, familiar, but slipping away. As they walked away from the temple, they left behind more than just a prayer. They left behind everything they had been. Siddu smiled, but his eyes were heavy with emotion. He said, “You know, Anu, I always believed that if you truly want something, you don’t wait for it to happen, you make it happen. That’s what I’ve always done. That’s what I thought we’d do. But maybe, maybe not everything in life bends to our will.”

He paused, looking at her with an affectionate but pained smile. “You once told me that you fear forgetting things. That you write them down so they don’t fade away. But, Anu, memories aren’t just words on paper. They live in us, in every moment we breathed together, in every fight, every laugh, every silly thing I did just to make you smile.”

His voice shook slightly, but he quickly composed himself, keeping his tone light, trying to make her smile one last time. “But I guess love isn’t always about winning, right? Sometimes, love is knowing when to stop fighting, when to let go, even if it breaks you.”

“You were not just a part of my life, you were the very breath of it. And now that you’re gone, I don’t crave closure or a new beginning. I crave silence, the kind that speaks only your name in my head, over and over again, until it drives me mad enough to feel alive again.”

He reached for her hand but hesitated, letting his fingers barely brush against hers before pulling away. He smiled, stepping back, his eyes filled with unshed tears. “And if life ever feels too heavy, just remember, somewhere out there, there’s one crazy architect who still believes in you.”

He smiled, not the playful Siddu smile, but a sad one. A smile with a goodbye buried underneath it.
“I don’t want you to hold onto me, Anu. I want you to hold onto yourself, the version of you who laughed freely, who dreamed endlessly, who believed in her heart even when the world didn’t. Find her again.”

Ananya hesitated for a moment, her fingers curling into the loose fabric of her kurta. There were a thousand things she wanted to say, questions, wishes, worries, dreams, doubts, but none of them reached her lips. Instead, she looked up at him and asked, her voice breaking slightly, “Siddu, I just want to know... were you ever planning to come back?” Her eyes held onto the last threads of hope.

Siddu looked at her, and for a moment, it seemed like he couldn’t breathe. He swallowed hard, his throat tight. And the word he had dreaded finally pushed itself out, a broken, almost inaudible whisper, “No.”

A bleeding, burning “No” suffocated him from within, never quite making it to the surface.
A “No” that trembled at the edge of his breaking voice. A “No” that carried the weight of all their shattered pieces.
A “No” heavy enough to drown them both, but too
fragile to leave his lips.
It wasn’t just an answer.

It was an apology. It was a goodbye.

It was the sound of something beautiful falling apart.

She lowered her eyes and whispered, her voice breaking. “That’s what I would always want for you, Siddu… even if it meant losing you.”
He turned to leave, taking one last deep breath before whispering to himself,

“Maybe in another lifetime, Anu.”

THE CLOSURE
It had been three months since that evening. Three months since Ananya last saw him.

Time passed slowly, heavily, and silently.
Ananya had started to believe that maybe that really was the end. Perhaps Siddu had vanished just as he had entered, unexpectedly, beautifully, and painfully.
Until one day, the doorbell rang.

Her mother opened the door to find a deliveryman
holding a brown box. “For Ananya Iyer,” he said.

There was no special occasion, no online orders. Ananya took the box into her hands. It was light and neatly wrapped, but there was no sender’s address or name, just her name on top, written in familiar handwriting. Siddu’s.

And below it, one more line:
“This has to reach the one it was written for.” Her breath caught in her throat.
“Where  did  this  come  from?”  she  asked  the deliveryman.
“No return address, ma’am. It was pre-paid,” he replied before walking away.

She sat on the edge of her bed, her fingers trembling as she untied the string.

Inside the box, there was something wrapped in soft white cloth. A letter lay atop it.

She unwrapped the cloth to reveal a miniature replica of the first school bench they had ever sat on together. It was crafted from wood, delicate, and hand-sculpted.
On the backrest, there was a carved inscription:
"Chota Teacher & Bench Partner Forever."

Her fingers traced the words. Beneath it, carefully wrapped in tissue, lay a pen, her old favourite, the one she lost in 6th grade. Alongside the pen was a small note: "You once said you’d finish our story when you found this pen again. Now… maybe you will."
Tears filled her eyes, not from pain, but from the realisation that he remembered the little things she had long forgotten.

She hugged the wooden bench to her chest, as if holding him close. Then, through her blurred vision, she unfolded the letter.

Anu,
I don’t know where to begin… maybe because I never imagined an end.

I’m writing this not because I expect you to read it, but because silence is heavy. And tonight, it’s heavier than usual. Even if you never read this, I had to write it. Because these words, they have always been meant for you. You’re probably confused right now, holding this letter with a hundred questions in your heart, wondering what it holds. I’d say… answers, maybe. Or just the pieces I never found the courage to say out loud. This is not just a letter. This is the breath I never got to take beside you, the hug I rehearsed but never gave.



So, if you’re reading this, it means I couldn’t say these words to you in person. I couldn’t look into your eyes and tell you how much it hurts to smile at a world that no longer has you in it.

I was always messy, you were always neat. Together, we drew a sketch the world didn’t understand, but I did. Because it was you. I’ve always found it easier to joke than to speak, because jokes made you smile, and your smile made my chaos quiet. But today, I want to be honest. They say architecture is about lines and balance, but no one tells you what to do when your most important line is left unfinished.

Do you remember the monkey toy I gave you? I lied, Anu. I didn’t ask for it back to see you again, I asked for it back because I didn’t know how else to let go. That toy, I kept one for myself too. It still sits on my shelf. Yours was to bring you back. That's the reason I told you to return it after the holidays, but deep down, we both knew that return never came. Fate had its own sketchbook. You see, some moments aren’t meant to be closed, they’re meant to stay open, unfinished. Like us.

Skyline Scholars. The bench fights. The jokes. The excuses. Your scoldings. Your laugh. Your absence. You were everything. I saw you, Anu. Every moment. Every quiet effort. Every silent scream you never let out. Every moment you loved me without saying it. I saw you, even when I was no longer nearby.

Even when we weren’t in the same school, the same city, or the same world… I still saw you. The way you kept checking the gate during lunch breaks, how your eyes searched for someone your heart refused to forget. And I wanted to scream, Anu. To run back. To shake your shoulders and say, “I’m here, Anu… I never left you. I just lost myself.” But I didn’t.

And you? You were still holding onto the pieces of us like they weren’t stabbing your palms every day. How do you love like that? So fully. So deeply. So… painfully... when I gave you nothing but confusion, absence, and unanswered days?

You didn’t deserve silence. You deserved a sky full of promises, poems instead of pauses. A thousand apologies won’t suffice for not being there when you needed me most. But Anu… I loved you in ways I can’t explain. I loved you when we fought for the window seat, when you scolded me like a teacher, when you laughed at my stupid “Michael Jackson” answer.
But this love shouldn't hold you back. So, smile, my Chota Teacher. Even if we never meet again, a part of me will always live in that sketchbook where you first wrote my name.

This is not a confession. This is closure. Mine. Yours. Ours. Please don’t cry reading this. But if you must, let this be the last time. And end this here. The pain you were holding in your heart. And when you’re done… Smile. Because you gave me more than I ever deserved, a place in your world and memories. And that’s enough. From today, I won’t search for you in crowds. I won’t look at every girl with jasmine hoping it’s you. I’ll carry you in silence. Like a song I don’t play, but still hum in the dark.

When someone asks you if you ever had a first love, just whisper my name once in your heart. I’ll hear it. I’ll always hear it. And if they ask who Siddu was, say, “He was a chapter… unfinished, but unforgettable.”

Anu, you were my prayer, I never knew how to chant properly. But you still held me in your memories like I was a gift you never wanted to return. And that’s why

it hurts more now.

Live beautifully, Anu. Laugh deeply, louder than you did with me. And, Love again, without fear or guilt. If you find love, don’t hold back because of me. You deserve a life that embraces healing, not one that remembers pain. So, if someday your heart races again for something, for someone, don’t feel guilty. I’ll be cheering from afar, even if my name is no longer written in your story’s next chapter. Just make sure you are.

Walk forward. I mean… March Forward, Anu... Because if there’s one thing I’m sure of, you were never a mistake. You were the miracle.
I wish I could hold your hand once. Just once. To see if it still fits the way it did in my dreams.
I don’t know who you’ve become after me. But I hope… I hope you learned to sleep without crying. To eat without checking your phone for a message that never came. To walk without waiting for footsteps behind you. I never got to say how your laugh became my favourite sound, even though it stopped echoing around me. I never got to say how I stood near your house once and didn’t ring the bell. You were never a page in my story. Nor a chapter. You were the pen. The ink. The story. The entire damn book.

Now, I’m closing the cover… with shaking hands and a heart that will never beat the same again, not because I stopped loving you, but because holding on feels like dying in slow motion. And, Anu… I want to live. Loving you silently has started to feel like breathing underwater, and I’m drowning in every word I never said.



So, I’ll stop here before this paper becomes too soaked with my own tears, before your name starts to shake in my handwriting. I don’t know if life will ever bring our paths back together. Maybe we’ll be strangers with familiar eyes one day. Perhaps you’ll walk into a building I’ve designed without ever knowing I was behind it. Walk ahead bravely. Smile for both of us, because this world still needs your kind of light. Let the last memory of me be not a confession but a release.

I’m not leaving you, Anu. I’m just stepping out of your story. This time, for real. You were my story. I was your chapter. And this… this is our full stop. If our story doesn’t end the way we dreamt, it doesn’t mean it wasn’t beautiful. This isn’t a goodbye. It’s a funeral for the version of me who kept joking just to see you smile and make you laugh one more time. Just remember that, no matter where I go or how far life pulls us apart, a part of my heart will always whisper your name. And it will never blame you.
Never.
Yours in every heartbeat you’ll never hear again,
Siddu.


Ananya clutched the letter to her chest and cried because this was not just the end of a story, it was the end of a version of herself that only he knew.
She wiped her tears and found another envelope. It held the sketchbook, worn, with folded corners, frayed edges, and a faded cover. But it felt warm, like it had been held for years. Most of all, it felt sacred.

The sketchbook lay on her lap like a heart that had stopped beating. The cover read, “This isn’t a gift. It’s everything I couldn’t say.”

She held the sketchbook tightly, as if it might disappear if she let go. She opened it, and with every page, she broke a little more.

On the first page:
I used to draw. You know that. But not everything I drew was for architecture.
The sketch:
Her in a school uniform, balancing two water bottles, looking annoyed. She remembered that day. He made fun of her, as always.
Page 3:
A sketch of her praying at school. Head bowed. Eyes closed.
Underneath:
Even gods must’ve paused to look at her.

Page 8:
She was laughing.
Eyes closed, mouth wide open.
There was a small line under that one, too:
The sound I’d trade all my tomorrows for.

Her first tears fell on a page where he had drawn her sleeping at her desk, head on books, hair resting lightly on her shoulders.

Page after page. Memories. Moments. Tears started rolling.
But the sketchbook… didn’t stop.

And then,

The last sketch.
The final page. A full-page sketch. One drawing.
Bigger than the rest.
Ananya.
In a bridal saree. Looking ethereal.
Hair adorned with jasmine. Eyes lowered.
But her face… It wasn’t drawn fully. The lines around her eyes were blurred. Like he didn’t want to finish her.
Or maybe… he couldn’t.

Below it, written in faint pencil:
She was everything I ever wanted… But in someone else’s forever.
And below that, scratched like he was crying as he wrote it: Not mine.

She couldn’t breathe.
The sketchbook slipped from her hands as her body folded into sobs. Not dramatic. Not loud. But the kind of crying that comes from a soul that knows, She was always his.
She hugged the book and cried into her pillow. And then, there was one last message:
Anu, I’ve seen the way your eyes light up when you talk about stories.
The way you remember even the smallest moments and turn them into something beautiful.
So, if we ever part ways… write me into your story.

Write about the girl who marched forward. Write about the boy who never stopped sketching her, even in silence.

Write it for the world… Or don’t.
Write it just for yourself.
So that when someone asks you years later, what made your heart ache and smile at the same time… You can hand them a book. Your book.
And maybe… just maybe, you’ll write the happy
ending that we never got.
I'll be on every page you dare to write.
With all my heart, Siddu.

He had asked her to write their story if they ever parted, and she would. Because, he had already parted… long before the words ever did.

Life writes endings we never signed up for.

title.stringValue: अब मैं मजबूर नहीं… मजबूत हूँ

content.stringValue:
अब मैं मजबूर नहीं… मजबूत हूँ
तूने मुझे मरने के लिए छोड़ दिया था।
एक-एक पैसे का मोहताज बना दिया था।
तुझे लगा —
या तो मर जाएगी…
या झुक जाएगी।
पर सुन…
मैं नहीं झुकी।
अब मैंने खुद के लिए जीना सीख लिया है।
भूखी मर जाऊँगी,
पर हाथ नहीं फैलाऊँगी।
मेरी बेटी को फूलों की तरह पालूँगी —
ये मेरा वादा है।
मैं उसे खिलाऊँगी।
मैं उसे पढ़ाऊँगी।
मैं उसे सपने दिखाऊँगी।
मैं उसे मेरी तरह मजबूर नहीं बनाऊँगी।
मैं खुद से जीना सिखाऊँगी।
प्यार के सामने झुकना सिखाऊँगी…
पर ज़ुल्म के सामने नहीं।
मैं उसे सिर उठाकर चलना सिखाऊँगी।
ताकि कोई मर्द
मेरी बेटी को तबाह न कर सके,
उसकी रूह को न मार सके।
मैं भी जियूँगी तेरे बिना।
और उसे भी जीना सिखाऊँगी —
नज़र उठाकर,
सम्मान के साथ।
अब मैं मजबूर नहीं…
तेरी ठोकर ने मुझे मजबूत बना दिया है।
तेरी ठोकर से ही
मैं अपनी ज़िंदगी बनाऊँगी।
तू मुझे तोड़ नहीं सका…
तूने मुझे जगा दिया।
आज मैं अकेली नहीं हूँ —
मेरे साथ मेरी हिम्मत है,
मेरी बेटी है,
और मेरा आत्मसम्मान है।
और यही काफी है।

title.stringValue: I talk to the moon about my moon

content.stringValue:
I talk to the moon about my moon.
I speak through my eyes,
His name knocks on my lips,
Everytime I hear the word love,
His face floats in my mind,
As if it knows before me,
What's love? Who I love?

Every time I feel heavy,
I feel his presence,
Not just beside me,
But inside my soul.

He - who owns my spirit,
My care, my heart with peace,
He - the one
For whom my heart beats,
Where life exists,
Where love breathe

And I hide him inside my warmth,
As for unmasking him,
I fear that this world will harm him.
His gentle presence, his gentle spirit.

But the universe has its  cruel way,
Everything i love it steals.

But who am I fooling?
When nothing is truly mine,
Not this heart,
Not even this mind,
Neither my soul.
It's his,
The one who rules my core.
My spirit.

And so i talk to the moon, about my moon.
Because everything about me,
Is him 🤍🌹

The air inside the underground vault of the Obsidian Club tasted like expensive gin and dangerous secrets. It was a room designed for two things: the accumulation of illicit wealth and the destruction of anyone foolish enough to try and steal it.

Mira’s hands shook as she fumbled with the dial of the heavy steel safe. The blueprints she had memorized were burning a hole in her mind, but the cold reality of where she was—and who she was stealing from—was suffocating her.

"You’re trembling."

The voice came from the absolute darkness behind her. It wasn't a shout. It was a low, gravelly baritone that vibrated straight through her spine and settled low in her stomach. It was the voice of a man who never had to raise it to get exactly what he wanted.

Ethan Vance.

He stepped out of the shadows, the dim overhead light catching the sharp, patrician angles of his face. He was dressed in a tailored, midnight-black suit that emphasized his heavily muscled frame. His silver eyes locked onto hers with the intensity of a predator.

"I... I can explain," Mira whispered.

"There is nothing to explain, Mira," Ethan said, stopping mere inches behind her. "You broke into my club to steal the ledger that contains my secrets. The deadliest currency in this city."

He reached out, his large, calloused hand wrapping around her throat—firm enough to establish absolute, undeniable control. He tilted her head back. "Why shouldn't I kill you right now?"

"Because you know why I'm here," Mira gasped. "My father. His debts."

"And your father sent his beautiful daughter to clear his ledger," Ethan observed smoothly. He pressed her back against the cold steel of the safe, his solid body trapping her completely. "Your father’s debt is erased. But you don't get to walk out of here, Mira. You belong to me now."

The transition from desperate thief to Ethan Vance’s captive was a whiplash of silk and steel. Ethan did not lock her in a cell; he locked her in his sprawling, fortress-like penthouse overlooking the city.

For the first few days, Mira treated the luxurious apartment like a high-end hostage situation. She quickly learned two things about Ethan: he owned half the city, and he was pathologically obsessed with controlling her.

On Tuesday morning, she wandered into the massive marble kitchen wearing one of his oversized black dress shirts. Ethan was leaning against the counter, impeccably dressed in a charcoal suit, sipping espresso while reading a dossier.

"Do you ever sleep?" Mira asked, crossing her arms. "Or do you just hang upside down in a closet like a very stylish bat?"

Ethan didn't look up, but the corner of his mouth twitched. "Bats are blind, Mira. I see everything. Including the fact that you’re wearing my shirt."

"Your closet is the size of my apartment. I didn't think you'd miss it."

He finally lowered the folder, his silver eyes pinning her to the spot. "I don't mind you in my clothes. But if you want to play dress-up, go to the master suite. I had a few things delivered."

Mira went. She found three rolling racks of designer gowns, silk lingerie, and stilettos that looked more like lethal weapons. She walked back into the kitchen holding up a terrifyingly small scrap of black lace.

"Ethan, what is this?" she asked deadpan. "An eye patch for a pirate? A hammock for a very small hamster?"

A low, dark chuckle rumbled in Ethan's chest—a sound that did unfair things to her pulse. He closed the distance between them, plucking the lace from her fingers.

"Put it on tonight, and I'll show you exactly what it's for," he murmured, his voice dropping an octave. The amusement vanished from his eyes, replaced by a heavy, claiming heat. He gripped her hip, pulling her flush against him. "Rule one of living with me, Mira: you wear what I tell you. And tonight, we have guests."

The "guests" were three rival capos. During the lavish dinner, Ethan commanded her to sit right by his side. He played the role of the ruthless boss flawlessly, discussing multi-million dollar shipping routes. But beneath the imported mahogany table, his large hand rested heavily on Mira's bare thigh.

Every time she tried to shift away, his fingers dug possessively into her flesh, a silent, electric warning. Mine. When a rival boss dared to look at Mira a second too long, Ethan didn't yell. He simply smiled a dead, cold smile, slid his hand higher up Mira's thigh, and casually threatened to burn the man's warehouses to the ground. The boss averted his eyes immediately.

Mira realized with a terrifying thrill that she wasn't just his prisoner; she was his queen, and he was daring the world to try and take her.

The boundaries of their twisted relationship were set in stone. Ethan didn't just want her physical presence; he demanded her complete submission in every aspect of her life.

One rainy afternoon, Mira was pacing the massive living room when one of Ethan’s heavily armed guards stepped through the mahogany doors. "Mr. Vance wants you in his study. Now."

Mira swallowed hard, smoothing down the dark silk slip dress Ethan had laid out for her that morning. She walked down the long corridor and pushed open the heavy oak doors to his office.

Ethan was sitting behind a massive desk scattered with blueprints, shipping manifests, and the very ledger she had tried to steal. He looked up, his silver eyes dark and calculating. He didn't say a word. He simply tapped his thigh twice.

It was a silent, absolute command.

Mira’s pulse fluttered in her throat. She crossed the room, stepping around the desk, and carefully lowered herself onto his lap. The moment she did, Ethan’s large arm wrapped around her waist like a vice, pulling her flush against his hard chest. He went right back to reading a document, his other hand casually resting on her bare thigh, his thumb drawing slow, distracting circles on her skin.

"You're dismantling my father's operations," Mira observed softly, looking at the papers on his desk. She recognized the names of her father's warehouses. "You're taking everything from him."

"I am severing your ties," Ethan corrected, his deep voice vibrating against her back. He dropped the pen and turned her slightly by the chin so she had to look at him. "I told you, your father's debt is erased. But I don't share what is mine, Mira. By tomorrow, your father won't have the power to protect a stray dog in this city, let alone come looking for you."

A shiver of fear and undeniable heat ran down her spine. "You want me completely isolated."

"I want you completely dependent," he murmured, leaning in until his lips brushed her ear. "You are the only valuable thing your father ever produced. And you are the only thing of his I decided to keep."

He bit down gently on her earlobe, making her gasp and arch into him. His grip on her waist tightened instantly, a silent warning to stay exactly where she was. He kept her on his lap for the next two hours while he ran the city's underworld, demanding her silence, and making sure she understood precisely who owned her.

Two days later, the emerald gown arrived for the annual Syndicate Masquerade.

Mira was in the master suite when Ethan walked in. She was standing in front of the floor-to-ceiling mirror, the deep green silk clinging to every curve. The dress was scandalously low-cut in the back, leaving her spine completely bare.

Ethan stopped in the doorway, his eyes darkening to the color of storm clouds. He walked up behind her, his reflection towering over hers. He didn't touch the dress. Instead, his calloused hands slid over her bare shoulders, his thumbs pressing into the sensitive skin of her neck.

"You look beautiful," Ethan said, though it didn't sound like a compliment. It sounded like a threat to anyone else who might look at her tonight. "But remember the rules for tonight, Mira."

"I know," she whispered, her eyes meeting his silver gaze in the mirror.

"Say them," he commanded, his grip tightening.

"I don't leave your side. I don't speak to your rivals unless spoken to. And I don't look at anyone but you."

"Good girl," he growled. He leaned down, his mouth pressing against the curve of her shoulder. He sucked a harsh mark into her skin, biting down just hard enough to leave a faint, blooming bruise right at the edge of the emerald silk. A brand. "Let the monsters in that ballroom wonder who owns the most beautiful woman in the city. And let this remind you of the answer."

But in the mafia, peace is just an illusion holding its breath.

The masquerade was dripping with crystal chandeliers and masked figures. Mira stood by Ethan’s side, a delicate lace mask over her eyes. Ethan’s arm was wrapped securely around her waist.

"Drink," Ethan murmured, handing her a crystal flute of champagne.

Before she could take a sip, a familiar voice cut through the hum of the ballroom.

"A beautiful bird for a gilded cage."

Mira froze. Standing a few feet away, in a silver wolf mask, was her older brother, Leo.

Ethan’s grip on Mira’s waist tightened to the point of pain. His silver eyes locked onto Leo, cold and dead. "Leo. I told you your family's debts were paid on the condition you never stepped foot in my city again."

Leo smirked. "Things change, Vance. The Rossi family is backing me now." He shifted his gaze to Mira, his eyes flashing with disgust. "Did you do it yet, Mira? Or did you let the monster distract you?"

Mira’s blood ran ice cold. The champagne flute felt like a lead weight.

Ethan went completely still. He slowly turned his head to look down at Mira. "Did you do what, Mira?"

The twist hit her with the force of a freight train. As past sins resurface, every choice could be their last. Her father hadn't sent her to steal the ledger. He had sent her to get caught. He had sent her to get close to Ethan. The Rossi family had promised her father protection if he assassinated Ethan Vance. And Mira was the weapon.

"The champagne," Leo sneered. "It's laced with aconite. Odorless. Tasteless. We knew he'd trust you enough to share a drink with you. Give it to him."

The ballroom felt entirely too quiet. A single drop would stop Ethan’s heart. She had the power to end the king of the shadows and free her family.

She looked up at Ethan. He wasn't looking at the glass. He was looking only at her. There was no fear in his silver gaze, only a dark, tragic acceptance.

"Do it," Ethan commanded softly, stepping back to give her space. "If that's what you want, Mira. Do it."

A tear slipped from beneath her mask. Trust was a luxury no one could afford, but she was about to buy it in blood.

Mira turned entirely toward her brother. With a fierce motion, she hurled the crystal flute directly into the blazing fireplace. The glass shattered, the poisoned champagne hissing violently in the flames.

"No," Mira said, her voice clear and steady.

Leo’s smug expression vanished into panic. "You stupid bitch! You just signed our death warrants!"

"No," Ethan’s voice boomed, completely devoid of mercy. He stepped in front of Mira, shielding her as he drew his heavy, matte-black Sig Sauer. "She just signed yours."

The ballroom erupted into chaos. Ethan fired twice. Leo dropped to the marble floor. Suddenly, Rossi men hidden among the guests broke cover. Gunfire shattered the chandeliers.

"Down!" Ethan roared, throwing Mira behind the heavy marble bar.

He didn't cower. He became the demon they all feared, returning fire with terrifying precision. He was a force of vengeance, protecting the one thing he had claimed as his own. Within minutes, the surviving Rossi men fled into the night, leaving the ballroom a smoking ruin.

The ride back to the penthouse was a blur of flashing city lights and deafening silence.

The adrenaline from the ballroom shootout was crashing hard. In the back of the armored Maybach, Ethan was a mess of ruined tailoring and blood. He had taken off his suit jacket, his white shirt stained with plaster dust and the blood of the Rossi men who had tried to kill them.

As soon as the car doors locked, he reached across the leather seats, grabbed Mira by the hips, and hauled her directly into his lap.

Mira buried her face in the crook of his neck, her hands gripping his broad shoulders. She was shaking. She had betrayed her brother to save the mafia king.

"He was my brother," she choked out, a dry sob escaping her throat. "Leo... he was my blood."

Ethan gripped her hair, pulling her head back so she was forced to look at his lethal, soot-stained face. There was no pity in his eyes, only a fierce, consuming obsession.

"He was a pawn," Ethan snarled, a low, terrifying rumble. "And he tried to take you from me. I would burn this entire city to the ground before I let them touch a single hair on your head, Mira. Do you understand me? Your blood doesn't matter anymore. I am your family now. I am your loyalty."

He crushed his mouth to hers, kissing her with a violent, desperate hunger. It tasted like cordite, expensive champagne, and survival. Mira whimpered, completely overwhelmed, and surrendered instantly.

By the time the elevator doors opened directly into the penthouse, the tension between them was explosive.

Ethan didn't let her walk. He carried her over his shoulder, kicking the door to the master suite shut behind them. The room was dark, illuminated only by the city lights pouring through the rain-streaked windows.

He dropped her onto her feet beside the massive bed. His silver eyes were wild, feral. He was a predator who had just protected his mate.

"Turn around," he ordered, his chest heaving.

Mira obeyed blindly. Ethan’s hands went to the zipper of the ruined emerald gown. He grabbed the fabric and ripped it completely, the sound echoing sharply. The silk pooled at her feet, leaving her in nothing but the black lace she had joked about days ago.

He spun her back around, lifting her off the floor and slamming her back against the cool glass of the floor-to-ceiling window. The entire city of shadows was spread out hundreds of feet below them.

"You saved my life," Ethan breathed, pressing his body entirely against hers. He unbuckled his holster, letting his heavy weapons clatter to the floor. "You killed your past for me."

"I chose my king," Mira gasped, reaching down to desperately undo the buttons of his ruined shirt.

Ethan groaned, shedding the shirt entirely. His scarred, tattooed chest was scorching hot against her bare skin. "Then let your king claim his prize."

He hooked his hands under her thighs, lifting her legs to wrap around his waist. Mira cried out as he entered her in one sharp, powerful thrust, completely filling her. It was raw, primal claiming.

"Look at me," Ethan commanded, setting a deep, punishing pace that made the glass rattle behind her. His hands gripped her hips, bruising her flesh, making sure she felt every single inch of his dominance. "Keep your eyes on me, Mira."

"Ethan—please—" she sobbed, throwing her head back, her nails digging half-moons into his heavy shoulders. The pleasure was too sharp, too intense after the terror of the night.

"Tell me whose life you saved," he demanded, thrusting upward.

"Yours! Only yours!"

"Tell me who owns you," he growled, his teeth sinking into the sensitive skin of her neck, right over the bruised brand he had left earlier.

"You do! Ethan, you own me!"

Her confession was the final push he needed. Ethan let out a harsh, guttural shout, burying himself as deep as he could go as he came undone inside her. The climax ripped through Mira a second later, a shattering wave of dark, consuming bliss that left her completely boneless.

Ethan didn't let her fall. He held her suspended against the glass, his massive chest heaving against hers. He pressed his forehead against hers, the ruthless mafia boss finally tamed by the woman in his arms.

"Some shadows never fade, Mira," he whispered hoarsely, carrying her away from the window and laying her gently amidst the dark satin sheets of his bed. He crawled in next to her, pulling her tightly to his chest. "But you are the only light I will ever allow in mine."


with love,
~MELORE~

I first met Arav at the wedding of our common friend, Radhika. He was tall, charming, and had an honest smile. Radhika introduced us casually, and the three of us chatted for a while. But soon, Radhika excused herself, saying, “I'll go help the bride,” and left the two of us alone.
That wedding night, I spent time with Arav. His sense of humor, his respectful way of talking — it all impressed me. He wasn’t the kind of guy who flirted around. He listened, he smiled gently, and when he spoke, it felt real.
Before leaving, we exchanged numbers and promised to stay in touch.
To be honest, I had started liking him that very night. It felt like love at first sight. I began looking for ways to meet him again. I asked Radhika to fix another meeting with him.
Soon, we met again at Radhika’s house. She made us sit together and served fresh juice, then cleverly disappeared inside, giving us some privacy.
I nervously started talking about random things — mostly Radhika — though I really wanted to talk about him and us. I’m not usually shy, but that day I was. Maybe that’s what love does.
Then I gathered all my courage and said, “Actually… I like you. Since that wedding night. I really wanted to meet you again.”
He looked at me with a teasing smile and said, “Is it? Really?”
He was pretending to be surprised, but I knew he wasn’t. And yet… I liked that playful attitude — his ada.
A few minutes later, he said with a soft voice, “I like you too.”
I don’t know what happened to me in that moment. I felt pure happiness rush through me. I couldn’t hold it in. I jumped forward, hugged him tightly, and said, “I love you, yaar!”
Chapter 1: The First Spark
That was the beginning of us.
We started dating — simple coffee shops, long walks, evening calls. Arav was always ready to meet me, even if it was late or he was tired. He gave me his time, his attention, his presence. I loved how he noticed even my smallest moods.

He couldn’t bear to see me unhappy. He would do anything to make me smile — cancel meetings, bring me my favorite food, or just sit quietly holding my hand.
I knew he truly loved me. And my love for him grew deeper each day.
Chapter 2: Us — In Love
One day, on a breezy romantic evening, while we sat on a bench waiting for coffee, I looked into his eyes and said with a little smile, “Arav, we’ve been dating for so long… we both love each other… so, will you marry me?”
He laughed gently, took my hand and said, “I was thinking the same. Let’s talk to our parents.”
Luckily, both families agreed. And soon, we got married.
We had a beautiful start — honeymoon trips, long drives, even a foreign holiday. I felt like I was living a dream.
But slowly, things changed.
Arav became busy with his business. Meetings, travel, phone calls. I understood at first, but gradually, I started feeling ignored.
He would come home late, tired. I would wait for him, only to eat alone. My smiles faded, my words turned into complaints. The silence between us became louder than our talks.
I wanted the old Arav back — the one who used to wait outside the café before time, who used to notice my smallest expressions.
I started arguing often.
He tried to explain — “It’s just a phase, Meera. I’m doing it for us…”
But I couldn’t accept it. I felt unloved, forgotten.
One day, after a particularly big fight, I lost control. I shouted, “There’s nothing left between us now.” I said it with fire in my voice… but inside, my heart whispered, “Except the love I’m too tired to fight for anymore.”
Chapter 3: When Love Goes Quiet
I called the driver, packed nothing, and left for my parents’ home.
Arav tried to stop me. He stood at the door, eyes pleading. “Meera, please don’t go. Let’s talk.”
But I didn’t stop.


At my parents’ house, I cried all night. My parents were shocked.
“This is not how marriages work,” my mother said gently.
“We’ll call Arav tomorrow. Don’t take decisions in anger.”
Next day, Arav came. He looked tired and broken. He said sorry.
My parents tried to convince me too — “Don’t leave your home for small fights, beta.”
But I had made up my mind… or maybe my heart hadn’t healed yet.
Days passed. Arav called, messaged… even his parents tried.
But I didn’t respond.
Eventually, the calls stopped.
I lived like a guest in my own life — quiet, cold, neutral. But I never thought of divorce. Because somewhere deep inside… I still loved him.
Then, one day, Sarla, my maid, unknowingly changed everything.
She was always smiling, even while working hard every day. Her husband worked two shifts, they had two kids, barely any time for each other — yet, she never complained.
I asked her, “Sarla, your husband hardly gives you time. Don’t you feel upset?”
She smiled and replied, “Didi, love isn’t just about sitting together or going out. Love is understanding, respect, and doing our duties with faith.”
She continued, “He works hard for us. I work hard for our kids. This too is love. When he makes tea for me after work, or I press his tired feet… that is our romance.”
Her words hit me like lightning.
And yet… I wasn’t ready to accept them.
How can a woman live without love? Without time, touch, and togetherness?
We women are not born just to give birth to children, raise them, cook meals in the kitchen, and serve our husbands’ relatives with smiles, even when we’re hurting inside.
I had dreams too… I had my own identity.
And in that identity, my husband was supposed to be a part of my life, not my whole reason for existence.
For centuries, women have been taught to adjust, to remain silent, to put others first — and they called it love.
But for me… I believed love should also mean equality, emotion, presence.
Sarla didn’t know the storm that had started inside me.
She kept talking, unaware that every word was piercing deep.
“Didi,” she said gently, “socho agar kisi fauji ki patni bole — mat jao border pe, mujhe akela chhod ke. To phir kaun bachaayega desh?”
What if a soldier’s wife stops him from going to the border? Then who will protect the country?
“Aur ek doctor ki patni bole, mat karo late night duty. To kaun bachaayega kisi maa ke bacche ki jaan?”
And if a doctor’s wife says no late shifts — then who will save someone’s child?
“Kabhi kabhi hume dusron ke liye bhi jeena padta hai, Didi. Pyaar har waqt saath rehne ka naam nahi hota.”
(Sometimes we must live for others too. Love isn’t only about always being together.)
Her words were hammering me, and I couldn’t listen anymore.
I stood still — silent on the outside, but breaking inside.
A memory flashed suddenly.
I was just a little girl. My father used to travel for months — far away, working hard to earn for us. There were no mobile phones then, no daily calls, just waiting.
And still, every time he left, my mother smiled and waved goodbye with hope in her eyes.
I remember asking her once,
“Maa, don’t you feel sad?”
And she had said,
“Of course I do. But he’s doing it for us. I’ll welcome him with a smile — and love, when he returns.”
And when he did return…
It was like Diwali in our home. My mother would light diyas, cook sweets, dress up — not out of duty, but out of pure love.
I had never seen her complain. Not once.
I sat down, slowly, as if the weight of truth was too heavy for my knees.
Sarla is right, I thought.
I had forgotten that love wears many forms — presence, absence, sacrifice, support, and sometimes waiting silently without resentment.
Maybe… I had made my love too loud.
Maybe, Arav had made his love too quiet.
But maybe — we both were loving in our own ways.
I looked at Sarla, who was now folding clothes, humming again.
So calm. So ordinary.
And yet, her understanding of love was far more extraordinary than mine.
Sarla Taught Me “Love doesn’t always come with flowers and dates. Sometimes, love wears the face of responsibility. Sometimes, love is quiet”.
Chapter 4: I Love You, Phir se
I sat alone that night, tears running down my face.
And then, with shaking hands, I called Arav.
He picked up after two rings. His voice… soft, unsure.
I whispered, “I love you, yaar…”
This time, with pain. With truth. With humility.
“Have you forgotten me? Don’t you remember anything? I tried… but now I can’t live alone. Please come take me back…”
Then I paused, smiled through my tears, and added, “No… don’t come. I’m coming myself.”
I rushed to the hall, asked the driver to start the car. My parents were shocked. “Where are you going, Meera?”
I just said, “Home.”
Even Sarla understood. She nodded silently, her eyes full of joy.
I didn’t pack anything. Just carried myself.
When I reached our flat, the door opened even before I rang the bell.
Arav stood there.
He looked like he hadn’t slept well for days. His hair was slightly messy, eyes tired but searching. He had the same T-shirt he often wore on Sundays — the one I once teased him about, calling it his “lazy charm.”
We looked at each other — silent, still.
I could smell that familiar scent of home — a mix of sandalwood incense, old books, and faint traces of his cologne. The air inside was warm. Familiar. It pulled me in before he even spoke.
My heart was racing — fast, loud, like it wanted to jump into his arms before I could.
His eyes softened the moment he saw me, as if trying to believe I was really there.
I stepped forward and hugged him tightly.
He froze for a second… then wrapped his arms around me, slowly but firmly — like holding something he had almost lost.
“I’m sorry… for not understanding, for leaving, for all those missed calls,” I whispered, my voice shaking.
I felt him breathe against my shoulder — deep and heavy, like he had been holding his breath for weeks.
“I never stopped loving you,” he whispered back.
We didn’t need more words. We just held each other in the doorway — not as perfect lovers, but as two people choosing each other again.
Later, we sat by the window, sipping tea — like old times. The cup trembled a little in my hand. He noticed.
“Still nervous?” he asked gently.
“No,” I smiled. “Just… feeling everything, all at once.”
And then I said, “This time, let’s love not like the movies… but like real life. Patient. Grown-up. Forgiving.”
Love doesn’t always need loud promises or perfect moments.
Sometimes, it needs a second chance.
A quiet return.
A hand held again.
A voice that says — “I love you… again.”

The last train to Varanasi always arrived at 4:17 a.m.
It did not matter whether the monsoon flooded the tracks or the winter fog thickened like milk over the river. At 4:17 a.m., the train would groan into the station, metal shrieking against metal, carrying with it the scent of faraway cities and the soft fatigue of travelers who had not slept well.
Arjun had memorized its rhythm.
He stood every morning near the chipped blue pillar at Platform Three, a red scarf wrapped around his neck even in the warmer months. He would pretend to read the headlines of yesterday’s newspaper, but his eyes were always fixed on the doors of the second general compartment.
He was waiting for someone who had promised to return.
Five years earlier, Meera had boarded that same train with a small suitcase and an ocean of stubborn hope. She had won a scholarship to study classical music in Mumbai, and Arjun had been proud of her—so proud that his chest had hurt.
“Three years,” she had said, her voice trembling between excitement and fear. “I’ll be back before you know it.”
He had laughed, pretending it was nothing. “Three years is nothing.”
But three years had stretched, thinned, and frayed like old cloth.
At first, letters came twice a week. Meera wrote about the dizzying pace of Mumbai—the crowded local trains, the salt in the air near Marine Drive, the way the city refused to sleep. She wrote about her guru, about rehearsals that lasted until midnight, about her dream of singing at the grand auditorium of Shanmukhananda Hall.
Arjun replied faithfully. He described the mornings by the Ganges River, how the sun would spill gold over the ghats. He told her about the old chai seller who still asked about “the singing girl.” He never wrote about the loneliness that had begun to take root inside him like a stubborn weed.
In the fourth year, the letters slowed.
In the fifth, they stopped.
There was no dramatic goodbye, no final explanation. Just silence.
Arjun had searched for her name online at the local cyber café. He found videos—grainy recordings of a young woman in a simple sari, her voice rising like prayer. He recognized her instantly. The tilt of her head. The way her fingers curved in the air as if conducting invisible threads of emotion.
She was no longer just Meera from the narrow lanes of Varanasi. She was Meera Rao, a rising classical vocalist. Her name appeared on posters. Her concerts were announced on social media pages he did not fully understand.
He watched every performance he could find. Each time she closed her eyes to sing, he wondered if she ever thought of the boy who had once waited outside her house with a borrowed bicycle and two cups of tea.
And so he came to the station every morning at 4:17 a.m.
Because hope is a stubborn thing. It does not care for logic.
On a particularly cold morning in January, fog wrapped the platform in a gray hush. The train arrived right on time, as it always did. Arjun barely breathed as the doors opened and passengers spilled out, rubbing their arms against the chill.
An elderly couple.
A man with a sleeping child.
A student dragging a guitar case.
And then—
A woman stepped down slowly, adjusting the strap of her bag.
Her hair was shorter now, grazing her shoulders. She wore a long woolen coat over a simple kurta. There was a tired elegance about her, a quiet confidence that hadn’t been there before.
Arjun’s heart slammed against his ribs.
It was her.
For a moment, he could not move. The world seemed to narrow to the sound of her boots on the concrete. She looked around the platform with searching eyes, as if expecting something familiar to appear.
Then her gaze met his.
The years between them cracked open.
“Arjun?” she whispered.
He dropped the newspaper.
“Meera.”
Her name felt fragile in his mouth, like a memory that might dissolve if spoken too loudly.
They stood there, two people separated by five years of silence, and neither knew how to bridge the distance.
“You’re here,” he said finally, hating how inadequate it sounded.
“I’m here,” she replied.
The announcement system crackled overhead. Porters shouted. Life moved around them, indifferent to their reunion.
“Why didn’t you write?” he asked before he could stop himself.
Meera looked down at her hands. “I tried. Many times. But I didn’t know what to say.”
He swallowed the bitterness that had been his only companion for so long. “You could have said anything.”
“I know.”
She lifted her eyes to his, and he saw something he had not expected: regret.
“Can we walk?” she asked softly.
They left the station and headed toward the ghats. The city was just waking up. Priests prepared for morning prayers. The river shimmered under the pale light of dawn.
They sat on the steps overlooking the Ganges, the same place where they had once spent entire afternoons talking about impossible dreams.
“I thought I would come back sooner,” Meera began. “After my course ended, I was offered more opportunities. Concerts. Recordings. It felt like everything I had ever wanted was finally within reach.”
“I saw,” Arjun said quietly. “You’re famous now.”
She gave a faint smile. “Not really. Just… visible.”
Silence settled between them again, but this time it felt less hostile.
“Why didn’t you come to my last concert in Varanasi?” she asked suddenly.
He stared at the water. “I didn’t know you were coming.”
Her brow furrowed. “I sent you an invitation.”
“I never got it.”
Understanding dawned slowly on her face. “I sent it to your old address.”
He laughed softly, though there was no humor in it. “I moved after Ma passed away.”
Meera’s breath caught. “Arjun… I’m so sorry. I didn’t know.”
He nodded. “There’s a lot you don’t know.”
The statement hung heavy between them.
He wanted to tell her everything—about the nights he had sat by his mother’s hospital bed, about how he had whispered Meera’s songs into the darkness as if they were prayers. About how he had almost boarded a train to Mumbai once, ticket in hand, only to tear it up at the last moment because he was afraid of what he might find.
But the words felt too large.
“And you?” he asked instead. “Are you happy?”
Meera took a long time to answer.
“I thought success would feel like arriving,” she said slowly. “Like stepping into a room where all the lights are on and everyone is waiting for you. And sometimes it does. When I’m on stage, when the music flows through me… I feel alive.”
She paused.
“But when the applause fades and I go back to an empty apartment, I realize I left pieces of myself behind.”
He looked at her then.
“In Varanasi?” he asked.
“In you,” she said.
The honesty in her voice struck him harder than any apology could have.
“I was afraid,” she continued. “Afraid that if I came back too soon, I would never leave again. That I would choose comfort over ambition. And I didn’t trust myself to balance both.”
“So you chose ambition,” he said.
“Yes.”
“And now?”
She met his gaze steadily. “Now I don’t want to choose between my dreams and the people I love.”
The sun had begun to rise fully, painting the sky in shades of gold and rose. The river caught the light like molten metal.
“I don’t expect you to forgive me,” Meera said. “Or to wait for me again. I just… I needed to see you. To tell you that the silence wasn’t because you didn’t matter. It was because you mattered too much.”
Arjun felt something inside him shift—a knot loosening after years of tension.
“I hated you,” he admitted, his voice trembling. “For a long time, I hated you for leaving. For not writing. For making me feel like I wasn’t enough.”
Tears welled in her eyes, but she did not look away.
“And then,” he continued, “I realized I wasn’t really angry at you. I was angry at myself. For building my entire world around someone else’s return.”
Meera reached out hesitantly, her fingers brushing his.
“I never asked you to wait,” she whispered.
“No,” he agreed. “You didn’t.”
They sat there, hands barely touching, both aware that love had not disappeared. It had simply changed shape.
“What will you do now?” he asked.
“I’ve been invited to teach here for a year,” she said. “At a small music school near the old market. It’s not as glamorous as Mumbai. But it feels… right.”
“For good?” he pressed.
She shook her head gently. “I don’t know. My life is still tied to concerts, to travel. I can’t promise permanence.”
Arjun nodded slowly.
Five years ago, he would have begged her to stay. He would have clung to her words like lifelines.
Now, he felt different.
“I don’t need permanence,” he said at last. “I need honesty. If we try again, it has to be as two people with their own paths. Not as one person waiting for the other to come home.”
A small, hopeful smile spread across her face. “You’ve changed.”
“So have you.”
A group of children ran past them, laughing, their voices echoing against the stone steps. Life moved forward, as it always did.
“Will you come to my class today?” Meera asked suddenly. “I’m introducing the students to a new raga. I could use a familiar face in the room.”
Arjun hesitated only a second before nodding.
They rose together and began walking back through the narrow lanes of Varanasi. Shopkeepers lifted shutters. The smell of fresh jalebis filled the air. A temple bell rang somewhere in the distance.
For the first time in years, Arjun did not feel like he was waiting.
He did not know what the future would bring. Perhaps Meera would leave again. Perhaps he would decide to travel with her someday. Perhaps they would discover that love, though strong, was not enough to bridge the differences that time had carved between them.
But as they walked side by side, their shoulders occasionally brushing, he understood something profound:
Love was not about holding someone in place.
It was about walking beside them, even if the road curved in unexpected ways.
When they reached the small music school, Meera paused at the entrance. She looked at him, her eyes shining with a mixture of fear and hope.
“Thank you for coming to the station all those mornings,” she said quietly.
He blinked. “You knew?”
She nodded. “The chai seller told me. I called him once… just to ask about you.”
Arjun felt a laugh rise in his chest, warm and surprised.
“So you were watching from afar too,” he said.
“Always,” she replied.
Inside the classroom, a dozen young students waited with eager faces. Meera stepped to the front, her posture straightening, her presence transforming as it always did when music claimed her.
Arjun took a seat at the back.
She closed her eyes and began to sing.
The first note filled the room, rich and resonant. It carried the weight of longing and the promise of return. It carried five years of silence and the fragile hope of a new beginning.
And as Arjun listened, he realized that the train at 4:17 a.m. had not just brought Meera back to Varanasi.
It had brought him back to himself.

I don’t remember when he became important to me.

There was no exact moment I could point to. No sudden realization. No dramatic beginning. He entered my life quietly, like something that was never meant to stay and yet never truly left.

The first time I saw him, he was just a stranger walking past me on an ordinary afternoon. The world around me was unchanged — the same road, the same air, the same distant sounds of people living their lives.

And yet, for reasons I still don’t understand, I noticed him.

He was taller than everyone around him, his presence calm, distant. He wasn’t smiling. He wasn’t trying to be seen.

But I saw him anyway.

I remember looking away quickly, almost annoyed at myself. I wasn’t the kind of girl who noticed boys. I wasn’t the kind of girl who looked twice.

But that day, something in me did.

I told myself it meant nothing.

I didn’t know then how wrong I was.

He returned into my life slowly, without warning.

First as a name.

Then as a conversation.

And eventually, as someone I couldn’t imagine my days without.

His name was Aarav.

Talking to him felt different from talking to anyone else. With others, I was careful. Measured. Afraid of saying too much or too little. Afraid of being misunderstood.

But with him, words came easily.

He listened. Not just to what I said, but to what I didn’t say. He understood silences. He noticed small changes in my voice. He remembered things I had forgotten mentioning.

He made me feel seen.

And without realizing it, I began to depend on that feeling.

One day, in the middle of an ordinary conversation, I told him something I thought would protect me.

“We should never fall in love with each other.”

He agreed without hesitation.

I smiled when he said it.

I didn’t realize my heart had already betrayed me.

He became part of my everyday life in ways I never intended.

In crowded hallways, my eyes searched for him automatically. I would find him standing among others, unaware of the way my world softened just by seeing him exist.

Sometimes, he would notice me too.

And when he did, he smiled.

It wasn’t a special smile. Not one that meant anything more than friendship.

But to me, it meant everything.

He called me cute when I was upset. He teased me when I was quiet. He spoke to me like I mattered.

And I held onto those moments longer than I should have.

There were days I hated myself for it.

Days I told myself I was imagining things. That I was creating feelings where none existed.

But no matter how much I tried, my heart refused to listen.

Because loving him didn’t feel like a choice.

It felt like something that had already decided itself.

There was one afternoon I never managed to forget.

It had been raining that day, the sky heavy and gray, the air filled with the quiet sound of falling water. Everything felt slower. Softer.

I had gone to see him for a reason I can no longer remember.

Maybe I just needed to see him.

We stood close, talking the way we always did. Nothing had changed. Nothing was different.

And then, suddenly, he leaned forward and pressed a soft kiss against my cheek.

It lasted less than a second.

But my heart didn’t understand time.

It stopped. Completely.

In that moment, everything inside me shifted.

Not because of the kiss itself.

But because of what I wished it meant.

He pulled away quickly, apologizing, his voice careful.

I smiled and told him it was okay.

I told him it didn’t matter.

But it did.

It mattered more than anything had ever mattered before.

Later that day, he called me again.

“I don’t want you to misunderstand,” he said gently.

And just like that, my heart broke in a way no one could see.

Because I had never said anything.

And yet, he was already rejecting something I hadn’t confessed.

After that, nothing changed.

And yet, everything did.

He was still there.

Still talking to me.

Still laughing with me.

Still calling me cute.

But I knew now.

I knew where I stood in his life.

I knew what I meant to him.

And what I didn’t.

I learned how to smile while hiding the ache inside my chest. I learned how to pretend his presence didn’t affect me.

I became good at pretending.

Too good.

Sometimes, I wondered what was wrong with me.

Why I wasn’t enough.

Why he could love others so easily but never me.

I never asked him those questions.

Because I was afraid of hearing the answers.

Time passed.

Life moved forward the way it always does, without caring who it leaves behind.

He became part of my past.

But he never became part of my forgetfulness.

I met new people. I lived new days. I smiled in ways that looked real enough to convince everyone around me.

I told him once that I had moved on.

He believed me.

I don’t know why that hurt more than anything else.

Maybe because it proved how easy it was for him to let me go.

Maybe because it proved how invisible my love had always been.

Even now, sometimes I hear his voice in my memories. Calm. Familiar. Safe.

And I realize something I spent years trying to deny.

He was never mine.

Not even for a moment.

I was just someone who loved him quietly, while he lived his life unaware of the way he had become my entire world.

He didn’t break me.

He didn’t betray me.

He simply never loved me.

And somehow, that hurt more than anything else ever could.

Because there was nothing to blame.

Nothing to hate.

Nothing to fight against.

Just a love that existed alone.

Sometimes, I wonder if he ever thinks of me.

If he ever realizes how deeply I cared.

If he ever knew that he was the first person who made my heart feel alive.

But I never ask.

Because some answers only make the silence louder.

And so, I live my life the way I was always meant to.

With memories I cannot erase.

With feelings I cannot explain.

With a love that was never returned.

And sometimes, late at night, when the world is quiet and no one is watching, I allow myself to admit the truth I hide from everyone else.

I never stopped loving him.

I just learned how to live without being loved back.

And that is the cruelest kind of love there is.

The kind that stays.

Even when the person is gone.

When I first opened my eyes in broad daylight,
I saw the face of a beautiful creature holding me with a gentle smile,
Eyes were sparkling bright,
A smile on her lips so pure and light.

When she lifted me with her adorable hands,
I held her lips to feel her visible stand.

Her smile was so gentle, her eyes were so tender,
I saw in her eyes and borrowed her smile as a vendor.

Her eyes were so sparkling and full of tears,
It was so easy for me to understand the pain she had to bear.

When she kissed my lips with an adorable touch,
I felt overjoyed by the cadence a lot.

When I held her breasts with my tender hands,

To quench my thirst and fill my can.
My famished can starts to fill with milk,
And I engrossed myself in a beautiful dream.

As I filled my can, I went to sleep,
She patted my back, and I fell into a deep sleep.

I slept for long, very long and long,
Until my can was empty, so strong.

I yelled for milk by crying high, 
The lady came quickly with a deep sigh.

That was the encounter with my first love,
When I first saw the world in a woman’s heart.
