प्रथम खंड: तिरस्कार की राख
उत्तर प्रदेश के पूर्वांचल का वह अनाम सा जनपद, जहाँ की हवाओं में आज भी सामंतवाद की सोंधी और कड़वी गंध घुली हुई थी। 'लोहियापुर' गाँव के क्षितिज पर जब सूर्य अपनी अंतिम लालिमा बिखेर रहा होता, तो ऊसर जमीन पर पड़ने वाली लंबी परछाइयां मानों सदियों के दमन की गवाही देती थीं। इसी गाँव की एक संकरी, कीचड़ भरी गली के अंतिम छोर पर 'फूलमती' का वास था।
फूलमती का जीवन संघर्ष की उस स्याही से लिखा गया था, जिसे अभाव की धूप सुखा नहीं पाई थी। वह एक ऐसी स्त्री थी जिसने अपनी देह पर मजदूरी के निशान और अपनी आत्मा पर जातिगत उपहास के घाव सहे थे। उसके लिए 'लोकतंत्र' शब्द रेडियो पर गूंजने वाली एक अमूर्त ध्वनि मात्र थी, जिसका उसकी भूख और नंगे पैरों से कोई संबंध न था।
वह वैशाख की एक दाहक दुपहर थी। गाँव के ऊंचे रसूखदार ठाकुर भीम सिंह के द्वार पर सन्नाटा था, जिसे केवल वहां लगे नीम के पेड़ पर बैठे कौवों की कांव-कांव तोड़ रही थी। फूलमती वहां अपनी रुकी हुई मजदूरी मांगने गई थी। उसकी बेटी बीमार थी, और घर में अन्न का एक दाना न था।
"सरकार, बिटिया को तेज तप (बुखार) है। पिछले हफ्ते की मजूरी मिल जाती तो दवा लाती," उसने अत्यंत विनीत स्वर में, अपनी फटी साड़ी के पल्लू को ठीक करते हुए कहा।
भीम सिंह ने हुक्का गुड़गुड़ाते हुए अपनी लाल आँखों से उसे देखा। "फूलमती, तू भूल रही है कि ये चौखट किसकी है। मजूरी तब मिलेगी जब हिसाब होगा। अभी जा यहाँ से, हवा मत रोक हमारी।"
जब फूलमती ने दोबारा विनती की, तो अहंकार की वह दीवार ढह गई। भीम सिंह के छोटे बेटे ने आव देखा न ताव, फूलमती को धक्का दे दिया। वह तपती हुई जमीन पर जा गिरी। उसके हाथ छिल गए, और साड़ी धूल से धूसर हो गई। वहां खड़े लोग ठहाके लगाकर हंसने लगे। उस हँसी में जो क्रूरता थी, उसने फूलमती के भीतर के 'मौन' को हमेशा के लिए दफन कर दिया।
उसने अपनी आंखों के आंसू पोंछे नहीं, बल्कि उन्हें पी लिया। गिरकर जब वह खड़ी हुई, तो उसके चेहरे पर दीनता नहीं, बल्कि एक भयावह शांति थी। उसने वहां बिखरी हुई अपनी गागर उठाई और बिना पीछे मुड़े चल दी। उस दिन 'लोहियापुर' ने एक मजदूर को खो दिया था और एक 'विद्रोही' को जन्म दिया था।
द्वितीय खंड: चेतना का जागरण
महीने बीतते गए। गाँव में प्रधानी के चुनावों की सुगबुगाहट शुरू हुई। इस बार सरकार ने एक बड़ा उलटफेर किया था—सीट 'महिला आरक्षित' (अनुसूचित जाति) घोषित हो गई थी। गाँव के दबंगों में खलबली मच गई। उन्हें एक ऐसी महिला की तलाश थी जो केवल कागजों पर 'प्रधान' हो और सत्ता की बागडोर उनके हाथों में रहे।
भीम सिंह की नजर फूलमती पर पड़ी। उन्हें लगा कि वह अनपढ़ है, गरीब है और उसे डराकर काम निकाला जा सकता है। उन्होंने फूलमती के घर प्रस्ताव भेजा।
फूलमती ने सुना, मुस्कराई और स्वीकार कर लिया। उसने नामांकन भरा। विरोधियों ने उसे डराने के लिए उसके छप्पर में आग लगवाई, उसके पति को डराया, लेकिन वह अडिग रही। उसने गाँव की हर उस दहलीज पर दस्तक दी जहाँ औरतें चूल्हे के धुएं में अपनी जिंदगी बिता रही थीं।
"बहनों, ये वोट कागज़ का टुकड़ा नहीं है। ये उस अपमान का बदला है जो हम हर रोज सहती हैं। अगर आज हमने अपना प्रतिनिधि नहीं चुना, तो कल हमारी बेटियों को भी वही अपमान सहना होगा जो मैंने उस दुपहर सहा था।"
उसकी वाणी में जो सत्य था, उसने गाँव के समीकरण बदल दिए। मतदान के दिन, चुपचाप घूंघट काढ़े महिलाओं ने वह क्रांति कर दी जिसकी कल्पना किसी ने नहीं की थी। फूलमती भारी मतों से चुनाव जीत गई।
तृतीय खंड: प्रशासन और प्रतिशोध
शपथ ग्रहण के दिन, जब फूलमती ब्लॉक ऑफिस पहुँची, तो वहां का वातावरण असहज था। अधिकारी उसे कुर्सी देने में हिचकिचा रहे थे। भीम सिंह का कारिंदा फाइलों का बंडल लेकर खड़ा था।
"प्रधान जी, यहाँ अंगूठा लगा दीजिये, बाकी काम हम देख लेंगे," उसने आदेशात्मक स्वर में कहा।
फूलमती ने कुर्सी की हत्थी को कसकर पकड़ा और उन फाइलों को एक तरफ धकेल दिया। "साहब, अंगूठा तो हम नहीं लगाएंगे। हमने अब अक्षर पढ़ना सीख लिया है। और हाँ, अब से प्रधानी चौपाल पर नहीं, पंचायत भवन में होगी।"
पूरे ब्लॉक में सन्नाटा पसर गया। अगले दो वर्षों में फूलमती ने गाँव का नक्शा बदल दिया। उसने उन रास्तों पर ईंटें बिछवाईं जहाँ कभी दलितों को चप्पल पहनकर चलने की अनुमति नहीं थी। उसने कन्या विद्यालय की नींव रखी और मिड-डे मील में होने वाले भ्रष्टाचार को जड़ से खत्म किया।
उसकी ख्याति अब जनपद की सीमाओं को पार कर लखनऊ के गलियारों तक पहुँचने लगी थी। वह अब केवल एक 'प्रधान' नहीं थी; वह 'परिवर्तन' का प्रतीक बन चुकी थी।
चतुर्थ खंड: सत्ता का शिखर
साल 2026 के विधानसभा चुनाव करीब थे। प्रदेश की राजनीति में एक नया उभार आ रहा था। एक बड़ी क्षेत्रीय पार्टी ने फूलमती को 'महिला सशक्तिकरण' का चेहरा बनाकर चुनावी समर में उतारने का निर्णय लिया।
उसे उस निर्वाचन क्षेत्र से टिकट मिला जहाँ जातिगत राजनीति की जड़ें बहुत गहरी थीं। उसके सामने वही भीम सिंह का परिवार था, जिनके पास अपार धन और बाहुबल था। चुनाव प्रचार के दौरान फूलमती पर हमले हुए, उसे 'नीच' और 'अछूत' कहकर संबोधित किया गया, लेकिन उसकी जनसभाओं में उमड़ने वाला जनसैलाब कुछ और ही कह रहा था।
अपनी अंतिम चुनावी रैली में, लखनऊ के ऐतिहासिक मैदान में लाखों की भीड़ के सामने फूलमती खड़ी थी। उसके सिर पर सूती साड़ी का पल्लू था और माथे पर आत्मसम्मान की चमक।
"भाइयों और बहनों, मुझे राजनीति का व्याकरण नहीं आता। मैं तो बस इतना जानती हूँ कि जिस मिट्टी ने मुझे अपमानित किया, उसी मिट्टी ने मुझे लड़ने की शक्ति भी दी। मैं यहाँ सत्ता भोगने नहीं, उस सिंहासन को 'शुद्ध' करने आई हूँ जिस पर बैठकर लोग गरीबों की कराह को भूल जाते हैं। मेरी जीत मेरी नहीं, उन करोड़ों पसीने से लथपथ चेहरों की होगी जिन्हें आज तक अनदेखा किया गया।"
परिणाम आए, तो राजनीति के पंडितों के सारे गणित फेल हो गए। फूलमती ने रिकॉर्ड मतों से जीत हासिल की।
पंचम खंड: सवेरे की पहली किरण
आज विधानभवन की सीढ़ियां फूलों से सजी थीं। फूलमती, जो कभी धूल में धकेली गई थी, आज एक गरिमामयी सफेद साड़ी में वहां पहुँची। जब उसने 'मंत्री' पद की शपथ ली, तो उसकी आवाज में कँपकँपी नहीं, बल्कि एक दृढ़ संकल्प था।
शपथ लेने के बाद, वह सीधे अपने गाँव 'लोहियापुर' गई। वह भीम सिंह के द्वार पर रुकी। भीम सिंह आज वृद्ध और शक्तिहीन थे। फूलमती कार से उतरी, उनके पास गई और शांति से बोली—
"ठाकुर साहब, आज हिसाब पूरा हुआ। उस दिन आपने मेरी मजूरी नहीं दी थी, लेकिन आज देखिए, समय ने मुझे पूरे प्रदेश की सेवा की जिम्मेदारी दे दी है। राजनीति में न कोई ऊंचा होता है, न नीचा—ऊंचा वही है जो सबके काम आए।"
भीम सिंह की गर्दन झुक गई। यह एक व्यक्ति की दूसरे पर जीत नहीं थी, बल्कि यह 'समता' की 'सामंतवाद' पर जीत थी।
फूलमती का सफर अभी खत्म नहीं हुआ था। वह जानती थी कि उसे अभी हज़ारों 'फूलमती' को उनके हक के लिए खड़ा करना है। वह उत्तर प्रदेश की राजनीति का वह नया अध्याय थी, जिसे अब कोई मिटा नहीं सकता था।

The markets in these Chinese towns are exhaustingly huge, you could walk for miles and still be seeing unique designs in every window pane. The wide roads stretched infinitely, flanked by tall glassy high-rises on either side, their reflections making the summer heat feel even sharper.

It was well past noon on the hot summer streets of Guzhen town. We had walked for miles but weren’t close to finding what we were looking for. I was walking ahead in my quest to cover more and my friends were closely trailing behind. Between the patches of tree shades and sharp sunrays, I was walking faster when I felt a freezing cold hand of a child hold my hand and run diagonally across. Involuntarily I just started running along the path he already was on. He dragged me for a few meters and took me inside a store, a one that was selling outdoor and solar lighting.

Once inside it felt much better than the street outside, the A/C running at a pleasant low. The kid left my hand and went and sat a small study table in the store’s corner. By the time I realized I was in a place which had nothing I wanted, my whole entourage had hurriedly followed me inside. A friend who was a local contact, a designated translator, another friend who was the client and a very dear friend of mine. All these five people inside this store and none having the slightest clue why we were inside other than following me. I glanced at the kid after picking up my senses, the boy of about four in a white tee and shorts stood before me. He gestured his parents who obviously owned the store to sell us something.

I was confused as to what this all meant but even in this confusion of sorts my parental instincts kicked in. The kid standing before me started to resemble my younger son about the same age then. Big broad forehead the twinkle in the eyes and the naughty smile. He walked up to me again and with his delicate pair of hands held my hand up and smiled, as if asking me to buy something from their store.

I had no good need for anything and neither did they look like they needed any business from me. But I still bought a solar powered light which had a camera installed on it. And I asked the kid’s mother to buy the kid some ice cream and handed her the biggest bill of their currency I was carrying. It wasn’t like it was a struggling store, everything was well placed and organized. The temperature inside indicated people working at full strength and could afford the power bills.

And once out of the store I walked much slower, more contemplative of the future I do not see. The kid’s efforts needed appreciation is what I kept saying aloud on our way back. But deep down it was nothing more than the lingering thought of my son, the same age yet walking a different path. He is nonverbal autistic. My son’s life would never be like that of this Chinese counterpart of his. His life will take a different shape. And mine as a father, will always follow.

The college campus stretched over ten acres and our company was awarded the tender for the new block. The institution had strict rules and we had to work in non operational hours. It was one of those sites that grew on me.

“Someone call up the plant, the vehicles are taking too long.” I yelled on the radio.

“ Sir, vehicle 15 and 16 loaded. Further vehicles will be dispatched from plant 2C.” Responded one of the white helmets from our team.

“QC! batch samples accordingly. I don’t want fuck ups like last time.” I ordered.

“Copy sir.” Came the response.

I clipped the walkie back in my waist band. The boom pump shot jets of concrete while reeling back at regularly spaced intervals. The diesel engines roared in the background, the concrete vibrators shaking the reinforcement under my safety boots. The commotion of the yellow helmets was getting a bit overwhelming for me. I gestured the pump operator to slow down the flow, un strapped the safety harness and gestured my boys that I will be downstairs for a while.

It was late in the January evening and despite running around for the past eight hours I felt the cold settling in. I walked around the block away from all the noise. I looked for a quiet corner under a tree by the internal campus road. Took off my helmet splashed some water over my face and settled on the curb stone. I lowered the volume on my walkie, there was too much noise on the radio communication. The road wore a deserted look as it was a holiday on the campus.

The only person I could see was a young boy walking down the road towards me. He wore a shirt well ironed on a fresh pair of blue jeans paired with leather boots. He was over the phone, smiling momentarily and looking around. Playing with the keys in his hands, he walked in a boisterous gait. As he got closer to where I was, he started to look irritated but was still keeping his tone pleasant over the phone.

I leaned back against the wall pulled out my phone and scrolled through the messages. After a while I raised my head to see a girl walking in the same direction. The girl was of a petite figure, a dainty gait, smiling playfully as she spoke over her phone. I turned around to see the boy, he had crossed my position and was close to the bike parking. I looked the other way and I realized the boy and the girl were on the phone with each other.

Mindful of who was watching them they maintained a safe distance in the campus. The boy conscious of his presence, the girl oblivious of hers. She probably was telling him she wouldn’t be able to meet him. He hung up his phone lowered his head and kept walking.

The girl playfully laughing at her prank picked up pace rushed to him and held his hand. He turned around pleasantly surprised at the shock and both of them laughed at her joke. They held hands and walked to the bike parking.

He kick started a red Royal Enfield and the girl hopped back on. They rode past me I smiled and the boy gave a slight nod as he crossed me. Looking back at them again I could see the sun setting slowly as it felt like they were riding straight into it.

I said a little prayer under my breath and heaved a sigh.

I got up, dusted my worn out dusty, denims and lit my cigarette. With the corner of my eyes I could see a few security guards rushing towards me. And when I raised my head I could see a couple of white helmets rushing at the guards. By the time they got up close, the guards took note of my position. Saluted me and left.

The white helmets turned to me and said,

“ Sir, you hadn’t been responding on the walkie. Should we switch from SCC to regular. The beams are done.”

I lowered my head to check the volume. I raised the volume.

“ Yeah change the batch. I’ll be joining in a minute.”

I finished my cigarette put on my helmet strapped it under my chin and headed back to all the action.

I looked up my watch, it had been only ten minutes down there but I had traveled back and forth a decade.

title.stringValue: The Bridge Between Revenge and Justice

content.stringValue:
It was morning. Soft sunlight was falling in the courtyard of the house, and inside one room there was complete chaos.

“Mummy! Where is my black jeans?”
Nagendra had already thrown the clothes from the cupboard onto the floor. His bag was lying open, and on his face there was both nervousness and excitement together.

A voice came from the kitchen,
“It’s on the bed! Look properly!”

He turned around. The jeans was right there.
He smiled lightly at himself.

Today he was leaving his village for the first time — for studies, for dreams, maybe for his identity.

As soon as he put the bag on his shoulder, his father’s loud voice came,
“Hurry up! The bus will leave!”

Nagendra quickly went and touched his father’s feet. His father placed his hand on his head. He didn’t say anything… but the weight of that hand felt like a blessing.

The road to the bus stand was short, but that day it felt strangely long.

As soon as he sat in the bus, he looked out of the window. The village was slowly being left behind.

“In the city I will study properly… see new places… make new friends… and one day I will return after becoming something.”

Thinking all this, the bus reached Deoghar.

The city was completely different.

Noise.
Crowd.
New faces.
New air.

Everything was unfamiliar to him, but somewhere in his heart there was a strange happiness.

First, he stopped a toto.
“Brother, will you go to Satsang?”

The toto started moving. Throughout the way, Nagendra kept looking at everything like a child. Big boards, bright shops, crowded streets — everything felt new to him.

After reaching Satsang, he paid and asked someone for his friend Aman’s address. Holding his bag carefully, he started walking on the road.

And then—

Thud!

He collided with someone.

Books scattered on the ground.

“I’m really sorry!” Nagendra quickly bent down and started picking up the books.

“Can’t you see? I was coming from the front!” the girl said angrily.

When Nagendra looked up—

For a moment, everything slowed down.

Her hair was moving slightly in the wind. There was anger in her eyes… but there was also a different kind of shine.

“How did I not see such a beautiful girl…” he thought to himself.

Then he immediately corrected himself—
“No. I have come here to study. Nothing else.”

“Hey hero! Where are you lost?” the girl waved her hand.

But by then, Nagendra was already lost — in his thoughts.

When he came back to his senses, the girl had left.

He whispered to himself,
“Who knows… if we’ll ever meet again.”

And then he walked toward Aman’s house.

“Aman! I’m here!”

The door opened. Aman came out, was shocked for a second… then laughed.

“Good that you came. Go get shampoo from the shop.”

Nagendra stopped.
“Did I come here to work?”

“Just bring it, bro!” Aman laughed.

Nagendra smiled too.

The city was new… but the friendship was old.

In the evening they went out a little. Nagendra thought they would roam around. But Aman bought vegetables on the way.

“That’s it? This was roaming?” Nagendra asked.

“That’s enough for today,” Aman replied casually.

At night they cooked together. Sat and ate together. There was tiredness, but there was hope in the heart.

While eating, Aman asked,
“Which coaching will you join?”

“We’ll see,” Nagendra said.

The next day they went to check coaching institutes. They liked two places. But hearing the fees, Nagendra became quiet.

“It’s out of budget…” he said softly.

Aman joked,
“Then study online.”

They both laughed. Nagendra didn’t even have a smartphone.

“Then what will you do?” Aman asked.

Nagendra stayed silent for a few seconds.

Just then his eyes fell on the coaching gate.

The same girl.

The one he had collided with.

She was laughing and entering with her friend.

A slight smile appeared on Nagendra’s face.

“I’ll take admission here,” he said firmly.

Aman was shocked.
“You just said you don’t have money?”

“It will be managed,” Nagendra replied.

But he didn’t tell the real reason.

That day, Nagendra didn’t just join a coaching institute—

He chose a new turn in his story.
And maybe in his life.

The next day, as Nagendra was getting ready to go to coaching, Aman said,
“Listen bro, you came here to study. Don’t get distracted in the name of a girl.”

Nagendra replied,
“You worry too much. Don’t think so much.”

“I won’t do anything like that…”
Nagendra said to himself, as if calming his own fear.

He left for coaching.

On the way, thousands of thoughts ran in his mind.

“How will the first day be?”
“What if sir asks me too many questions?”
“And that girl… will she come?”
“Did I take admission for the wrong reason?”
“Later people will say — he ruined his future for a girl…”

While thinking all this, his eyes suddenly fell ahead.

The same girl.

The same face.

The same fast walk.

Simran.

She was walking ahead of him on the same road.

Nagendra said nothing. He just silently followed.

Simran felt that someone was behind her. She increased her speed and reached the coaching gate.

When she turned back—

It was the same boy.

“Are you following me?” she asked firmly.

“I study in the same coaching,” Nagendra replied awkwardly.

“Since when?”

“Since yesterday… I took admission yesterday.”

Simran said nothing and went inside.

Days passed.

Slowly, conversations increased between them.

First, notes were shared.
Then small talks.
Then laughter.
Then long walks.
Then tea after coaching.

They became best friends.

And as it often happens—

Friendship slowly turned into love.

But they decided—

“This will remain secret.”

One day, a boy from class made a wrong comment about Simran.

Nagendra’s blood boiled.

The boy laughed,
“What happened? Are you her boyfriend?”

Nagendra grabbed his collar.
“Why are you talking nonsense about her?”

The boy glared,
“I’ve been telling her for months that I like her. But she doesn’t agree.”

Nagendra pushed him.
“It’s her choice. Who are you to force?”

The boy said with a strange warning,
“You’ll find out what I am when the time comes.”

And left.

After class, Nagendra and Simran met in the park.

“Why didn’t you tell me someone was troubling you?” he asked angrily.

Simran looked straight into his eyes.
“I can handle my own problems.”

That one line turned into an argument.

The next day Nagendra didn’t go to class.

Evening passed. Aman hadn’t returned home.

Night fell. Phone switched off.

Fear settled in his heart.

He went out searching.

Near a bridge, he saw a crowd.

He went closer—

And froze.

Aman’s dead body was lying on the ground.

Nagendra screamed.

Police asked,
“Do you know him?”

“He’s my friend…”

Police asked again,
“Do you know the girl?”

“Which girl?”

“A girl’s body was found with him.”

Nagendra’s heart stopped.

When he saw the body—

His world shattered.

Simran.

He held her and cried.

Days later, news came on TV.

Police announced:

“Aman and Simran were boyfriend and girlfriend.”

Nagendra’s blood boiled.

“Is this true?”

Or was it a lie?

Then an unknown number called.

“Do you want to know the truth?”

“Who are you?”

“Come where I tell you.”

The man said—

“The boy you hit in class… he did all this. With his friends. They forcefully took Simran. Aman saw it. He tried to save her… so they killed him too.”

Something broke inside Nagendra.

No tears now.

Only fire.

“Now it’s my turn…

SUPER SQUAD-GO

When courage meets friendship, chaos doesn’t stand a chance.

By  Serena Geraldin. S

PREFACE

Welcome to Freedonia, a land of lavender hills, sparkling rivers, and hidden wonders. When four friends—Mike, Rose, Lilibet, and Dahlia—stumble upon a mysterious treasure chest, their ordinary lives turn into an extraordinary adventure. With new powers and courage, they face challenges, discover true friendship, and learn that even the smallest heroes can shine bright. Join them as they uncover secrets, battle chaos, and restore balance to their beloved country.

Part 1 – Light from the Chest

Chapter 1: The Lavender Hills

The sun hung high over Freedonia, painting the sky in hues of gold and pale blue. It was a bright, breezy day, the kind of day where the air felt charged with a strange, electric anticipation. The country was famous for its lavender-scented hills; the purple blooms stretched as far as the eye could see, waving in the wind like a fragrant sea.

Four friends—Mike, Rose, Lilibet, and Dahlia—were trekking up the steepest ridge, their laughter echoing against the crystal-clear rivers that snaked through the valley below.

Mike led the pack. With his messy brown hair and eyes that constantly scanned the horizon, he was the group’s unofficial protector. He spent his mornings helping his father haul heavy timber in their village, but his heart always yearned for something greater. He felt a restlessness in his bones, a feeling that he was meant to be more than just a labourer.

Rose followed close behind, her long red hair caught in the breeze. She carried a leather-bound journal, her curious nature always driving her to look under every rock and behind every waterfall. She had read every legend in the village library twice over, dreaming of the days when magic walked the earth.

Lilibet walked with a gentler pace, her soft blonde curls framing a face that always held a kind smile. She had a natural gift for nurturing life; even without magic, the flowers seemed to bloom brighter when she was near. She helped her mother, the village healer, but she often looked at the dying crops on the outskirts of town and wished she had the power to wash away the grey blight that was starting to spread.

Dahlia brought up the rear, her bright, inquisitive eyes sharp and focused. She was the thinker of the group, a lover of puzzles and ancient riddles. While the others saw a forest, Dahlia saw a map of secrets waiting to be solved.

As they reached the summit, the wind suddenly died down. The silence was heavy. There, half-buried in the rich, dark soil and tangled in silver vines, sat an old treasure chest. Its wood was dark as midnight, carved with symbols that seemed to pulse with a faint, rhythmic light.

“Whoa, what’s that?” Mike whispered, his voice hushed with awe.

“It looks... ancient,” Rose said, her fingers already reaching for the lid.

Together, they cleared the vines. With a collective breath, they heaved the lid open. A blinding pillar of light erupted from the chest, smelling of ozone and wildflowers. Four glowing symbols floated into the air, spinning slowly before darting toward each friend.

Mike’s symbol, a Golden Shield, settled onto his chest, and he felt a surge of heat and iron-like strength fill his limbs. Rose felt a Swirling Feather brush her fingertips, making her feel as light as a summer breeze. Lilibet caught a Silver Heart in her palm, its warmth radiating through her body, while a Radiant Star hovered near Dahlia’s forehead, opening her mind to a thousand invisible connections.

Chapter 2: First Tests

The following days were a whirlwind of discovery. The four friends met in the secret clearing behind the Lavender Hills to test the limits of their new gifts.

Mike stood before a massive boulder that had fallen during the last landslide. With a grunt of effort, he placed his hands against the stone. The Golden Shield on his chest flared, and to his amazement, the ton-weight rock rose into the air as if it were made of parchment. He laughed, the sound booming through the trees, feeling a sense of purpose he had never known.

Rose sat atop the highest cliff, closing her eyes. She focused on the Swirling Feather. Suddenly, she felt the wind answer her call. With a flick of her wrist, she directed a gale upward, lifting herself off the ground. She didn’t just fly; she danced with the air, weaving between the clouds and sending gentle breezes down to help the village windmills spin faster than they ever had before.

Lilibet knelt by the "Dead Creek," a patch of water that had been poisoned by a strange, oily shadow for weeks. She dipped her hand into the water, and the Silver Heart glowed with a soft, pulsing light. The grey murk vanished instantly, replaced by water so clear it looked like liquid diamond. She felt the earth breathe a sigh of relief beneath her feet.

Dahlia practiced the most mysterious gift. By focusing on the Radiant Star, she could see "echoes" of things that weren't there. She looked at a wide, impassable canyon and concentrated. A bridge of solid, shimmering light formed under her feet, crossing the gap with ease.

But their celebration was cut short. A shadow began to grow on the northern horizon. Reports reached the village of a man named Riven, a sorcerer who lived in a palace made of obsidian. He was using a dark, chaotic energy to "rewrite" Freedonia, turning the lavender fields into ash.

“We have to stop him,” Mike said, his voice deep and serious. “These powers weren't just a gift; they were a preparation.”

They marched toward the Obsidian Palace, but they were overconfident. As they crossed the threshold, Riven appeared—a tall, gaunt man with eyes like cold embers. With a flick of his wrist, he summoned a vortex of violet energy. Dahlia, sensing a trap, tried to warn them, but it was too late. The violet light solidified into a cage around her.

“One down,” Riven sneered, his voice like dry leaves. “The star is extinguished. Let’s see how the rest of you fare in the dark.”

The remaining three tried to fight, but without Dahlia to coordinate them, their attacks were messy. They were forced to retreat into the woods, the sound of Riven’s cold laughter ringing in their ears. Heartbroken and exhausted, they slumped under an old willow tree.

“You’re doing it all wrong,” a voice whispered from the branches.

A woman stepped out, cloaked in a mantle of shifting colours. Her eyes were ancient and wise. “I am Zara,” she said. “And if you want to save your friend and your country, you must learn that a squad is not just four people—it is one soul.”

Chapter 3: Meeting Zara

Zara’s hidden sanctuary was a cave deep within the Whispering Woods, protected by a veil of mist. Inside, the walls were covered in glowing moss that reacted to their symbols.

“Riven draws his power from the Shadow Crystal,” Zara explained as she stirred a pot of glowing herbs. “It is a mirror of the heart’s deepest fears. He has hidden it in the Caves of Echoes, where the walls amplify your doubts until they break you.”

For the next week, Zara put them through rigorous training. She didn't just teach them to use their powers; she taught them to merge them.

“Mike, your shield is not just for you,” she commanded. “Rose, your wind must carry Lilibet’s light.”

The model expected movement,
a signal clean and sure,
a start that curved toward outcome,
predictable, secure.

Instead, there was waiting,
a pause prolonged, unscored,
a silence stretched so perfectly
it registered as void.

This was recorded as error.
The signal dimmed by scrutiny,
grew fragile when observed.
Each effort to contain it
only blurred what it preserved.

Each instruction trusted speed,
response, compliance, proof.
The system asked for evidence
and met a quiet truth.

This was not collapse.
It was misfit.

What could not move remained.
What could not close endured.
What could not finish outward
folded inward, compressed, secured,
until intention learned its weight,
its discipline, its force.

It did not begin as darkness,
but pressure held in line:
a thought trained into stillness,
a will refined by time.

What could not surface did not fade,
it narrowed, thinned, and stayed.

They called this inefficiency.¹

The model refined by subtraction:
anything slow was cut,
anything resistant flagged interrupt.

Residuals gathered anyway,
if only one had checked the footnotes.

They pooled beneath unfinished tasks,
inside deferred starts,
between thoughts that knew precisely how
and bodies stalled at parts.

This was not silence dressed as lack,
but order forced on fire,
the burnt out, visible at a distance,
compression without crack.

The graph appeared immaculate.
The curve behaved.
The page was satisfied,
the burnt out, now flawlessly masked.
its hunger neatly saved,

Margins thickened.
Small doubts learned to breed.
These were not corrections.
They survived.
Rage was loud.
Grief too wide.
Both spent too much to build
what learned how not to speak.

So the obscure chose discipline,
trimmed noise, refused display,
kept only what could tolerate
being shaped this way.

They called this dysfunction.²
Pressure continued.
Limits stayed.

This was not tragedy
just math completing thought.

When it moved,
it did not feel like change,
only consequence:
something long misunderstood
continuing to do
exactly, what it was built to do.


¹ Often confused with lack of capacity.
² Defined as absence of response rather than presence of resistance.

title.stringValue: L’Art - un bébé orphelin qui voit la Guerre

content.stringValue:
La moitié du monde aujourd’hui est sous un état de guerre, ou au seuil d’une instabilité civile. On se demande si cela indique un avance vers la troisième guerre mondiale. Les philosophes disent que c’est à cause d’une tendance de ‘virage à l’intérieur’ chez toutes les nations puissantes au niveau international. De leur avis, c’est une conséquence directe d’ un ego gonflé de chefs d’états, qui, au nom de «l’intérêt national», sont en train de grignoter la valeur critique «d’humanité». 


C’est évidemment l’inverse d’un monde qui une fois se trouvait au sein de la mondialisation, où les frontières nationales devenaient moins visibles et on devenait un citoyen mondial. Cependant, nous voyons que les racines de cette «crise civilisationnelle» sont plus profondes. Une négligence systématique du rôle d’art dans nos vies a causé cette fissure socioculturelle. Dans cet essai, nous allons essayer d’explorer les raisons sous-jacentes.


La plupart des sociétés à travers le monde croient qu’il y existe trois forces majeurs à fin d’assurer un bon fonctionnement de l’univers: l’énergie qui crée, l’énergie qui préserve et l’énergie qui détruit. Dans la philosophie d’hindouisme, cela correspond à Seigneur Brahma, Seigneur Vishnu et Seigneur Mahesh. Alors, c’est le Dieu ou bien la Nature, qui est tout-puissant et qui est responsable pour bien maintenir l’équilibre de ce cycle éternel de création, préservation et destruction.


Le devoir primaire d’être-humain consiste à embrasser en entier tous ces trois processus du cycle de tout cœur et non à y intervenir. La pratique d’art, dès les temps anciens, émerge comme un outil très efficace de célébrer cet équilibre universel. La richesse de plusieurs mouvements artistiques dans l’histoire: Humanisme, Romantisme, Symbolisme etc. mettent en valeur les thèmes comme l’être-humain, l’état d’esprit, les sentiments, la nature, la spiritualité, la mort etc. Une étude en cas est «l’Homme de Vitruve» par Léonardo da Vinci qui met en analyse l’anatomie humaine.

En outre, l’art avait aussi fait preuve de son potentiel en tant qu’une force de changement. Autrement dit, dès qu’il y avait une situation de désordre dans l’histoire, c’étaient les œuvres venant du Réalisme, Surréalisme, Modernisme, Postmodernisme etc. qui ont mis en question les extrémités comme la pauvreté, la misère, le racisme, le colonialisme etc. Les idées dans Du Contrat Social par Rousseau alimentaient le feu de la Révolution Française. La Liberté guidant le Peuple par Eugène Delacroix  nous rappelle des sacrifices du peuple français pendant La Révolution de Juillet de 1830.  


Un autre exemple est le tableau «Bharat Mata» (‘Mère Inde’) par Abanindranath Tagore, représentant l’Inde comme une déesse hindoue, un symbole puissant du nationalisme indien, qui enflammait davantage le mouvement Swadeshi. «Le Deuxième Sexe» par Simone de Beauvoir a fait des vagues dans le monde de Féminisme. Nous constatons alors que le rôle d’art a toujours été héroïque et celui d’un saveur pour maintenir le bon fonctionnement des civilisations.


Par ailleurs, les études montrent que l’art sert aussi à être un moyen formidable de canaliser notre énergie. Les être-humains ont une envie irrépressible de s’engager aux activités qui fournissent leur besoin de la sécrétion d’hormone dopamine dans le cerveau. Cela stimule une émotion de contentement chez l’individu. L’absence systématique d’opportunité artistique à travers le monde empêche l’individu à vivre cette émotion. Par conséquent, cette énergie débordante, stockée à l’intérieur, sort en forme de violence, dépendance, agression et d’autres 
comportements extrêmes.


Alors, nous pouvons être d’accord sur le point que l’art est un bébé dont la nourriture de temps en temps est important pour assurer l’harmonie et le bonheur dans l’univers. La création et l’alimentation de ce bébé permettaient d’établir de grandes civilisations dans l’histoire. Malheureusement, ce bébé est devenu orphelin aujourd’hui. Peu de nations du monde veulent investir dans la prolifération des œuvres artistiques. De plus en plus des projets artistiques sont mis à côté. L’enthousiasme pour lire et pour écrire chez les individus existe à peine.Les ministères de culture de plusieurs pays se rendent redondants. Les universités dédiées aux études d’art manquent l’infrastructure de base. Les gouvernements hésitent à lancer des bourses pour recherche en art.Les artistes ont du mal à trouver l’emploi. Les visites aux musées sont limités à fin éducatif.


Par contre, le développement de la technologie ne connaît pas de limites. D’une part l’art remet l’équilibre dans les civilisations, d’autre part la technologie le dérange en emportant les sociétés aux extrémités. Des projets technologiques attirent de millions de dollars d’investissement. On se prépare pour la guerre, la pandémie, les troubles civils, le coût élevé de la vie, les invasions, le radicalisme et le commercialisation. Mais, dans le processus, on perd l’humanité.


Nous ne dépendons plus de la Nature pour créer, préserver et détruire.
L’intervention technologique effectuée par des humains dans chacun de ce processus aggrave la situation. L’émergence de l’intelligence artificielle (IA), qui est capable de créer tout seul n’importe quel œuvre d’art, tue la moindre possibilité de la réanimation de la tendance artistique. Au lieu de transférer la connaissance à travers les générations au moyen de l’art, les gens au présent utilise la technologie pour rejeter les idées existantes, devenant subversifs et intolérants.L’intelligence artificielle domine la création, les technologies comme la robotique, l’apprentissage automatique («machine learning»), la réalité virtuelle ainsi que la réalité augmentée gèrent nos vies et la guerre cybernétique et technologique assume le rôle de destructeur.


Nous pouvons dire qu’à fin de rétablir l’équilibre civilisationelle du monde il faut que l’art se fleurisse. Nous devons tous faire un retour vers les études des beaux-arts, de l’architecture, de la sculpture, de l’histoire, de la géographie, des sciences sociales, des science politiques, du sens moral et civique. L’heure est venue de lancer une «révolution artistique» au niveau mondial et de rendre la responsabilité de gérer le monde à la Nature.Le rôle de la technologie doit être limité à un catalyseur dans ce processus et non le remplacement de Dieu. L’heure est venue de réadopter l’orphelin.

In room 116 of the city's multispecialty mental hospital, the noise and screams carried across the room and reached the staff room at the end of the corridor. Ramakrishnan and Sugunan rushed to where they heard the sound. Room 116 is at the end of the corridor on the first floor. Ramakrishnan is trying to open the door by taking a set of keys from the bag. He has the keys to all 20 rooms on that floor. It was difficult to find the key of room number 116 from it amidst the worry. Pappan fell on the ground and screamed loudly, frothing and bleeding from his mouth. Pushing open the door, attender Ramakrishnan and nurse Sugunan rushed to Pappan. Ramakrishnan tried to hold Pappan by force and put him on the bed. He took Pappan's right hand behind his back and put one hand on his neck and laid him on the bed. By that time, nurse Sugunan filled the syringe with medicine and injected it into Pappan's buttocks. His body trembled and groaned and his strength waned and Pappan fell into a slumber.

Padmakumar is the only son of Shanti, the youngest of the four daughters of Madhavan Karanavar of Kunnath family. Padmakumar's grandmother Janakiyamma was the first to call him Pappan, which later became a nickname. Pappan has completed his B.Tech studies and is pursuing his Diploma in Visual Media.

Kunnath Tharavadu is a large Nalukettu compound. That ancestral home is centuries old. On the west side, behind the Nalukettu home, There are approximately ten acres of wet land. Beyond that, the Bhagavathikunnu, the hill the Theyyam is observed there.

            Sitting amidst the fallen leaf litter inside the kavu, Pappan said to himself while looking at a copper plate and holding it in his hand.

            “Gotta get it this time”

            Sunset rays extending beyond Bhagwati hill.   There are a lot of letters and symbols on the copper plate. Something vaguely written in small letters and capital letters is on it. It's a sketch. Sketch of the vault under the puja room at Nalukettu. Pappan rubbed lime on the copper plate and wiped it; the lines and letters on it became clear. What you see as "squares" are individual chambers in the vault. The primitive Malayalam script is also written in each square. The vault houses many centuries-old artifacts. Pappan's grandfather's grandfather had this vault built by carpenters and masons to store the antiquities. There are even precious books that no one has seen before. One of them is Swatvaviprastitha.

Pappan took his mobile phone, scanned the writings on the copper plate, and started searching on Google. It was able to understand the part written on the copper plate that says "North." Moreover, it was possible to understand in which chamber the object that Pappan was looking for.

Raghunandan, the boy from the neighbouring house, called loudly while coming on his bicycle.

“I got it. I got it... Oh, he kept asking, What is this key? and Where did you get it from?”

Leaning the bicycle under a tree, he walked towards Pappan and handed him the big key in his hand. Pappan looked at the key again and again. a big, iron key about six inches in size.

"Where is the old one?"

Pappan asked Raghunandan without raising his head.

Raghunandan took out the paper wrapped around his waist and opened it. It contained a key with all its rusted teeth rotting away. Pappan double-checked his work with both keys. 

Pappan said to Raghunandan as he got up from under the Elanji tree and walked out of Kavu with his keys tucked into his waist.
            “You have to come home at half past ten tomorrow.”
            Raghunandan doubts “Then.. there..?”
            Pappan explained as he stepped over the Stone steps.
            “Tomorrow is the day Surya sankranthi. Everyone will go to pray at Bhagwati Hill. will return only in the afternoon.”

That night was over. A crow pheasant called from the bushes beyond the kitchen. The sun is only getting hotter. A squirrel jumped out of the house from a tree branch. The location of the pooja room is beyond the atrium of the house.

            The puja room is filled with copper pots, copper lamps, and scriptures. It is filled with the smell of sandalwood, camphor, and burning lamps filled with sesame oil. The floor of the puja room is made of wood. A lamp on a chain hangs near a large wooden storage box beside the right wall. Pappan put the copper plate on the wooden box and pondered on it.

            “Underneath this large wooden box is the passage to the vault.”

            Raghunandan and Pappan took hold of one side of the wooden box and moved the tray. Years of dust lay on the door. Pappan opened the cellar door with his left hand and the key. Vijakiri's noise and dust flew all over the place. Pappan instructed Raghunandan before starting to descend into the vault.

            “Stay here, and I will try to come back in 10 minutes max.”

                 In the flash of his phone, Pappan descended the stairs to the cobwebbed cellar.

            The cellar has been closed for a long time. There is a possibility of toxic gas.

 He turns left after 8 steep steps, and there are 8 more steps. Reaching down, he took out a lighter from his pocket, lit it, and looked around, checking for the presence of sulphur gas. After taking a towel and tying it on his face, he searched around with the flash light of his mobile phone. After 10 feet from the bottom of the cone, two narrow corridors open to the left and right. Pappan looked at the compass on his wristwatch and understood the direction of north. By taking the copper plate and keeping it in line with the north direction, an impression of the vault was made. After some thought, Pappan walked into the corridor on the right. There are small chambers on both sides. After four chambers, the corridor turns left. Breathing becomes very difficult as the air circulation decreases. Oxygen levels are very low. Pappan took a deep breath.

            Pappan realised that he could stay here for a maximum of 2 more minutes. Get it within that time.

            Walking forward again, Pappan stood in front of the second chamber in the corridor to the left. He took the copper plate and checked it with the flash light of the mobile phone.


            “Yes, this is it.”

            a four-foot-high, double-panelled door in front. The door is locked. Pappan felt weary.

            “How do I open it?”

            Eye sight is beginning to decline. and his legs became weak. As he leaned against the wall and took a deep breath, the mobile phone and the copper plate fell to the ground. The deep breathing sound of Pappan echoed through the cellar. When he inhaled for the third time, Pappan collapsed on the ground.

            A spark of thought came to Pappan's mind when the flash light of the mobile fell on the copper plate. He took the copper plate in his hand and checked it again. Three letters are written in the primitive Malayalam script on a copper plate similar to the one column on which he stands.

            Pappan knelt down and checked the lock. Three rings of the rotatable type Each ring is engraved with numbers in primitive Malayalam script. Pappan rotated the rings and arranged them according to the numbers on the copper plate.

            A screaming sound was heard inside the lock. It opened. Vijakiri responded with a loud voice as the door was pushed open. Pappan was surprised to see the view inside the chamber. He built an ashram here and imparted knowledge to the low-caste children. It was a revolution. sometimes an unrecorded revolution in history. Brahmadevananda gained popularity among the people. Those who did not like it tried to attack him. But no one had the courage to stand face-to-face with the fervour in those eyes. A conspiracy was formed against him. About 100 Mallans were imported from Kaliyakavila in the south. They surrounded the ashram to kill Brahmadevananda. The spirit of the ashram frightened them. After a long wait, they set fire to the ashram. Brahmadevananda was also gone when the ashram burned down. He was burned without even becoming a part of history. But one thing remained. A box that was left inside the ashram did not catch fire. The casket in which the book 'Swatva Viprastita' was contained. It later became an asset in our vault.”

            “I can't find the word ‘Swatva Viprastitha’ on Google.”

            “It is a rare book, Doctor.”


            Raghavan said


            “It has a strong magnetic field.”

            Deepa stepped in and said


            Deeparaghav is a lecturer in the Malayalam Department of Government College.

            Through this, we can recognise the mental strength and ability of a yogi named Brahmadevanandan who lived in the seventeenth century. This book will steal our minds through hypnotism. If you chant the mantra 'Swatva Viprastitam Astu', written at the beginning of the book, 101 times and start reading the book, your mind will reach the land of Thali in the seventeenth century. The body here and the mind in the land of the scriptures will drift apart from each other. The truth and the secret are that those who enter the book will never be able to return.

            “If he has such knowledge and consciousness and has written such a book, he must have found a solution to this problem.”

“What is the solution?”
Deepa asked eagerly.

    The doctor looked at the faces of the three
    “I don't know, but the solution will be in that book like a puzzle.”

    Raghavan's mobile rang before another silence began. As he answered the phone, Raghavan's brow furrowed and his face looked very worried.

    Raghavan found it difficult to speak because his breathing was so fast.

    “My son, Rishi, is reading that book. The book Swatva Viprastita.”

            Rishi was walking along the dark path. Rishi felt as if he himself was trapped in a cave. Only the cry of crickets and darkness. He discovered the trace of light only after a long walk. A light from the cave entrance. Rishi walked there. slowly came out of the cave. Fog around. They wait for the sun to come out so they can dissolve. The birds chirped and went out in search of prey. The Rishi realised that he had reached the middle of a forest. The Rishi walked along a path covered with fallen leaves. Wrapping a thin shawl around his neck, he folded his arms and walked through the cold. Peacock's feathers are lying on the path. A vine tries to climb up the mango tree. Rishi felt many eyes were watching him from within the bushes. After walking a long distance, Rishi reached the border of the forest.

            The sun got hotter and hotter. Rishi is walking through a wide arecanut grove. The ripe arecanuts are falling off. A small stream flows through the middle of the garden. Beyond the arecanut garden is a vast paddy field. A kingfisher had arrived on a wheel near the field. A lamp is hung from a stick stuck near the wheel. They say memory fades — that your mind stitches holes over the worst parts so you can
keep breathing. Mine never did. Every night, when the lights go out, I feel the cold marble under my knees. I see Cook Marla’s glassy eyes, my mother’s hand reaching for me, my father’s blood spreading like ink. Some nights I think the smell of smoke is still tangled in my hair.

Fourteen years. That’s how long I’ve been living with ghosts.

maps, my notes, the photos spread like a deck of sins. There he is.
Drake Ashford
The favorite nephew of the mastermind: Ben Ashford. The first time I saw him in person,
he was laughing under neon lights in a club I’d set on fire ten minutes later. White shirt, sleeves rolled up, whiskey glass balanced between elegant fingers. He’s beautiful — not the pretty kind, the dangerous kind. Eyes like a storm rolling in over a calm sea. A smile like a blade pressed to your throat — soft, careful, then gone when you blink.
People call him untouchable. I call him next.
I flick open my lighter. The flame dances, tiny and defiant against the dark. I hold it under the corner of a photo — Ben Ashford. With his nephew, stepping out of a sleek black car, eyes hidden behind tinted sunglasses. The paper curls, darkens, then crumbles into ash.
One by one, I burn the rest. His name. His nephew’s name. His company. His endless string
of spotless, gilded alibis.
I’ve spent too long playing chess in the shadows. Tonight, the board flips.

A soft buzz in my ear — comms crackle alive. “Ezri, you in position?”
It’s Cedric. Older now, more lines around his mouth, same skeptical tone. He’s good at
pretending I’m still that trembling girl in the stables.

I shove him back, hard enough to hear the thud of his shoulders hit the wood. He stays upright — a flicker of surprise buried under that infuriating smile.
I sprint for the window. Curl my body tight as I crash through the glass — it explodes in a shatter of diamonds and rain. The night air hits me like ice.
I twist midair — one heartbeat of freefall — then aim. My gloved finger pulls the trigger on the grappling gun strapped to my belt. The suction-cup tip snaps against the glass behind me, the rope screaming through the winch as my fall slows, slows — stops inches from the wet pavement.
I drop. Roll. My boots slap the concrete. I look up — he’s there, a silhouette framed by
jagged glass, watching me with that calm, curious expression.
I lift my hand — two fingers to my temple in a mock salute. Next time.
I spin on my heel and run for the van waiting in the shadows. I slam the door shut behind
me and punch the metal partition.
“Drive!”
The engine snarls to life — the city blurs past. My pulse is thunder in my ears, the USB
warm against my chest.
They’ll know my name soon enough. But for now, I am still the ghost in their walls — and I
just stole the first piece of their kingdom.



P.S. ✉️ I am an Architecture student, and I am also an author. This is an extract from my debut novel, ‘Phantom Edge’ 😃
I have self published it on Amazon Kindle, and am currently still working on improvising it 😄
Thank you, Indian Writers League, for this wonderful opportunity! 😊

In the bustling markets of Goa, where the air carried the scent of spices, sea breeze, and fresh ambition, two men ran electronics shops barely twenty steps apart. No one knew much about their pasts, and neither spoke of family or history. They were simply two traders sharing the same street, the same customers, and the same dream of prosperity.

John’s shop stood at the corner, bright with flashy posters and loud discounts scribbled in red ink. “Unbelievable offers!” “Lowest price in Goa!” he would shout, waving passersby inside. He had charm, quick wit, and a smile that could sell almost anything. To customers, he sounded confident—almost reassuring.

“This phone?” John would say, holding it up like a prized trophy. “Best battery in the market. You won’t find better at this price.” He rarely mentioned that the battery drained quickly in humid weather. Nor did he explain the limited warranty that came with it. A half-truth here, a careful omission there—his business strategy rested on persuasion, not precision.

Across from him stood Joseph’s modest stall. No bright banners. No blaring offers. Just neatly arranged boxes and a small wooden counter polished by time. Joseph didn’t chase customers; he waited for them.

When someone walked in, he would ask questions first. “What do you need it for? Calls? Gaming? Just daily use?” Then he would explain patiently.

“This model works well for basic use,” Joseph would say calmly, “but the battery drains faster during heavy usage, especially in the heat. If you need longer backup, you might want this one instead.”

Sometimes customers would leave his shop after hearing such honest details, tempted by John’s louder promises. Joseph never stopped them. “Better you choose what fits you best,” he would smile.

For a while, John’s shop seemed unstoppable. Money flowed like the Mandovi during high tide. He expanded his inventory, took bigger consignments from Roy, a supplier from Panaji, and extended informal credit to regular buyers like Sunil, who always promised to settle accounts “next week.”

John liked the thrill of quick growth. He believed speed was success.

Then came the monsoon.

It began with Thomas, a fisherman who had purchased a refrigerator from John just before the rains. Within a week, the fridge began malfunctioning. The cooling system failed, and the fish Thomas stored spoiled overnight.

“You said it was top quality,” Thomas confronted John.

“It must be voltage fluctuation,” John replied casually. “Not my fault.”

Thomas left disappointed, but he didn’t stay silent. In the marketplace, news travels faster than wind. By the next week, whispers began.

“Be careful with John’s products.”

“Warranty doesn’t cover half the issues.”

Roy, the supplier, soon heard the murmurs. Payments from John had been delayed as well. Concerned about his reputation, Roy tightened his terms. “No more deliveries without clearing dues,” he told John firmly.

At the same time, Sunil, who owed John a considerable amount, stopped answering calls. The informal trust John had placed in him vanished like smoke.

Within months, the once-crowded shop grew quiet. Posters faded. Dust settled on unopened cartons. Customers passed by without stopping. Some still entered—but mostly to argue about defective items.

John’s confidence began to crack. Quick profits had brought quick collapse. Every shortcut he had taken returned as a consequence. The market had weighed him—and found him lacking.

Across the street, Joseph’s journey looked different.

Thomas, after his bitter experience, visited Joseph’s stall. “I need a reliable fridge,” he said cautiously.

Joseph didn’t rush. He explained voltage compatibility, cooling capacity, and maintenance tips. “It costs a bit more,” he admitted honestly, “but it will handle coastal humidity better.”

Thomas bought it. Months passed. It worked smoothly. He returned—not with complaints, but with gratitude. Soon, he brought friends.

Maxwell, who ran a small café nearby, needed durable kitchen equipment. Rajaram, a schoolteacher, wanted a dependable laptop for online classes. Each left Joseph’s stall informed, not dazzled.

Roy noticed the difference too. Joseph always cleared payments on time, even if it meant smaller orders. Impressed by his consistency, Roy extended flexible credit and offered better stock options.

Sunil, who had disappeared from John’s radar, walked into Joseph’s shop one afternoon. “I’ve heard you explain things properly,” he said quietly. “I want to start fresh.”

Joseph listened. He didn’t judge. But he set clear terms.

Over the years, Joseph’s small stall transformed—not overnight, but steadily. The wooden counter was replaced with glass displays. The faded signboard gave way to a simple, elegant nameplate. More importantly, his name became synonymous with reliability.

Customers didn’t just buy products; they bought peace of mind.

John, meanwhile, continued operating, but the sparkle was gone. Regret lingered heavier than unpaid bills. He realized too late that business is not merely about transactions—it is about trust. Once trust cracks, it is harder to repair than any faulty circuit.

In the end, both men remained in the same market, under the same sky, facing the same tides of fortune. Yet their journeys diverged sharply.

One chased immediate gain and lost lasting respect.

The other chose honesty, even when it slowed his rise, and gained something far more valuable than profit—credibility.

In business, as in life, the scales may tip slowly, but they always balance. And when they do, integrity weighs the most.

In a cramped studio apartment in ‘Auravana’, three young filmmakers sat surrounded by coffee cups and chaos. Devdutt, the visionary director. Maruth, the sharp-eyed cinematographer. Krish, the heart of their stories. They were determined to create a blockbuster; something bold, something unforgettable.

One rainy evening, a brown envelope appeared at their doorstep. No sender. No return address. Inside was a script.
The title page read: “The Forsaken Light” 

They began reading.
It told of a divine incarnation - a god born quietly in a struggling nation. A land once crawling through mud, burdened by slavery, poverty, corruption, and doubt. But under the unseen protection of this incarnation, the country rose.

From dust to dominance.

Within decades, it became a global power in Science &Technology, education, space research, and defense . Satellites pierced the sky. Universities flourished. Innovations stunned the world. 

While other Neighboring nations, once confident and stable, crumbled into famine,  financial collapse, and internal conflict.

Developed countries watched in disbelief.
“How can a developing nation compete with us?” they wondered.

Yet, the people of that land never recognized the divine force shielding them. Politicians claimed credit. Leaders declared themselves saviors of the land. Global leaders admired and praised them for governance. Campaign speeches echoed with self-praise. No one acknowledged the real divine power protecting them from all misfortunes and disasters that almost rooted out other nations.

Then the script darkened.  
Envy grew. Power-Evil hungry ties turned against the very incarnation that protected them. Lies spread. Accusations were hurled. The divine presence was insulted, attacked, and cornered.

Decades passed. Seasons shifted ..People who absolutely done nothing for the land embraced positions, high-class security,  and praises that they never deserved. 

And then came the warning written in bold ink: 
“You dare call this your power? I AM the Sovereign of Ages. Power is Mine alone. I have seen what you have done to My chosen. With a breath, I shall return this land to its former dust. If you claim strength, then raise it again to the glory you now behold.”

Overnight, disaster struck.
A greater, unimaginable calamity. Economic collapse, natural catastrophes, system failures. The mighty nation fell silent.
Devdutt stopped reading. The room felt heavy.
“This feels… too real,” Krish whispered.
They looked at headlines flashing on their phones. Political turmoil. Economic tremors. Natural disasters in neighboring regions. The parallels were unsettling. 
                                         
                                      Confused and disturbed, they sought guidance from an old scholar known simply as Acharya Dev, a retired historian and mystic.
He read the script slowly.
His face paled.
“This..,” he said quietly, “resembles interpretations of the quatrains of Nostradamus.”

All three froze.
“You mean prophecy?” Maruth asked.
“Not prediction,” the Acharya replied. “A pattern. A warning. Nations rise. Pride blinds them. They forget the unseen forces - faith, unity, moral spine -that carried them.”

                                        Days passed. News intensified. Political leaders resigned in shame as crises deepened. People blamed each other. Trust eroded.

The trio faced a dilemma.
Should they release the film?
Would it ignite tension? Or awaken conscience?
Krish finally said, “What if the movie isn’t about destruction… but prevention?”

They rewrote the ending.
                                   In their version, before the fury descends, the people of the land recognize the divine spark within their land -  as collective integrity. They protect and honour it . They humble themselves. The disaster pauses.

                                                       The film released.
                                              It did not preach. It provoked.
                                       Audiences left theaters silent - reflective.
                                 Some called it fiction. Others called it warning.
But something shifted. Conversations began. Leaders softened their tone. Citizens questioned blind pride. Small acts of unity emerged.

Did the movie really stop Divine Fury?
No one knew.!
But perhaps, Devdutt thought as he watched crowds gather outside cinemas, salvation doesn’t descend from the sky.
Maybe it rises from awareness.
And maybe… that was the real prophecy.   

A whisper rose from the crowd, fragile yet piercing: “What if this film is never released? What if the truth remains locked away?” The celebration dimmed for a heartbeat. Would silence invite the old curse back upon the land? Would the unspoken truth reopen the gates of punishment? 

The camera did not turn to the heavens -it turned to the reels of film, resting like destiny in human hands. 

The message was clear: miracles are not merely sent; they are revealed.
If courage fails, grace may wait. 
 
                          The screen faded into darkness, asking-will you let the light be seen? .....

Crumbling beneath the weight of my years, I tenderly walk alone.
Dodging the faint shadows of some dreams that could not stay
Joy, an eternal nemesis, has set itself in stone,
As the final echoes of my laughter silently draw away.

My heart, my very will to continue walking on in this familiar yet alien world,
Has learnt to beat stronger than my fears by shatters and by scars
Every fragile beat is a lesson forged after an obstacle hurled
Every day i draw on, I feel closer to the amber sky and its persistent stars

How many loves have i lost
Before I could perceive the shape of what remains?
How many promises broken, trust decayed,
Before my soul learned the innate beauty of pain?

For every time I lost a piece of myself, I gained more
This is sorrow's cruel, fateful design
Every fracture, every tear is a reminder of the pinnacle in store
When you evolve within to carve something divine

Tempered was my heart, in growth's euphoric fire
It yearned to soften with every reason life gave it to turn hard 
It has bled, but with every drop soared a little higher
As it confronts itself daily through my soul's inner shard

I still tenderly walk alone, having had my share of life and loss and love
Yet I still hold my heart high, as I look beyond the ruins of joy, for I have found myself.

Light casts shadows of all it finds
– Never its own !
You may dislike liking me;
But can’t stop me liking you !
Life, neither an analogy
Nor an anomaly,
It’s an imagery – all along ;
All left single, aloof and alone!
Others stand by you
When you stand strong !!.

Flying high in sky, kite sees the World
Falling down and lie,kite sees itself !
Stay ahead of us
Tens of thousands of years.
Most precious yet, the moment present!
Bees kiss and quit the flowers for the next.
Nectar tasted never, sweeter than ever !
Love, – lovable than Love,
A cunning opportunist –
of greed, grudge and lust !
-Fall in not, before test.
Spring calls on us
Bringing breeze at ease
Let us patch up hearts’
Frets, burns and wounds!
Let us bury the past
Left dull and dead !
Plant the pain now;
Reap the gain later !!
All come and go, including I and you;
Tides float the boat, for the voyage next !
Come, closer than close
Unveil – mask and gloves.
United we stand….
Go hand in hand
For a stride…. beyond !
– To a world ….in-errant !!

though nobody dares her to fute.
